en: Preface to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Precepts*:
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* taught by the Buddha is the fundamental source of all Buddhas, the intrinsic nature of sentient beings, and the vast net of the precept-mesh.
This is the essential gateway of the Vinaya school. Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, traveled back and forth eight thousand times and manifested through ten billion transformations;

it was none other than for the sake of the one great cause and condition that he appeared in the world. He gathered all those with the capacity for transformation and suddenly clarified their Buddha-nature, briefly opening the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground to reveal the perfect luminosity of one's own nature, enabling sentient beings to attain the rank of the precepts as soon as they enter them.

Among all the Great Awakened Ones, there is no scripture superior to this sutra. To explain its title: the Buddha observed the net of the Brahma Heaven King and spoke of immeasurable worlds as being like the mesh of a net;
this metaphor illustrates the vastness of the gateway of the teaching. Yet, when investigating its ultimate reality:
Thus, the radiant Vajra Jewel Precepts are, from the very beginning, perfectly realized in every individual; this is a metaphor for the single essence of sentient beings and Buddhas.
It is because sentient beings are deluded regarding the Truth and pursue the False that they are unable to manifest Unsurpassed Bodhi.
Therefore, the Tathāgata descended from the celestial palace to the human realm and revealed the Buddha-precepts to ordinary people, explaining the [precepts] within the minds of sentient beings.
The Buddha-dharma delivers sentient beings within the hearts of all Buddhas. For the sake of Prince Miaohai, it suddenly established the fifty-eight precepts for Bodhisattvas.
Whether as ordinary beings or as Buddhas, all enter into the Buddha-nature precepts. Whether form or mind, all return to the fundamental source, the ground of the heart.
How great! The Bodhisattva precepts—surely they are the root of all precepts? There is no teaching that does not encompass them.
Inanimate matter is not included [in this category]. Since I first received and upheld it, I have made this *Śīla-sūtra* my daily practice.
However, I regret that my wisdom and nature are shallow and my understanding of the principles difficult to clarify. Fortunately, my resolve to study the precepts has never ceased for even a moment;

burning oil lamps to extend the light of day, I have carefully read various texts. Yet, as the ocean of the Dharma is vast and deep, it is ultimately difficult to fathom its depths; therefore, I have here provided a brief [account].

I have selected several passages and composed this as a bridge for crossing over. Unintentionally, as days and years passed, it accumulated into eight fascicles, titled *The Initial Ford of the Brahmajāla*.

Although the underlying principles are not yet exhaustive, the ritual aspects are no different [from the original]. This work is intended merely to provide a record for my own clarity and to serve as an aid for recitation.
I do not dare hope that this will be transmitted to future students.
Written on an auspicious day in the ninth month of the thirty-eighth year of the Kangxi era by the disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts, Shaoqing Shuyu.
General Principles:

This scripture’s chapter on the "Mind-Ground" (*citta-bhūmi*) is divided into two volumes. The upper volume contains the thirty minds and ten stages (*bhūmi*), clarifying the levels of cultivation and realization for Bodhisattvas.
The lower volume contains the ten grave and forty-eight light offenses, revealing the conduct of the Buddha’s sons.
One should study the precepts of the Dharma. Although the stages [of realization] are manifested through the Dharma, these stages must necessarily rely upon the cultivation of the precepts.

Therefore, the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai composed a commentary solely on the lower fascicle, which has been the practice venerated by his time; this was because he regarded the precepts as the foundation for attaining the stages.
Now, I shall follow the established precedent to suit the needs of the present age. Should one wish to fully elucidate the meaning of the sutra in its upper fascicle:
Please consult the remaining commentaries.

Regarding the preliminary discourse preceding the sutra: in the *Vinaya-śīla-sthiti-saṃgraha*, our late Preceptor followed the ritual methods of the Xian school and briefly opened seven gates to clarify the universal and the specific.
In the *Śīla-ṭīkā-fayi*, Master Yunqi relied upon the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

This brief commentary establishes five sections in advance to harmonize with other schools. Now, following the Great Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, these are expanded into ten meanings to manifest their essential points.
Whether one prefers brevity or detail, one may choose accordingly according to one's inclination.

In traditional commentaries on the sutras, there are those that employ topical outlines (*ko*) and those that do not. It is said that an outline can segment the text, while a commentary can explain the meaning;

therefore, I have now added these topical divisions. Furthermore, the precepts of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not transcend the two methods of restraint (*śamatha*) and practice (*pratipatti*); to depart from these is to deviate from the principles of the Vinaya.
Herein, by analyzing the characteristics of the grave and light precepts through the lens of restraint and practice, I enable those who have not yet examined the texts [to understand them].
The general outline has already been presented. As for the remaining structural details, they are largely identical to those of other schools.

Regarding the Bodhisattva Mahāśīla, Śākyamuni transmitted it directly to Samantabhadra, who heard it from him personally; it was passed down through successive generations until Master Kumārajīva recited it.
However, there exist Southern and Northern versions of the canon with differing additions and omissions. For now, I shall explain the scriptural text based on the currently circulating edition.
I did not dare to alter a single character. First, because this has been recited for a long time and its transmission is already well-established;

second, fearing that later imitators might gradually cause the scriptural model to be lost. Although it may be argued that what is logically superior should be adopted, one must not permit the reckless alteration of sacred scriptures.

The main text of the sūtra and its title are both written flush with the left margin (at the top level). The commentary is indented by one character, and the topical outline (ke-wen) is indented by another character.

This is done, first, out of reverence for the Buddha’s words; and second, so that the sūtra text, the topical outline, and the commentary may each remain distinct and not be confused with one another.

In explaining the text and clarifying its meaning, it is most excellent to prioritize directness and lucidity. If one forces the language through artificial twisting and contortion, the meaning of the text will not be revealed;
when the facts are not clear, how can the principle be thoroughly penetrated? Therefore, this book does not concern itself with the chronological order of various commentators;
rather, whatever serves to elucidate the meaning of the original scripture shall be recorded accordingly. However, people today for the most part grow weary [of such works].
Because the [Mahāyāna] is extensive, its explanations likewise follow a concise path. It does not prize exhaustive verbal detail, but rather strives for the fullness of meaning.

Thus, the Mahāyāna Vinaya laws differ fundamentally from those of the Hīnayāna; consequently, its rules regarding what is permitted or prohibited, what is maintained or transgressed, and the gravity of such acts, are distinct.
It is not determined by the Śrāvaka precepts, but relies solely upon the Bodhisattva Precept Sūtras.

Furthermore, within the detailed regulations, there are many instances where offenses are established through conditions, as well as citations regarding karmic retribution; these are fully present in the ten grave prohibitions, as they are in the minor precepts.
Thus, existence and non-existence are not fixed.
The three trainings of the outflows-free path take the precepts as their foundation. The Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa universally covers all realms of existence;

anyone who can understand the language may receive it. Therefore, we know that according to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, among the fourfold assembly of devas and humans, anyone who possesses a mind [is eligible].
All should observe this. Nevertheless, it must be received first before one may begin to study it.

If those who have not yet received the precepts were to peruse it prematurely, there is a fear that when they later receive the precepts, they will be unable to give rise to a heart of profound reverence.

Yet, if one drinks only after feeling thirsty, the flavor of the water becomes all the sweeter; if one lights a lamp only after falling into darkness, the utility of the lamp becomes all the greater. It is solely through such reverence...
Regarding the discernment of the occasion: furthermore, when delivering a lecture, one does not exercise such discernment because the aim is to inspire the seeds of goodness;
however, when reciting the precepts, one must exercise discernment for fear that contempt or negligence might arise.

This is just as those such as Tanyou and others, who upon seeing this sutra immediately resolved their great minds and received the Bodhisattva Great Precepts—such cases do not require discernment. Those below this level may not do so. Thus it is said.
Those who [wish to practice] should rely upon this sutra and contemplate it with focused intent.

Recorded by the Vinaya-transmitting Śramaṇa Shuyu of the Ancient Hangzhou Zhaokong Wanshou Precept Platform, based on the first fascicle of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (The First Ford), translated by the Buddha. Pure.

In order to explain this sutra, I shall first open ten gates: First, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, its classification within the Piṭakas and Vehicles; third, the determination of the time and assembly;

fourth, the depth and breadth of the teaching and contemplation; fifth, the appropriate capacities of those to be converted; sixth, the essential nature of that which expresses it; seventh, the scope of its primary tenets and purpose;
eighth, the translation and transmission; ninth, a general explanation of the title; and tenth, a detailed interpretation of the text.
Regarding the meaning: prior to the title of this text, I shall also provide a preliminary exposition of the eight thematic gates.
First, concerning the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching: the *Avataṃsaka* states that the appearance of a Tathāgata is not accomplished through a single cause or a single event.
The present sutra’s emergence likewise has many causes and conditions, which are categorized separately into ten. The first is: Propagation.
1. Because it is the eternal Dharma transmitted between all Buddhas; 2. Because it indicates the fundamental basis for sentient beings to enter the Path;
3. Because it reveals that the Great Precepts arise from the Mind-ground; 4. Because it briefly opens up the vast practices and vows of Bodhisattvas; 5.

Because it extensively manifests the gateway of the precepts to universally embrace all living beings; 6. Because it protects and sustains Bodhisattvas so that they certainly do not fall back or decline.
7. To inspire those of the Hīnayāna to study the Mahāyāna; 8. To directly point out to ordinary beings that they themselves are Buddhas;
9. To provide support for the final dharma period by acting as a great guide; 10. To circulate the holy precepts so that they may be transmitted endlessly from one to another.

Second, regarding the classification according to the Pitakas and Vehicles (*yāna*): there are two parts to the first [classification], the Pitakas. First, the three Pitakas: Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.

Within this section, the "Mind Ground" (*cittabhūmi*) explained above is subsumed under the Sūtra Piṭaka; the "Precept Piṭaka" (*śīlapiṭaka*) within the Buddha-dharma explained below is subsumed under the Vinaya Piṭaka.
It is subsumed within the Vinaya Piṭaka, yet because it lacks formal interrogation and debate, it is not subsumed under the Śāstra Piṭaka. Second, there are two [types of] Piṭakas:

those of the Śrāvakas and those of the Bodhisattvas. As the Sūtra says: "All you Bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds should recite this, and even the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages should recite it.
Because it is subsumed within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, it is not for the Śrāvakas. Second, regarding subsumption by vehicle, there are also two.
First, the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*): namely, the human, celestial, śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva vehicles. As the sutra states:
"When first establishing the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa, [the practitioner] joins their palms and listens with a sincere mind as the Buddha recites the Mahāyāna precepts of all Buddhas;
this belongs to the inclusion of the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna. Second, the four vehicles: after the three vehicles, one adds the Buddha vehicle.

This refers precisely to the Great White Ox-Cart of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. As the Sūtra says: "When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
Therefore, this is subsumed within the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and not the three provisional vehicles mentioned previously.

Third, the classification by division (*vibhāga-viniścaya*), which refers to the twelve divisions of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*). These are: 1. prose (*sūtra*); 2. verses (*geya*); 3. prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*); 4. independent verses (*udāna*); 5. causes (*nidāna*).
6. Nidāna; 7. Avadāna (unasked self-explanations); 8. Itivṛttaka (past events); 9. Jātaka (birth stories); 10. Vaipulya (extensive teachings); 11. Adbhutadharma (marvelous occurrences).
11. Parables (Avadāna). 12. Exegesis (Upadeśa). These can be understood from the prose and the verses.

"You shall become a Buddha" and "I have already become a Buddha" refer to the prophecy (Vyākaraṇa). Therefore, the light of the precepts issues from the mouth. It has a condition; it is not light without a cause.
This light is not blue, yellow, red, white, black, or the like; this refers to the causal conditions. It enters the celestial palaces and descends to Jambudvīpa.

*Fú* (Extensive): This refers to the teachings on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the *Jātaka*, and the *Itivṛttaka*. It briefly opens the *Cittabhūmi* (Mind-Ground), which is the gate of the ineffable Dharma, and further elaborates upon the "Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of Precepts.
This constitutes the *Vaipulya* (Extensive) class. Śākyamuni’s body emits rays of wisdom-light that illuminate the palaces of the Heavenly Kings;
these rays then return to the world-system of the Lotus-Flower Terrace Treasury (*Padmagarbhalokadhātu*), where they are presided over by the Lord of Profound Penetration and Flower-Light.
The Bodhisattva emits light the color of white clouds of vajra, which universally illumines all worlds; this is truly unprecedented.
The sutra uses metaphors such as the Brahmajāla-net, the precepts as the sun and moon, necklaces, and enlightenment as sprouts—these are analogies.
Therefore, it is subsumed within the nine divisions of scripture (*navāṅga*) and does not arise in isolation. It belongs to the three categories of teaching: Sūtra, Vyākaraṇa, and Upadeśa.

Third, the analysis of the timing and assembly of the teaching. There are three periods of time: first, the period of initial illumination, which refers to the "goodness in the beginning" and corresponds to the entry [of the sun] during the first watch of the day.
Second, the period of transformative illumination, which refers to the "goodness in the middle" and corresponds to the entry [of the sun] during the middle watch of the day.
Within this single period, there are three successive illuminations. During the first transformative illumination, the wheel of the Dharma of the Hīnayāna is turned for those of inferior faculties.
When it turns and illuminates during the middle period, it turns the wheel of the Dharma of the three vehicles for those of middling faculties.

When it subsequently turns and illuminates, it turns the wheel of the Dharma of the one vehicle for those of superior faculties. Third, when it returns and illuminates—this is what is called "good at the end"—it enters during the latter part of the day.

This shall first be explained according to the timing of its manifestation, for there are five such assemblies: First, the Avataṃsaka Assembly, which is the teaching that directly reveals [the truth]. Second, the Āgama Assembly, which is the teaching that conceals the reality.
Third, the Saṃdhinirmocana Assembly, which is the teaching that guides and gathers [beings]. Fourth, the Prajñāpāramitā Assembly, which is the teaching of harmonious integration.
Fifth, the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Assembly, which is the teaching of opening and revealing. This [present case] is subsumed under the Avataṃsaka Assembly. Furthermore, the Nirvāṇa...
The *Pāṇḍaravāsī-sūtra* discusses the five flavors. The text states: "For example, from a cow comes milk; from milk comes curd; from curd comes fresh butter (*navanīta*);
from fresh butter comes clarified butter (*ghṛta*); and from clarified butter comes the finest essence (*sarpis*). This corresponds to the flavor of the initial milk."
Fourth, the teaching on the profound and vast [nature of reality] is divided into two parts. First, the teaching on the characteristics [of the teachings], which is further divided into two. One:

the teaching on the ritual of transformation (*saṃdarśana-vinaya*), which is categorized into ten gates: 1. The gate of the distinction between the root and the branches; 2. The gate of the arising of the branches based upon the root; 3. The gate of subsuming the branches back into the root; 4.
The gate of the non-obstruction between the root and the branches; 5. The gate of indeterminacy according to the capacities of beings; 6. The gate of the simultaneity of the manifest and the secret.
7. The Gate of Simultaneous Manifestation; 8. The Gate of Silent Wordlessness; 9. The Gate of Pervading the Three Periods of Time; 10. The Gate of Infinite Layering. As the Sūtra says:
"I, now as Vairocana, sit upon the lotus pedestal; upon the thousand petals surrounding me, I further manifest a thousand Śākyamunis.
The division of the former two and the latter two constitutes the Gate of Differentiation. They are connected...
[The preceding section] is the "Gate of Unifying the Branches. Furthermore, it says: "Thus, the thousands, hundreds, and ten millions [of manifestations] are the original body of Vairocana;
this is the 'Gate of Returning to the Source' and the 'Gate of Non-obstruction. The teaching at the Ten Abodes is the 'Gate of Adapting to Capacities.

The transformation of Māra through the Four Dhyānas and the exposition of the Mind-Ground are the 'Gate of Revealing the Esoteric. The simultaneous and sudden proclamation of the heavy and light precepts is the 'Gate of Sudden Manifestation.'"

Entering the celestial palaces to manifest as a Māra, descending to birth and attaining enlightenment to preach the Dharma—his entry and exit never depart from the *Huaguang Samādhi* (Flower-Light Samādhi), which is the Gate of Stillness and Emptiness (*jimo men*).
All Buddhas of the three periods of time—past, present, and future—have already, are now, and shall hereafter recite it. All Bodhisattvas have already, are now, and shall hereafter study it;
this is the Gate of the Three Periods (*sanji men*). This is the *Cittabhūmi* (Ground of Mind) among the Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha. And...
The Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of the Precepts: A thousand billion Śākyamunis also speak thus.

This extends even to all the Buddhas’ Treasury of the Mind, the Treasury of the Earth, the Treasury of the Precepts, the Treasury of Immeasurable Vows and Practices, and the Treasury of the Ever-Abiding Buddha-Nature of Cause and Effect.
All such immeasurable treasuries of all dharmas spoken by all Buddhas are the Gate of Inexhaustibility. Thus it is cited.

Regarding the meaning of the text, all ten meanings apply. As for its specific categorization according to time, it is subsumed under the seventh, ninth, and tenth gates, as well as a portion of the "Distinctions" within them;
this is because it suddenly expounds the fundamental One Vehicle (Ekayāna) to directly benefit those with the capacity for the sudden and perfect teachings.
One should contemplate this in accordance with the Dharma. Second, the gate of the teaching on the methods of transformation opens as follows:

Second: First, regarding the classification of teachings, we shall clarify the distinctions between the universal and the specific in their exposition of the Dharma. There are five categories of teaching. First, within the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teaching, all four vehicles are contained:
1. The Human Vehicle, which discusses the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions; 2. The Celestial Vehicle, which discusses the four dhyānas and the eight concentrations;
3. The Śrāvaka Vehicle, which discusses the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths; 4. The Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, which discusses the twelve links of dependent origination.

The first two [stages] involve the existence of a self and still belong to the ordinary beings within the realm; the latter two are without self and are termed the noble ones who have transcended the realm.
Therefore, this Hīnayāna speaks only of the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Second, the Initial Teaching merely clarifies the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);

it is also called the Partial Teaching, as it only explains the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*). Third, the Final Teaching fully expounds the Middle Way; it is also called the Real Teaching, as it extensively discusses the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
1. Nature (Xing). 2. Sudden Teaching (Dun Jiao), which exclusively elucidates the true nature. 3. Complete Teaching (Yuan Jiao), which fully discourses upon the Dharma-realm.

The first is the Small Vehicle; the second, third, fourth, and fifth are the Great Vehicle. The fourth and fifth belong to the Complete Teaching, because the fundamental source—the mind-ground—is non-dual and indistinguishable from the mind-nature of the Dharma-realm.
It may also encompass the preceding Final and Sudden teachings, yet it is not the Small or Initial [vehicles]. This is provisional.

Within the *shijiao* (the teaching of reality), that which is subsumed under the *shijiao* is as stated in the Sūtra: "When sentient beings receive the Buddha-precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
This belongs to the *dunjiao* (sudden teaching). Furthermore, when one Śākyamuni manifests a thousand billion emanations, those thousand billion are none other than the very body of Śākyamuni;
this belongs to the *yuanjiao* (perfect teaching). As the verse says: "One should calmly observe the true nature of all phenomena. This is called...
The first path is also called Mahāyāna; it is the ultimate, true meaning. The text states: "All sentient beings enter into the Buddha-nature precepts. The verse says:
"By constantly maintaining such faith, the category of precepts is already fully perfected. This is the meaning of the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*). The sutra says:
"To open the ground of the mind (*citta-bhūmi*) within the dharma-gates of inexpressible teachings as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of Ganges Rivers."
It even proceeds to explain that immeasurable worlds are like the holes in a net; each world is distinct from the others.

The gateways of the Buddha’s teaching are likewise so—this is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Thus, there is what was previously understood, but no longer what was previously restricted.
Next, regarding the sequence of the arising of phenomena from their origin to their end, the distinctions are revealed. There are also five aspects to the meaning of these phenomena.
First: There is only the one mind as the fundamental source. This is what is called the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
It is the mind of the One True Dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, corresponding to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Second: Based on the one mind, two gates are opened.
The first is the gate of the True Suchness of Mind (*cittatathatā*), which refers to the nature of the mind being neither arising nor ceasing. [This is the teaching of] Sudden Enlightenment.
This teaching is for the purpose of leveling [the understanding]. The initial teaching explains the meaning of emptiness;

it speaks of this gate in a concealed manner because those [at that stage] do not know that the Tathāgata has dispelled all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) in order to reveal the true nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is not their portion. Second is the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind.

Because it relies upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is a mind that arises and ceases—namely, that which is neither-arising-nor-ceasing yet is in union with arising and ceasing, being neither identical nor different.

It is called the *ālayavijñāna*. This concludes the section on the Shared Teaching (*sāmānya-śāsana*). Regarding the doctrine of consciousness according to the Distinct Teaching (*prabheda-śāsana*), this gate is taught esoterically.
Because they do not know that the Buddha taught the *tathāgatagarbha* as the *ālaya*, it is not their domain.

Third, based on the subsequent gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), two meanings are clarified. The first is the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*), which refers to the essence of mind being free from thought, equal to empty space.
The realm (*dhātu*). Second is the meaning of non-awakening, which refers to not knowing reality as it truly is (*yathābhūtam*) because the *dharmatā* is one.

In the Śūnyavāda of the Initial Teaching, the meaning of awakening is limited to this point, taking it as the ground of the original awakening of true emptiness; however, that school has not yet clarified the characteristics of true emptiness.

This is the very nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, it is said that there are no phenomena that are not empty. Fourth: based on the meaning of subsequent non-awakening, the three subtle states arise:

first, the phase of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*); second, the phase of transformation (*pravṛttilakṣaṇa*); and third, the phase of manifestation (*nirbhāsalakṣaṇa*). According to the teachings of the Nikāya schools, they stop at this phase of karma.
[The treatise] regards these as the fundamental basis for the arising of all phenomena; therefore, it has not yet clarified that the three subtle states are identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Because it takes the One Mind as the source, it describes True Suchness as immutably quiescent and the eight consciousnesses as subject to birth and death. Fifth, based on the subsequent manifestation of appearances, the six coarse states arise: first, the state of discernment (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*);

second, the state of continuity (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*), which is the attachment to dharmas (*dharma-grāha*); third, the state of grasping (*upādāna-lakṣaṇa*); fourth, the state of calculating names (*nāma-saṃkhyāna-lakṣaṇa*).

The characteristic of names (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*). The first four stages are all the path of delusion; those of the Two Vehicles only reach the third stage, as they merely sever the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) but have not yet realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Fifth, the characteristic of the arising of karma (*karma-samutthāna-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the path of karma, humans and devas are equal to this stage, as they merely know the characteristics of good and evil karma.
Because one does not recognize the two types of grasping and the afflictions. Six: the characteristic of suffering bound by karma; this is the path of suffering.
Śamatha briefly opens the mind-ground to the extent of a hair-tip, up until the fundamental source-nature which is pure; this is the single general characteristic of the mind.
"You Buddhas, turn what I have spoken and open the path of the mind-ground for all sentient beings; this is the second gate.
This refers to the single precept that Śākyamuni Buddha constantly recites within the *Śīla-citta-bhūmi* (Mind-Ground Precepts) at the stage of initial aspiration.
The Radiant Vajra Precept of the Jewel is the source of all Buddhas, the source of all Bodhisattvas, and the seed of Buddha-nature;
it is precisely the meaning of awakening to non-awakening. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
All consciousness, form, and mind—whether they be the emotions or the intellect—all enter into the precept of Buddha-nature; this refers to the three subtle states. It is as follows:
These ten *pratimokṣa* rules emerge from within the world; they are the dharma-precepts. They are to be revered, upheld, and maintained by all sentient beings of the three periods of time.

It is even said: "If there be any who violate them, they shall not be able to give rise to the bodhicitta in their present body, and they shall follow along within the three evil realms for two or three kalpas, not hearing the names of their parents or the Triple Gem."

The "characters" (or syllables) refer to the six coarse aspects (*ṣaḍ-audārika*). Since the Sūtra provides complete evidence from beginning to end, its profound and vast meaning and principles are clearly manifest.

Subsequently, the path of contemplation (*dhyāna-mārga*) is opened into three gates: first, the contemplation of non-arising; second, the contemplation of non-extinction; third, the contemplation of the one mind. Alternatively, they may be:

first, the contemplation of non-difference; second, the contemplation of non-identity; third, the contemplation of true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*). As the verse says: "One should contemplate in stillness."
Examine the true nature of all phenomena: they neither arise nor cease; they are neither identical nor different.

Within this single mind, one should diligently adorn it through skillful means. Furthermore, there are three [contemplations]: first, the contemplation of extinguishing evil; second, the contemplation of bringing forth the Buddha; third, the contemplation of the Single Path. As the verse says:
"Regarding those in training and those beyond training, do not give rise to discriminatory thoughts; this is called the primary path."
It is also called Mahāyāna. All evil conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are extinguished from this source; the *sarvajñā* of all Buddhas emerges entirely from this source.
Furthermore, it may be viewed in three ways: first, as the contemplation of non-existence; second, as the contemplation of non-non-existence; third, as the contemplation of the fundamental source.
Alternatively, it is said: first, the contemplation of non-form; second, the contemplation of non-mind; third, the contemplation of the light of precepts. The text states: "the light of precepts."
It issues from the mouth; it is neither form nor mind, neither existent nor non-existent. It is the fundamental source of all Buddhas. There are three aspects:
first, the contemplation of "neither [existent nor non-existent]"; second, the contemplation of causes and conditions; third, the contemplation of the precepts of the mind. As the text says:

whenever they requested him to preach the Dharma, they would invariably kneel long at the side of his seat and have the Master step upon them to ascend. In the ninth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era, the Grand Astrologer submitted a memorial.
It was said: "A virtuous star has appeared in a foreign land; there shall surely be a man of great virtue and wisdom who enters to assist the Central Kingdom. Yao Xian said:
"I have heard that in the Western Regions there is Kumārajīva, and in Xiangyang there is Dao'an. Could it not be one of these two?
He then dispatched General Lü Guang and others with seventy thousand troops to campaign westward against Kucha, requesting those masters to propagate the Dharma. Lü Guang and—
As soon as the Master had reached the midpoint of his journey, Yao Xing succeeded to the Qin throne and welcomed the Master back to his kingdom, honoring him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
He treated him with exceptional favor and distinguished patronage, inviting him to reside in the Ximing Pavilion and the Xiaoyao Garden, where he was accommodated in a separate villa.

There, he consulted with eight hundred śramaṇas on the Master’s teachings and was commanded to translate over three hundred and ninety volumes of sūtras and śāstras. This occurred in the tenth year of Hongshi.
In the eighth month of the first year [of the Yongchu era], on the twentieth day, he passed away in Chang’an at the age of seventy.
The Patriarch of the Nanshan Vinaya school asked the celestial being Lu Yuanchang: "The sutras translated by Master Kumārajīva remain as fresh as ever to this day;

why is it that their practice and upholding have become so flourishing? He replied: "That man was skilled at understanding the Mahāyāna and had grasped the intent entrusted to him by the Buddha. It ceased there.

Surpassing all that came before and shining upon all that followed, he is something that even those who look up to him cannot reach. He is a treasure of this age, a master translator of scriptures since the time of Vipaśyin Buddha.
Furthermore, it is said that Master Kumārajīva’s rank was equal to the Three Sages (Tri-vidyādhara), and that Mañjuśrī personally instructed him to edit and finalize [the texts];
this is no mere general assessment. △ Third, the explanation of the title of the chapter.
The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Ground, Part Two.
This chapter is titled according to both person and dharma. "Bodhisattva" refers to the person; "ground of the mind" refers to the dharma. First, I shall explain "bodhisattva."
A personal name. In Sanskrit, it is fully called *Mahābodhisattva*. This translates as "One who Accomplishes Sentient Beings through the Great Path of Enlightenment.
It means that because one possesses the great mind, one enters the Buddha-way. It is also called "Awakened Being" (*Bodhisattva*).
Here, *bodhi* has the meaning of "that which can awaken," and *sattva* has the meaning of "sentient being. It refers to one who is able to cause all sentient beings to awaken.
Because they awaken to the Buddha-way. In the Eastern Land (China), there is a preference for brevity; therefore, they simply say "Bodhisattva" (Pusa).

They are also called "Mahāsattva" (Dashì), meaning that they are able to seek the Way above and transform beings below, thereby establishing great undertakings. They are also called "Kāśyapa" (Kaishi), meaning that they are able to enlighten and transform all sentient beings.
In summary, based on the realm of the Four Noble Truths of Non-arising, one gives rise to the Four Great Vows. [Thus] it is composed.
He is a great armor-clad one who is capable of performing difficult deeds: above, he propagates the Buddha-dharma; below, he transforms sentient beings.

Because he unifies wisdom and compassion, he has obtained this title. Within this, there are both general and specific aspects. Generally speaking, from the moment he first resolved to attain enlightenment...
Up until the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), all are termed Bodhisattvas; yet, specifically, the stages and positions of the Bodhisattvas differ from one another.
Next, the "Mind-Ground" (citta-bhūmi) is explained. Regarding the name of the Dharma: it is called "mind" because it is that from which the myriad dharmas arise;
it is called "ground" because it is that upon which both ordinary beings and sages rely and are sustained. Indeed, this Mind-Ground is what is elucidated within the "Parable Chapter."
It is essential for the Great Being (mahāsattva), just as the heart is to the human body. It can coordinate all affairs and produce superior fruits;

it is that upon which the Great Being relies. In meaning, it is like the earth. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva vow (saṃvara) universally guards the three types of action: body, speech, and mind. The mind and the intellect...
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is a single essence with different names. Among the three types of karma, mental karma (*manas-karman*) is primary, while bodily and vocal karma are secondary.
This is discussed according to what is most preeminent; therefore, it is called the "mind-ground" (*citta-bhūmi*). Indeed, the Buddha is the mind, and the mind is the Buddha.

The mind attains Buddhahood to manifest the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and the Buddha relies upon the mind to transform and deliver humans and devas. Thus, whenever a Buddha appears in the world, he speaks only of this.
This mind—apart from this mind, there is no dharma that can be spoken of. One who understands this meaning may be discussed with regarding the Brahma Net Sūtra.
Furthermore, this ground of mind is the fundamental source of all ordinary beings and sages; when among the ordinary, it is because they are deluded regarding this mind.
Thus, one transmigrates through the three realms, the six paths, and the four modes of birth.
For the sages, because they have awakened to this mind, they return to the original source of truth and attain ultimate purity.

Bodhisattvas who wish to return to their original source-world take these correct precepts of the mind-ground as the supreme cause to realize the ultimate fruit of Vairocana. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "I have already..."
Having practiced for a hundred kalpas in this mind-ground, I am named Vairocana.
You, my sons of the Buddha, shall propagate what I have taught to open the path of the mind-ground for all sentient beings. Furthermore, it says: "All consciousness, form, and mind..."
These emotions and this mind both enter into the Buddha-nature precepts. Having received these precepts, they persist until the attainment of the Buddha-body;
throughout the interval between them, the essence of the precepts remains ever-present. Therefore, one knows that these precepts are precisely the ground of the mind. As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says:
The liberation attained by all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings.
From the fundamental ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*), all stages of a bodhisattva’s practice arise, each distinct from the others.

Within these bodhisattva stages, the dharma-gates for practicing the ground of the mind at each successive level are likewise immeasurable. Without relying on the dharmas of the ground of the mind, who could ever achieve enlightenment?
Regarding the name "Bodhisattva": were it not for the person who is a Bodhisattva, who would uphold the Dharma of the mind-ground?
The person is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is itself the person. Because of the person, there is Great Bodhi; because of the Dharma, there is Great Nirvana.
Bodhi is wisdom (*jñāna*); Nirvana is principle (*tattva*). Since wisdom and principle are one and the same, it is called the "Mind-Ground of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore:
The source-ground of the mind not only gives rise to the stages and positions of bodhisattva practice,
but also universally gives rise to all dharmas— namely, from the mind of hell up to the mind of a Buddha, and from the ground of hell up to the ground of a Buddha. Now,

it is referred to specifically as the "Bodhisattva Mind-Ground" because the Bodhisattva, above, accords with the power of compassion, and below, accords with the longing for mercy, thereby universally encompassing [all beings].

Regarding the meaning of the ten realms: since these ten realms are none other than the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground, if this mind were not the ground, from where would the precepts be upheld, and how could a Buddha be realized? In the Sanskrit language, this is called *parivarta*.
This term is translated here as "pin" (chapter). A "pin" refers to a category; it is so named because various categories of meaning follow one another.
It is traditionally said that the full version of this sutra consists of one hundred and twelve fascicles and sixty-two chapters.
This present work is but a single chapter, the "Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind," comprising two fascicles. The upper fascicle elucidates the thirty minds and ten stages of the Bodhisattva.

This chapter serves as the gateway and the very source for entering the fruit of Buddhahood. The subsequent fascicle clarifies the Bodhisattva’s ten grave and forty-eight light precepts, which likewise constitute the foundation for practicing the Bodhisattva path.
By taking up this single chapter, one understands the ultimate aim of the entire treatise;
through this single treatise, one comprehends the ritual methods of all generations; and by contemplating a single Buddha, one comes to know them all throughout the ten directions.

This is the model and standard for all Buddhas of the three periods of time. By observing a single Bodhisattva, one comes to know the mental ground of the ten stages of Sages and the three grades of Worthies.
Speaking in relation to what precedes it, it is therefore called "The Chapter on the Mental Ground of Bodhisattvas, Part Two. The general explanation of the title is hereby complete.
△ Tenth: Explaining the Text and Meaning Individually.
In preparing to explain the scriptural text, it is divided into three major sections: first, the Introduction (Nidāna); second, the Main Body (Śarīra); and third, the Dissemination (Pariṇāmanā).
The establishment of these three divisions began with the Dharma Master Dao’an of the Jin dynasty; his sublime judgment was as vast as the heavens. Later, in the Western Regions...

The commentaries and sub-commentaries on various Bodhisattva treatises transmitted from the East all divide [the text] into three parts. Only then did one come to know that the Jin dynasty was in accord with the Buddhist teachings of the West;
this is truly an unchanging constant rule throughout antiquity and the present. Regarding the "Preface" (*xu*): it means to describe or narrate, and it also implies a beginning or a sequence.
It refers to the origin and purpose of a single scripture. Furthermore, there are both general and specific types. As for the general type, at the beginning of every scripture, there are...
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was at a certain place together with a great assembly. This is called the "General Introduction" (*sāmānyamukha*).

As for the "Specific Introduction" (*viśeṣamukha*), it refers to the fact that the introductory circumstances (*nidāna*) for each sutra are different; thus, it provides the specific preface for a single sutra or a single chapter.
This is called the "Specific. Regarding the "Main Body" (*śarīra*): "Body" (*śarīra*) means the primary subject or what is honored, referring to that which the Buddha [taught].

In expounding the Dharma, one must invariably honor the meaning spoken according to the specific capacity of the audience as the primary essence; this constitutes the fundamental purport of a single sutra.
Regarding "circulation": "flow" (liu) means not stagnating, and "penetration" (tong) means not being obstructed, because the correct meaning has already been set forth.

It is intended to be transmitted to future generations for the benefit of sentient beings, so that the source of the True Dharma may circulate without obstruction, spreading throughout the ten directions without end.
From the beginning of this chapter up to the phrase "The First Purity," it is called the Introduction (Nidāna).
From the words "The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddhas" onwards, there are ten levels of *prātimokṣa*.

[The word] "Next" [marks the transition]. From the point where the various Bodhisattvas of the present recite it—namely, from the section on the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts up to the end of the verses—it is called the "Section on the Correct Teaching" (Zhengzongfen).

Although this constitutes but a single fascicle among the sixty-two fascicles, and specifically the lower volume of that single fascicle, the Prologue, the Correct Teaching, and the Dissemination together comprise the complete scripture in its entirety.

However, regarding this lower fascicle, its three divisions are perfectly distinct, just as in the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and other sūtras, where every chapter begins with the words "At that time.

This present sūtra is likewise so; that is, the "Correct Teaching" (śāsanamūla) and the "Circulation" (parivarta) here clarify the nature, characteristics, phenomena, and principle of this single chapter alone, rather than the "Correct Teaching" and "Circulation" of the entire work. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka*...

The Commentary states: "Now, when the Sages establish their teachings, there must necessarily be a gradual progression. When they intend to transmit subtle words, they first clarify the underlying principles.

Once these principles are clarified, those whose capacities correspond to them receive the Dharma; thus, the True Doctrine (Zhengzong) is bestowed. Once the True Doctrine is set forth, the aim is to provide salvation and relief.
This not only consolidates the assembly of the present age, but further ensures that future generations shall transmit its fragrance, so that the Lamp of the Dharma shines eternally."

Because its illumination is inexhaustible, it is entrusted for circulation; this applies not only to a single section, but also to the various assemblies and chapters, all of which may contain it. Thus it is said.
The first part, the Preface, is divided into two sections: first, the initiation by Vairocana; second, the exhortation by Śākyamuni. Within the first section, there are two further parts.
The first part consists of the long prose; the second, the verses. The long prose has three sections: first, the entrustment by Vairocana; second, the propagation by Śākyamuni;

third, the exhortation to believe, accept, and uphold. Within the first section, there are again two parts: first, the oral exhortation and instruction; second, the entrustment through the emission of light.

First: At that time, Vairocana Buddha, for the sake of this great assembly, briefly opened up the *Cittabhūmi* (Mind-Ground), which is among the hundreds of thousands of *Ganges-sand* numbers of ineffable Dharma-gates, to the extent of a mere hair-tip.
This has already been taught by all Buddhas of the past and will be taught by the Buddhas of the future.
It shall now be spoken. The Buddhas of the present speak it now. The Bodhisattvas of the three periods have studied, are studying, and will study it.
For a hundred kalpas I have practiced this Mind-Ground; I am named Vairocana. You, my sons of the Buddha, propagate what I have taught.
"To all sentient beings, he opens the path of the mind-ground.
"At that time" refers to the moment when Vairocana Buddha was about to reveal the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground.

The general introduction to all sutras possesses six kinds of accomplishment; this present sutra is likewise so. "At that time" refers to the time. "Buddha" refers to the Lord. "Great" [refers to the Great Vehicle].

Therefore, it is called "At that time. In the Sanskrit language, *Vairocana*; this is translated here as "Universal Illumination by Light. There are two meanings to "illumination":
first, internally, illuminating the true *dharmadhātu* with the light of wisdom—this refers to the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment body).

Second, externally, illuminating those with great capacity through the light of the body—this refers to the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (other-enjoyment body). It is also translated as "Pure and Full," meaning:
All evils are exhausted without remainder; hence it is called "Pure" (*śuddha*). This is the retribution for ceasing evil.
All virtues are perfectly complete; hence it is called "Full" (*pūrṇa*). This is the retribution for practicing good. Because practice is fulfilled and the fruit is perfected, one is called a Buddha.

This is also the designation for one in whom delusions and karma have both been exhausted, and whose merit and wisdom are fully perfected. This [attainment] is mostly derived from the enjoyment of one's own realization (*svasaṃbhoga*).

As for its name, its radiance shines everywhere, and it is most commonly designated as the *parabhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). According to the *Cittabhūmi-darśana-sūtra*, the *dharmakāya* is also called the *svabhāvakāya* (Self-Nature Body);

Seated upon a great jewel lotus flower—namely, the throne of the Great Jewel Flower King—it is surrounded by an ocean-like assembly of immeasurable beings.
They will surround him, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising him; this is called the benefit of future retribution.
At that time, the Bodhisattva enters the Vajra-samādhi, severing all subtle cognitive afflictive obstructions and attaining unexcelled Bodhi;

Furthermore, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says: "The eighty-four thousand dharmas are all subsumed under the single dharma of the 'Dharma-gate of the Non-destruction of the Mind. This is also to include the extensive within the concise. Also, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says: "The eighty-four thousand dharmas are all subsumed under the single
The grasses, trees, and leaves of the great earth are said by sentient beings to be like the leaves in one's hand; this is precisely the same analogy.
As for "gate" (mōn), it carries the meaning of "that which enables passage. This refers to the Dharma of the One Vehicle taught by the Tathāgata, all of which issues forth from this;
therefore, it is called a "Dharma-gate" (hōmon). The "Ineffable Dharma-gate" is vast. The mind-ground is like a hair-tip.
“Granted. This refers to the abbreviated [teaching]. Because it is derived from the extensive and opened up through abbreviation, it is called the “abbreviated opening.
That all Buddhas of the past have already spoken it shows that the Dharma has something transmitted; that the Buddhas of the future shall speak it shows that the Dharma has something received;
and that the Buddhas of the present now speak it shows that the Dharma has something realized. The Buddha is one who has attained the fruit.

Citing those who are the same as oneself to provide proof is an exhortation to believe. Stating that "Bodhisattvas" are those on the path of practice is an exhortation to accept the teachings by citing those who have likewise practiced and studied.
Regarding the phrase "Bodhisattvas of the three periods," this refers to those who have attained the fruit in the three periods;

if even they still comply with the teachings, how could there be any among the causal practitioners of the three periods who do not study accordingly? However, the mind is the source of all phenomena; when the mind is raised, all phenomena [are revealed].

Since both are exhausted, all Buddhas teach this in common, and Great Beings study it together. When I say "I" have practiced this Mind-ground for a hundred kalpas, this "I" is the true self of the eight masteries;
it is not the deluded self of ordinary beings that clings to the body and mind of the five aggregates.
"A hundred kalpas" distinguishes this from the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of the provisional teachings. The Sanskrit term is *kalpa*, which here means "differentiation."
Regarding the time periods: at the beginning of the kalpa, when the human lifespan is ten years, a son’s age is double that of his father’s.
In this manner, it increases until it reaches eighty-four thousand years. Thereafter, it decreases by one year every hundred years, continuing until it returns to ten years.

This single period of increase and decrease is called a minor kalpa (antarakalpa). Twenty minor kalpas constitute a middle kalpa (madhyakalpa). [There are four such middle kalpas for] the formation, the abiding, the destruction, and the voidness [of a world system].
Twenty increments and decrements each constitute one *mahākalpa*. An incalculable number of *mahākalpas* constitutes one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.
Therefore, the superior text states: "I have practiced the Mind-Ground for a hundred *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, taking this as the cause."
Initially abandoning the state of an ordinary person and attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, one is named Vairocana and dwells within the ocean of worlds of the Terrace Treasury;

this is taken as the fruit. This refers to the period from the time one is a Bodhisattva by name until reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) while practicing the precepts of the mind-ground.
In each stage, one cultivates with firm accomplishment and enters the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). The essence of the precepts becomes perfectly complete;
all evils are eternally purified, and all myriad virtues are fully realized. For this reason, he is named Vairocana Buddha. As for the "one hundred kalpas" mentioned now:
Alternatively, the text may be abbreviated. According to other sutras, it is generally said that the Tathāgata practiced for three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;

or, having completed those three great kalpas, he further cultivated the causes for the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) during one hundred kalpas. Therefore, it says "one hundred kalpas.
Tiantai cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and other treatises, stating that the Tathāgata [descended] from the ancient Śākya...
From Kāśyapa Buddha up to Śikhin Buddha, he encountered seventy-five thousand Buddhas; this is called the first asaṃkhyeya.

From Śikhin Buddha up to Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he encountered seventy-six thousand Buddhas; this is called the second asaṃkhyeya, during which he received the prediction (vyākaraṇa) that his name would be Śākyamuni.
From Dīpaṃkara Buddha up to Vipaśyin Buddha, he encountered seventy-seven thousand [Buddhas].
The Buddha is said to have completed three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. From the beginning until this point, he finished cultivating the six *pāramitās*.

He then remained for another hundred *kalpas* to cultivate the causes for the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Thus, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* records that the Buddha said:

"Throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I practiced with diligent austerity; for a hundred *kalpas*, I cultivated merit. During the first *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa, I made offerings to eighty-eight thousand Buddhas."
During the middle asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he made offerings to ninety-nine thousand buddhas; during the subsequent asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he made offerings to one hundred thousand buddhas.
He left the household life, upheld the precepts, fulfilled the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), and mounted the chariot of the six perfections.
Donning the armor of patience, he sat upon the Vajrāsana beneath the Bodhi tree, subdued Māra, and attained the path of Buddhahood.
According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when the Buddha first resolved his mind, he was intent on seeking the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
He dwelt in quietude for forty-four billion kalpas, during which time there were no Buddhas, Dharma, or Saṅgha. After seventy kalpas within that period, he encountered a Great...

The Buddha Tonghui (Universal Wisdom) extensively expounded the Mahāyāna, yet [the king] understood it only with slight faith. He established meritorious deeds and, after further nineteen kalpas, became a great king.
He made offerings to the pure assembly and provided for the poor and destitute. Renouncing his throne, he left the household life to dwell in tranquility and practice silent contemplation.
However, his mind gradually grew weary; wandering through birth and death, he underwent countless retributions because his intention lacked a great vow.
Desiring to escape his own afflictions, he passed through another sixty kalpas until he encountered the Buddha Ratnamālā.
There, in the One Vehicle where there is no second path, even the name of the "lesser vehicle" was unheard of. From that time he first resolved his mind; his great vow has been difficult to thwart.
From then until this day—seven hundred million asaṃkhyeya kalpas—he has protected and followed the True Dharma, and now he has attained self-awakening. You must know this.

Prior to seven *koṭis* [of kalpas], although one may have diligently practiced the path with hardship, in the absence of firm vows, one ultimately cannot achieve Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Based on this, even one hundred *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* would still be insufficient. This, too, is spoken according to the capacities of sentient beings;

the provisional and the real, as well as the two vehicles of the Great and Small, differ in their methods of transformation. Now, Śākyamuni [the Buddha] has verified this through his own practice and realization.
Having established the Dharma, he proclaims it to others so that they may give rise to faith; they shall rely upon this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground to emulate his cultivation and realization.

When he says, "You, my sons of the Buddha, who transmit what I have spoken," the term "Buddhas" refers generally to the Buddhas of the thousand-petaled lotus, as well as the hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis.
This means that while the previous teaching was given universally for the great assembly, the present entrustment of the mind-seal is not for anyone else.

This is what people can endure; therefore, I have specifically entrusted it to the thousand Śākyamunis to transmit the words of me, Śākyamuni Buddha, to show to all sentient beings, so that they may receive it from above and spread it below, thereby seeing that the reception of the Dharma has its own origins. One who receives the Dharma and attains benefit is called a "disciple" (*putra*).
"Transmitting" (*zhuan*) means to pass on; it refers to transmitting the Buddha-Dharma to sentient beings. Now, since the seal of mind (*cittamudrā*) has been transmitted... [text ends]
This may be considered ordinary; hence I address you as "sons. Regarding the opening of the path of the mind-ground for all sentient beings: "opening" refers to the act of revealing what was closed.
This means that I, Śākyamuni Buddha, have already, together with the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, cultivated and realized this Dharma-gate of the mind-ground.
Therefore, you should likewise take my mind as your own mind, and transmit what I have taught.
All sentient beings who cultivate and realize this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground each perceive their own original source-ground.
Yet this original source-ground is that which all sentient beings share in common; it is merely that, from time immemorial, it has been long obstructed by delusive emotions and karmic afflictions.
This is what is meant by the statement: "The Buddhas have already awakened, while sentient beings still remain deluded."—The Sovereign Mind.
Once [the teaching] has been received, the Dharma King does not appear; therefore, he causes the Buddha’s words to be transmitted so that they may be fully understood and penetrated. Thus it is said:
"Hearing the path of the mind-ground" is precisely the opening of the Buddha's knowledge and vision. △ Next, the emission of light and the entrustment.
At that time, within the Lotus Treasury World, from the lion throne of blazing celestial light, Vairocana Buddha emitted radiance.
This light addressed the Buddhas upon the thousand petals of the lotus, saying: "Take this 'Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Ground of My Mind' and depart.
He then further transformed into the billions of Śākyamunis and for all sentient beings, sequentially expounded this "Chapter on the Superior Ground of My Mind. You—
Thus they receive, uphold, read, and recite it, practicing with single-minded devotion.
As for the "World-System of the Lotus-Womb Treasury" (*padmagarbhalokadhātu*): it is called "Lotus" because it dwells amidst the dust [of the world] without being defiled.

It is called a "Womb" (*garbha*) or "Pedestal" (*maṇḍala*) because it is solid, firm, lofty, and eminent, serving as the ultimate source and pinnacle of all phenomena. It is called a "Treasury" (*kośa*) because it contains infinite world-systems (*kṣetraprakāra*). Thus it is named.
It is said: "Vertically encompassing what has no beginning or end is called a *loka* (world); horizontally extending across all quarters and corners is called a *dhātu* (realm).

The "Lotus-Womb Treasury World" (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*) refers to the *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* (the environment or dependent retribution). "Vairocana Buddha upon the lion throne" refers to the *mūla-vipāka* (the primary retribution or the principal subject).

Furthermore, as for the place where the lotus contains its seeds, it is termed a "Womb Treasury" (*garbha*) because it possesses the meaning of "enveloping. Now, regarding these world-systems (*kṣetra-jāti*) and their worlds...
The earth is contained within a single great lotus flower; all worlds of the ten directions are entirely within it.
Therefore, it is called the "Lotus-Womb Treasury World" (Padmagarbha-lokadhātu), which is the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu).

While this may be so from the perspective of conventional phenomena (*dharma*), when speaking according to principle (*tattva*), for what reason does the ocean of lands (*kṣetrasāgara*) have such a form? Briefly stated, there are two reasons. First, regarding the cognition of sentient beings...
The ālayavijñāna is the fragrant ocean. Within this ocean, there exist the characteristics of cause and effect, as well as the nature-virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
these are the flowers of the primary cause (*dharmatā-hetu*). All future fruits, both mundane and supramundane, are fully contained within them;
therefore, it is called a "store" (*garbha*). If one takes the *dharmatā* to be the ocean, then the mind is the flower; the manner of containment is likewise so. However, this...
Within the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), half constitutes the external environment because it is not grasped as a self;

half constitutes the internal body because it is grasped as one's own nature and gives rise to sensation and awareness. For what reason is the Tathāgata’s storehouse consciousness thus? Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Because it is drawn forth by karmic actions, there are two [aspects]. Second, within the great ocean of the Buddhas' great compassion, the flowers of boundless practices arise, containing within them the dharmas of the fruits of both self-benefit and benefit for others, as well as the defiled and pure states, all layered together without obstruction; therefore, the characteristics of the lands they manifest correspond to this.
Furthermore, the lotus flower is the various radiant stamens and fragrant banners, while the pedestal is the fruit of the lotus. Ten unspeakable numbers of Buddhas...
In its center lies a sea of fragrant water as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field. "Hèhè" (赫赫) describes its magnificent and blazing splendor.

"Celestial light" refers to the natural light of the merit of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), which shines forth universally and brilliantly. As for the "lion throne," it is so named because its form resembles a lion;
it symbolizes fearlessness in preaching the Dharma. When the Tathāgata preaches this fearless Dharma, the non-Buddhist heretics and the Māras—
All submit to his command. Like the roar of a lion, all birds and beasts crouch in hiding.
Therefore, every seat upon which a Buddha sits is called a "lion throne" (*siṃhāsana*). It is also called the "throne of the emptiness of phenomena" (*dharmasūnyatā-āsana*), signifying fearlessness;
for it is because the Tathāgata has realized the emptiness of phenomena that he possesses nothing to fear. As the *Upadeśa* (Shangpin) says: "The [Buddha]..."
That which is within the palace of a hundred trillion purple-gold vajra radiance is this:
the majestic seat of light upon a hundred trillion exquisite jewel lotuses. When the Light addresses the Buddhas atop the thousand petals, it refers to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground.
Originally, it transcends all names, words, and sounds. Now, wishing to manifest the True Dharma of the Mind-Ground, one performs Buddha-work once again by means of the light of the mind;
thus, it is not proclaimed by speech, but proclaimed by light. This precisely manifests the matter of the entrustment.
Yet, since the formal conclusion has already been reached, the reason for emitting light once more to proclaim it universally is that this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground is, in its essence...
Whether it be the traces [of the Buddha's teaching], the causes, or the fruits, there is nothing that does not have wisdom as its precursor.

Yet, even the preaching at the Cloud-Palace (Megha-kuṭa) in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and the teachings in the Light-Sound (Ābhāsvara) Heaven of the dhyāna realms constitute established doctrine; how much more so the light of the Buddha’s body?

This also has two meanings: first, that for those nearby, he teaches through speech, while for those far away, he teaches through light; second, that for those of inferior capacity, he teaches through speech, while for those of superior capacity, he teaches through light.
Now, the simultaneous practice of body and speech manifests this Mind-Ground Precept Dharma as the essential path to supreme virtue.
If categorized according to its response to capacities, it refers to the Buddha of the Body of Other-Enjoyment Land;

if categorized according to self-realization, it is the Dharma-body in the unobstructed land, the inexhaustible lion throne, the Buddha of Perfect Interfusion and Non-obstruction, the light that universally illumines the Dharma-realm—this is the general characteristic.
The Dharma of the Mind-Ground belongs entirely to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); it is not provisional or gradual. Regarding the name of the Buddha, Śākyamuni:

according to the *Benqi jing* (Sūtra on the Original Arising), "Śākya" is translated as "Capable Benevolence" (Nengren); according to the *Benxing jing* (Sūtra on the Original Deeds), "Muni" is translated as "Silent Stillness" (Jimo).

"Capable Benevolence" is his clan name, signifying his benefitting of sentient beings through compassion and manifesting his non-abiding in nirvana. "Silent Stillness" is his personal name, derived from his wisdom.
The wisdom illuminates the principle; the manifestation of non-abiding in birth-and-death is the Great Transformation (Mahāpariṇāma) of the Buddha upon the thousand-petaled lotus.

The thousands of billions of Śākyamunis are the Small Transformations (Kṣudrapariṇāma). The term “and” (*ji*) signifies succession. There are two meanings for the phrase “expounded in sequence”: first, [the first meaning is...]
Regarding persons: first, the teaching on *śamatha*; next, the transmission of the thousand Buddhas; next, the ten billion Buddhas;
next, the Bodhisattvas; and finally, sentient beings. Second, regarding the Dharma: first, the thirty minds; next, the ten stages (*bhūmi*); next, the ten grave [offenses];

and finally, the forty-eight light [offenses]. Recitation and chanting mature the seeds of the Path within. Mental practice is the external verification of one’s conduct. This is called "receiving and internalizing."

To receive [the teachings] is called "receiving" (*śruta*). To hold them firmly is called "retaining" (*dhāraṇī*). To face the original text is called "reading" (*pāṭha*). To recite from memory is called "chanting" (*svādhyāya*). Receiving and retaining pertain to the mind; reading and chanting pertain to the mouth.

When mind and mouth advance together in practice, there is neither duality nor distinction; therefore, it is said that one practices with a single mind (*ekacitta*). Furthermore, regarding the sequential explanation:

the perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) does not obstruct the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*). One who practices with a single mind finds that the sequential arrangement does not obstruct the perfect interfusion.

"China" (Chīnā) is sometimes called "Zhì-nà. In the language of the Flower [China], it means "the Land of Refined Culture" (*wénwù guó*).
This praises this region as a land of ceremonial caps and robes and refined culture. The *Xīyù jì* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
"Mahācīna," which here means "Great Tang," is also named "Zhèndàn" or "Zhēndān. Master Lín said: "The East belongs to the direction of Zhèn; it is where the sun rises."
It is square; therefore, it is called Zhendan (China). The *Loutan jing* states: "To the east of the Onion River lies that which is named Zhendan.
It received this name because when the sun first rises, its radiance shines upon the eastern corner.
The "one great causal condition" (ekamahākaruṇā-hetu-pratyaya) is none other than the one true reality (eka-tathatā). Its nature is vast and expansive, hence it is "great.
The Tathāgata’s appearance in the world and his ritual for saving sentient beings constitute the "matter" (artha). Sentient beings possess this true reality;

their capacity to respond and move the Buddha constitutes the "cause" (hetu). The Tathāgata realizes this true reality; his ability to manifest responsive transformations to save sentient beings constitutes the "condition" (pratyaya). All...
The Tathāgata appears in the world universally to reveal to all sentient beings the originally existing true reality,
so that they may all attain awakening and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" (Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment) is here translated as "the Path of Awakening. Regarding "unsurpassed":
it refers to the attainment of the Buddha of Wondrous Enlightenment, whose wisdom is pure and uniquely exalted, with nothing superior above it; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed."
"Burning fat to continue the daylight": "Fat" refers to oil; "daylight" (guǐ) refers to the shadow of the sun. As the ancients said: "The daylight is insufficient;
therefore, one continues it into the night"—this is precisely what that means.

Regarding the "General Principles" (*fán lì*): *fán* means "in general," and *lì* means "to take as a model. The preface to the *Zuǒzhuan* states: "To establish the general principles and initiate the models.

In ancient times, Hangzhou was called Fángzhōu during the Sui dynasty and Yúháng during the Táng dynasty. During the Southern Song, Emperor Gāozōng established his capital there after the southward migration.
At this point, the name was changed to Lin’an; during the Ming dynasty, it was again called Hangzhou, hence the term "Ancient Hang" (Guhang).
According to the gazetteer, Zhaokong Temple was established by imperial decree in the first year of the Tiānfú era of the Shíjìn dynasty as a great temple of the Vinaya school.
"Zhao" signifies the merit and achievement of manifesting myriad virtues, while "Qing" signifies the celebration of the great virtue of a single person.
The Wanshou Precept Platform is, in fact, the Earth-Sprung Precept Platform. Its formal name is the Ancient Buddha’s Precept Platform.
In the third year of the Taiping Xingguo era of the Song dynasty, Vinaya Master Yunkan diligently practiced the Way day and night in accordance with this site.

He was moved by the manifestation of the deity Vaiśravaṇa, who said: "The place where the Great Master now practices the Way is the precept platform of an ancient Buddha; it is a most auspicious ground."
This is the place where Dīpaṃkara Buddha was born. I pray that you, Master, will extensively propagate the *śīla* (precepts) so as to perpetuate the life of wisdom of the Tathāgata.
As for me, your disciple, I have obtained soil from beneath the seat of the World-Honored One’s enlightenment and heart-water from the four great oceans in West India.
I shall construct an altar and invite you to transmit the precepts, so that those who ascend it to receive ordination may forever be liberated from the sufferings of the hells.

As soon as he had finished speaking, a ritual platform surged forth from the earth. The seven treasures emitted radiance, and at the break of dawn in the east, the Veda-deva joined his palms in the void to bear witness.
Five-colored auspicious clouds formed a canopy to cover it, and all people marveled at this; thus it was called the "Earth-Surging Precept Platform.
When the matter was reported to the Emperor, an imperial edict granted it the name "Wanshan (Ten Thousand Goodnesses) Precept Platform," for the precepts are the foundation of all goodness.

In the thirty-third year of the Wanli era, he was granted the imperial edict bestowing the title of "Wanshou Jietan" (The Ten-Thousand-Year Longevity Precept Platform), because he ascended this platform to recite the precepts and pray for the prolongation of the Emperor’s sacred life.

Regarding the three trainings free from outflows (*trīṇi śikṣāṇi anāsravāṇi*), they are: precept (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Concentration arises because of the precepts; wisdom is produced because of concentration. [The precept...]
One emerges from the three miserable realms, certainly transcends the six heavens of desire, and through wisdom attains liberation from the three realms. These three factors support one another;

when afflictions are completely purified, one does not fall back into the cycle of birth and death. Thus, it is called "learning" (*śikṣā*). It is like adornment: if a vessel is not adorned, there is no way to achieve a beautiful appearance.
If one does not study, there is no means by which the fruit of sainthood can be realized.
Regarding the "ten gates": "gate" (mèn) refers to the act of gathering and encompassing without obstruction.

This means that when one intends to explain a sutra, prior to the actual text, one first employs these ten gates to encompass the meaning of the scripture, to clarify its sections and chapters, and to reveal its general outline, so as to enable all [beings]...
Scholars enter into understanding by means of the gates [of interpretation], so that the essential purport of the sūtras has a point of reference and is free from obstruction.
"Pari" (譬) refers to using categories for comparison; "yāya" (喻) refers to opening up a path to lead one to realization. This describes the manner in which the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma.
For those of dull faculties, [the Buddha] employs provisional parables to instruct and enlighten them, so as to cause them to attain understanding;
such is the case with the parables of the burning house, the medicinal herbs, and others found within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The "three periods" refer to the past, the present, and the future. King Prasenajit said: "When one contemplates the true mark of the body, one contemplates the Buddha in the same way:
there is no prior limit, no middle limit, and no subsequent limit."
Regarding the "four dhyānas and eight samādhis," this refers to the principle of gathering the distracted mind and returning it to stillness. There are four in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*):

namely, the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna. There are four in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): namely, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Thus, they are called the "four dhyānas and eight samādhis."
The *Sicidi of the Dharma-realm of the Four Truths* states: These four are collectively termed "truths" (*satya*) because their meaning is "thoroughly real.

These four truths were specifically taught for the sake of those who follow the Śrāvaka vehicle; wishing to give rise to understanding through hearing, they must necessarily rely on the teachings to manifest the principle.
Now, it is clarified that the teachings and the principle are not empty, hence they are called "thoroughly real. Suffering arises when causes evoke their results; thus, one should...

Originally, cause was presented first and effect later; now, all cases present the effect first and the cause later. This is because the gates of teaching employ this method as a skillful means to guide sentient beings;
therefore, they all present the effect first and the cause later. The former two truths pertain to worldly phenomena;

they lead one to know suffering so as to abandon its origin, and thus the effect is presented first, followed by the cause. The latter two truths pertain to supramundane phenomena, intended to enable [the practitioner] to...
Cessation is attained through the Path; therefore, it is also presented first as the fruit and followed by its cause. First, the Truth of Suffering: suffering is the fruit of suffering.
Second, the Truth of Origination: origination is the cause of suffering. Third, the Truth of Cessation: cessation is the fruit of bliss. Fourth, the Truth of the Path: the path is the cause of bliss.
Emptiness of self refers to the absence of the fourfold views of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Emptiness of phenomena refers to the absence of the five aggregates: form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

The one true Dharma-realm is called "one" because it is free from duality; it is called "true" because it is not false; and it is called the "Dharma-realm" because its elements interpenetrate and harmoniously encompass one another.
This is precisely the equal Dharmakāya of all Buddhas. From the very beginning, it is neither born nor extinguished;
it is neither empty nor existent; it is free from names and free from marks; it has no interior and no exterior; it is solely the one reality, for it is inconceivable.
Regarding the "Gate of the Suchness of Mind": the Suchness of Mind is the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-Gate of the One True Dharma-Domain.
That is to say, the nature of mind is neither born nor extinguished; it is neither defiled nor pure; it is ultimately equal and without change or alteration.
It is solely this one mind, and for this reason it is called the Gate of the Suchness of Mind.
The Tathāgata’s “expelling of marks” refers to the expelling of phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), because he reveals only the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
That is to say, all phenomena are fundamentally characterized by nirvāṇa. If one were to cling to nirvāṇa, then even nirvāṇa would become a mere category of phenomena.
