Therefore, it is further expelled by saying, “There is no nirvāṇa. “There is no Buddha in nirvāṇa” expels the subject; “there is no nirvāṇa of the Buddha” expels the object.

"Buddha" means that which is capable of awakening. "Nirvana" is that which is awakened to. Because neither existence nor non-existence can be apprehended, both the subject (the awakener) and the object (that which is awakened to) are transcended.
The Tathāgatagarbha is precisely the nature of True Suchness; it is the support of the eighth consciousness, replete with all dharmas and encompassing all things.
It is like an elephant treasury; therefore, it is called a "treasury. All Buddhas realize this treasury-mind to benefit all sentient beings, its application being inexhaustible;
it is the very essence of the single true reality (*ekadharmatā*). This essence can give rise to all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
Therefore, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The *ālayavijñāna* is the name for the eighth consciousness; it is translated as the "non-perishing consciousness" (*amukta-jñāna*), taking the sense of "not losing" [seeds] as its meaning.
It is also translated as the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*), because it is able to contain and store the various seeds of both good and evil. It is also called the "seed consciousness."
It is also called the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
"True emptiness" refers to the fusion of mind and objects; yet, true emptiness is signless, which is precisely what is termed the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

"Precepts coexistent with the Path" refers to the state in which, during the stages of the Path of Vision and the Path of Cultivation, one does not intentionally maintain them, yet naturally commits no transgressions.

Precepts and the Path arise together; therefore, they are called "concomitant. Since these precepts are obtained through the first, second, and third fruits [of the path], they are untainted (anāsrava) precepts.

Precepts concomitant with meditative concentration (samādhi-samvara) are also called "dhyāna-precepts. This refers to the time when one attains the first, second, third, or fourth dhyāna concentrations; at that time, [one does not...]

It is maintained through mental attention (*manasikāra*). One naturally refrains from transgressions; since both precept and meditative concentration arise together, they are termed "conjoined" (*sādhāraṇa*).
These precepts do not yet exhaust the afflictions (*kleśa*) nor bring about liberation from birth and death; thus, they are known as "outflow-tainted" (*sāsrava*) precepts.

The untainted dhyāna-precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) refer to the "superior path" (*uttara-mārga*), which is a collective designation for both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the two types of precepts.

Regarding the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), a verse states: "The ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) mutually form one hundred; The ten realms (*dhātu*) form one thousand; The seven branches [of action] form seven thousand;
Across the three times, this becomes twenty-one thousand. Including the three poisons (*viṣa*) along with the equal portion (*sabhāga*), This constitutes the eighty-four thousand."
"Dust" (*rajas*) refers to that which defiles the true nature. "Labor" refers to being driven and enslaved by the cycle of transmigration.
The eighty-four thousand *dharmaparyāyas* refer to the Tathāgata’s attainment of the Way. Therein are three hundred and fifty *pāramitās*.
As for "pāramitā," it means the fulfillment of practice through both phenomena and principle, crossing over the flow of birth and death to ascend to the shore of *nirvāṇa*.
These merits are inexhaustible; therefore, they are called "Pāramitās" (Infinite Transcendences). The verse says:
From the arising of the first radiance up to the distribution of the śarīra relics, there are three hundred and fifty Pāramitā dharma-gates.
Each gate contains the six pāramitās, totaling two thousand one hundred. By adding the four great elements and the six sense-decays, they total twenty-one thousand. Plus...
Those with equal proportions of the three poisons constitute eighty-four thousand [types].
Those of indeterminate nature are so called because they encounter conditions and habituate themselves to them heavily; thus, their practice is not fixed.

If they associate with śrāvakas, they practice the Dharma of the śrāvakas; if they associate with pratyekabuddhas, they practice the Dharma of the pratyekabuddhas; if they associate with bodhisattvas, they practice the [Dharma] of the bodhisattvas.
Sentient beings each develop their own nature according to what they have practiced; this is called the indeterminate nature.

In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is no existence; in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is no non-existence. Being neither existent nor non-existent, this is called the Middle Way, the ultimate truth.
Original enlightenment refers to the essence of the sentient beings' mind. It is numinous, luminous, and vast, equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception;
it is precisely the Tathāgata’s impartial Dharmakāya. Based upon this Dharmakāya, it is designated as "original enlightenment."

Initial awakening refers to the sentient beings' fundamental awakening, the source of the mind. Due to being stirred by the permeation of ignorance, awakening does not manifest as awakening, and they remain lost in delusion for many kalpas.
Now, for the first time, they awaken; this is called initial awakening. When the initial and the fundamental are non-dual, it is called ultimate awakening.
This is precisely the attainment of Buddhahood.
The thirty-two marks refer to the Tathāgata’s body of transformation and response; by possessing these thirty-two marks, he manifests the Dharma-body, in which all virtues are perfectly fulfilled.
He is the most honored among gods and humans, the sovereign king of all sages. These are what are called the "stable feet."
The mark of level feet; the mark of wheels with a thousand spokes on the soles of the feet; the mark of long and slender fingers; the mark of soft and supple hands and feet;
the mark of webbed hands and feet; the mark of full heels; the mark of high and well-formed insteps; the mark of calves like those of the king of deer;

the mark of standing with the hands reaching the knees; the mark of the male organ being concealed within a sheath; the mark of the body being proportionate in height and breadth; the mark of the pores emitting a blue-green light; the mark of the body...
The mark of body hairs curling to the right; the mark of a golden-colored body; the mark of a fathom-wide radiance extending from the body and face;

the mark of skin so fine and smooth; the mark of seven parts of the body being level and full; the mark of the two armpits being full; the mark of a body like that of a lion; the mark of a well-proportioned body;
the mark of rounded shoulders; the mark of having forty teeth; the mark of teeth that are white, even, and closely set; and the mark of pure white canine teeth.
The jaw is like that of a lion; the throat possesses the mark of obtaining supreme flavor; the tongue is broad and long; the Brahma-voice is deep and far-reaching;
the color of the eyes is like refined gold; the eyelashes are like those of a bull king; there is a white tuft of hair between the eyebrows;
and the crown of the head is formed as a fleshly protuberance, also known as the "invisible crown" mark. These constitute the thirty-two marks.
Furthermore, there are the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), namely: the mark of the invisible crown of the head; the mark of the body being straight and the nostrils not protruding;
the mark of eyebrows like the crescent moon; the mark of the spokes on the ear-lobes; the mark of the body being firm and solid; and the mark of the joints of the bones being like hooks and chains.
The turning of his body is as excellent as that of an elephant king. When he walks, his feet leave the ground four inches while the auspicious marks of the soles appear beautifully.
His nails are the color of red copper and are excellent. His kneecaps are firm, well-attached, and perfectly rounded. His body is pure blue and excellent. His body is supple and excellent.

His body is straight and not bent, and excellent. His fingers are slender, round, and excellent. The lines on his fingers are concealed within them and excellent. His veins are deep-set and do not show, and excellent.
The ankles are not prominent; his body is well-lubricated and radiant; his body is self-sustained and does not waver;
his body is fully developed; his deportment is complete and excellent; his deportment is perfect and admirable; his dwelling place is peaceful and cannot be disturbed;
his majesty overawes all; he is pleasing for all to behold; his face is neither too long nor too large; his countenance is upright and his expression is untroubled.
Excellent. His face is perfectly full and excellent. The color of his lips is crimson and lustrous like the *bimba* fruit, excellent.
His voice is deep and resonant, excellent. His navel is deep, spiraling to the right, and wonderfully round, excellent. The hair of his body is dark blue-black, radiant and glossy, excellent.

His hands and feet are perfectly rounded, excellent. His hands and feet are as he wishes, excellent. The lines on his palms are clear and straight, excellent. The lines on his palms are deep and long, excellent. The lines on his palms do not...

He is excellent in his abandonment [of faults]. He is excellent in having a face that is harmonious and pleasant for all sentient beings with evil minds to behold, being broad, sublime, and beautiful.

His face is excellent like the full moon. He is excellent in speaking with harmony and joy according to the inclinations of sentient beings. He is excellent in constantly emitting a wondrous fragrance from his pores.
He is excellent in emitting unsurpassed fragrances from his mouth. His deportment is excellent like that of a lion king; his gait is excellent like that of an elephant.

The king is excellent; he is excellent in his conduct like a king of swans. He is excellent with a head like a *mātuluṅga* fruit. He is excellent in being fully endowed with all the limbs of his body.
He is excellent with four white, beautiful tusks. He is excellent with a tongue that is long, broad, and red in color. He is excellent with a tongue that is thin and exquisite.

He is excellent with body hair that is reddish. He is excellent with body hair that is soft and pure. He is excellent with eyes that are elegant, wide, and long. [He is excellent] with the characteristics of the orifices.
He is endowed with excellent qualities: his hands and feet are red and white like the color of a lotus; his navel is deep and does not protrude; his abdomen is unexposed;
his waist is slender, square, and well-proportioned; his body is steady and does not sway; his body is dignified and majestic;
his stature is tall and grand; his form is exceptionally sublime; his hands and feet are soft and smooth; and he possesses a circular halo extending one fathom on all four sides.
Excellent is the radiance that illuminates the body as one walks; excellent is the impartial regard for all sentient beings; excellent is the refusal to disparage sentient beings;

excellent is responding to the voices of sentient beings without increase or decrease; excellent is preaching the Dharma without attachment; excellent is preaching the Dharma according to the languages of sentient beings;
excellent is emitting sounds to respond to the multitude; excellent is preaching the Dharma through successive causes and conditions; excellent is [all of this].
Sentient beings cannot exhaustively perceive his marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). These include: the mark of being never weary of being gazed upon; the mark of long, flowing hair;
the mark of hair the color of blue pearls and smooth to the touch; and the mark of virtuous characteristics on the hands and feet. These constitute the eighty [minor] marks.
All such marks and signs as these above are the result of pure observance of the precepts throughout many lifetimes.

Regarding the names of Bodhisattvas who are equal to the Fully Awakened One (Samyaksambuddha) and are in their final birth before Buddhahood—such as the present Bodhisattva Maitreya and others—from the perspective of those on lower stages, they are equal to the Buddhas.
Yet, because they still possess a single most subtle grade of ignorance that has not yet been exhausted, they are still called Bodhisattvas.
The contemplative wisdom they have cultivated is purely singular, firm, and sharp; it is likened to a vajra and is thus termed the "Vajra-mind. Furthermore, it is also...
He is called a Superior Being (*uttamapuruṣa*).

"Sublime Enlightenment" (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) refers to the mind after the diamond-like [samādhi] (*vajropama-citta*). It is a vast and luminous great awakening; sublime wisdom has exhausted the source, and the habitual tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*) are completely eliminated.
This is called true liberation. Therefore, it is termed "Sublime Enlightenment."
The three obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and retribution (*vipāka*). They are called "obstacles" because they obscure the right path.

The divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) refers to the sense organ of pure matter (*rūpa-indriya*); it is called the "eye" because it illuminates objects and gives rise to consciousness. It is attained through cultivation based on the heavens.
Therefore, it is called the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*).

India is newly called *Bhāratavarṣa* (Tianzhu). In the language of Tang, it means "moon. This is because the sages and worthies of that land have succeeded one another in their tracks, guiding ordinary people and governing all things, just as the moon shines upon and oversees everything.
"Model" (*muke*) means to take as a standard for emulation.
Regarding the True Pure Land, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the "body of enjoyment for others" (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) resides in the "land of enjoyment for others.

This body of enjoyment for others refers to the manifestation of this body due to the resonance of the stimuli from other sentient beings; it is the "excellent response-body" (*viśiṣṭanirmāṇakāya*). "Other... [text continues].

The Land of Enjoyment is also the Land of Real Reward. This means that by the power of great compassion, the Buddha transforms it into a pure land according to what is appropriate for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages; it may be small or large, inferior or superior.
The Body of Other-Enjoyment dwells therein, and thus it is said that he "resides in the truly pure land. (From the *Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation of Amitāyus*)
It is said: "This refers to those who, by practicing the Dharma of reality, have attained superior retribution.

These are the various Bodhisattvas, specifically those of the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi), as well as those of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten transferences of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), up to and including the Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi).

*Asaṃkhyeya*, here translated as "innumerable" (*wúyāngshù*), refers to a number that even those among gods and humans capable of calculating cannot comprehend through the utmost limits of calculation;
this is called one *asaṃkhyeya*. This is the first of the ten great numbers in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The ten great numbers are: first, *asaṃkhyeya*; second, immeasurable (*apramāṇa*); third, boundless (*ananta*); fourth, incomparable (*asama*).
Five is incalculable; six is incomparable; seven is inconceivable; eight is immeasurable; nine is ineffable;
ten is ineffably ineffable. These are the ten great numbers.

Regarding the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): it is also called the obscuration to knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*). This refers to the attachment to the phenomena that are realized, which obstructs the nature of wisdom;
this is termed the cognitive obscuration. It is identical in root to the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), consisting of the twenty-six secondary afflictions.

Because they possess a function of agitation upon the basis of craving, they are called the afflictive obscurations; because they possess a function of covering, they are called the cognitive obscurations.

There are two obstructions: the afflictive obstruction (kleśāvaraṇa) which obstructs nirvāṇa, and the cognitive obstruction (jñeyāvaraṇa) which obstructs bodhi. These consist of the conceptualized and the innate.

This explanation concerns, for the time being, the abandonment [of these obstructions] during the stage of the Mahāyāna path of vision (darśanamārga). The Tathāgata is eternally free from these two obstructions;
his mind is perpetually pure, devoid of the characteristics of subject and object.
The four wisdoms are: first, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; second, the Wisdom of Equality; third, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; and fourth, the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done.
Regarding the "Clear Gate of the Hundred Dharmas," the hundred dharmas are condensed into five categories: namely, eleven material dharmas (*rūpadharma*) and eight mental dharmas (*cittadharma*).
There are fifty-one mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), twenty-four dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma*), and six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*);
together they constitute one hundred. The details are as found in the *Mahāyāna-śatadharma-vyākhyāna-mukha-śāstra*.
The "Three Sages" refer to the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications; all are called "sages.

This is discussed from the perspective of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), which holds that while the bodhisattvas at these stages have completely severed the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-kleśa), they still possess the affliction of ignorance (avidyā).
Because they have not yet entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), they are called "Worthy Ones" (*bhadra*).
The "Ten Noble Ones" are the truly noble. This means that these Bodhisattvas, having fulfilled their cultivation and practice, have already entered the state of correctness;
therefore, they are called "Noble Ones. These are the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

The term *siddhānta* (四悉檀) means "universal" (*si*). *Siddhānta* is a compound of the Sanskrit *siddha* and the Chinese *tan* (from the Sanskrit *dāna*), meaning "bestowal. Because it combines both the Sanskrit and Chinese terms, it is called *siddhānta*.
This refers to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma through these four methods, universally bestowing them upon all sentient beings;
hence they are named the Four *Siddhāntas*. First is the *loka-siddhānta* (世界悉檀). *Loka* signifies "separation" or "distinction," while *siddhānta* means "division" or "classification."

This is because the faculties and capacities of sentient beings are shallow; therefore, the Buddha, in accordance with what they desire and wish to hear, explains the teachings by distinguishing them in sequence to inspire joy in them.

This is called the *loka-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the universal standpoint). Second is the *pudgala-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the individual standpoint), which means that when the Buddha wishes to preach the Dharma, he must first observe the magnitude of the sentient beings' faculties and capacities, as well as their past seeds [of cultivation].
[He examines] their depth and shallowness, and then explains the Dharma according to their specific capacities, causing them to increase in right faith and cultivate roots of goodness;
therefore, this is called the *pudgala-siddhānta* (the standpoint of the person). Third, the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remediation):

for example, those among sentient beings who have much lust are taught to contemplate impurity; those with much anger are taught to cultivate a mind of loving-kindness; and those with much delusion are taught to contemplate...
The *hetu-pratyaya* (causal) [Siddhānta]: This refers to the teaching of these medicinal Dharmas in response to these various illnesses and their bestowal universally upon all sentient beings;
therefore, it is called the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (remedial Siddhānta). Fourth is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (ultimate Siddhānta). *Paramārtha* means principle (*tattva*).

This refers to the Buddha’s knowing that the roots of goodness in sentient beings have already matured, and thus he teaches the Dharma for them, enabling them to realize the Noble Path; this is called the first [Siddhānta].

The *arthasiddhānta* (the established truth of meaning) is as follows: "The self that is sovereign" refers to the sense of "self" within the body; it is the "self" of the four virtues—permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*)—of the Tathāgata.
This is because the Tathāgata, possessing great supernormal powers and wisdom, manifests with mastery according to the capacities of sentient beings. First, he is able to...
1. Manifesting a single body as many bodies. 2. Manifesting a body the size of a single atom filling the great trichiliocosm.

3. A massive body rising lightly and traveling afar. 4. Manifesting infinite forms while constantly dwelling in a single land. 5. The mutual functioning of the sense organs. 6. [The power of] non-obstruction.
1. Attaining all dharmas while remaining free from the conceptualization of dharmas; 2. Expounding the meaning of a single verse for immeasurable eons;
3. One’s own body pervading all places, just like empty space. Because one possesses these eight qualities, one is called "I" (Ātman).
Śikhin is here translated as "Jewel Topknot" (Bǎoji). It is also rendered as Śikhi, which translates as "Fire. Fire has two meanings:
first, it can illuminate so that various evils do not arise; second, it burns away all afflictions so that they do not arise. Thus, the name was established according to its meaning.
"Dīpaṃkara" in Sanskrit is translated here as "Ran Deng" (Lamp-Lighter). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that when the Prince was born, his bodily radiance was like a lamp;
he is also called Dīpaṃkara (Flame-Light).
Vipaśyin is also called Vīkṣin; in the language of China, it means "Victorious Vision" (Shèngguān) or "Universal Vision" (Biànjiàn).
The six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) refer to generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; by means of these, one delivers oneself and delivers others.

The causal characteristics for cultivating the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*) are as follows: the primary marks refer to the thirty-two marks, and the secondary signs refer to the eighty minor marks.

By practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), one accomplishes a hundred merits; using these hundred merits, one produces one primary mark. Thus, they serve as the causes for the thirty-two primary marks.
The Prince Wondrous Ocean (*Sāgaraprabha*) is called *Mañju* in the Sanskrit language, which means "Wondrous," and *śrī*, which means "Ocean. As for "Prince," he is the son of the Dharma King.

Since the Tathāgata is the Great Dharma King, and since Wondrous Ocean was the first to request from the Buddha the bestowal of the bodhisattva precepts and enter the stage of the correct position of the Dharma (*dharmasamyaktvaniyāma*), he is thus named a prince.
Verses on the Flow of the Three Teachings (Extracted from the *Zhou Shu Yiji*) The fourth emperor of the Zhou, Jiayin year: Śākyamuni descended into birth at Kapilavastu.
The fifty-third year of King Mu, Renshen year: The Tathāgata returned to the limit of truth at eighty years of age.
One thousand and eighty years after the Parinirvāṇa, the teaching flowed into the world during the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty.
Four hundred and twenty-two years before that, Laozi was born during the reign of King Ding;
four hundred and seventy-seven years before that, Confucius was born during the time of King Ling.
This is the record of the clear sequence of events before and after the birth of the Triple-Sanctified One.

Recorded by the Vinaya-transmitting Śramaṇa Shuyü of the Wanshou Precept Platform at Shaoling Temple in Ancient Hangzhou, based on the first volume of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* as expounded by the Buddha. Part Two. Pure.

△ Second, the extensive transmission by Śākyamuni, in two parts: first, a general enumeration of the many Buddhas in all realms; second, a specific manifestation of the one Buddha in this realm. Within the first part, there are four sections:

first, receiving the Dharma and preparing to depart; second, returning to one’s own realm; third, benefiting sentient beings in accordance with the command; fourth, concluding by analogy with the other Buddhas. Now, the first section: 1. Receiving the Dharma and Preparing to Depart 2. Returning to One's Own Realm 3. Benefiting Sentient Beings in Accordance with the Command 4.
Concluding by Analogy with the Other Buddhas Now, the first [of these four].
At that time, the Buddhas upon the thousand-petaled lotuses—the hundreds of thousands of myriads of Śākyamunis—rose from their majestic lion thrones in the Lotus Treasury World.
Each withdrew in turn, and from every part of their bodies they emitted inconceivable rays of light.

From each ray of light were manifested immeasurable Buddhas, who simultaneously offered immeasurable flowers of blue, yellow, red, and white to Vairocana Buddha, receiving and upholding [the teachings].
The "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" as explained above is concluded.
As for the Buddhas upon the thousand petals rising from their seats, the matter of receiving the Dharma is finished.
As for each of them paying obeisance, taking leave, and withdrawing before Śākyamuni, the etiquette between teacher and disciple is exhausted. Their entire bodies emit inconceivable light.
Thus, the heart that repays the source is made manifest. Furthermore, the light of the Buddhas is of two kinds: first, constant light; second, emitted light.

Constant light is the perfect clarity of original enlightenment (*mūla-āśraya*), which universally illumines the Dharma-realm. Emitted light refers to the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) that arise, whose manifestations are manifold;
all of these emerge without departing from the precept-body (*śīla-tattva*) of the fundamental mind-ground. Now...
Regarding the term "inconceivable": it means that this light is not something known by those of the provisional or limited vehicles.

Because the manifested light is no different from the fundamental light, they are both the secret treasury of the three virtues and the illumination of subtle, wondrous wisdom; thus, it cannot be grasped by the thinking mind.
It cannot be expressed through words; therefore, it is called "inconceivable.
That "each light transforms into immeasurable Buddhas" is intended to reveal that this wisdom is the mother of all Buddhas, for all Buddhas are born from it.
Thus, the mind-ground of Śākyamuni transforms into a thousand Buddhas, and those thousand Buddhas transform into ten billion Buddhas. Ten billion...

The billions of Buddhas manifest as immeasurable Buddhas. Furthermore, this represents the ten inexhaustible treasuries of the precepts, for they all arise from the light of the adamantine jewel-precept.
Blue, yellow, red, and white represent the stages of abiding, practice, orientation, and the grounds (*bhūmi*).

The flowers represent the wondrous causes of the myriad practices, and the offerings represent the fruit of the Buddha’s One Vehicle. Since these wondrous causes arise from the virtues of the fruit, [the offerings are placed first].
This is further used to adorn the fruits and virtues [of Buddhahood]. Previously, Vairocana signaled with light; now, all Buddhas respond with light.
This represents that the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground is fundamentally beyond words and thought. The Buddha-nature and the essence of the precepts are neither form nor mind.

Only this single ray of Prajñā-light is such that the fundamental is never separate from the traces, and the traces are never separate from the fundamental; fundamental and traces shine together in offering.
Vairocana Buddha thus repays the milk of the Dharma. △ Second, returning to the original realm:

each of them vanishes from this Lotus-womb World. Having vanished, they enter the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature-Space and return to their original source-world, Jambudvīpa, beneath the Bodhi tree. From the Essential Nature-Space...
The Flower Radiance Samādhi emerges.

Its initial concealment is called "submergence," and its final disappearance is called "completion. Although there is thus emerging and submerging, concealment and manifestation, because the Buddhas have awakened to the mind, they possess sovereign and unimpeded mastery.
As for the Flower Radiance Samādhi whose essential nature is like space, it refers to the thorough illumination of the original suchness.
Within the essential nature of space, the flower-light manifests spontaneously and naturally. The essential nature represents the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

the flower represents the virtue of liberation (*vimuktikāya*); and the light represents the virtue of wisdom (*prajñākāya*). Because these three virtues are perfectly integrated, it is called *samādhi*.
Furthermore, this essential nature is the Dharma, common to both sentient beings and Buddhas; it is the essential nature of the eternally abiding true mind. This is the flower-light.
This is a metaphor. This metaphor illustrates that the substance of the mind is vast, empty, and tranquil, possessing no boundaries or external manifestations; therefore, it is called "empty space.

Although the substance of the mind is empty, it is fundamentally endowed with the wondrous functions of the light of nature, virtue, and wisdom as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, such that thousands of branches and ten thousand leaves can all pierce through the dust of emotional attachments;
therefore, it is called "the Flower-Light of Essential Nature. Stillness is not separate from illumination, and movement...

This is precisely concentration; therefore, it is called *samādhi*. *Samādhi* is a general term. Here it is translated as "equipoise" (*samāhita*), also as "the sphere of right mental application," and also as "right reception.
However, the names and essences of *samādhi* are manifold, and the methods of cultivation and realization vary accordingly.

For instance, all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are also termed *samādhi*. What is now referred to as the "Flower-Light Body-Nature" (*Huaguang Tixing*) is intended to distinguish this from other types of *samādhi*.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s samādhi is fundamentally neither entering nor emerging. Thus it is said: "The Nāga is always in meditative concentration;

there is no time when he is not in concentration. It is also said: "Without arising from the extinction-concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*), he manifests all modes of deportment and displays the forms of the ten Dharma-realms to guide and benefit all sentient beings.
What is now called "entering" refers to the fact that essence and function are darkly one; what is called "emerging" refers to the fact that essence and function are fully manifest.

This is because it manifests what is thus: namely, that the hundreds of thousands of gates of meditative concentration all return to the same stillness, and the boundless ocean of wisdom does not depart from its original source.
Guifeng said: "To cease all conceptual discrimination so that wisdom merges with principle is called 'entering. This is precisely it.
If one integrates the preceding three contemplations, then emptiness is the contemplation of non-arising; by contemplating the unconditioned dharma-realm mind, the flower is non-extinguishing.
Contemplation: Contemplating the mind of the conditioned dharma-realm, its nature is precisely the contemplation of the one mind;
contemplating the mind of the unobstructed dharma-realm, the three and the one are perfectly interfused and sovereign. This is called the Samādhi of the Essential Nature of Empty-Space Flower-Light.
Regarding "returning to the source world of Jambudvīpa, beneath the Bodhi tree," this refers to Śākyamuni Buddha being at [Bodh Gaya] in Magadha.

In the palace of the deity Śiva, together with immeasurable Brahma kings and an unspeakable multitude of Bodhisattvas, [Vajrasattva] finished expounding the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" as taught by Vairocana Buddha.

He then lifted up this world’s great assembly and returned to the Palace-Treasury World (Kūtāgāra-lokadhātu) to pay homage, inquire after the Dharma, and now come to Jambudvīpa; hence it is said he "returns. Furthermore, regarding the Flower Treasury (Huāzàng):
This is the fundamental realm where the Original Teacher received his training: the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa). It is the fundamental realm for one’s own practice and transformation;
therefore, it is called "returning to the original source realm. Nevertheless, whether returning or coming forth, one does not depart from this single realm of the original source-nature.
If discussed in terms of principle, then the essence of the body is the Samādhi of Empty Space and Flower-Light.
Regarding the source-worlds of all Buddhas, speaking in terms of phenomena: the thousand Buddhas, as well as the hundreds of billions of Buddhas, each previously had their own native land;
because they heard the precepts, they all came to the abode of Śākyamuni (Sana). Now that they have completed receiving the Dharma, they each return to their respective original lands of retribution.
Jambū is the name of a tree; this is translated as "Superior Gold" (Shengjin). Tīra... [text ends].
It is a continent. This means that to the north of this Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa) there is a great tree named Jambu;

its branches and leaves are all golden, and when the water dripping from them enters the soil, it becomes red gold because it is superior to other gold. Alternatively, it is said that beneath the tree there is a river.
The juice of the Jambu fruit, when dropped upon objects, turns them into gold; because it flows into a river, the sand becomes golden in color.

Thus, the tree gave its name to the river, and the continent derived its appellation from the tree; hence it is called the "Continent of Superior Gold" (Jambudvīpa), which is the Southern Continent of Jambudvīpa.
Regarding the Bodhi tree, the *Xiyuji* states that it was a Pippala tree, several hundred feet high, upon which the Buddha sat.
Beneath it, he attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*; thus it is named Bodhi, which translates as "Path of Awakening. As it is the ultimate of all paths, it is also called the "Tree of the Path.
Its trunk is yellowish-white, while its branches and leaves are lush green; they do not wither in winter or summer, remaining radiant and unchanged.
Every year on the fifteenth day of the second month—the anniversary of the Buddha’s *parinirvāṇa*—the leaves all fall away, only to grow back again shortly thereafter.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The Bodhi tree is lofty, prominent, and extraordinary;

its trunk is of diamond, its main stem is of lapis lazuli, and its branches and twigs are composed of various exquisite jewels. Its precious leaves are lush and spreading, casting a shade like clouds.
Its precious flowers are of manifold colors, casting shadows as they branch out. Furthermore, it has mani-jewels as its fruit. This is the [Buddha-]field.
That is his Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which is the realm of Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and cannot be perceived by ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles.
Nevertheless, it manifests the Buddha’s samādhi, supernormal powers, and the light-reflections of wisdom, adorning the ground of the mind;
thus, it is identical in essence to the Flower Light [World]. Because Śākyamuni cultivated the Way through this, it is called the "Returning to the Original Source World of Bodhi."
It is beneath the *tī* tree. Regarding "emerging from the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of the Void-like Essential Nature":

returning to the original source-nature is "entering," while arising from the fundamental to manifest illumination is "emerging. The former "entering" was to demonstrate the samādhi of self-enjoyment;
the present "emerging" is intended to cause sentient beings to likewise enjoy this samādhi. Furthermore, it is called the "receptive karma" and the "progressive karma."

To "enter" means to respond to conditions and initiate transformation; to "exit" means to manifest. This has three meanings: first, when observing the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is no characteristic of entering or exiting, yet for the sake of skillful means (*upāya*), one speaks of entering and exiting.
Second, when observing the time of preaching the Dharma, there is a distinction between the appropriate and inappropriate timing for teaching; therefore, there is entering and exiting.
Third, when observing how to adapt the teaching to the capacity of the recipient—administering medicine according to the illness—there is exiting [from the state of non-manifestation].
The characteristic of entering. Although entry and exit are thus demonstrated, movement and stillness share a single source; going and returning are non-dual in their certainty.
△ Third, the section on benefiting sentient beings in accordance with the imperial decree, in ten parts; now, the first location.
Having emerged, he then sat upon the Vajra-Thousand-Rays King Throne and in the Hall of Sublime Light, where he expounded the ocean-like dharma-gates of the ten worlds.

"Emerging" refers to the departure from thought; "having completed" refers to the conclusion of the task. The preceding section clarified the thousand Śākyamunis and the hundreds of thousands of billions of Śākyamunis.
Having first received the Bodhisattva-piṭaka of precepts before Vairocana, they entered samādhi and returned to their original source-worlds.

Now, it clarifies that they have emerged from samādhi and manifested their bodies in ten locations to preach the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "just now sitting upon the Vajra-Thousand-Rays King Throne":
"just now" (fang) means "correctly" (zheng). Because they dwell securely in the True Dharma, it is said they "just now sit. It signifies ultimate firmness.
It is truly named the Vajra; it is the seat upon which the thousand Buddhas emitted light and attained the Way, and is therefore called the Seat of the Thousand-Light King (*Sahasraraśmiprabhārāja*).

According to the *Lüshu* (Abridged Commentary), this seat is located in Central India, in the kingdom of Magadha, more than two hundred *li* to the southwest of the city of Rājagṛha, beneath the Bodhi tree. Long ago, when this world was first formed, the seat and the Great...
It arises simultaneously with the earth. Situated within the trichiliocosm, it extends downward to the golden wheel (*kāñcanacakravāḍa*) and upward to the surface of the earth.

Composed of diamond (*vajra*), it spans over a hundred paces. All one thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa sit upon this seat, enter the diamond-like concentration (*vajrasamādhi*), emit great radiance, and attain unsurpassed enlightenment; therefore, it is called the "Diamond Thousand-Radiance King Seat. This is as follows:
This is the place for coming to cultivate and realize the Way of Principle; it is also called a *bodhimaṇḍa* (place of enlightenment). As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon this seat and attained supreme perfect enlightenment regarding all dharmas. Regarding what is meant by "attaining": there is no attainment in the *dharmakāya*; it is called "attainment" because it has emerged from obstructions.
In the *saṃbhogakāya*, the four wisdoms are first perfected, which is called "attainment. In the *nirmāṇakāya*, there are the eight phases [of a Buddha's life].
He sat beneath the Bodhi tree and severed the fetters to achieve completion. Although the circumstances differ, the principle remains one. As for "the Hall of Sublime Radiance" (*Miaoguang Tang*):
*ji* (及) is a term denoting succession, meaning that from beneath that tree he proceeded to this place to preach the Dharma.

It is called "Sublime" (*Miao*) because it is adorned with various jewels; it is called "Radiance" (*Guang*) because the brilliance of the jewels illuminates one another. [The assembly consists of] the holy and the ordinary...
Because it is a place where [beings] gather, it is called a hall (*maṇḍapa*); it is also named the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-maṇḍapa*).

This hall is located not far to the west of the Bodhi tree. In the past, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, Brahmā established this hall with the seven treasures, and Śakra established a throne of the seven treasures that emitted extraordinary light, illuminating the Bodhi tree. He then invited [the Buddha].
The Buddha ascended the throne and turned the Great Wheel of Dharma. Seated upon that seat, he emitted light for seven days and expounded the sublime Dharma;
this place is also called the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsamaṇḍapa*). As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "At that time, the Tathāgata was in the Hall of Universal Radiance."
This refers to sitting upon the lion throne of the Lotus Treasury. Regarding the "Ocean of Dharma-Gates of the Ten Worlds," "ocean" signifies depth and vastness;
it means that all dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are fully encompassed within these ten.
First, the ocean of worlds; second, the ocean of sentient beings; third, the ocean of the establishment of the dharma-realm; fourth, the ocean of Buddhas.
1. The ocean of the five Buddhas’ *pāramitās*; 2. The ocean of the six Buddhas’ liberations; 3. The ocean of the seven Buddhas’ transformations; 4. The ocean of the eight Buddhas’ expositions; 5.
The ocean of the nine Buddhas’ names and titles; 6. The ocean of the ten Buddhas’ lifespans. The *Necklace Sūtra* (*Ratnavyūha-sūtra*) states:
When the Buddha first attained the Way beneath this tree and expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Ocean-like Worlds, there were eighty thousand stainless bodhisattvas...

The Bodhisattva at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) manifests his body and attains Buddhahood. Nine billion people enter the gate of illumination of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Thus, the Flower Treasury Adorned Ten Worlds-Oceans are the self-realized noble wisdom of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time;
it is the realm of enjoyment. All Buddhas rely upon this Dharma-gate to turn their chariots backward [toward the world].
The Compassionate Vessel: Broadly Delivering All Beings. All Bodhisattvas cultivate this Dharma-gate until they reach the ultimate ocean of fruition.
Because all sentient beings are deluded regarding this mind, they transmigrate endlessly within the sea of birth and death.

Rather than speaking of "sentient beings," the term "worlds" is used to refer to the *pariṇāmanabhoga* (the environment) so as to encompass the *upabhoga* (the physical body). Furthermore, the Avataṃsaka...
The Commentary states: "The ten world-oceans refer to the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). 'Faith' takes the sense of compliance;
it means complying with the principle of Buddha-nature without doubt. To speak in terms of the number ten is precisely to clarify the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths.

The stages of Abiding, Practice, and Direction (*vihāra-caryā-pratipatti*) are largely the same as those in the *Avataṃsaka*, with only minor differences. [This refers to] the Bodhisattva of the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*)."
Through the accumulation of merit and by the power of his original vows, he took his station within the human vehicle as the King of Jambudvīpa.

He cultivated the ten wholesome actions to transform sentient beings and practiced the dharma of the perfection of giving to adorn the wondrous fruit. Thus, he governed all the lands of the southern continent.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment and initially turned the wheel of Dharma, he first preached it in this very place.
The ocean of dharma-gates of ten worlds serves as the bodhisattva’s true cultivation of skillful means.

Because these various worlds are all formed by the two kinds of delusion—common and individual—of sentient beings, there are ten locations from the Hall of Sublime Light up to the Heaven of the Fourth Dhyāna.
The first six locations constitute six assemblies; the seventh and the subsequent four dhyānas together constitute one.
The seventh assembly summarizes and further explains the preceding thirty minds and ten stages (*bhūmi*). The first six assemblies explain this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground individually;

all take faith as their foundation. According to the *Avataṃsaka*’s seventh assembly, the "Certainty" (*niyata*) and "Pervasive Patience" (*vyāpti-kṣānti*) stages should also include the explanation of the thirty minds and ten stages.
Master Qingliang’s commentary states: "Certainty and Pervasive Patience correspond to [the stages of] Equality (*samatā*)."

The Dharma of Awakening (*bodhi-dharma*). The remaining [stages] shall be the Dharma of Sublime Awakening (*vibodhi-dharma*). Taking those as examples for these, it may also be that in the first three dhyānas, the dharmas of *kṣānti*, *praṇidhāna*, and *vidyā* constitute the Dharma of Awakening;
in the fourth dhyāna, the stage of the mind-ground (*citta-bhūmi*), the *vidyā* constitutes the Dharma of Sublime Awakening.

However, this is both different from and the same as the *Avataṃsaka*. In the *Avataṃsaka*, Vairocana is none other than Śākyamuni; while preaching the Dharma in all assemblies, he remains unmoving yet pervades everywhere. This pertains to the stages prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*).

The Perfect Interfusion (yuanrong) occurs on the stages (dìshàng), while the Sequential Arrangement (xíngbù) pertains to the present stage. In this sutra, Vairocana sits upon a lotus pedestal while Śākyamuni occupies a thousand-petaled lotus;

rising from his seat to reach the other [Vairocana] represents the Sequential Arrangement, whereas being on the stages represents the Perfect Interfusion. One should know that the ten inexhaustible precepts are, in their entirety, the ground of the one mind;
this is the Sequential Arrangement that does not obstruct the Perfect Interfusion. Only when these two are non-obstructive can they be called the Perfect Teaching (yuánjiào). Therefore...

Vasubandhu [explains] that through the six aspects of perfect interfusion, taking up one encompasses the whole; yet, according to the capacities and inclinations of beings, there are differences in their explanations.
Here, we clarify the sequential order; therefore, the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) are taught first, followed by the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).
This enables sentient beings who have already resolved upon the Great Mind to enter the stage of the perfect ten faiths before attaining the perfect ten abidings. △ Second Section.
He rose again from his seat and went to the palace of Śakra, where he preached the Ten Abodes.
Regarding the palace of Śakra: in Sanskrit it is called Śakradevendra, which is translated here as "The Lord of Gods.
This means he is able to act as the sovereign of the Heaven of the Thirty-three. In the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, there was a bhikṣu who asked the Buddha: "What..."
Therefore, he is named Śakra Devānām Indra. Answer: When he was formerly a human being, he practiced sudden and complete giving and was capable of acting as a sovereign;
thus he is named Śakra Devānām Indra. His palace is named Vaijayanta (the Victorious Palace), which is the second heaven of the desire realm, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Because he cultivated the ten wholesome paths of action in their superior degree, he attained birth therein. Thus it is said that Bodhisattvas on the Stainless Ground (Vimalā-bhūmi) [attain this].
Through the practice of meritorious deeds, one frequently becomes a King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; for this reason, World-Honored One, you have taught the Ten Abodes in this second stage.
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s progressive cultivation according to the stages, one proceeds from the shallow to the deep, taking Subtle Enlightenment (Miao-jue) as the ultimate fruit.
Yet, at the outset, one must take the Ten Faiths (Shi-xin) as the precursor. Thus, Subtle Enlightenment enters through faith; once entered, [one attains it].

One is able to abide [in these stages]. As for the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*): first, the abiding of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*); second, the abiding of purifying the ground (*viśuddhibhūmiviśodhanavihāra*); third, the abiding of cultivation (*caryāpratipattiviḥāra*); fourth, the abiding of noble birth (*janmakulavihāra*);

fifth, the abiding of the perfection of skillful means (*upāyasaṃbhāravihāra*); sixth, the abiding of the correct mind (*samyakcittavihāra*); seventh, the abiding of non-retrogression (*avinivartanīyavihāra*); eighth, the abiding of youthful truth (*kumārabhūtavihāra*);

ninth, the abiding of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputravihāra*); and tenth, the abiding of consecration (*abhiṣekavihāra*). These refer to abiding in the stage of faith in the Dharma and cultivating it oneself.

Because it involves the realization of severance, these ten abodes are taught so that Bodhisattvas who have already entered the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā), such as the celestial kings, may enter the Dharma-gate of the perfect ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"At that time, by the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual authority, throughout all worlds in the ten directions, in each of the four continents, within Jambudvīpa, they all saw the Tathāgata seated..."

Beneath each tree, there was a bodhisattva who, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, expounded the Dharma; none of them failed to feel as though they were constantly in the presence of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, without leaving the foot of any of the Bodhi trees, ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru and proceeded toward the palace of Śakra.
Each of the other bodhisattvas likewise ascended individually in this same manner. (Commentary)
It is said: The Tathāgata does not move from the Bodhi tree, yet he ascends to the Śakra Heaven; his essence and function are without fixed direction, responding to the desires of sentient beings.
This is like the single moon over a clear river observed by three boats: one boat remains stationary while two boats drift south and north.

To the one drifting south, the moon appears to follow it for a thousand li; to the one drifting north, the moon appears to follow it for a thousand li; yet to the stationary boat, the moon remains as it is.

It does not shift; this is what is meant by "this moon. Without leaving the middle of the stream, it appears in both the north and south. The manifestation of the Tathāgata may be understood through this analogy:
the function of the essence is universally pervasive, yet its coming and going depend on conditions; the Buddha is neither moving nor still.
It is unmoving yet pervasive, responding to the capacities of sentient beings. Thus, a sutra says: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, universally appearing before all multitudes of beings;
responding to conditions and meeting with stimuli, there is nowhere it does not reach, yet it ever remains upon this seat of Bodhi.
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not depart from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet he brings universal benefit to all living beings. △ Third Section.
Again, he rose from his seat and went to the Yāma Heaven, where he preached the Ten Practices.
As for the Yāma Heaven, in Sanskrit it is called Yāma, also known as Nyama; here it is translated as "Time-Portion" (Shifen). This means that there is happiness at every moment.
It does not rely on the light of the sun or moon; rather, day and night are distinguished solely by the opening and closing of lotus flowers. This is so.
This is the third heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This heaven dwells supported by space, and its palaces are called "Jeweled Halls" (*ratnabhavana*).
One is born there by practicing the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) of the superior grade and concurrently attaining the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Therefore, Bodhisattvas on the Radiant Stage (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), through their cultivation of meritorious practices, frequently become Kings of the Yama Heaven (*yāma-devendra*), occupying this celestial station as a provisional state. Thus, in the world...

Venerable One, the third [section] herein explains the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*). Following the previous ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), one’s cultivation has reached fulfillment and one has already become a child of the Buddha;
having personally attained one's own benefit, the practice of benefiting others has not yet been perfected.

Therefore, one extensively performs acts of great benefit, acting in accordance with sentient beings to cause them to rejoice. However, as these practices vary in depth and subtlety, they are established as ten kinds. First:
1. The practice of joy; 2. The practice of benefiting others; 3. The practice of freedom from malice and resentment; 4. The practice of inexhaustibility; 5.

The practice of freedom from delusion and confusion; 6. The practice of excellent manifestation; 7. The practice of non-attachment; 8. The practice of reverence; 9. The practice of wholesome dharmas; 10.
The practice of reality—namely, the practice of teaching and transforming others for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. These ten practices are called the Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices.
This is for the purpose of enabling the celestial kings of Bodhisattvas who have already entered the Ten Abodes to attain entry into the Dharma-gate of the Perfect Ten Practices.
△ Fourth Section: Again rising from his seat, he proceeded to the fourth heaven and expounded the Ten Transferences.
The fourth heaven is the Tuṣita Heaven of the desire realm. In Sanskrit it is called Tuṣita;

here it is translated as "Contentment" (Zhi-zu), meaning that its inhabitants know contentment regarding the five sensual desires. This heaven dwells supported by space, and the practices cultivated there are the same as those previously described.
Within it is an inner courtyard, the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas in their last birth before Buddhahood, also known as the abode of Bodhisattvas in their final body.
Therefore, Bodhisattvas on the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi), while performing their spiritual practices, often manifest as the King of Tuṣita Heaven;

they are able to eliminate the view of a self in sentient beings and contemplate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), which is equivalent to the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) in the first fruit. For this reason:
World-Honored One, the fourth [chapter] here explains the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). "Dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*) means turning back and directing toward.

That is to say, it refers to giving rise to the mind of great compassion in order to rescue and deliver sentient beings. Furthermore, it involves turning the merit of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and directing it toward three points:

first, the precious limit of true suchness (*tathatā-ratna-koṭi*), which is that which is realized; second, unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*), which is that which is sought; and third, the one...

All sentient beings are those to be saved. By means of the mind that is capable of turning [merit] and the virtuous deeds to be turned, one directs them toward all classes of beings so that they may equally enter the Dharma-realm.
This is the dedication of saving all sentient beings while remaining free from the conceptualization of "sentient beings."
2. The dedication of non-destruction; 3. The dedication equal to all Buddhas; 4. The dedication reaching all places; 5.
The dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit; 6. The dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality; 7.
The dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings; 8. The dedication of the mark of *tathatā*; 9. The dedication of neither bondage nor liberation.
The Dedication of Liberation. The Ten Infinite Dedications of the Ten Dharma Realms.
These ten dedications are taught so that the celestial kings of bodhisattvas who have already entered the ten practices may attain entry into the dharma-gate of the perfect ten dedications.
△ Fifth Section.
He rose again from his seat and went to the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), where he taught the ten dhyānas.
The Heaven of Delighting in Emanations is the fifth heaven of the Desire Realm; it is so called because its inhabitants delight in the five objects of desire that they themselves emanate.

Thus, Bodhisattvas on the Ground of Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā), through their cultivation of meritorious practices, frequently become Kings of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, taking this as a provisional station.
The vehicle of the Arhats: once their practice of contemplating the Four Truths is completed, they are identical to those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) who have attained the four fruits.

Therefore, World-Honored One, at this fifth stage, you teach the ten gates of dhyāna-concentration so that the great Bodhisattvas and celestial kings who have already entered the stage of the ten dedications may attain perfect knowledge of the dhyānas of all Buddhas and perfectly enter the [realms] of all Buddhas.
The *kṣetra* is the realm of the perfectly realized *dharmakāya*. The ten meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are also called the ten great *samādhis*.
Only the great bodhisattvas are able to skillfully enter them. Upon entering these *samādhis*, they attain the power of the *dharmadhātu*, which is inexhaustible;
they attain the rank of Dharma King with immeasurable sovereignty; they are born into the family of the Tathāgata; and they manifest all manner of vast [transformations].
The supernormal powers: first, the samādhi of universal light; second, the samādhi of wondrous light; third, the samādhi of sequentially visiting all buddha-lands;
fourth, the samādhi of the practice of the pure profound mind; fifth, the samādhi of knowing the treasury of past adornments;
sixth, the samādhi of the treasury of the radiance of wisdom; seventh, the samādhi of thoroughly knowing the buddha-adornments of all worlds.
The third is the Samādhi of the Differentiated Bodies of Sentient Beings; the ninth is the Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharma-realm;

and the tenth is the Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel. These are detailed in the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. However, the *Avataṃsaka* was composed after the [Daśabhūmika] Sūtra.

This refers to what other sutras state: that when the practices of the three stages of worthiness are fulfilled, one cultivates the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*) before ascending to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
△ Sixth location:
He again rose from his seat and went to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), where he preached the ten stages.

The Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) is the highest heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Its palace is named the Treasury of Maṇi Jewels (*maṇiratnagarbha*).

There are two types of this heaven: first, those who exclusively cultivate the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*), relying on the transformations produced by others to achieve their own pleasure; these are the Heaven of the Māra King (*mārarāja*).

Second, those who correctly cultivate the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions and additionally practice the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), relying upon which they attain [this state].

Accomplished. They naturally experience bliss. Therefore, when Bodhisattvas on the Stage of Presence (Abhimukhī-bhūmi) cultivate their practices, they frequently become Kings of the Heaven of Mastery over Others’ Emanations (Vaśavartin), presiding over the Desire Realm.

They rely upon the Vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas; that is to say, these Bodhisattvas cultivate the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, which is identical to that of the Pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason, World-Honored One, the sixth [stage] explains the Dharma-gate of the ten stages at this point.

This is for the sake of enabling the celestial kings who are Bodhisattvas already entered into the ten concentrations to attain the dharma-gate of the perfect realization of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The "ten stages" refers to the positions realized by Bodhisattvas; they are like the great earth because all Buddha-dharmas arise in dependence upon them.
The *Ratnavyūha Sūtra* states: "The name 'stage' (*bhūmi*) means 'support,' meaning it supports all one million asaṃkhyeya [dharmas]."
These are the merits; they are also called "births," meaning that because they give birth to all causes and effects, they are named "grounds" (*bhūmi*).
They are: first, the Ground of Joy; second, the Ground of Purity; third, the Ground of Radiance; fourth, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom; fifth, the Ground Difficult to Conquer;

sixth, the Ground of Presence; seventh, the Ground of Far-Going; eighth, the Ground of Immovability; ninth, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence; tenth, the Ground of the Dharma Cloud. That is to say:

Because wisdom and compassion arise equally as the support for the Buddha-nature, according to this sutra, it begins from the Ground of Equality and culminates in the Ground of Entry into the Buddha-realm.
The Dharma-gates taught in the six aforementioned locations are primarily intended for Bodhisattvas from the first ground up to the sixth;
they provisionally rely on the stages of humans, devas, and the two vehicles to simultaneously sever their delusions. Therefore, the World-Honored One...
World-Honored One, herein, within these six locations, you have expounded the Dharma-gate of the ten stages of faith arising up to the ten bhūmis,
so as to cause those ordinary beings, devas, humans, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas to turn toward the Mahāyāna and realize the ten bhūmis. Below,

you speak of the "Golden Patience and Vows," whereby bodhisattvas of the seventh, eighth, and ninth bhūmis take their stations within the One Vehicle to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, in order to—

Attaining mastery over the arousal [of activity], one spontaneously manifests bodies and preaches the Dharma, causing the permanent severance of the two innate attachments to self and dharmas, as well as the ignorance of the arising-characteristic.
Thus, one enters the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous enlightenment fruit. △ Seventh Section.
Furthermore, one reaches another dhyāna where the ten vajras are taught.
Regarding "furthermore reaching another dhyāna": this refers to the first dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha-bhūmi*).

This means that because these devas have already abandoned the desires and evils of the lower realms and rejoice in the sublime meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they correspond to the merit of the Bodhisattva on the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*) in their practice.
He practices and frequently becomes a Heavenly King of the First Dhyāna. Relying on the Bodhisattva Vehicle, he gathers and transforms sentient beings through the Dharma-gate of his own realization.
For this reason, World-Honored One, at this seventh stage, ten adamantine qualities are taught:
namely, that the Bodhisattva’s vow-mind is firm and immovable like a vajra; first, awakening to all dharmas in a single moment; second, bringing sentient beings to parinirvāṇa; third...
1. Adorning the world; 2. dedicating the four roots of goodness; 3. making offerings to all Buddhas; 4. realizing all dharmas in reality;
5. extensively practicing patience; 6. practicing transformation for a long duration; 7. fulfilling one’s own practice; 8. fulfilling the vows of others.
According to this present sutra, these are called the ten minds of faith and so forth, which are termed the "ten vajras" in order to cause those who have already ascended...
The Bodhisattva Heavenly King of the Seventh Ground attains the realization of the Vajra Contemplation Wisdom and enters the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment.
△ Eighth Section.
Again, proceeding to the Second Dhyāna, he expounds the Ten Patiences.
"Furthermore, as for 'reaching the second dhyāna': this refers to the second dhyāna of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), the stage of joy and bliss born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

It means that these devas have already departed from the joy of the first dhyāna; with their minds gathered in concentration, they are serene and tranquil, giving rise to superior meditative absorption.

Prior to the seventh ground, one has not yet departed from conditioned activity (*abhisamskāra*); only upon ascending to the eighth ground is one designated as 'Immovable' (*acala*). Therefore, it is called the Immovable Ground."
Bodhisattvas who cultivate merit frequently become kings of the Second Dhyāna Heaven, presiding over a small chiliocosm.

Relying on the stage of the One Vehicle, they preach the dharma-gate of self-realization to transform sentient beings. For this reason, World-Honored One, at this eighth stage, you speak of the ten kinds of patience (*kṣānti*).
Patience here refers to *anurakṣaṇā-kṣānti* (patience as endurance), meaning that the bodhisattva severs the delusion of ignorance and realizes the [unconditioned].

Having thoroughly realized that all phenomena are originally quiescent and extinguished, one thus perceives forms and hears sounds as being like illusions and transformations, giving rise to no deluded thoughts or discriminations.

Having attained this patience (*kṣānti*), one reaches the stage of unimpeded patience (*anāvaraṇa-kṣānti-bhūmi*) of all Bodhisattvas and realizes all Buddha-dharmas, which are unimpeded and inexhaustible; this is the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
This is that which is realized when the Bodhisattva’s final mind has severed all subtle ignorance: first, the patience of a single sound; second, the patience of compliance;
third, the patience of the non-arising of phenomena; fourth, the patience of being like an illusion; fifth, the patience of being like a flame; sixth, the patience of being like a dream.
7. The patience like an echo; 8. The patience like a shadow; 9. The patience like a transformation; 10. The patience like space.

These ten patiences are taught so that those who have already attained the true patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)—the Bodhisattva Heavenly Kings—may practice the Dharma-gate of the ten patiences and enter the ocean of the fruit of Sublime Enlightenment. △ Ninth Section.
Furthermore, he proceeds to the third dhyāna and speaks of the ten vows.
Regarding "further proceeding to the third dhyāna": this refers to the stage of sublime bliss free from joy within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

Having already transcended the agitation of joyful exultation found in the first and second dhyānas, these devas enter meditative absorption in a state of total stillness and attain a superior, wondrous bliss.

Therefore, Bodhisattvas on the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (Sādhumatī-bhūmi) cultivate meritorious virtues and frequently become Kings of the Heaven of the Three Dhyānas, presiding over a medium chiliocosm.
Abiding in the position of the One Vehicle, they expound and reveal the Dharma-gates of their own realization for the sake of all sentient beings.
For this reason, World-Honored One, at this ninth stage, ten vows are taught. The first vow is to bring sentient beings to maturity without end.
1. May there be freedom from weariness. 2. May I vow to practice all virtues and purify all worlds. 3.
May I vow to serve the Tathāgatas, always generating reverence. 4. May I vow to uphold the True Dharma, not sparing even my own body or life.
5. May I vow to enter all Buddha-lands by means of wisdom-insight. 6. May I vow to be of one and the same essential nature as all bodhisattvas. 7. May I vow to enter the Tathāgata...
[He] entered the gate [of the Dharma], comprehending all phenomena. He made eight vows so that those who see him might give rise to faith and none fail to obtain benefit;

he made a ninth vow that his spiritual power might abide in the world for as many eons as there are in the future; and he made a tenth vow to fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra and purify the gateway to all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*).
By proclaiming these ten great vows, he caused that Deva-king Bodhisattva, who had already realized the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), [to attain further progress].
Furthermore, one attains the power of the ten great vows and enters the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous enlightenment-fruit.

The preceding nine locations explain the sequential progression (*xingbu*) within the context of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*); this final location explains the perfect interfusion within the context of sequential progression.
△ The Tenth Location.

Again, he proceeded to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara within the Fourth Dhyāna, where he expounded the Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground as taught by Vairocana Buddha in the Lotus-Pedestal Treasury World, the source of his own origin.

Furthermore, regarding "reaching the fourth dhyāna": this refers to the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the stage of purity through equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*).

Having already abandoned the joy (*prīti*) of the second dhyāna and the bliss (*sukha*) of the third dhyāna, the mind is free from aversion and attachment; it is equanimous in every thought-moment, pure and unmixed.
Abiding in this dhyāna, space is luminous and tranquil, and all phenomena manifest therein. Thus, [it corresponds to] the Bodhisattva stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
Sā. Having cultivated many merits, he frequently becomes the Heavenly King of the Four Dhyānas, presiding over the great trichiliocosm.
While his rank is entrusted to the Buddha-vehicle, he expounds the dharma-gate of self-realization for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and heavenly kings.
Maheśvara—here translated as "Great Power"—has three eyes and eight arms; holding a white whisk in his hands, he possesses great majestic power and is therefore also [referred to as such].
It is called "Great Sovereignty" because it attains the eight masteries (*aṣṭavaśitā*), wherein its desire, liberation, and radiance surpass all others,

and it dwells at the summit of the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*). Therefore, World-Honored One, in this tenth stage, you have suddenly expounded the chapter on the Dharma-gate of the forty stages of practice within the Mind-Ground,
so that those Bodhisattvas who have fully realized the ten stages may enter the ocean of the fruit of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
In the past, when the former Buddha was in the fourth dhyāna, he taught various Dharma-gates such as the stages of abiding, practice, and realization (*sthiti-caryā-pratipatti*).

Now, at the very end, while in the fourth dhyāna, he teaches this Mind-Ground Dharma-gate. This means that originally, light was emitted from within the fourth dhyāna to initiate [the transmission], reaching as far as the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang-shijie*) where he received this Dharma; therefore, he now once again teaches this Mind-Ground Dharma within the fourth dhyāna.
He opened the gate and comforted them. This also demonstrates that all phenomena ultimately converge within the single mind to reach the ultimate pinnacle;
it is most honored and unsurpassed, for there is no phenomenon superior to the mind. Now, this fundamental source is a dharma that is unconditioned and formless.
It cannot be fathomed by the mind-consciousness of ordinary beings of the lower realms; only Buddhas and Buddhas can know it.
Furthermore, this fourth dhyāna is the ultimate summit of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). This palace of the Heavenly King lies above the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*).
There is no heaven higher than this; therefore, within the teachings of the Three Vehicles, this is established as the Pure Land where the Sambhogakāya Buddha resides.
The Secret Mantra (Guhyatantra) states that beyond the Five Pure Abodes lies the palace of Vairocana; it is this very place.
Furthermore, the palaces of Śakra and others are explained as being divisions of this Dharma of the Mind-Ground within the four dhyāna heavens.

In this section, the Dharma of the Mind-Ground is explained both collectively and individually. Explaining it individually signifies the sequential progression (*xingbu*), while explaining it collectively signifies perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*).
This means that although the stages of this Dharma of the Mind-Ground are differentiated, they all collectively lead to the ultimate fruit of Samantabhadra.

Furthermore, the explanation of the ten patiences (*kṣānti*), the ten vows (*praṇidhāna*), and the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground is intended to cause the severance of [delusions] at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
By eliminating ignorance regarding appearances, one enters the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous fruition of enlightenment. △ Fourth, the general conclusion for the remaining Buddhas:
The other thousands of billions of Śākyamunis are likewise thus; they are non-dual and without distinction, as explained in the "Chapter on the Worthy Kalpa."
As for the remaining thousands of billions of Śākyamunis, this seal—the teaching spoken by every Buddha—is identical.
That is to say, just as the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground taught by one Buddha upon a thousand-petaled lotus is thus, so it is with what is taught by the thousand Buddhas;
and just as what is taught by the thousand Buddhas is thus, so it is with what is taught by the hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas throughout the hundred billion worlds.

Since what has been explained is thus, the restatement of the teaching in this manner serves as an analogy for the fact that the Buddhas preaching the Dharma in thousands of billions of worlds do so in exactly the same way; hence it is said that there is neither duality nor distinction.

The above scriptural passage constitutes the concluding words at the end of the preceding chapter, yet the ancient commentaries place them at the beginning of the following chapter to manifest the fundamental and manifested traces of Śākyamuni, thereby enabling people to...

[This matter] is as clear as looking at the back of one's hand; therefore, it remains as it was originally. The phrase from the "Chapter on the Worthy Kalpa" (Bhadra-kalpa-parivarta) is extracted from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (Daben jing);
it is a statement by Master Kumārajīva citing scriptural evidence, not the word of the Buddha. Next, specifically revealing that this world has one Buddha [and two bodhisattvas].

This section has two parts: first, the formal explanation of how the mind-ground benefits sentient beings; second, the subsequent discourse on the precepts and laws for gathering and transforming living beings. Within the first part, there are again two sub-sections.

First, the section on the horizontal pointing; second, the detailed account of the vertical progression and its reciprocal relations. Within the first [section], there are four parts: first, the subduing of Māra in the heavens;

second, the attainment of enlightenment among humans; third, the turning of the Dharma wheel in thirty locations; fourth, the teaching of the realms through analogies. Now, the first [part]: the subduing of Māra in the heavens.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, having first appeared in the Lotus-Pedestal Treasury World and come from the east to enter the celestial palace,
had finished preaching the *Sūtra on the Demon’s Conversion*.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha refers to the moment when the function arises from the essence.
Previously, the thousand Buddhas, as well as the thousands of billions of Śākyas, were described as preaching the Dharma within thousands of billions of worlds;
now, this single Śākyamuni within one solar system is described—his birthplace, his parents' names, and his renunciation and cultivation.

This is the general outline of the Way: attaining Buddhahood and benefiting sentient beings. "From the initial manifestation in the Lotus-womb World" refers to the events from the emission of light that thoroughly illuminates the Four Dhyāna Heavens at the beginning of the upper fascicle, up until the lifting and receiving [of the assembly] and their return.
The Flower Treasury (Huazang) is the place of origin; the celestial palace is the place of abiding. "Initial" refers to the rising from the seat, taking leave, and departing.

"Manifest" refers to the emanation of light and transformation-buddhas. As for "coming from the east and entering," this means that this world of one sun and moon is situated to the east within the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu). There are two meanings for "east":

first, the meaning of "vibrating," which signifies shaking down and subduing all evil māras; second, the meaning of "growing," which signifies initiating the precepts and virtues of sentient beings. However...

Having already grasped the mind through the Dharma-gate of entering the essence of the void-like flower-light samādhi (*ākāśa-puṣpa-prabhāsa-samādhi*), he returned to this land from within that very samādhi.
The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states: "Within all dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), there is one realm of retribution;
among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), whether mundane or supramundane, whether ordinary beings or sages, whether views and attachments or the laws of cause and effect."

There is no one outside the Dharma-realm except for the Buddha alone. Only after being outside the Dharma-realm does he again enter the treasury of the Dharma-realm to manifest, for the sake of sentient beings obscured by ignorance, the immeasurable distinctions in the retributions of all good and evil paths.
As for "within the celestial palace," whenever a Buddha appears in the world, he always first resides in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.
Having completed the transformation and instruction of the various devaputras, he then descended to be born in Jambudvīpa.

Regarding the *Māra-parivarta-sūtra*, the Sanskrit term is *māra*; in the Qin language, it means "killer. This refers to his constant desire to sever the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*) in human beings.
