The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: namely, the *skandha-māra*, because they give rise to all forms of grasping; the *kleśa-māra*, because they are perpetually defiling; and the *karma-māra*.

The māra of birth, because it creates obstacles; the māra of the mind, because it gives rise to arrogance; the māra of death, because it abandons the place of birth; the māra of the devas, because of self-indulgent pride;
the māra of roots of goodness, because of excessive grasping; the māra of samādhi, because of long-standing attachment to its flavor;
the māra of spiritual friends, because it gives rise to a mind of attachment; and the māra of the wisdom of bodhi-dharmas, because of the lack of desire to relinquish them. — *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*
It is said: Gain and offerings, honor, praise, negligence, stinginess, longing desire, anger and resentment, vexation, concealment, arrogance, and deceit—all these are Māra.
For this reason, the Tathāgata first subdued them and only then descended to be born [in this world].
This is because Tuṣita is free from Māra; the devaputras there constantly cultivate the samādhi of contentment. As for the Mahesvara Heaven...
The Royal Palace is located in the Heaven of the Fourth Dhyāna, at the pinnacle of the Realm of Form (Rūpadhātu). There are nine heavens in total within the Fourth Dhyāna;
the upper five heavens are all inhabited by noble Arhats who have attained the third fruit of the Non-returner (Anāgāmin).

At the summit of the Realm of Form is the palace of Vairocana, where the great Bodhisattvas constantly assemble. Furthermore, there is certainly no Māra present, nor is he found in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
Having preached the Dharma within the palace of Māra, King of the Gods, and having caused Māra to be transformed by his teaching, he then proceeded to Tuṣita;

or perhaps it was Māra himself who went to Tuṣita to receive transformation. The *Jizhu* (Collected Annotations) states: "Tuṣita is among the six heavens of the Desire Realm and the seven heavens of the Brahma World.
Because the Buddha always dwells in the middle path, the palaces of Māra are included therein. Furthermore, or...

For those of sharp faculties, he manifested the teaching of the Dharma separately; it was only after he had finished subduing Māra in the Heaven of the Fourth Dhyāna that he descended again to be born below.
This differs from what is seen by those of dull faculties, for whom the subduing of Māra occurs only upon reaching the foot of the tree.
△ Second, attaining enlightenment among humans.
I was born below in Jambudvīpa, in the kingdom of Kapilavastu. My mother’s name was Māyā and my father’s name was Śuddhodana;
my own name is Siddhārtha. At the age of seven I left the household life, and at thirty I attained the Way; I am called Śākyamuni Buddha.

Regarding "descending to be born": The *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds) states that the Bodhisattva Huiming, while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven for a full four thousand years, observed the sufferings of the lower realms and descended to be born in order to rescue and deliver them.

The *Dabei-en-jing* (Sutra of Great Gratitude) states that when a Tathāgata appears in the world, he does so necessarily for five purposes: first, to turn the wheel of Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings; second, to deliver [them]...
1. To repay the kindness of their parents from many lifetimes; 2. To establish those without faith upon the ground of faith; 3.
To cause those who have not yet resolved to attain Bodhicitta to do so; 4. To bestow upon them the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood in the present or the future;
5. For these five reasons, he appears in the world. Regarding Jambudvīpa, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: [The text continues with the citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.]

In three respects, this continent surpasses even the various heavens, let alone the other three continents: first, the ability to sever sexual desire; second, the power of mindfulness and recollection;
and third, the capacity for diligent effort. For these reasons, all Buddhas appear only in Jambudvīpa. Kāyila is also called Kapila, which means "yellow.
This refers to the fact that in ancient times, there was a yellow-haired *ṛṣi* who relied upon this place to cultivate the Way. Therefore, it is so named.
This is taken as its name. It is within the territory of Central India. There are twelve kingdoms in Central India in total.
Kānyakubja is located in the center of the land of Jambudvīpa. It is also called Vārāṇasī, which means "Abode of the Sage.
In the Sanskrit language it is Mahāmāyā, which means "Great Illusion," and is also called "Great Wisdom."
The Mother refers to her accomplishment of the bodhisattva’s liberation door of the wisdom-illusion of great vows;
by means of this great illusory artifice, she is eternally the mother of all Buddhas. As the sutra says:

when the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra descended from Tuṣita on the eighth day of the seventh month, those of limited capacity saw him riding a six-tusked white elephant, accompanied by immeasurable devas performing various [rites].
As for the arts and music, [the Bodhisattva] entered through the mother’s right side; his body was reflected outside as if he were dwelling within lapis lazuli.
Those of great capacity saw the Bodhisattva riding upon a sandalwood pavilion and the like while residing in the womb. The *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* states:
When Lady Māyā’s months of pregnancy were nearly complete, she desired to wander within the garden. She immediately raised her right hand and grasped a branch of an *aśoka* tree;
from her right side, the Prince was born. The Lord of Devas received him with his hands wrapped in celestial, exquisite garments.
The celestial deities held a golden-handled parasol; the various devas, nāgas, and spirits scattered fragrant flowers and played musical instruments.
The great earth shook in six ways. As the *Āgama* Sūtras state: when the Bodhisattva was born, he emerged from the right side [of his mother], mindful and undisturbed.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mother stood holding a tree branch, neither sitting nor lying down. The Four Heavenly Kings held fragrant [substances] in their hands.
The water stood before his mother and spoke, saying: "Indeed, O Celestial Mother, a noble son has been born today; do not harbor grief or distress.
As soon as the Prince descended to the earth, he walked seven paces and, raising his hand, declared: "In all that is above heaven and all that is below heaven, I alone am the most honored."
In Sanskrit, *Śuddhodana* means "Pure Rice" (*Net-ban*); the current term "White Pure" (*Bai-jing*) conveys the same meaning.
*Siddhārtha* means "Sudden Auspiciousness," referring to the fact that on the Buddha’s birthday, the eighth day of the fourth month, all manner of auspicious omens appeared instantaneously;
it is also called "Accomplishment of All Meanings. This was his childhood name. At the age of seven, he left the household life.

This refers to his seven years as a renunciant. It means that at the age of nineteen, on the fifteenth day of the second month, at midnight, he mounted a celestial horse and leaped over the city wall.
He entered the mountains and first studied the *ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi* (the concentration of the sphere of nothingness), attaining realization before long;

yet he knew it was not the ultimate goal. Next, he studied the *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi* (the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception), again attaining realization before long, and knowing that this too was not the ultimate goal.
Subsequently, he traveled through various kingdoms for five years; as these were not matters pertaining to his renunciation, they are not mentioned here.

Furthermore, in order to subdue the various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas), he manifested six years of ascetic practice. Thus, it was only upon reaching the age of thirty that he attained perfect enlightenment.
It is therefore clear that his seven years of renunciation are well-established. As for why I am called Śākyamuni Buddha, this reveals both my manifest traces and my original name.
Each is distinct. It is by virtue of the prediction received from ancient Buddhas that he attained this sacred title. As the sutra states:
"In the past, when the Tathāgata was a potter, he made offerings to the ancient Śākya Buddha and personally made a sincere vow, wishing to share the same name and clan as that Buddha.
Prior to this point, all were of the nature of empty space; these matters pertain to the state within the Flower-Light Samādhi.
Having manifested the attainment of Buddhahood, it is said that he has emerged from samādhi. △ Regarding the turning of the Dharma at thirty locations:

from sitting upon the Vajra-flower Radiance King Throne at the Site of Enlightenment (Śītavana), up to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara—in these successive ten dwelling places, the teachings were expounded.

The "Site of Quiescent Extinction" (*śānti-maṇḍala*) is the place where the Tathāgata attained the Way. "Quiescence" (*śānti*) refers to the quiescence of the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra-kleśa*).

"Extinction" (*nirodha*) refers to the extinction of the two kinds of birth-and-death (*dvividha-jāti-maraṇa*). "Way" (*mārga*) is *bodhi*; "site" (*maṇḍala*) is the location; and *bodhi* is wisdom (*jñāna*).

Quiescence is the principle. By sitting in this place, one realizes the principle of quiescence through the wisdom of bodhi; thus, the great afflictions of birth and death are forever severed, and all Buddha-dharmas manifest before one.
Therefore, it is called the *śānti-maṇḍala* (the site of quiescence), and is also named the *bodhi-maṇḍala* (the site of enlightenment).
It is where one sits upon the Vajra-flower-light-king throne, extending even to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara.
This clearly explains the place where the Dharma is preached. Because his mind is firm and dwells in immovability, it is called "Vajra" (Diamond).

Because the jewel of the mind is like a lotus and its precious radiance emits flames, it is called "Flower Light. Because he arises from the essence to manifest function with sovereign non-obstruction, he is named "King.
Because he sustains and maintains all Buddha-dharmas, it is called a "Seat. Furthermore, the thousand Buddhas...
He preached the Dharma, all of which issued from the Flower Radiance Samādhi (*Puṣpaprabhāsa-samādhi*). While he sat upon this seat, the great earth shook, yet this seat remained unmoved.
This signifies that the essence of the precepts of the mind-ground of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is like a vajra:
it can destroy all afflictions (*kleśa*) and cannot be moved by afflictions; therefore, it is named the "Flower Radiance King Seat. It precedes the "Thousand Radiance King [Seat]."
This is the seat of realization; this is the seat of preaching the Dharma.

Having sat upon this seat, he preached the Dharma in succession from the Hall of Sublime Light up to the fourth dhyāna. Within this, there are ten dwelling places where ten types of Dharma gates were taught;
therefore, it is said: "The successive teachings given at the ten dwelling places. △ Fourth, the teaching by means of analogies.
At that time, the Buddha observed the net-bannered staff of the Great Brahma Kings and, on that account, spoke of immeasurable worlds. He said that they are like the mesh of a net;
each and every world is distinct from the others, differing in infinite ways. The gateways of the Buddha’s teaching are likewise so.
This is so. The passage beginning with "The Buddha observed" and so forth is the point where the main body (*śarīra*) of this sutra is initiated.

According to the meaning of the preceding text, [the Buddha] came from the east of the Terrace Storehouse (*tāizàng*), entered the Heaven of the Fourth Dhyāna, observed the Brahma-net, and preached the *Māhavaineya-sūtra* and other such scriptures.
The Flower-Light Samādhi is contemplation. Even when descending eight thousand times, he does not depart from this samādhi; it is merely that his entering and emerging differ.
Mahābrahmā—here translated as "Pure Body" or "Pure Conduct"—the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "Brahmā" is a Western term; here it means "Free from Desire.
He is the lord of the Sahā world, dwelling in the intermediate stage of the first dhyāna, presiding over and encompassing those above.

Because they have descended from the lower realms, they are called "Great. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states: "Having abandoned the fetters of the lower stages and ascended to the Form Realm, they are thus called 'Free from Desire.

As for the mention of the 'various Great Brahmā Kings,' this refers to the fact that within this Sahā world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds, there are ten billion Great Brahmā Kings;
when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, they all assemble together, and therefore [the text] mentions them collectively."
Furthermore, that which is being discussed here is not the Great Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna Heaven, but rather the Great Maheśvara Brahmā King of the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven.
As for the "net-banner," its full name is Indra-jāla; this is translated here as "celestial red pearl.
At that time, the Buddha was in the palace of the Great Maheśvara Brahmā King and beheld it.
This jewel banner is composed of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of maṇi jewels.
Each individual jewel differs in its radiance, color, and patterns; they reflect one another, interpenetrate one another, and do not obstruct one another.
Such is the jewel banner of a single Great Brahmā King, and so it is for the jewel banners of all the Great Brahmā Kings.
It is all thus. Therefore, the Buddha, based on this, spoke of immeasurable worlds, which are like the meshes of a net;
each and every world is distinct from the others. The Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma-gates is likewise so.

As for what is called "immeasurable worlds," they extend vertically through the three periods of time without end and horizontally throughout the ten directions without interval. Thus, the worlds of the ten directions are established...
The teachings established by all Buddhas are immeasurable; the practices and realizations devised for Bodhisattvas are immeasurable;

and the variations in their cultivation and attainment are immeasurable. Nevertheless, the world is the sentient being who is to be reached, while the Buddhist teachings are the Dharma that reaches them.

By observing the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, one sees its myriad nets layered upon one another; through this, one comes to know that worlds and teaching-gates are distinct and immeasurable. Thus, [the sūtra contains] hundreds and thousands...
Within billions of lands, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis proclaiming and transforming beings. △ Next, to detail the vertical progression of the exchange:
I have now come to this world eight thousand times for the sake of this Sahā world, sitting upon the Vajra-flower Radiance.
From the royal throne up to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, he has briefly expounded the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for the entire great assembly.
"Eight thousand times" means that one complete cycle of going and returning is called a "turn. This refers to the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood and his saving of beings.

Regarding the matter of birth, there are approximately eight thousand cycles of coming and going. This represents the transverse opening of the fundamental and the trace—the one thousand times ten billion worlds—revealing the distance between the fundamental and the trace.

When the *Tāizàng* (Garbha) realm subsides and emerges in Jambudvīpa, passing through eight thousand returns, this represents the vertical opening of the fundamental and the trace, revealing the distance between them.
These eight thousand cycles in the Sahā world serve to open the ground of the mind; is this not the number that reveals and manifests [the truth]?
Is it through the accumulation of the factors of enlightenment? However, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is, in essence, as profound and empty as space;

it is fundamentally free from the characteristics of subject and object, arising and ceasing, coming and going, or movement and stillness. Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata comes from nowhere."

Furthermore, there is nowhere to which it goes. As for the statement that [the Buddha] returns eight thousand times, this is the great function of the Tathāgata’s compassion and wisdom in benefiting sentient beings.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata has no body; for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests a body.
This is precisely the Dharmakāya: unborn, yet not that which does not arise; signless, yet not that which does not manifest signs. By means of the Nirmāṇakāya, the Dharma...
The body has no distinct essence. Due to the karmic conditions of sentient beings, they perceive the Buddha appearing in the world;

when those conditions are exhausted, they perceive the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. It is like the sun shrouded by clouds: the ignorant and deluded think the sun has vanished, yet when the clouds part and the sun appears, they say it has returned once more.
Sentient beings are likewise: when their obstructions are heavy, they do not behold the sun of the Buddha; when their karma is light, they see the Buddha appear in the world. In reality...

Due to the karmic resonance and capacity of sentient beings, it is not that the Buddha comes or goes; his appearance in the world and his passing into parinirvāṇa are nothing other than for the benefit of sentient beings.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, act in order to cause sentient beings to give rise to joy."
He appears in the world; desiring to cause sentient beings to give rise to longing and devotion, he manifests *nirvāṇa*. This is it.
If one relies on other sutras, the number "hundreds of thousands" is merely spoken according to worldly convention as a great number. Furthermore, as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Although I am here in Jambudvīpa, I repeatedly manifest entry into *nirvāṇa*, yet in reality, I do not [pass away]."
Nirvāṇa. Yet all sentient beings believe that the Tathāgata has truly entered extinction; however, the nature of the Tathāgata does not actually perish.
Therefore, you should know that it is an eternally abiding dharma and an immutable dharma. Great Nirvāṇa is precisely the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
All sentient beings say, "I have only now attained Buddhahood," yet I have already [attained it]...

Throughout immeasurable kalpas, he has already accomplished what was to be done; yet, in accordance with worldly conventions, he again manifests in Jambudvīpa, leaving the household life and attaining enlightenment. Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says:

"In truth, since I attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas. I have always remained here in this Sahā world, preaching the Dharma."
He teaches and transforms beings, and in other places as well—through hundreds of thousands of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya lands—he guides and benefits sentient beings.
My lifespan is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas; I abide eternally and do not perish. It is not that I have truly entered parinirvāṇa, yet I proclaim that I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
This is because the Tathāgata uses skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings. [Question: As for this...

Question: Since you have already attained Buddhahood long ago, why do you not simply manifest your body and preach the Dharma directly, rather than taking birth through parents and leaving home to practice the Way?

Answer: If it were not so, ordinary people, lacking wisdom, would suspect that the Buddha is a conjured being, or they might claim that one can only attain the Way by having no parents, wife, or children, and thus would be unwilling to emulate and cultivate themselves. This is as follows:
This manifestation is the wondrous function of employing skillful means to benefit sentient beings. "Saha" (娑婆) is translated here as "Capable of Endurance" (能忍) or "Able to Withstand" (堪忍).

This refers to the fact that the sentient beings of this world are able to endure and tolerate the suffering of the three poisons—greed, hatred, and delusion—as well as all other afflictions, yet they do not give rise to weariness or renunciation in order to seek liberation. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (乃至): it refers to the ten...
He teaches the Dharma in eight locations. First, he mentions the Vajrāsana; later, he mentions the palace of the Heavenly Kings; and the remaining eight locations are included therein.
Regarding "all the great assemblies therein," this refers to the great assemblies of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*).

Although he has briefly explained the *Cittabhūmi* (the Ground of Mind) from among the hundreds of thousands of *Gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* Dharma-gates as being no larger than the tip of a hair, nevertheless—

Thereafter, he expounded the precepts of heavy and light offenses for the sake of ordinary beings on earth. △ Second, the turning of the teaching of the precepts to gather in sentient beings has two parts.
First, identifying the source of the precepts.

Furthermore, descending from the Palace of the Heavenly King to Jambudvīpa, beneath the Bodhi tree, for the sake of all sentient beings upon this earth—those ordinary people shrouded in the darkness of ignorance—I shall speak of that one precept which I, as the original Buddha Vairocana, constantly recited at the moment of first generating the bodhicitta within the Mind-Ground:
the Radiant Vajra Jewel Precept, which is the source of all Buddhas. One...
The fundamental source of all bodhisattvas and the seed of buddha-nature.

Regarding the phrase "returning from the Palace of the Heavenly King": "returning" (fù) means descending again after having ascended. This refers to the Ground of Mixed Dwelling among the Five Destinies on earth.
As for "all sentient beings," this encompasses the nine realms and eight classes of beings, as well as the fourfold assembly, with the single exception of the Buddha himself.
Previously, it was taught for the assembly of celestial bodhisattvas; now, it is taught for ordinary beings on the ground.
To practice improper dharmas and falsely give rise to deviant views is called "delusion. The afflictions of ignorance close off the ground of one's own mind, and thus it is called "darkness.
Out of compassion for these beings, the Tathāgata has transmitted the Samantabhadra’s correct precepts eight thousand times throughout the three periods of time.

The Buddhas all first receive these precepts as the primary cause for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that from the moment of first generating the bodhicitta, they constantly recite this one precept.
Furthermore, this single precept is the Radiant Vajra Jewel Precept, which constitutes the essence of the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts.
Moreover, after the ten assemblies have concluded, the reason the Chapter on Precepts is taught subsequently is because...

These stages of dwelling, practice, and orientation toward the grounds and so forth—though all these subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates are inherently possessed by every person—have long been obscured by delusion, such that one remains seated upon the ground of ignorance; how, then, could one gain entry? Nevertheless, it is not difficult to enter them.
There is indeed a skillful means; I fear only that you are unwilling to resolve your mind [to enlightenment]. Take, for example, Vairocana Buddha:

he was originally an ordinary person shrouded in ignorance, yet as soon as he first resolved his mind, he received the precepts. After receiving the precepts, he constantly recited and practiced them.
It is by this alone that he was able to realize the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground, proceeding directly until his attainment of Buddhahood. It is all due to this one thing.
Precepts are the most supreme causal condition. Yet, those who are mired in delusion and lack awakening are called ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).

That Śamatha is the root is a traditional teaching; it correctly reveals that Śākyamuni is the manifested trace. Regarding the "mind-ground" (*cittabhūmi*), there are two aspects: first, the mind-ground of the original source, which is the nature (*prakṛti*);
second, the thirty minds and ten stages, which are cultivation (*bhāvanā*). "To develop" (*fa*) means to open and unfold, referring to initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*).
This refers to when Śākyamuni, during his time as an ordinary person shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, first dispelled delusion and gave rise to the bodhicitta;
at that time, he constantly recited this one precept, the "Luminous Vajra Jewel Precept," which is primordial enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). This has two meanings.
First, explained in terms of phenomena: because this precept can shatter the darkness of ignorance, it is called "luminous"; because it can crush afflictions (*kleśa*), it is named "vajra."

Because it is fully endowed with immeasurable merit and the wealth of the Dharma, it is said to be "like a treasure. Furthermore, because this precept is supreme and foremost, it is called "the one precept.
Since all Buddhas of the three periods of time first receive this precept as their primary cause, it is called "the initial arousal of the mind.
Next, to clarify it through principle: this precept illuminates all phenomena and is thus named "light," and it encompasses all that is wholesome.

The precepts (*śīla*). Their essence is untainted (*anāsrava*), and thus they are called "vajra. The *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint precepts) provide relief to sentient beings and are utilized for their benefit;

thus they are called "jewels. The *upapatti-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precepts for sustaining life) [function similarly]. Regarding the *saṃvara-śīla*, it means that there is no evil that is not ceased. Through the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), one shall realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Now, non-action is itself upholding, while action constitutes a transgression. Regarding the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precepts for gathering wholesome dharmas), it means that there is no wholesome [dharma]...
If one does not cultivate wisdom-virtue, one shall realize the fruit of the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha; yet, to act [in accordance with it] is to maintain [the precept], while to refrain is to transgress.

Regarding the precept of gathering sentient beings (*saṃgraha-śīla*), this means that there is no being who is not delivered; as for the virtue of grace, one shall realize the fruit of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha;
yet, to act is to maintain, while to refrain is to transgress. The ocean of the *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) of all Buddhas takes these precepts as its source. Thus, the Bodhisattva...
Among the myriad practices of the six perfections, this precept is the foundation.
Not only is Samantabhadra accomplished through these precepts, but all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time are likewise accomplished without exception by means of them.
All Bodhisattvas also cultivate and arise without exception by taking these precepts as their foundation. Therefore, it is said: "This is the root of all Buddhas."

"Source": This refers to the source of all bodhisattvas. If one practices apart from this precept, then the dharma-gates of the thirty minds and the ten stages will not be accomplished; even all the merits of the Buddha-stage will fail to arise.
Regarding the "seed of Buddha-nature": the precept is the seed of Buddha-nature. This means that although Buddha-nature is inherent...
The spiritual [nature] is universally complete; it is produced by means of the precepts and may thus be called the "seed. This is as it is said: "The Buddha-nature arises from conditions.
Therefore, this root of the precepts takes the primary cause of Buddha-nature (*zhengyin foxing*) as its seed. Now, the primary cause of Buddha-nature is the nature itself.

This means that all sentient beings are fully endowed with this nature; yet, by turning their backs on awakening and aligning themselves with the sensory dust, they are constantly obscured and obstructed by afflictions.
If they cultivate in accordance with the Buddha-nature, they will be able to transcend birth and death and awaken into entry into nirvana.
This is to realize the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground together with the Buddha. Thus, the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:

"Because one knows the Dharma and has faith that it is free from defilement, one practices the *śīla-pāramitā* in accordance [with that truth], thereby taking the Buddha-nature as the object of perception.
Furthermore, there is nothing that does not take this precept as its seed for cultivation. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Although all sentient beings possess the Buddha..."
The Buddha-nature must first be realized through the observance of the precepts; by seeing the Buddha-nature, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
△ Second, the explanation of the benefit of the Dharma.
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. All consciousness, form, and mind—whether they be emotional or cognitive—all enter into the precepts of Buddha-nature.
Because there is always a cause for each and every instance, there is always the eternally abiding Dharma-body for each and every instance.
The statement that "all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature" means that all sentient beings shall eventually become Buddhas.
This single phrase is most intimate and essential; it constitutes the orthodox core of this great scripture. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"Within the bodies of all sentient beings, the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata are fully present. However, because of [ignorance]..."
At the very first thought, one fails to awaken and gives rise to ignorance, forming a state of delusive darkness that acts as a self-imposed obstruction.
Therefore, by causing one to receive these true precepts, this self-imposed obstruction is removed and the Buddha-nature spontaneously manifests.

Because one sees that the Buddha-nature is impartial and pervades all phenomena—whether they be mind, consciousness, form, or heart; whether they be sentient or insentient—it encompasses everything without exception.
This is entry into the Buddha-nature precepts. All consciousness, form, and mind are fundamentally the substance of the One True Dharma-realm;
because they do not maintain True Suchness, they are given the names "mind," "consciousness," and "awareness. Although these names are divided into three, their substance is fundamentally non-dual.
Furthermore, "consciousness" (manas-vijñāna) is a secondary name for the "mind" (citta), referring to the sudden, deluded thoughts of ordinary beings.

The gathering and arising [of phenomena] is called "mind" (*citta*); next, the mental deliberation is called "thought" (*manas*); and finally, the discernment by the mind is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).

"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the substance of form, namely the physical body composed of the four great elements. "Sentiment" (*qing*) refers to deluded sentiment; it is an alternative name for the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).
That these sentiments and minds all enter into the Buddha-nature precepts means that they correctly reveal and manifest all forms and minds.
Sentient beings all possess Buddha-nature. Apart from this mind, there is no other Buddha-nature to be found;
therefore, it is said that the *ālaya-vijñāna* is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha*. To say here that these are "sentient" (*qing*) serves to distinguish them from the non-sentient (*wuqing*).
This refers to the mind; it is distinguished from being without mind. That which is insentient and without mind, such as wood or stone, is incapable of receiving the precepts.
Since one possesses Buddha-nature, one shall enter into the Buddha-nature precepts. Regarding the phrase "constantly abiding in the Dharma-body at every moment":
"at every moment" (dang-dang) means precisely and certainly. This refers to the wondrous nature of this ground of the mind.
The precepts arise entirely from the fundamental substance of the Buddha-nature; they are truly the eternal true cause. Furthermore, they reveal and manifest the Buddha-nature to adorn it;
they are certainly the eternally abiding wondrous fruit of the Dharma-body. Moreover, they point back to and verify the dharma of the precepts.
Furthermore, they are decisively and definitively called "the ever-present" (*changdang*), meaning they are constantly present and not something that occurs only occasionally.
It is neither sudden nor non-existent; it is eternally abiding. This distinguishes it from that which comes or goes. Precepts are the seeds of the Buddha-nature;
therefore, those who receive them possess the eternal, direct cause for attaining Buddhahood. They do not fall into false causes, but dwell forever in the pure Dharma-body, untainted by desire.
It is like gold extracted from ore, which never again becomes ore. The *Sutra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground* says: "Sentient beings are originally..."

The seeds of Bodhi all reside within the *ālayavijñāna*. If one encounters virtuous friends and gives rise to the Great Mind, practicing the three types of refinement and cultivating sublime conduct, one will forever sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), thereby realizing the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding body.
This is it. △ Third, exhortation to believe, accept, and uphold.
Thus, these ten *pratimokṣa* emerge in the world; they are the Dharma-precepts. They are to be reverently received and upheld by all sentient beings of the three periods of time.
Now, for the sake of this great assembly, I shall again expound the chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of Precepts.
These are the precepts of all sentient beings, pure by their original source and intrinsic nature.
"Thus" (iti) is a summary of the preceding text. "Ten" refers to the enumeration of the major items, which thereby encompasses the minor ones.

*Prātimokṣa* is translated here as "Guarantee of Liberation. This means that for one who receives these precepts, the Tathāgata guarantees that they will certainly attain liberation from ignorance, afflictions, delusions, and karma, and realize the pure Dharma-body; thus, it pertains to the causal stage.
That which can be maintained is called *pratimokṣa*. That which is attained upon reaching the fruit is called the pure *dharmakāya*.
Regarding its emergence from the world: this great precept of the mind-ground is difficult for the world to encounter; it has now emerged because a Tathāgata has appeared in the world.
You should give rise to joy and gratitude, and not treat it with negligence. This dharma-precept distinguishes itself from those of the two vehicles.
The *Prātimokṣa* is precisely the true Dharma precept for attaining Buddhahood. "Wearing it on the crown" refers to the utmost respect;
"receiving and upholding it" refers to firm adherence. Such being the seed of Buddhahood, one ought to respect and firmly uphold it.
It must not be forgotten for even a moment; therefore, it is said that all sentient beings of the three periods of time wear it upon their heads and uphold it.
"I shall now, for this great assembly" means "in the future. "To speak again" means to proclaim these precepts once more;

that is to say, having already explained them briefly above, they are now proclaimed a second time. Or, [it may mean] that previously [they were taught] for the sake of bodhisattvas and devas, and now...

Because it is for the sake of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is said to be "repeated. Nevertheless, since the precepts are the foundation for attaining the Way, they should not be weary of being proclaimed repeatedly.
Thus, the Tathāgata himself recited them every half-month; the Patriarch Xuan of Nanshan took ten recitations as his standard.
Therefore, what is now called "repeated exposition" is not considered much. As for the "Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of Precepts," although this chapter is so named...
These ten encompass the inexhaustible Bodhisattva precepts and fully embody immeasurable Dharma-gates. The *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* states:
"All the precepts of Bodhisattvas—whether mundane or supramundane, ordinary or holy—take the mind as their essence. If the mind were to have an end, the precepts would also have an end;
because the mind is inexhaustible, the precepts are likewise inexhaustible. Therefore, they are called the "Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries" (daśākṣaya-kośa) of the Chapter on Precepts.
Furthermore, this "precept of all sentient beings" refers to this Dharma of precepts which, above, has been transmitted by the thousand Buddhas, and below, universally covers all capacities.
It is received together by monastics and laypeople, humans and devas; it is likewise accepted by spirits, ghosts, and animals. It is not like the limited scope of the Śrāvaka precepts.
"The fundamental source and original nature are pure" means that not even a single speck of dust can be established therein. This is to say:
This precept is such that the Buddha and sentient beings share the same source; its nature is fundamentally pure. When present in the Buddhas, they have already returned to this source;
when present in sentient beings, they must uphold and receive it before they can restore their original state.
Yet, as for this fundamental nature, its nature is fundamentally pure; there is no self-nature existing apart from the source, nor is there any purity to be attained apart from this nature.
Furthermore, these ten inexhaustible treasuries of the dharma of precepts take the fundamental source and the inherently pure nature as their supporting essence.
Therefore, receiving and upholding these precepts now is to restore that originally pure essence. △ Second, the verse summary has three parts.

First, the initial bestowal by Śāntamati; second, the transmission by Śākyamuni; third, the exhortation for the assembly to believe and accept. Regarding the first [of these three], there are two parts:

first, clarifying the primary and secondary [realms]; second, clarifying the person and the Dharma. Regarding the first of these, there are again three parts: first, the primary Buddha-land; second, the secondary Buddha-land;
third, the conclusion regarding the primary and secondary. Now, the first [part].
"I, now Vairocana, am seated upon the lotus pedestal.

Here, "I" refers to the Tathāgata himself manifesting as the sovereign who expounds the Dharma; it does not refer to the Buddhas upon the thousand petals, nor to the thousands of millions of Śākyamunis.
As for "Vairocana," it signifies that the defilements of ignorance have been forever exhausted, and wisdom and merit [are fully perfected].

All are perfectly complete, like the pure full moon; this expresses his virtue through his name. Furthermore, the body of Vairocana is the fruit of the precepts, which is the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vedanīya*);
the lotus pedestal is the virtue of the precepts, which is the secondary retribution (*āśraya*). The thousand Buddhas and the ten billion Buddhas are the primary retribution;

the thousand petals and the ten billion lands are the secondary retribution. Vairocana is the fundamental essence, while the thousand Buddhas are the manifested traces. Moreover, as for the thousand Buddhas...

The hundred billion Buddhas of the fundamental [reality] serve as the traces. Without the fundamental, there would be no way to manifest the traces; without the traces, there would be no way to reveal the fundamental.
Although the fundamental and the traces differ, the fruition-virtue is non-dual. Within this, there are four points of analysis. First: the fundamental within the fundamental.
Second, the trace within the fundamental; third, the fundamental within the trace; fourth, the trace within the trace. "Direction" (fang) refers to the ultimate return to the *dharmatā*;
"sitting" (zuo) refers to abiding immovably. As for the "lotus pedestal," it signifies that the form of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang Shijie*) resembles a lotus.

Because the flowers support [the body] from below, they are called a "pedestal" (*maṇḍala*). The pedestal resides in the center, symbolizing that the precepts are the primary cause of the Middle Way, capable of giving rise to the fruit of Buddhahood of the Middle Way.
The *Vairocana* body is termed the "flower-pedestal," which also signifies the non-differentiation between the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*).
Furthermore, the fact that the fundamental Buddha Vairocana sits upon the flower-pedestal as the sovereign of all Buddhas precisely symbolizes this.
The Dharma of precepts is the foundation of all virtues. Form and mind are non-dual; the environment and its inhabitants are mutually interpenetrating in infinite layers.
This arises from the manifestation of the sentient beings' own mind-nature, and it abides in reliance upon that very same mind-nature. The mind-nature of sentient beings is like a lotus flower:
dwelling amidst the dust, yet unstained by it. Cause and effect are simultaneous. Because of this wondrous lotus of the mind-nature, it is therefore...
He causes the world to be like a lotus flower; this very nature of mind is the supreme Middle Way.
Because he is thus ultimately in accord with it, it is said that he "sits upon a lotus pedestal. △ Second, the Buddha-land of the traces.
Upon the thousand petals surrounding [the central one], there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis. On each petal are ten billion lands;
in each land is a Śākyamuni, each sitting beneath a Bodhi tree, simultaneously attaining the Way of Buddhahood.
"Surrounded by a thousand petals" means encircled on all sides. "A thousand petals" refers to a flower possessing one thousand leaves;
a petal of a flower is called a "leaf. Flowers in the human realm have only ten or so leaves, whereas flowers in the heavens have more than a hundred leaves.
The flowers of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess a thousand petals. Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of the thousand Śākyamunis:

since all these thousand Buddhas emerge from the single Buddha Vairocana, they first manifest the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environmental retribution) and subsequently manifest the *mūla-vipāka* (the primary retribution);
hence the word "furthermore" (*fu*). The Buddha-body possesses four aspects: first, Vairocana, whose body is the True Dharma; second, Śākyamuni...

The fulfillment of practice results in the body as the fruit of retribution; this is the third [category]. Śākyamuni’s manifested trace (saṃbhogakāya) takes the response to sentient beings' needs as its body;
this is further divided into two: first, the response body (nirmāṇakāya) receiving the offerings of Cunda; second, the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) receiving the offerings of the great assembly.

What is now called the "thousand Śākyas" refers to the response body Buddha; the "ten billion Śākyas" refers to the transformation body Buddhas. The thousand-petaled [lotus] represents the thousand Śākyas.

This means that each petal contains one Buddha-world; thus, there are the pure lands of the thousand Buddhas, representing the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), which constitute the fundamental ground where the causal stage reaches completion and gives rise to the responsive fruit.

That "one flower contains ten billion lands, and in each land there is one Śākyamuni" reveals the realm of the transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*). The above clarifies that a single flower and petal represent one world-system.
Because there are [ten] directions, there are one thousand Śākyamunis. Now it is clarified that upon a single petal there are further ten billion lands;
therefore, there are ten billion Śākyamunis. Because there are one thousand petals, there are one hundred trillion Śākyamunis.

This means that as soon as Vairocana sits upon the flower pedestal, one thousand Śākyamunis appear surrounding him. Each of these Śākyamunis, in turn, manifests a transformation of one thousand Buddhas surrounding them.
Each transformation Buddha is further surrounded by a thousand Buddhas. Thus, one Buddha sits upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower;

on each petal there are a thousand Buddhas, on ten petals there are ten thousand Buddhas, on a hundred petals there are one hundred thousand Buddhas, and on a thousand petals there are one million Buddhas.

It dispels the mist of transgressions; it is like the sun, for it can remove darkness. It is likened to the moon, adorning the *dharmakāya*.
