The same term [when applied to the fruit] refers to the ultimate fruit of attaining realization; this is termed "revealing the real" (*xianshi*). As for "sons of the Buddha" (*fozi*), the meaning is that of succession.

All sages of the three vehicles have their understanding born from the Buddha and are transformed by the Dharma; thus, they all possess the sense of being "sons. Now, they have given rise to the Mahāyāna mind.

Because they receive the Mahāyāna precepts, they are called "true. There are three kinds of sons of the Buddha: those who practice like ordinary people and have not yet entered the Way, yet continue and uphold the lineage of the Buddhas, are called "external sons of the Buddha";
those Śrāvakas who uphold the teachings of the Hīnayāna and cause the Dharma-body to grow are called "commoner sons of the Buddha";
and Bodhisattvas who receive the Mahāyāna precepts and give rise to the Buddha-Dharma-body are called "true sons of the Buddha."
"Status" is the great treasure of the sage. Yet, as soon as one receives the Buddha-precepts, one's status becomes equal to that of the Great Awakened One.

This is truly because the source of birth and Buddhahood is the same, and the nature of the mind is non-dual. To turn one's back on awakening and unite with the sensory dust is what is called being a sentient being.
Turning one's back on defilement and uniting with awakening is what is called being a Buddha. Now, by receiving the Buddha-nature precepts, one suddenly returns to the source of the original mind;
is this not to occupy a station identical to that of all Buddhas? Question: Since one’s station is thus identical to that of the Buddhas, why is one still called a "son of the Buddha"?
Answer: Although the great station is the same, one’s Buddha-virtues are not yet perfected; therefore, one receives the title of "son. This is analogous to the East [where the sun rises].
The Prince of the Palace has already received consecration and will eventually succeed to the royal throne; for now, he is merely called the Prince and not yet the King.
The great assembly all pay him respect—this is the exhortation. Listen with a sincere heart to my recitation—this is the admonition to listen.
If you do not listen with a sincere heart, then deluded thoughts will block the ground of the mind, and the Dharma of the precepts will have no way to enter. Before long, then...
One cannot restore oneself to the original source. Now, those who wish to hear the precepts must first externally solemnize their physical demeanor and internally arouse a sense of reverence.

"Reverence" refers to the external decorum; "sincerity of heart" refers to the internal attitude of respect. When the internal and external are one and the same, the Great Dharma may then be bestowed.
*The Buddha’s Exposition of the Brahmajāla Sūtra:

Initial Ferrying, Volume Two, Phonetic Explanations.* **Master (Shī):** One who transmits the Way. **Aid (Zī):** To assist. This means to assist in bringing forth the karmic practices of one's own person.
Furthermore, it is said: "The teacher possesses the merit of craftsmanship and completion; the disciple possesses the virtue of innate endowment.
The country of Magadha is also called Makhāṭa, which translates as "Excellent Victory" (Śubhavijaya).
It is also called Makatī; "Maka" means "great," and "Kati" means "essence. This signifies that among the five regions of India, this country is the greatest, encompassing and governing all others.

The country is therefore called Mahādeha (Great Body). Alternatively, *maha* means "pervasive" (*vyāpti*) and *keti* means "intelligent" (*prajñāvat*); thus it signifies that intelligent people pervade the entire kingdom.
It is also called Avihimsaka (Non-Harming), meaning that according to the laws of this country, capital punishment is not carried out;
those sentenced to death are sent to the Śītavana (Cold Forest). It is further called Anupadrava (Without Affliction) or Avihethana (Non-Injury); all these names refer to the *kalpa*.
From the beginning, there was no infliction of harm or injury. However, when it reached King Bimbisāra, he employed the mutilation of fingers as a form of punishment.

Later, because the king himself suffered the pain of biting his own finger, he abolished this punishment once more. Since the Buddha was destined to be born in that land, these auspicious omens manifested in advance;
for this reason, the name "Non-Harming" (Ahiṃsā) was established first.
Rājagṛha is the same as Rājagiri; it is the name of a city in the kingdom of Magadha.

According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya- vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun), this country originally had a malevolent dragon that caused various calamities and destroyed the houses and dwellings of the people, yet the royal palace alone remained undamaged;
it was named for this reason. Furthermore, it is said that because a thousand kings once resided together there, it is called the City of Royal Abodes (Rājagṛha).
Furthermore, regarding the eight aspects: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that Śākyamuni Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment countless kalpas ago;
yet, out of the power of his great compassionate vows, he has repeatedly appeared in lands throughout the ten directions to benefit sentient beings.
He manifests birth and manifests extinction, differing in every place. It is not merely that he appears in this single region of Jambudvīpa in the south;
when discussing the beginning and end of his manifestation, it possesses eight phases, all of which serve to demonstrate that he conforms to the human way.
First, the phase of descending from Tuṣita; second, the phase of entering the womb; third, the phase of emerging from the womb; fourth, the phase of leaving [the household]...
The mark of the household; fifth, the mark of subduing demons; sixth, the mark of attaining the Way; seventh, the mark of preaching the Dharma; eighth, the mark of entering nirvana.

Regarding the two types of delusion—the collective and the individual—the individual karma of deluded vision refers to all sentient beings who, having lost their true nature, give rise to deluded visions of their own accord, perceiving all manner of illusory realms, whether of suffering or pleasure. It is like one with diseased eyes at night.
One sees the light of a lamp and perceives two distinct circular shadows; this is a common deluded vision.

It refers to all sentient beings who, having lost their true nature, collectively perceive all manner of illusory objects and collectively experience suffering and pleasure, as induced by shared karma.
This is like the people of a single country who collectively see pestilence, calamity, and inauspicious events.
The Six Aspects in Perfect Interfusion: The "Six Aspects" refers to the substance of the one true Dharma-realm possessing six kinds of aspects consisting of names and meanings.
Although the substance of the Dharma-realm is identical and originally devoid of differentiated aspects, as the phenomena enter into their meanings, six names consequently arise.
Though there are six names, they do not depart from the single substance; they interpenetrate and harmonize, such that the one and the many are without obstruction.

Therefore, it is called "perfect fusion" (*yuanrong*). First, the general characteristic; second, the specific characteristic; third, the common characteristic; fourth, the distinct characteristic; fifth, the characteristic of formation;
sixth, the characteristic of destruction.
*Trāyastriṃśa* (忉利) is translated here as the Heaven of the Thirty-three. It resides on the summit of Mount Sumeru, at a distance of eighty thousand *yojanas* from the human realm.
The Ten Directions: In each of the four directions, there are eight heavens, with Śakra residing in the center. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:
"In the past, after the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a woman who resolved to build a stūpa. Furthermore, thirty-two people resolved to assist in its construction.
By virtue of her merit in building the stūpa, she became the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, while those who assisted in the construction became his ministers."
The ruler and his ministers combine to form the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa).
There are five [objects]—form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch—which constitute the five desires (*kāma*). "Desire" (*kāma*) refers to that which is sought after. As the *Zhiguan* states:
"The five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are not themselves desire; rather, they possess within them flavors that can give rise to the mind of seeking and desiring in the practitioner."
The "view of a self-body" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of sentient beings refers to the false conceptualization of [the aggregates] as a body, forcibly establishing a sovereign master.

One who is in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*) is said to have one more birth because they still possess a single grade of ignorance; once this one birth has passed, [they attain liberation].
This refers to the attainment of the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Regarding the "four preparatory practices" (*catvāri prayogāṅgāni*): they are *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgra-dharma*, which constitute the four.

They are called "preparatory practices" (*prayoga*) because one’s spiritual effort increases therein. *Uṣmagata* (Heat) is named after a metaphor: it is like a person drilling wood to produce fire; although the fire—though...
It has not yet emerged. First, one attains the sign of "warmth" (*ūṣmagata*). This is like the stage of application (*prayoga*), where the fire of wisdom burns the fuel of afflictions;
although one has not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one has already attained the precursor to the fire of wisdom. As for the "summit" (*mūrdhan*):

This refers to the stage where contemplative practice becomes increasingly clear; it follows the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), just as when one has ascended a mountain peak and gazes upon the four directions, seeing everything with complete clarity.
"Patience" (*kṣānti*) has two meanings. First, it carries the sense of "sealing" or "affirmation. This means that within this stage, one is able to affirm the principle of the Four Noble Truths:
that the truth of suffering is indeed suffering, and so on, up to the truth of the path, which is indeed the path.
Furthermore, there are two [meanings]: first, the meaning of certainty, because these roots of goodness are certain not to regress;

second, the meaning of being the highest in the world, because although one has not yet realized the principle of the Four Truths while in this stage, one is nonetheless the most excellent within the mundane world.

"Preparatory concentration" (*anāgamya-dhyāna*) refers to that which has not yet entered the fundamental dhyānas. This means that while one is in the desire realm, one cultivates the form-realm concentrations;
although the body has not yet reached those [higher realms], the mind has already realized them beforehand.

There are two types of innate grasping: first, innate grasping at a self; second, innate grasping at phenomena. First, innate grasping at a self refers to forcibly establishing a sovereign controller within the aggregates (*skandhas*) and other such phenomena, falsely clinging to them as a "self" that arises simultaneously with the body. This is called innate grasping at a self.

Second, innate grasping at phenomena refers to the false conceptualization that arises toward all phenomena due to the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of beginningless time. This is called innate grasping at phenomena.
It is attached and always coexists with the body; therefore, it is called the "innate attachment to dharmas" (*sahaja-dharma-grāha*).
"Arising-phase ignorance" refers to the single grade of the ignorance of the arising-phase that remains after the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samaya-jñāna*).
Ignorance has the meaning of "non-awakening. Because of this non-awakening, the three subtle states arise. This ignorance persists until the final moment of mind of the Vajra-like Samādhi.
Now, regarding the five types of Non-returners (*anāgāmin*): *anāgāmin* is the Chinese translation for "not coming. "Not coming" carries the meaning of "not returning.

This refers to one who has completely severed the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is born into the form (*rūpadhātu*) or formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), where they exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*) and do not return again.

This is because they come to receive rebirth there. They are also called the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*), namely: Avṛha (No Affliction), Atapa (No Heat), Sudarśana (Good Vision), Sudṛśa (Good Appearance), and Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form).
"Leaving home" means departing from the house of birth-and-death and entering the house of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the afflictions of the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*): the delusions of views within the three realms constitute one abode;

the delusions of thought within the three realms are divided into three—namely, craving for desire, craving for form, and craving for existence—and the delusions of ignorance as numerous as motes of dust are combined into one abode, thus forming five in total.
Sentient beings abide [in saṃsāra] because these five afflictions cause them to cling to birth and death.

There are two types of birth and death: first, the *pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth and death), which refers to the sentient beings of the six realms who receive retribution according to their karma;
for these beings, the physical segments of the body vary in length, and the limits of their lifespan vary in longevity or premature death. Second...
Regarding birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma-vaśitā-maraṇa*): this refers to Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas.

Although they lack birth-and-death through fragmentation (*bheda-vaśitā-maraṇa*), they possess birth-and-death characterized by the shifting of causes and the changing of effects. For instance, an earlier stage serves as the cause and a subsequent stage as the effect;
furthermore, a subsequent stage serves as the cause and a further subsequent stage as the effect. Therefore, it is called "transformation."
The term *zhuchi* (abbot/resident preceptor) means to dwell securely in virtue and morality, to uphold and maintain the teachings so that the Dharma may endure for a long time;
it is also said to mean dwelling in ultimate truth and maintaining it without loss.
The afflictions bound to the ground refer to dwelling in bondage due to the predominance of afflictions.
Regarding the "ground of the five destinies where beings dwell together," the five destinies are the six heavens of the desire realm, humans, hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings.
Originally, this includes all six destinies; however, because asuras are included within these various destinies, only five are mentioned here. They dwell together in a mixed fashion.
As for "the [five] destinies": although the karmic retributions of suffering and pleasure differ among them, they are collectively situated within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As for "the nine realms," this refers to the three vehicles and the six destinies; because the divisions of the realms of retribution differ, there are nine realms.

The Buddha’s manifestation of transformation extends to the eight classes of beings; his Way brings salvation to the hundred spirits. The transmission of the Dharma through the ages nurtures all things with compassion.
The worthies and sages of the Three Vehicles have already reverently taken refuge, and the gods and ghosts of the eight classes likewise stand in solemn array as protectors.
Therefore, in many sutras, the assembly of eight classes is frequently enumerated. These eight classes are:
devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
The fourfold assembly consists of: first, the initiating assembly (*prasthāpaka-parṣad*), which refers to the assembly that initiates the discourse.

This means those who stimulate and inspire [the Buddha], causing the Tathāgata to have something to teach and the great assembly to hear it, as well as those who initiate questions and answers, and so forth.

Second, the assembly of those with the capacity (*yathābhavya-parṣad*), which refers to the assembly of those present who possess the requisite capacity. This means those who have planted roots of virtue in the past and whose conditions have converged.
At that time, those who were spiritually mature did not rise from their seats; upon hearing [the teaching], they immediately attained the Way.

Third are the "shadow-and-echo" assembly, referring to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past who concealed their perfectly consummate fruits and manifested themselves as being identical to the assembly of ordinary beings to assist the Dharma King.
They are like shadows following forms and echoes responding to sounds, or like the many stars surrounding the moon; though they perform no deliberate action, their presence is manifest.
This is of great benefit. Fourth are those who form karmic connections through the Dharma. This refers to those who establish the causal conditions for hearing the Dharma.

Generally, because their faculties were shallow in past lives, the three types of wisdom did not arise; thus, although they see the Buddha and hear the Dharma in the present life, they are unable to obtain benefit, serving only as causal conditions for attaining liberation in the future.
Regarding "True Suchness (tathatā) and the Limit of Reality (bhūtakoṭi)": True Suchness is like space merging with space or water poured into water;
its nature does not undergo false change, and is therefore called True Suchness. The Limit of Reality is the ground of the principle of Buddha-nature.
"Ten recitations as the standard period"—this was the practice of Master Xuan of Nanshan. Whenever he transmitted the Sūtras or the Vinaya, he invariably set ten recitations as the required limit;
he did so because he feared that fewer would leave the teachings vague and obscure.

The four kinds of provisions (*saṃbhāra*) are also called the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). The first is the provision of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*), which refers to that cultivated through past lives.

Regarding the various merits: in this present life, one possesses abundant wealth and treasures, encounters virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), remains free from all obstacles, and is able to practice diligently;
this is called the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*). Second is the accumulation of wisdom (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*):
having cultivated wisdom in previous lives, one is now intelligent and quick-witted in this present life, understanding the meaning of the Dharma; this is called wisdom.

The equipment of wisdom. Third, the equipment of previous lives: this refers to having accumulated roots of merit in past lives such that, in this present life, one’s faculties are complete and one’s family and wealth are sufficient; this is called the equipment of previous lives. Fourth, the equipment of the present life:
this refers to possessing wholesome dharmas in this present life, whereby roots of merit have matured and one is endowed with the restraint of ethical discipline; this is called...

The provisions for the present life consist of four roots of goodness: first, dwelling joyfully in the forest; second, gathering beings through the four means of attraction; third, sacrificing one's body to seek the Dharma;
and fourth, practicing with diligent vigor.
Vairocana is translated here as "Pervasive Illumination" (Bi-lu-cha-na) and is also called "Great Sun.
This refers to the Tathāgata’s form-body and dharma-body, which universally pervade the entire dharma-realm and illuminate all worlds throughout the ten directions.

If a person invokes his name, takes refuge in him, and pays him homage, they shall receive the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy sages of the dharma-realm, as well as the eight classes of beings.
"Guarding and protecting.

*Pāramitā* is translated as "reaching the other shore. This means that when a bodhisattva cultivates these dharmas, they transform and deliver sentient beings, transcending the ocean of birth and death to reach the other shore of nirvāṇa.
Regarding the Wheel-Turning Kings (*cakravartin*) of the Ten Wholesome Paths, there are four types: first, the Gold-Wheel King, who rules over the four great continents;
second, the Silver-Wheel King, who rules over three continents, excluding the northern continent; third, the Copper-Wheel King, who rules over two major continents, the eastern and southern;
and fourth, the Iron-Wheel King, who rules over the southern continent alone. All four possess the precious wheel (*cakra-ratna*), which appears in the sky.
He traveled through the air by means of a wheel; therefore, he is called a "Wheel-Turning Emperor" (Cakravartin). As for the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*):

three of the body—namely, refraining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; four of speech—namely, refraining from false speech, frivolous chatter, divisive speech, and harsh speech; and three of the mind.
This refers to not giving rise to greed, hatred, or wrong views. By means of these ten dharmas, one governs the world; therefore, it is called the "Ten Wholesome Acts of a Wheel-Turning King.

Governing through worldly speech means exhorting and transforming others through words of filial piety and fraternal duty, loyalty and trustworthiness, benevolence and righteousness, propriety and wisdom.
Regarding the precepts of the ox, the dog, and so forth, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* mentions six types of ascetic practitioners (*tīrthika*).

First is self-starvation, which means abstaining from food and drink and enduring hunger for a long time. Second is plunging into deep pools, which means casting oneself into deep waters during the cold season to endure the suffering of freezing.
Third, entering fire: this refers to constantly scorching the body with heat and fumigating the nose, and so forth. Fourth, self-seclusion:

this refers to constantly remaining naked, regardless of cold or heat, and sitting in the open air. Fifth, silence: this refers to making cemeteries and burial grounds one’s dwelling place, remaining still and not speaking.
Sixth, the ox and the dog: they claim that in their previous lives they came from among oxen and dogs.
They immediately observe the precepts of cattle and dogs, eating grass and consuming filth, hoping solely for rebirth in heaven.
As with the six types of non-Buddhists mentioned above, they cling to these ascetic practices as the cause for attaining the fruit [of liberation].
The First Tide of the Brahmajāla Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Three.
Recorded by the Vinaya-transmitting Śramaṇa Shuyù of the Wanshòu Precept Altar at Zhāoqìng Temple in Ancient Hangzhou.
△ Second, the Section on Śākyamuni’s Exhortation and Inspiration, in two parts: first, the narrative provided by the sūtra compiler; second, the words spoken by the World-Honored One himself. First:
The middle section has three parts. First, regarding the Buddha’s desire to establish the precepts:

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, having first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained unsurpassed enlightenment, initially established the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa, which consists of filial obedience toward one's parents, teachers, and the Triple Gem, and filial obedience toward the Dharma of the Ultimate Path.
Filial piety is called the precepts; it is also called restraint.
"At that time" refers to the period when [the Buddha] descended from the Palace of the Heavenly King to Jambudvīpa.
Śākyamuni is the transformational master who recites the precepts; he is the primary retribution body (*vipākaphala*). The Bodhi tree is the transformational land where those precepts are recited.

This refers to the *niṣyanda-phala* (retributive environment). "Unsurpassed Awakening" (*anuttara-bodhi*) means awakening and enlightenment; it refers to the Dharma realized by the sages of the Three Vehicles.

Because there is nothing that surpasses the Tathāgata’s realization, it is called "unsurpassed. For instance, *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* only awaken to the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and do not yet know the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);

this is termed "partial awakening. As for those from the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*) through the ten stages of sanctity (*daśa-bhūmi*), up to the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-samādhi-samāpanna*), [their realization is likewise incomplete].
Although this awakening is correct, it still pertains to the stage of a cause and is termed "partial awakening" (*sufen-jue*); it remains surpassed by what lies above it.
Only the Tathāgata has realized the fruit of wondrous awakening (*miaojue-guo*), wherein wisdom is exhaustive and uniquely sovereign; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed awakening" (*wushang-jue*).

Regarding the initial formulation of the Bodhisattva *Prātimokṣa*: "formulation" (*jie*) means "prohibition" (*zhi*). That he formulated these precepts immediately upon attaining the Way of the Buddha is precisely...

The manifestation of the *prātimokṣa* is the most urgent preliminary task for entering the Path. Furthermore, the term "Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa" is used specifically to distinguish it from the precepts of the Śrāvakas;
this is because the intended recipients of these precepts are exclusively Mahāsattvas, not those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
However, the stages and positions of a Mahāsattva are not within the scope of the two vehicles, and thus the gravity of the prohibitions and precepts is likewise [different].
This is not that which is studied by the Hīnayāna; therefore, for the sake of the Mahāsattvas, fifty-eight precepts are established instantaneously.
This differs from the Śrāvakas, who incur offenses one by one as they arise. However, because Śrāvakas loathe and fear birth and death, they regard self-benefit as the primary concern;

thus, the precept against sexual misconduct is placed at the head of their code, since sexual desire is the root of saṃsāra and the source of birth and death. The Bodhisattva, however, does not fear this.
In the cycle of birth and death, taking up the welfare of sentient beings as one’s primary duty, the precept against killing is established first.

Moreover, killing severs the seed of Buddha-nature and violates the fundamental vow of compassion. Regarding the principles, it concerns the suitability of the occasion; regarding the facts, there are three meanings:
first, that a Bodhisattva possesses deep faith and will not be repelled even upon hearing [the teaching] all at once; second, that the Bodhisattva’s work of benefiting sentient beings is urgent.
One cannot always attend by the Tathāgata’s side to report matters as they arise.
(3) When Śākyamuni conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon Prince Miaohai, he expounded these fifty-eight precepts all at once; such was the ancient custom.

Furthermore, while the Śrāvakas formulated rules one by one as circumstances arose—each being comprised of ten topical points—the present system establishes all the precepts simultaneously, precept by precept.
These should likewise be fully possessed. Although the Sūtra does not explicitly state this, the principle necessarily requires it.

Therefore, I shall now briefly set forth the names, characteristics, phrases, and meanings, so that one may understand their benefits and facilitate study and practice. First: "Inclusion within the Saṃgha.
This means that by establishing these grave and light precepts, all sentient beings are gathered and received, led back into the ranks of the Mahāyāna, and caused to embrace the Great Vehicle.
First, because it is the fruit of the Jewel of the Saṃgha. Second, it causes the Saṃgha to rejoice;

that is to say, by the power of the aforementioned gathering [of beings], it enables all bodhisattvas to be joyful and delighted, as they do not stagnate in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Third, it causes the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness;
that is to say, by the majestic power of the prohibitive precepts, it enables the lineage of bodhisattvas to flourish with benefit and attain a state of peaceful dwelling.

4. To cause those who have not yet developed faith to do so. This means that by the power of the prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepa-śīla*), one is able to purify both natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed (*prajñapti-sāvadya*) karmas, thereby giving rise to the mind of right faith in all sentient beings. 5. To cause those who already possess faith to increase it.
This means that by means of the pure discipline (*viśuddha-vinaya*), one is able to strengthen the resolve of those who have long been immersed in the Buddha-dharma, preventing them from wavering.

Sixth, because of regret and remorse. Regarding those who are difficult to discipline and bring into subjection: there is a class of individuals who, though nominally called bodhisattvas, have generated the great resolve yet possess powerful afflictions and habitual tendencies.
Now, they are disciplined by means of the various precepts—both grave and light—and through repentance and self-reproach.
7. It causes one not to dare to violate the law, for this reason. 8. One who possesses a sense of shame and remorse attains peace and happiness;
that is to say, by means of taming those things difficult to tame, such a person possesses shame and remorse and is thus free from disturbance and confusion. 9. It severs present outflows (*āsrava*);
that is to say, the precepts restrain the three types of action and the ten branches, ensuring that karma and afflictions do not leak forth. 10. It severs future existence.
10. The exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava*). This means that by permanently severing the seeds of the two types of grasping, the bodhicitta is no longer lost. 10.

The ability for the True Dharma (*saddharma*) to abide for a long time. This means that by virtue of embracing the Sangha Jewel of the Mahāyāna, one ensures that the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is not interrupted, establishes and propagates the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, and thereby enables the True Dharma to abide for a long time. These are the ten.
This refers to the meaning of the phrases. Because there are these ten meanings, the Tathāgata first established the precepts immediately upon attaining perfect enlightenment.

Regarding "filially obeying one's parents and serving one's teachers, monks, and the Three Jewels": although the Buddha had already established the Bodhisattva precept system, he had not yet revealed its essential core.
Therefore, filial obedience is now established as the governing principle of the precepts. Filial obedience is goodness.
To serve and nourish them is filial piety; to receive their countenance without opposition is obedience. Parents are the heaven and earth of a person;
they give birth to and nurture one’s physical body, and their kindness is boundless. Thus, Śyāmaka gouged out his own eyes to save his father, and his chronic illness was cured in a single day.
Through the aspiration of a compassionate heart to take suffering upon himself, the wheel of fire was extinguished in an instant. Although the marks of the precepts—
"Much" refers to filial piety and obedience, which encompass everything; therefore, filial piety and obedience are raised collectively as the central theme.
"Teacher" refers to the preceptor who confers the precepts and the ācārya; these are one's supramundane parents. Thus, a sutra says:

"They give birth to and nourish the Dharma-body, and sustain the life of wisdom. Such is the power of the teacher; their merit is unsurpassed. "Sangha" refers to the assembly of fellow students and the like.
Teachers possess the grace of instructing and perfecting one’s virtue; monks possess the merit of assisting and supporting one’s cultivation.
If one can respect and make offerings to them without violating their teachings, this is called filial piety. As for the Three Jewels, they are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The Buddha is the compassionate father of the three realms; the Dharma is the heroic standard for transcending the world; and the Sangha are the younger brothers of the Tathāgata.

Child, your parents gave birth to your physical body (*rūpakāya*); you rely upon it to cultivate the Way. If there were no physical body, the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body would have nothing to rely upon;
likewise, there would be no basis for serving the Buddha or hearing the Dharma. Your teachers and preceptors gave birth to your precept-body (*śīlakāya*);
through this, one attains Buddhahood. If one lacks the precept-body as the foundation for practice, then all virtuous merits will be unable to arise.

Because they arise [from them], the Three Jewels give birth to my life of wisdom and bring about the fulfillment of Bodhi. If there were no cultivation through the Three Jewels, from where would this life of wisdom be obtained?
Therefore, one must be filial toward each of them. Furthermore, there are three distinctions in being filial to one's parents:
first, providing warmth in winter and coolness in summer; settling them at dusk and attending to them at dawn; serving and nourishing them in every way, and performing labor for them without fail.

Second, establishing oneself in the practice of the Way so as not to bring shame upon one’s parents. Third, employing skillful means to draw others close to the Way. Filial piety toward the Three Jewels is likewise threefold:
first, making offerings and serving them without weariness or fatigue; second, practicing according to the teachings so as not to defile the Dharma-transformation;
and third, preventing wrongdoing and reforming abuses to establish and propagate the teaching. This is the matter of following [the path].
This is an explanation. If one explains this according to the Dharma-gates: skillful means (*upāya*) is the father; the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the mother.
Not departing from the profound meaning constitutes the preceptor (*upādhyāya*). Self-mind’s awakening is named Buddha; the principle-body of self-nature is named Dharma;

the oneness of wisdom and principle is named Saṃgha. Contemplating through reflection in accordance with reality is named filial piety; entering realization in accordance with reality without turning back is named... [reverence].
This is "conformity. The Dharma of the Ultimate Way refers to the unsurpassed and supreme Dharma of the Way.
This means that by means of the two kinds of filial piety—those pertaining to prior matters and principles—one is certainly able to attain the unsurpassed, supreme path of Great Bodhi.
This Way is pure and vast, like empty space; its essence is free from faults and transgressions, and its function is without obstruction or hindrance. [The virtue of] filial piency...

The mind precisely accords with this meaning; therefore, it is called "the Dharma of the Ultimate Way. The Tathāgata, through kalpas of accumulated merit, repaid the kindness of his parents and perfected the cause of Right Enlightenment;

thus he is titled the Great Filial Śākyamuni Buddha. Regarding the statement that "filial piety is named the precepts," it means that if one can practice even this single matter of filiality, then all other precepts will be fully complete. Thus, the subsequent fifty-eight...

Regarding the precepts, they primarily refer to a mind of filial piety and obedience. Furthermore, not contradicting the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts is precisely to accord with the fundamental source-ground of the mind, which is also to accord with the threefold pure precepts (*tri-śikṣāpada*).
For instance, in accordance with the principle of restraining evil, fearing to bring disgrace upon one’s parents is called the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint).
In accordance with the principle of practicing good, intending to bring glory to one’s parents is called the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas).
This accords with the principle of universal salvation and extends its benefits without end; it is termed the "precept of sustaining life. To summarize:

if one can simply practice filial piety, the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) is naturally perfected, and for this reason it is called a "precept. Thus, the *Fayuan* states: "The precept is filial piety itself.
This means that all sentient beings are our parents; therefore, not killing and not stealing constitute filial piety. The meaning is correct.
The same applies here. It is also called "restraint" (*zhi-zhi*). "Restraint" (*zhi*) means strict regulation; "stopping" (*zhi*) means prohibition.
This refers to strictly regulating the three karmas so they do not arise, and prohibiting deluded thoughts so they do not occur; therefore, it is named "restraint. Furthermore, as for "restraint":

This means that the wholesome is regulated so as to be practiced, and the unwholesome is regulated so as to be severed. "Stopping" (zhi) refers solely to the cessation of evil; it clarifies what is openly permitted while implicitly forbidding what is not.
Filial piety and obedience constitute the essence (*tǐ*) of the precepts, while regulation and cessation constitute their function (*yòng*).
When both essence and function are fully manifested, one immediately perceives the original source, the ground of the mind. △ Second, the emission of light as an auspicious omen.
The Buddha immediately emitted immeasurable light from his mouth.

Regarding "the Buddha immediately emitted immeasurable light from his mouth": this means that because the Tathāgata wished to preach the Great Dharma, he first emitted light as an auspicious omen to cause the assembly of listeners to give rise to profound reverence and faith, and furthermore, to manifest that these precepts are most supreme. Thus it is said.
Because it gives rise to the dharma of inexhaustible precepts. As for "emitting from the mouth," it signifies that these precepts were personally proclaimed by the Tathāgata’s golden mouth.
"Immeasurable" signifies that these ten inexhaustible treasuries of precepts are without limit or measure. "Radiance" [signifies...]
This manifests that the fundamental source and original nature are pure, for there is no defilement.
In the past, Śākyamuni entrusted [the teaching] by bestowing it through the transmission of light; now, Śākyamuni upholds the doctrine and likewise radiates light to proclaim it.

When a Bodhisattva hears and receives this precept, they are born directly from the Buddha’s own mouth; therefore, they are called true sons of the Buddha. △ Third, the great assembly desires to hear.
At that time, ten million billion members of the great assembly— bodhisattvas, the eighteen Brahmā heavens, the sons of the gods of the six heavens of desire, and sixteen great kings—
joined their palms with single-minded devotion and listened as the Buddha recited the Mahayana precepts of all Buddhas.
"Ten million billion" is stated merely as a large number to indicate that those with a common affinity have gathered together.
"The great assembly" refers to the fact that humans and devas meet together, and ordinary beings and sages are intermingled.

"The various bodhisattvas" specifically points to those on the thirty stages of mind (*citta*) and the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Regarding the "eighteen Brahmā heavens": *brahma* means "pure," signifying that their sensual desires have already [ceased].
"Pure. Because they still possess a physical body (*rūpakāya*), the *Miaoxuan* states: "The body of direct retribution is a pure form (*viśuddha-rūpa*), unlike the defiled bodies of the desire realm;
therefore, it is called 'Brahma' (*brahman*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because it is pure, radiant, most excellent, and most venerable, it is called 'Deva' (Heavenly Being).
This specifically refers to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). First, the Brahmakāyika [Heaven] is that which...

The subjects governed by him are twofold: first, the Brahmā-purohita (Ministers of Brahmā), who are the ministers and aides of the Brahmā King; second, the Mahābrahmā (Great Brahmā), who has attained the intermediate dhyāna and serves as the lord of the world.
He was born at the beginning of the kalpa and perishes at its end. Because his majestic virtue is preeminent, he is praised with the title "Great. He presides over a great trichiliocosm;
however, in general discourse, there are ten thousand billion Brahmā kings, yet it is this one alone who rules the great trichiliocosm.

Within this world-system, there is a king named Śikhin who has attained sovereignty over the great trichiliocosm; he cannot descend from here. These three [heavens] are collectively called the First Dhyāna.
In the Sanskrit language, *dhyāna* is translated here as "concentration" (*samādhi*), because the mind is gathered and focused without distraction.
Because they attain meditative concentration while seated, they are therefore called "devas. Fourth is the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*). Within the Second Dhyāna, there is light...

9. Śubhakṛtsna (Utterly Pure): Because it can be measured; because the experience of pleasure is most excellent and purity is all-pervasive. These three are called the third dhyāna. 10. Anabhraka (Cloudless):
Because the previous three dhyānas all dwell supported by clouds, whereas upon reaching this fourth dhyāna, one finally dwells in the celestial abodes.
11. Puṇyaprasava (Merit-Born): Because one must possess the power of superior merit to be able to attain rebirth there. 12. Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit). [The following] differs...
The fruit of rebirth is most excellent here; therefore, these three belong to the fourth dhyāna. They are the abodes of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Those who practice the ten superior wholesome deeds and engage in seated meditation attain birth therein. Thirteen is the Abode of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), the dwelling place of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who reckon it to be *nirvāṇa*.
However, it is merely a temporary interval during which mental activity and perception do not function; thus, it also belongs to the fourth dhyāna. Ten...
14. Untroubled (*anāvilā*): because it is not mixed with the afflictions of views and mental defilements (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). 15. Without feverish distress (*atapanīyā*):

because the mental disposition is harmonious and supple, being free from the distress of fever. 16. Of excellent appearance (*sudarśanā*): because the obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) gradually diminish, and vision becomes extremely clear and penetrating.
17. Of excellent manifestation (*suvibhaktā*): because the physical form becomes increasingly superior, and one is well able to manifest transformations. 10.
Eighth is the Ultimate (Akaniṣṭha) Heaven. It is called the ultimate because it is the most supreme among all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and is the final destination.
These five heavens also belong to the fourth dhyāna and are the abodes of noble ones who have attained the third fruit; they are thus named the Five Non-returner Heavens (*pañca-anāgāmin*).

Although these eighteen heavens differ in being either mundane or noble, they are all free from the defilement of desire and have attained pure meditative concentration (*samādhi*); therefore, they are collectively called the Brahma Heavens. [The above are] the Six Desire Heavens.
As for the "Heavenly Son" (devaputra), it refers to the various devas who fully experience the subtle pleasures of the five sensory objects; therefore, this is called the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
There are six heavens in total: first, the Four Kings (Cāturmahārājika), who dwell on the middle slopes of Mount Sumeru; second, the Trāyastriṃśa, who dwell on the summit of Mount Sumeru.
These two are called the "earth-dwelling" heavens. Third is Yāma; fourth is Tuṣita; fifth is Nirmāṇarati; and sixth is Paranirmitavaśavartin.
These four are the "sky-dwelling" heavens. Although these six heavens still possess the five sensual desires, their rewards are spontaneous.
Because they do not rely on effort or seeking, they are all called "devas" (heavenly beings).
Regarding the kings of the sixteen great nations, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that among the various kingdoms of the Western Regions, there are sixteen nations that are particularly large.
These are: first, Śākya; second, Magadha; third, Kāśi; fourth, Kośala; fifth, Vṛji; sixth, Malla; seventh... [text truncated].
1. Cīna; 2. Aṭala; 3. Oḍra; 4. Aparāntaka; 5. Vatsa; 6. Kāmboja; 7. Sindhū; 8. Vārṣa;
9. Nīla; 10. Pāñcāla; 11. Āśmaka; 12. Vatsa; 13. Sura; 14. Gandhāra; 15. Kamboja; 16. Aparāntaka.
When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, all these regions were moved by the resonance of his karmic affinity; thus, humans and devas alike—
The sages gathered like clouds to form a great assembly. Question: How was it possible for a million members of the great assembly to gather like clouds beneath the Bodhi tree?
Answer: As the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states: "Under the tree, palaces and multi-storied towers filled the ten directions."
Furthermore, through the empowerment of the Buddhas' spiritual power, within a single thought-moment, they completely encompass the entire dharma-realm.
Thus, at the assembly of the *Nirvāṇa*, between the twin *śāla* trees, infinite multitudes sat upon the tip of a single needle.
How could this be measured by ordinary sentiments or deliberated upon by the conscious mind? As for "joining the palms," the hands are originally left and right; having joined them...

To act as one signifies the utmost gravity and reverence; this is the purity of the physical action (*kāyakarman*). To have a "most sincere mind" means to concentrate the mind with single-minded intent;
this is the purity of the mental action (*manaskarman*). To "listen with the ears" means that speech naturally becomes still; this is the purity of the verbal action (*vākkarman*).
When these three actions are thus solemnly purified, one listens to what the Buddha teaches, and the light of the precepts will spontaneously shine forth from the source of the mind. All Buddhas...
Regarding the Mahāyāna precepts: this means that these precepts have been transmitted from Buddha to Buddha. △ Second, the World-Honored One’s own exposition has three parts.
First, clarifying his own recitation and exhorting others.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "I now recite these Dharma-precepts of the Buddhas every half-month.

You all, bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds, should also recite them; even the bodhisattvas of the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten vajra-stages, and the ten bhūmis should likewise recite them."

The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas. "Addressed" means to inform or exhort. "All bodhisattvas" refers to them collectively by name, which will later be detailed individually according to their ranks.
Now, when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, humans and devas assemble together; yet, he mentions only the bodhisattvas for four reasons:
first, because the bodhisattvas are the primary audience (*yogya-pudgala*); second, because they serve as the leaders of the great assembly.
Third, they are honored by humans and devas. Fourth, although the ranks and positions of Great Beings (mahāsattva) differ, they are all termed Bodhisattvas;

therefore, by mentioning "Bodhisattvas" in general, the great assembly of humans and devas is encompassed. Regarding the phrase "every half-month," Zhi-chi says it refers to the two halves of the month, the dark and the bright.
Regarding "reciting twice every month," this refers to good and evil karma, which one should [examine] for oneself...

Because they are filial and discerning, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: From the first day to the fifteenth, the light of wisdom gradually increases, symbolizing the virtue of knowledge (*jñāna-guṇa*).
From the sixteenth to the thirtieth, the light of the false gradually diminishes, symbolizing the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

Those who recite the precepts during these two periods do so because they desire their white karma to be perfected and their black karma to be exhausted. Thus, one personally recites the Dharma-precepts and the Buddha-precepts.
This indicates that each Buddha holds the *prātimokṣa* in the highest esteem. Furthermore, the Sanskrit name for this recitation of the precepts is *poṣadha*;
Nanshan translates it as "Pure Abiding" (*jìngzhù*). This refers to the bi-monthly recitation of the precepts to purify both body and mind.
Because one abides according to the precepts, it is correctly named *poṣadha*. *Poṣa* has the meaning of "nourishing," and *dha* has the meaning of "holding.

Because the assembly gathers to recite the precepts, they are able to nourish wholesome dharmas and maintain their own minds. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (or *Samantapāsādikā*, here referred to as the *Sudarsana-śāstra*) states:
"What is meant by 'the True Dharma abiding for a long time'? The Buddha said, "It is this: that the method of the *poṣadha* is not corrupted.

"All of you Bodhisattvas who have resolved to attain enlightenment and who recite it" refers specifically to Bodhisattvas at various stages of their progress; they too should recite it in this manner.
If even the Buddha, who has attained the fruit of Buddhahood, still recites it himself, how much more so should Bodhisattvas, who are yet on the path of practice? It goes without saying.
Recite "Ye. This is the constant practice of all Buddhas; therefore, the Tathāgata now also recites it himself every half-month.

This serves as a model for the great assembly before whom the Dharma is manifested, as well as for those who will receive the precepts in the future. Furthermore, regarding those bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds:
this refers to those who have first generated the Great Mind, namely persons at the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Taking faith as the foundation for the Three Worthies (*tri-satpuruṣa*).

The initial stage is the preliminary step for the ten sages. To have faith is to be free from doubt; it means believing that these Bodhisattva Great Precepts are definitively the seeds for attaining Buddhahood.
The *Yingluo Sūtra* states: "From the stage of an ordinary person, one encounters a Buddha or Bodhisattva preaching the Dharma;
within the teachings, they give rise to a single thought of faith and immediately resolve upon the bodhicitta. At that time, such a person..."
Prior to abiding [in the stages], one is called a "bodhisattva by name. Such a person briefly practices ten mentalities, namely:

the mentality of faith, the mentality of mindfulness, the mentality of diligence, the mentality of wisdom, the mentality of concentration, the mentality of non-retrogression, the mentality of protecting the Dharma, the mentality of dedication, the mentality of precepts, and the mentality of vows.

Because they practice these mentalities, they are called "one who has generated the mind" (*cittotpādaka*) and a "bodhisattva. The phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*) is a term indicating that [the list] is not exhaustive.

This means that not only Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, but even those Bodhisattvas dwelling in the stages of abiding, practice, heading toward, and the grounds, should likewise recite it.
As for the "ten emergences," these are the first ten mental states, namely: relinquishment, precept, patience, diligence, and concentration.
Wisdom, Vow, Protection, Joy, and Summit—these ten minds of the Bodhisattva take the preceding ten faiths as their foundation.
By means of these ten minds, one enters from the conventional into the empty; as each mind unfolds and progresses toward the fruit of Buddhahood, it is called "Progression" (*pratipatti*).

This is also the stage of the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*). Because wisdom abides in the principle after faith has been established, one attains non-retrogression regarding the stage; therefore, it is so named.

Regarding the ten types of nurtured states (*daśa-poṣaṇāni*): these are the ten mental states of the middle [dhyāna], namely: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), generosity (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and impartiality (*samānārthatā*).

Concentration and wisdom consist of ten minds. By means of these ten minds, the Bodhisattva proceeds from emptiness into the provisional, diligently and vigorously increasing the Buddha-way and nurturing sentient beings;
therefore, this is called "Nurturing" (*chāng-yǎng*). It is also the stage of the Ten Practices (*shí xíng*).

Because one has attained true awakening to the principle through the preceding Ten Abodes (*shí zhù*), one advances from there; hence it is called "Practice. As for the Ten Vajras, they follow... [the subsequent section].
These are the ten minds: namely, faith, mindfulness, dedication, penetration, rectitude, non-retrogression, the Mahāyāna, signlessness, wisdom, and the indestructible—these are the ten minds.
By means of these ten minds, the bodhisattva practices Madhyamaka, subdues ignorance, and becomes like a diamond in nature, incapable of being thwarted or destroyed;
thus they receive this name. Furthermore, faith and the others are all likewise characterized by their initial arousal and subsequent cultivation.
The meaning of these [ten stages] is that they are all dharma-gates of essential nature (*dharmatā*).

While the thirty [stages of] mental application (*cittotpāda*) serve as seeds, it is precisely these ten minds that are doubly firm and stable; therefore, they are named "Vajra" (Diamond). Their meaning is that which is indestructible.

This is also the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*). It means that by means of these ten minds, the Bodhisattva turns phenomena toward principle, turns causes toward the fruit, and turns the self...
The merit is dedicated toward sentient beings, while the ability to cultivate and that which is cultivated are redirected toward the *dharmadhātu*.

A "Son of the Buddha" refers to one who has generated the bodhicitta and received the great precepts of the Buddha; such a person is born from the Buddha, and their practice shall succeed him.

Committing an offense and ceasing to maintain [the precepts]; 2. Maintaining [the precepts] and ceasing to commit offenses; 3. Violating the teachings and incurring an offense.
First: whether one kills by one's own hand, instructs another to kill, employs the means of killing, praises killing, rejoices in seeing it committed, or even kills through incantations—
regarding the cause of killing, the conditions for killing, the method of killing, and the karma of killing— one must not intentionally kill any living being whatsoever.

Regarding "if one kills oneself": this is an expression used for illustration, meaning that if there were someone who committed such an act of killing, they would be defined by the Vinaya according to their offense.

For all sentient beings take the five aggregates as their body and mind; thus, to destroy those five aggregates by giving rise to anger and malice is what is called "killing.

To instruct another to kill means to verbally command another to carry out an act of killing—whether by teaching them face-to-face, by dispatching a messenger, or by writing a letter—and so forth. Expedient means of killing refers to various...
Employing skillful means to ensure that death occurs—such as binding, seizing, and tethering, or indicating the path so that others may capture the victim—and praising the killer.

"Praising" refers to extolling their superior strength; using flowery words and clever speech to offer various forms of flattery and praise to one who originally had no intent to kill, thereby inciting them to give rise to the murderous mind and bring the act of killing to completion.

Furthermore, "to lament" means to lament their inability [to refrain]. This refers to someone who already harbors a murderous intent toward another, and who, whether the act has been committed or not, employs various forms of disparagement to incite them to commit it.
Alternatively, it may refer to praising the virtues of one who desires death before them, saying such things as:
"You have already performed many meritorious deeds; you will suffer immediately upon being born [in a lower realm], but upon dying, you shall be reborn [in a higher realm]."

O Deva, you shall enjoy inexhaustible bliss. Thus, one causes them to die by either speaking with the mouth, manifesting signs of praise through the body, sending someone to speak on one's behalf, or sending someone to deliver a letter to them, thereby causing them to take their own life.
As for "rejoicing upon seeing [the act] performed," this refers to when one sees another person committing a killing and the mind immediately follows suit, giving rise to joy. Therefore...
The term "etcetera" (*ādi*) is an incomplete expression, meaning that the various types of killing within this category cannot be fully enumerated.
These include: constructing fire pits or traps to cause one to fall; setting up mechanical devices to cause death; using snares, gallows, or nooses; administering poison;
inducing abortions, and so forth. "Killing by incantation" refers to the use of extremely malevolent spells and sorcery.
He casts a spell to cause that person’s death. In foreign lands, there exists a corpse-raising mantra known as the *Vetāla*.
By means of this spirit-summoning mantra, he recites it for twenty-nine days over an undecayed, intact corpse until the corpse rises. It then washes itself with water and puts on clothes.
He hands over a sword, places it upon a carriage, and instructs him to go and kill; this constitutes "killing by incantation.
To personally devise the means constitutes a transgression of the body; to praise and extol the incantations and prayers constitutes a transgression of speech;

to see the act performed and rejoice in it constitutes a transgression of the mind—and when this is combined with speech, all such acts are subsumed under the karma of killing. As for the "cause," this refers to the seeds and habitual tendencies planted in previous lives.
It is not forgotten. When a single thought suddenly arises that manifests as a murderous intent, it is called the "cause" (*hetu*).
As for the "condition" (*pratyaya*), it refers to the continuity of that murderous intent which assists in the completion of the act of killing; thus it is called the condition.

As for the "method" (*dharma*), it refers to the contemplation and preparation of the means and implements [of killing], such as swords, staves, nets, spells, pits, and traps; thus it is called the method. As for the "action" (*karma*), it refers to these three conditions [coming together].
Through conjunction, one severs that life-force; therefore, it is called "karma. This karma has its cause in the past, its conditions in the present, and its effects extending into the future.
These factors mutually support one another, leading to mutual slaughter in the future and causing the cycle of *saṃsāra* to remain unceasing.
That initial sprout of a single thought of killing is termed the "afflictive obstruction" (*kleśāvaraṇa*). When the deed is accomplished, it becomes [the karmic obstruction].

The severance [of life] is called the karmic obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*). That which invites the suffering of the three evil realms in the future is called the retributive obstruction (*vipākāvaraṇa*).

Thus, the revolving of these three obstructions all arises from the initial arising of a single thought of unwholesomeness. If the initial thought is extinguished, the subsequent thought will not continue;
then there will be no volitional construction, and the karma of killing will not be established. Without this, there is no way for the retributive obstruction to arise.
The nine subsequent precepts should be understood according to this principle. The *Yishu* states: "The immediate cause is proximate while the contributing conditions are remote.

The primary cause is the murderous intent; the others act as auxiliary factors that bring it to completion. The 'proximate' refers to that which actively brings about and invites the retribution of future results."

It is like a shadow following a form. As for "conditions" (*pratyaya*), they are remote because they merely assist in the accomplishment [of the result]. Within the context of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), all acts of volitional construction (*abhisamskāra*) carry the meaning of karma.
The phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*) refers back to the harming of humans and forward to the inclusion of even the most minute sentient beings.
"All" (*sarva*) excludes only the human realm; it refers to the rest, such as ghosts, animals, insects, and so forth. "Those possessing life" (*sajīva*) refers to a single...
All sentient beings maintain a continuous succession through the six sense organs and six consciousnesses;
this is called "life. When this succession is severed, it is called "death. Of these two characters, the former is the most significant; this phrase first clarifies the precept.
Therefore, "killing" refers to intentionally taking life, not killing by accident or unintentionally. Although killing animals and the like may be...

One must repent and seek auspicious signs for one's offenses to be extinguished. The Bodhisattva, however, thoroughly understands the nature of karma and regards all sentient beings with equanimity, making no distinction between great and small, high and low.
It is due to wholesome karma that one is born in the realms of humans and devas; it is due to unwholesome karma that one is born in the paths of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
All alike possess the nature of consciousness, and there is no difference between them regarding suffering and pleasure.
Therefore, all who kill commit an offense. Furthermore, all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
they share a single original source, and those with Buddha-nature shall all become Buddhas. To kill another is thus to harm oneself and to harm the Buddhas of the future.

And there is no transgression. These two types [of offenses] largely produce merit; for a Śrāvaka after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, stealing the Buddha’s property is light, whereas for a Bodhisattva it is always grave.
Furthermore, one ought to give external life to others, yet instead one steals it away—how could this be the mind of a Mahāsattva?
This constitutes both a natural and a proscribed offense (*prakṛti- and prajñapti-sāvadya*), as it invades another's *upabhoga* (enjoyment) and seizes another's external [possessions].

It brings suffering and distress to others and is not tolerated by the laws of the state; furthermore, it is established as a transgression. This precept constitutes a grave offense when five conditions are fulfilled:
first, the object has an owner; second, one perceives the object as having an owner; third, one takes it with the intent to steal; fourth, its value is five coins or more;
and fifth, it is moved from its original location. Regarding "an object that has an owner," the owners are divided into three grades: superior, middling, and inferior.

Things have degrees of importance, distinguished into four categories. Regarding the three grades of objects: the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, sovereigns, parents, and teachers constitute the superior grade;
officials, subjects, humans, and devas constitute the middling grade; ghosts and spirits, bandits, and birds and beasts constitute the inferior grade.

There are four kinds of objects: first, those that are heavy in substance and heavy in value, such as gold and silver; second, those that are light in substance but heavy in value, such as silk and brocade;
third, those that are heavy in substance but light in value, such as wood and stone; fourth, those that are light in both substance and value, such as grass and leaves.
"Objects belonging to the Buddha" refers to items used for the worship of Buddha-stūpas and images, including incense, flowers, and ritual implements.

...as well as the remaining provisions offered by donors to the Buddha. Regarding "Dharma objects": these refer to items used for making offerings to the scriptures, as well as the materials for producing the scriptures.
The Vinaya states: "If one steals a scripture or book, the offense is determined by calculating its value. If one steals a Buddha image, it is of no benefit for making offerings;
yet to destroy it for the sake of profit constitutes a grave transgression. Regarding "Sangha property": this refers to items used for making offerings to the community of monks, and...
Regarding permanent property (*sthāvara-vastu*) and so forth: there are four types of permanent property.
First is the "permanent-permanent," referring to the dwellings, utensils, flower and fruit groves, fields, gardens, servants, livestock, and so forth belonging to the Saṃgha.

Because their substance is restricted to their specific location and does not extend to other boundaries, they are called "permanent. They may only be used; they may not be divided or sold. They must be preserved for all time. Therefore...

Furthermore, it is called "permanently abiding" (changzhu). Second is the "permanently abiding for the ten directions. This refers to the regular meals provided for the monastics within a monastery and so forth;

since visiting bhikṣus may all partake of them, they are called "for the ten directions. Since the food and drink of this location may not be moved elsewhere at will, they are called "permanently abiding.
These two types are known as the property of the *saṃgha*. Third is the "present before one" (*pratyutpanna*).
This refers to when a donor gives goods specifically to those residing in this location, or designates certain individuals by name; thus it is called "present before one" (*saṃmukha*).
Because the gift is bestowed at that very moment and not kept in reserve, it is further termed "present before one. Fourth is the "present before one" of the ten directions.

For example, when the light belongings of the five groups of monastics (*pañca-saṃgha*) pass away, they should be divided through *karmavācanā*; however, if the *karmavācanā* has not yet been performed...
Regarding the distribution before the grinding [of the offerings]: it belongs to the Sangha of the ten directions; all who arrive from various quarters shall have a share.

If the *karmavācanā* has already been performed, the distribution belongs only to those present, and those who arrive later have no share. If there is a thief, if the *gandi* has not yet sounded, the offense is incurred against the Sangha of the ten directions;
if it has already sounded, the offense is incurred against the Sangha present. The retribution for such acts is as that of the blind dragon girl.
One undergoes suffering. This is the immediate retribution for violating the sublime Dharma-eye. The *Zhuangchun lu* states:

"If one steals even a single coin from the permanent property of the Sangha, the interest accrued over one day and night will be three fen and seven li. On the second night, the interest upon the interest increases; in a future life, one must repay this as an ox or a horse.
Conversely, if a single coin is offered to the permanent property of the Sangha, the merit accrued over one day and night will double that amount. Observe this.
The *Buddhasamādhi Sūtra* states: "One who steals property belonging to the Sangha (the permanent endowment) commits a sin greater than that of killing eighty-four thousand parents.
The *Vaipulya Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva Puṣpakūṭa said: 'I am able to save even those with the five heinous crimes and the four grave offenses;
however, I cannot save one who steals the property of the Sangha. The *Compendium of Essential Passages from Various Sūtras* asks: "For what reason does stealing [monastic property]..."

"Is the offense particularly grave for using the property of the Sangha? Answer: "When a donor originally gives away even a single hair’s breadth or a single grain of rice, it is intended as an offering to the ten directions.
At the first sound of the *ghanṭā*, it is heard alike by those far and near; when both the holy and the ordinary partake of it, it collectively becomes a means for the path.

It provides secret support to the donor, enabling them to attain boundless merit. Since the good karma summoned is so great, how could the offense incurred be anything but slight? As for 'the ruler's property,' it refers to..."

Regarding property belonging to the king, as well as matters such as evading taxes or crossing ferries by deception, the Vinaya states that one should first inform them and subsequently seek a skillful means.
By praising the merits of the Triple Gem, the benefit is vast; if permission is not granted, one must pay the tax before passing through.
As for "property of relatives," this refers to the property of one's parents or the assets they manage. If the parents use it as they see fit...
If one takes [these items] with the knowledge that they are for the sake of a relative, it is also permissible and incurs no offense. Regarding the property of a teacher:

this is considered even more serious than the property of a relative, because such property was bestowed by a donor out of faith and a desire for the Path. Regarding the property of officials: this refers to the goods belonging to the nine grades of officialdom.
Regarding the property of the people: this refers to the goods belonging to the common folk. Regarding the property of spirits: this refers to the ritual implements within shrines and temples.

Regarding objects guarded by someone: as for the property of a robber, if it were my own property that was stolen, once I have formed the notion of loss and the object has already passed into the possession of another, it no longer concerns me. If one then uses force to seize it back, this constitutes "a thief robbing a thief";
the offense is determined according to the value of the money. As for the property of animals, it includes even what is held in the mouth of the six domestic livestock.

One must not seize such things. According to the *Wujiexiang jing* (Sutra on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts), killing a bird with an owner constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*), while killing a bird without an owner constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).

If one steals birds or beasts, the crime is determined by calculating their value. Furthermore, there are five ways of stealing: first, taking by force face-to-face; second, taking secretly and stealthily;
third, taking through trickery or jest; fourth, taking what has been entrusted; and fifth, taking after having already received it [but then misappropriating it].
Regarding the offense of taking [what is not given]: if one steals an item of superior quality (*uttama*), or an object belonging to a person of middle quality (*madhyama*), it is grave.

If one steals an object belonging to a celestial being (*deva*) of middle quality, or an item of inferior quality (*hīna*), the offense is light. Or, even if it is grave, the precept is not lost. Second, regarding those who have the perception that there is an owner:

this also applies to the four permutations of certainty and doubt. There is an owner; one has the perception that there is an owner; one has doubt as to whether there is an owner—these constitute two [cases].

The first two cases constitute a grave offense: taking what belongs to another when there is no owner, or taking it with the perception that there is an owner, or with doubt as to whether there is an owner. The next two cases constitute a light offense: taking what belongs to another with the perception that there is no owner, or taking it with the perception that there is no owner. The final two cases are non-offenses:

taking what belongs to another with the perception that there is no owner, or taking it with the perception that there is no owner. Furthermore, this applies to persons and their belongings: perceiving them as persons and belongings, or having doubt regarding them as persons and belongings.
Two phrases constitute a grave offense: taking what belongs to another while perceiving it as such; taking what is not one's own property while perceiving it as such;

taking with doubt while perceiving it as belonging to another; and taking while perceiving it as belonging to another. Four phrases constitute a light offense. Third, regarding taking with the intent to steal:

it is when there is no perception of having been given, no perception that it is one's own property, no perception that it is refuse-rag material, no perception that it is for temporary use, and no perception of close intimacy; [the object] is precisely the owner’s property.
Regarding "five coins worth four *dīnāras*": one large coin in the Western countries is equivalent to sixteen small copper coins here in this land.
If one takes five coins, or objects worth five coins, it constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). Taking four coins or less constitutes a light offense (*duṣkṛta*).

Even if it is a grave offense, the precept is not lost. If the object taken is not worth five coins in its place of origin, but is worth five coins in the place where it is taken, [it is a grave offense].

Regarding the gravity of the offense: if one passes directly through this location with an object worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, but the place from which it was taken is not worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, the offense is light.

Regarding "the fivefold lifting and moving from its original place": when another's property is placed in this location, one moves it so that it exits its original boundary, whether by oneself or [through others].
Whether one instructs another to move it, employs skillful means to move it, or uses incantations to move it—from that moment, the offense of theft is established.

This is detailed in the *Sūtra on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts*. If a debt is not repaid, the offense is established at the moment the creditor forms the certain conviction that they have lost it.

If one receives a deposit and does not return it, it is also as described above. If one evades taxes and has already passed through a customs post or ferry crossing, the offense is established at the time one no longer faces interrogation.
If one instructs another to steal, the offense is established at the moment the instructed person takes the object and removes it from its original location.

If one instructs someone to take a specific object from a specific place, yet that person takes it from a different location or takes a different object, the [instructor] is still held accountable for the offense.

It is a grave offense. If the instructor acts with the intent to steal, while the one being instructed lacks the intent to steal—meaning they believe they are taking what ought to be taken—then at the moment the object is removed from its place, the instructor commits a grave offense, while the one being instructed is without offense.

If the instructor lacks the intent to steal, while the one being instructed believes it is an act of theft—at the moment the object is removed from its place—[the instructor is without offense, while the one being instructed commits a grave offense].

The one who receives the instruction commits an offense; the one who gives the instruction commits no offense. If one instructs another to steal five *kārsāpaṇas*, but only four *kārsāpaṇas* or less are obtained, both are charged with a light offense.

If one instructs another to steal four *kārsāpaṇas* or less, yet the one who receives the instruction obtains five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, the one who receives the instruction is charged with a heavy offense, while the one who gave the instruction is charged with a light offense.
If the original intention was not to distinguish between the amount, but merely to take [the object] and move it away...

Regarding the original location: if two people together plan the theft and move the object from its place, even if the value is five *kārsāpaṇas*, they both commit a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) when dividing it, even if each receives less than five *kārsāpaṇas*.

Whether these individuals possess the precepts (*saṃvara*) or lack them, whether they remember [the offense] in a future life or not, and so forth, are all to be distinguished as in the section on the precept against killing. This constitutes an offense. As for what does not constitute an offense:

[The following thoughts apply: the thought that [the object] belongs to another, the thought that it is one's own property, the thought that it is refuse-rag-like (pāṃśukūla), the thought of temporary use, the thought of close intimacy, as well as states such as insanity and delusion.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, in the "Second Stage" chapter, says: "The sin of stealing also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.
If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, poverty; second, being unable to enjoy wealth independently."
Regarding "common wealth": worldly material goods are shared among five parties—namely, kings, thieves, water, fire, and unworthy descendants.
Only the wealth of merit and the Dharma is not shared with others. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever the habit of stealing, they will inevitably fall into heterodox paths; at best they become high-grade spirits, or middle-grade..."
Regarding "demonic spirits": these are persons of inferior and depraved character who are possessed by various demons.

According to this precept, [these virtues] arise from the mind of precepts within the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground, specifically from the mind of loving-kindness, the mind of compassion, the mind of benefit, and the mind of filial piety.
△ Third: The Precept Against Sexual Misconduct (Three Parts). First: The commission of the offense and the observance of restraint.

If a disciple of the Buddha, whether engaging in sexual misconduct oneself or instructing others to do so—even with any woman—one must not intentionally commit sexual misconduct. This is the cause of sexual misconduct.

The conditions for sexual misconduct, the nature of sexual misconduct, and the karmic actions of sexual misconduct—even engaging in it with the female of an animal, the female of a deva or ghost, or through improper orifices—constitute sexual misconduct.
Sexual misconduct refers to impure conduct; that is, defiled copulation, which is base, vulgar, and shameful, termed "non-celibate conduct" (abrahmacarya).
"Brahma" means purity. Since sexual conduct is inherently impure, it defiles one's own essential nature and pollutes the mental ground of others;
it is precisely the primary cause of birth and death and the very root of saṃsāra. To engage in sexual misconduct oneself is to perform an act of defilement;
