if they do not recognize their errors, the teacher shall expel them and no longer dwell with them. This is the Dharma of the Buddha, wherein the pure and the turbid are clearly distinguished.
How can this be compared to those who, out of private malice, propagate evil and refuse to tolerate the faults of others?
Failing to fear the retribution of karma and its fruits, they speak of others' transgressions with a heart of personal resentment, uttering venomous words with no fear that they are not deep enough.
They desire the sound of their accusations to pervade the entire earth, seeking only momentary gratification; how could they know that after death they will suffer calamity?

Yes. If categorized according to the three aggregates (*tri-skandha*), one does not speak of the faults of others. The *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint precepts) consists of constantly generating a mind of compassion.

The *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precepts for gathering wholesome dharmas) consists of teaching others to give rise to faith. This is the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precepts for benefiting sentient beings). These precepts are collectively established for the seven assemblies of bodhisattvas; however, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ.

In the Hīnayāna, it is said that violating the first category constitutes the first *pārājika*; violating the second aggregate constitutes the second category; and violating the third aggregate constitutes the third category.

Regarding the discourse on the three categories below, all constitute an offense of the seventh aggregate (*saptama-varga*). A Mahāsattva should conceal evil and promote good; therefore, [the Buddha] speaks of gravity.

Where there is gravity, it is grave; where there is lightness, it is light. If what is said is true, it constitutes the highest degree of divisive speech (*paiśunya*) and is also accompanied by harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).

If what is said is untrue, it is further a false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). This possesses both the nature-born (*prakṛti-saṃvara*) and the proscribed (*pratikṣepaṇa-saṃvara*) karmas, as is the case in the world.
When a person falsely speaks of misfortune or fortune, they incur the retribution of being ensnared and submerged. This precept constitutes a grave offense when six conditions are met:

first, a sentient being; second, the perception of that being as such; third, the intention to speak of their transgression; fourth, the specific transgression spoken of; and fifth, the person to whom it is directed.

Sixth, regarding the understanding of the preceding [sections]: first, concerning sentient beings. Regarding the two higher and middle objects, if they possess the Bodhisattva precepts or the Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī precepts, the offense is grave;
if they lack such precepts, it is light. Regarding the lower object, previously it was said that whether they possess the precepts or not, the offense is always light.
Now it is said that if they possess the Bodhisattva precepts, it is appropriate that the offense be grave; however, this does not necessarily imply they have lost their vows. If...

Regarding the first case, if a person has actually committed a grave offense (*guru-apatti*) and has already lost their precepts (*śīla*), it is said that they have committed a grave offense. Alternatively, if one has committed only a light offense; or if, despite committing a grave offense, one has not lost the precepts;

or even if one has lost the precepts, but has received them again according to the Dharma—in all these cases, it is said that they have committed a grave offense. Second, regarding the perception of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃjñā*):

whether there are precepts or no precepts, there are two instances of grave offenses and four instances of light offenses. Third, regarding the mind of confession (*āpatti-citta*), there are two types: first, "sinking" (*nimagna*).
First is the mind that wishes to cause another to lose their reputation and gain; second is the mind of punishment, wishing to cause another to be bound in fetters.
These two minds are precisely the primary factors of the offense. Whether the matter is true or false, one commits a grave offense in either case. Regarding the fourth point, "the faults spoken of":

this refers either to speaking of the specific transgression or speaking of the name of the offense. Each has its corresponding application, and there are six permutations involving doubt and perversion.
Regarding "offensive matters": these include killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, drinking alcohol, eating meat, and so forth. Regarding "offensive names":

on the heavy level, there are the seven reversals (*saptānantarya*), the ten grave offenses (*daśa-guru-dharma*), and the secondary stains; on the light level, there are the names of the five categories (*pañca-varga*) and the seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*).

If one speaks of a heavy offense while it is a heavy name, a heavy matter, and with a heavy perception or heavy doubt, one commits a grave offense. If one speaks of it with a light perception, one commits a light offense. This applies likewise to light names and light matters.

If one speaks with the perception of it being light or with light doubt, one commits a light offense; if one speaks with the perception of it being heavy, one commits a heavy offense. Regarding the fifth point, "the person to whom it is directed":
if one speaks of the seven classes of bodhisattva offenses and transgressions to those of the upper or middle [levels] who do not possess the bodhisattva precepts, one commits a heavy offense.

There is no offense for a bhikṣu regarding a bhikṣuṇī. To speak of the grave transgressions and faults of the two assemblies [of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs] constitutes a violation of the precepts if what is said is untrue;
this belongs to the category of slandering the precepts. Regarding those of lower status, whether they possess the precepts or not, speaking toward them in such a manner is always minor.
Because the damage is not profound. Sixth, regarding "the other person understands": when the matter is accomplished through verbal action, the offense is incurred at that time.
It is an offense according to the words spoken; it is an offense according to the person addressed. If they do not understand, one incurs only the preliminary offense (*prayoga*).

This constitutes an offense. One does not commit an offense if one speaks truthfully and in accordance with the Dharma toward those who possess Mahāyāna precepts or those who possess the full set of precepts.

One should cause them to repent by commanding it, or encourage them to speak with a sincere heart. If one has been appointed by the Sangha, one should speak with a public mind and not speak with a private mind.

This is like when Devadatta committed a crime of immediate retribution; the Buddha had the Sangha perform a *karmavācanā* (formal act) and appointed Śāriputra to go to a layperson's home to proclaim [the verdict]. This is an example of that.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Second Stage," states: "The sin of divisive speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.
If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, their retinue will be estranged; second, their kinsmen will be wicked.
The sin of harsh speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two..."
The various karmic fruits and retributions are as follows: first, one constantly hears unpleasant sounds; second, one’s speech frequently leads to disputes and litigation.

The *Sūtra on the Ten Paths of Wholesome Action* states: "If one abandons divisive speech, one will immediately obtain five kinds of indestructible qualities. First, one obtains an indestructible body."
1. Because they cannot be harmed; 2. They obtain an indestructible retinue, because it cannot be divided; 3. They obtain indestructible faith, because it accords with their original karma; 4.
They obtain indestructible practice of the Dharma, because what they cultivate is firm and solid; 5. They obtain indestructible spiritual friends, because they do not deceive or delude them.
If one can dedicate these toward Bodhi, then at the time of attaining Buddhahood, one will obtain the Right [Dharma].
One's retinue and all demons or non-Buddhists will be unable to obstruct or destroy them.

Adhering to this precept, it emerges from the precept-mind within the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground, arising from the mind of compassion, the mind of faith, the mind of protection, and the mind of delight in teaching.
△ Third: The Precept Against Praising Oneself and Slandering Others. First, regarding the commission of offenses and the maintenance of restraint:

If a disciple of the Buddha praises themselves and slanders others, or teaches others to praise themselves and slander others—whether by means of the causes for slandering others, the conditions for slandering others, the methods for slandering others, or the karmic actions of slandering others.
To praise oneself means to extol one's own merits and rely upon one's strengths, desiring that fame and profit accrue to oneself.
To disparage others means to mock their faults and expose their shortcomings, causing them to lose their fame and profit.

A Bodhisattva should instead attribute straightness to others and draw the crookedness toward themselves; how could they allow themselves to praise themselves and disparage others, comparing and contrasting each other in this way?
To manifest one’s own virtues while exposing the faults of others constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*).

If one merely praises oneself out of greed or disparages another out of anger, each case constitutes a defiled offense (*kliṣṭa-āpatti*). This specific provision exists separately in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, yet in the present sutra, this precept also governs such conduct.
Regarding "teaching others," there are two meanings: first, teaching others to praise oneself and disparage [others].
He either appears in person, manifests signs, or dispatches a messenger with a letter. Second, this refers to instructing others to praise one's own virtues and disparage others.
Regarding the karma of the conditioned phenomena (dharmas): the initial arising of a single thought of praise or disparagement constitutes the cause.

Next, the continuity of the mind serves as the contributing condition. Taking various skillful means of praise and censure as its method, it functions to cause the other person to understand and gain conviction.
Among these four phrases, the text specifically mentions censuring others without mentioning praising oneself;
this is because it follows the wording of the sūtra. However, censuring others implicitly reveals one’s own superiority, and this very superiority is—
This is a praise of the meaning. Furthermore, the thought of praising oneself is slight, whereas the malicious intent to disparage others is preponderant;
therefore, the more serious case is cited to encompass the lighter one. △ Second, the performance of observances and the cessation of transgressions.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should undergo all forms of injury and humiliation on behalf of all sentient beings; they take evil upon themselves and give good to others.
That one should undergo all forms of injury and humiliation on behalf of all sentient beings is precisely the root of the right view of a bodhisattva for benefiting living beings.
This refers to mindfulness. It means not only refraining from praising oneself and disparaging others, but also being willing to take upon oneself the insults and humiliations that others may suffer.
Who but a Great Being could act with such resolve? To direct misfortune toward oneself is precisely what it means to not praise oneself;
to bestow good fortune upon others is precisely what it means to not disparage them.
That is to say: "When there is good, attribute it to the ruler; when there is fault, attribute it to oneself. △ Third, the conclusion regarding the offense for violating the teaching:
If one exalts one's own virtues while concealing the good deeds of others, thereby causing others to suffer defamation, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
"Exalting" refers to praising oneself; "concealing" refers to hiding others' virtues. To exalt oneself is merely to fear that one does not surpass others;

to conceal the merits of others is solely out of anxiety that they might excel me. However, to exalt one's own virtues is not true virtue, and to conceal the good deeds of others serves only to obscure one's own mind while causing others to suffer defamation. Therefore, it is said: "This is a transgression of the Bodhisattva."

Regarding transgressions, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva is praised by others as being one of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) or an arhat, and accepts this praise in silence, they commit an offense. Based on this, it follows that even accepting praise from others is not permissible.
How much less should one praise oneself while simultaneously disparaging others; for how could such an act be the conduct of a Mahāsattva seeking to benefit sentient beings?

If one were to subsume this under the three clusters of pure conduct (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), not praising oneself and not disparaging others would constitute the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint). To endure humiliation on behalf of others constitutes the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas).

To do good for others is the precept of preserving life (*śīla*). This precept is established as a common discipline for all seven assemblies of Bodhisattvas, though there are differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

For the Great Being (*mahāsattva*), benefiting living beings and bringing peace to all things is fundamental; therefore, this precept is held in high regard. In the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), praising oneself constitutes an offense of the seventh category (*saptama-varga*), while disparaging others constitutes an offense of the third chapter (*tṛtīya-pada*);
thus, it is not appropriate to combine them [into a single precept]. This precept possesses both natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed (*prajñapti-sāvadya*) karmic consequences. As...
People of the world compete for fame and scramble for profit; it is difficult for them to avoid the calamity of physical injury. Five conditions constitute a grave offense: first, a sentient being;

second, the perception of that being as a sentient being; third, the intention to praise or disparage; fourth, the utterance of words of praise or disparagement; and fifth, the understanding by the person addressed. Regarding "first, a sentient being":
offenses involving superior or middling objects are grave, while those involving inferior objects are light. Second, the perception of that being as a sentient being.
Regarding these: [if one] perceives an object of the upper or middle grade with the thought that it is upper or middle, or with doubt, there are two grades of gravity;

the remaining four cases are all light. Or, if one perceives an object of the lower grade as being upper or middle, it is also grave. Third, regarding the mind of praise or disparagement: this is precisely the primary factor for the karmic result (*karmādhipati*).

That is to say, one desires to expose the faults of another so that fame and profit shall all accrue to oneself; it is not for the purpose of suppressing them, nor for their benefit. Fourth, the act of praising or disparaging...
There are seven types of endowment: first, lineage, whether noble or lowly; second, occupation, whether honorable or base; third, technical skill and craftsmanship, whether superior or inferior;
fourth, transgressions, whether present or absent; fifth, the underlying fetters (*anuśaya*), whether light or heavy;
sixth, physical appearance, whether handsome or ugly; and seventh, wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*), whether complete or incomplete. These are the five preceding [categories].
Regarding those who understand and accept [the teaching]: if the verbal karma is completed, a heavy offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) is incurred for every word spoken. The *karmavācanā* text states:
"If one commits an offense with a superior degree of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*), one loses the bodhisattva precepts and must receive them again.

If one commits an offense with a middling degree of entanglement, one should confess and eliminate it before three or more persons. If one commits an offense with an inferior degree of entanglement, one should confess before one person. Thus it is said.
The three precepts are identical in this regard. Furthermore, not following the goodness of others should also be governed by this precept. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:
"If one knows that another sentient being possesses genuine merit, yet out of a heart of resentment does not speak of it to others, nor praises it;
or if there is someone who praises it, one does not exclaim 'Excellent!'—this constitutes an offense arising from defilement (*kliṣṭa-āpatti*). If [the failure is due to] laziness or indolence..."
Through negligence or heedlessness, one commits an offense that arises from non-affliction; this constitutes an offense. There is no offense in the following cases:
if one knows that the other person has few desires and acts thus to protect their feelings; if one is ill; if one lacks the strength; if one is observing a monastic regulation (*saṃgha-vidhi*);

if one fears it would cause that person to give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*), excessive joy, pride, or what is unbeneficial; and if one acts to eliminate these various faults. If it concerns actual merit that merely appears as...
This is not a merit. If it is a truly well-spoken discourse, it may appear as though it were not well-spoken. This is for the purpose of subduing the false views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
It is like waiting until their discourse has concluded. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:

"If one disparages non-Buddhists and extols the Buddha-dharma, or employs skillful means (*upāya*) to bring them under discipline, causing them to abandon unwholesome states and cultivate wholesome dharmas, yet they still remain faithless..."
This is faith; for one who already has faith, it causes it to increase and expand. This constitutes no offense.

Furthermore, there is no offense if, in order to entice those on heterodox paths back to the Right Path, or to disparage the Two Vehicles so as to lead them to the One Vehicle, one’s words may seem like slander or praise while the mind is actually one of great compassion.
This is the compassionate heart of a Mahāsattva who, out of pity for sentient beings, establishes the banner of the Dharma to propagate the transformation [of others].

Can the great vows of such a person be judged as faults by equating them with ordinary praise and blame? Question: The World-Honored One declared, "In the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the most honored.
Yet he rebuked those of the Two Vehicles and rejected the non-Buddhists. Is this not nearly equivalent to praising oneself and disparaging others? Answer:
Praise and disparagement occur when one harbors the notions of self, person, victory, and defeat, knowing only how to benefit [oneself]. [The Buddha’s actions were not of this nature.]
Furthermore, he does not harbor thoughts of harming others. Now, the World-Honored One regards himself as a Buddha because he desires to cause all sentient beings to become Buddhas;
he disparages others as being heterodox because he fears that sentient beings might enter into heterodoxy. This is the full manifestation of great compassion;
how can it be called praise or slander? If one were to cause him to cling to the minor point of deprecating oneself and exalting others, then sentient beings would remain ignorant [of the truth].
From this transgression, ten thousand ages will be like a long night; what is gained is little, while what is lost is much. How could this be the essence of a Great Being?
According to this precept, one must protect the mind from within the precept-mind of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.
The mind of joy arises from a fondness for speaking.
△ Eighth: The Precept Against Stinginess and Slandering Others. Part One: Committing Offenses and Ceasing to Maintain [the Precepts].

If a Buddha’s disciple is stingy themselves, teaches others to be stingy, or engages in the causes of stinginess, the conditions of stinginess, the methods of stinginess, or the karmic actions of stinginess.
"Being stingy and adding insult" means that when someone begs for wealth or seeks the Dharma, one begrudges it and refuses to give it; hence, it is called "stinginess.
Furthermore, to respond with anger and verbal abuse is called "adding insult. Stinginess belongs to the category of greed (*lobha*), while adding insult belongs to the category of hatred (*dveṣa*).
Greed and hatred arise from a lack of wisdom and thus belong to the category of delusion (*moha*). An inherent tendency toward greed leads to rebirth as a hungry ghost (*preta*);
if one adds slander, one falls into hell. Delusion leads to rebirth as an animal. These three unwholesome poisons all originate from a continuous thread of greed.

When a Great Being practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), they do not discriminate between kin and stranger, bestowing everything upon those who ask. If one fails to give and instead adds slander, it is a profound violation of the Bodhisattva path.

Regarding the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), what is meant by "son of the Buddha"? One who is stingy themselves—being miserly regarding wealth and the Dharma and refusing to bestow them upon others;
one who teaches stinginess to others—either teaching them to be base and miserly regarding wealth and the Dharma and not to give, or teaching them to further disparage it;

whether through verbal instruction or by dispatching a messenger with a letter to instruct them and so forth—this is what is called "like things gathering with their own kind. This is the law of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-dharma*).

As for its function (*karma*): first, the initial arising of a single thought of stinginess serves as the cause; next, the continuity of that mind which assists and completes that stinginess serves as the condition (*pratyaya*);
various clever words and methods of parsimony serve as the method (*dharma*); and the other person’s comprehension and acceptance of the matter of stinginess serves as the function.
These four phrases do not mention "inflicting harm," because it is only due to prior stinginess that harm is subsequently inflicted. If...
This is not merely a minor transgression; it belongs to the category of light defilements (*āpatti*). The *Upāliparipṛcchā Sūtra* asks:

"Among the root offenses, which is the most grave? The Buddha replied: "If a bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna commits as many instances of greed as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River..."
When comparing these two offenses within the category of anger, anger alone is the more grave. Why is this?
One who manifests anger abandons sentient beings, whereas one who manifests greed protects sentient beings and thus does not become a source of affliction.
Consequently, for a bodhisattva, there is no fear of calamities or misfortunes. Therefore, the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* asks: "What is the meaning of anger? It says: "The root..."
It is a grave offense by nature not to give rise to skillful compassion. To act with anger is not beneficial;

it nourishes afflictions and diminishes compassion, which constitutes a great fault. Because of stinginess regarding this precept, one is parsimonious with wealth and proceeds to inflict harm and insults.
If one were able to practice giving despite greed, then there would be no faults such as inflicting harm, malice, and so forth. This is correct.
The *Dharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "If one has first formed a slight intention [to give] but later fails to practice giving, one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

If one has promised to give but does not do so, one falls into the realm of hell (*naraka*). How much more so for the unsurpassed *bodhi*, which involves fully promising to give to all sentient beings throughout the entire world without exception.
2. Distinguishing between the performance of what is to be maintained (*dhāraṇīya*) and the commission of what is to be avoided (*pratikṣepya*).
When a bodhisattva sees any poor person who comes to beg, they provide everything according to that person's needs.
"Everything" means they should give to all without discriminating between enemies and kin, or those far and near. There is no such thing as poverty for one who has no [attachment to] dharmas.
Wealth is called "exhaustion. Some are impoverished in terms of the Dharma, while others are exhausted in terms of material wealth;
both wealth and the Dharma possess the two sufferings of poverty. Those who come to beg: if they are poor in body, they beg for wealth, and one gives them wealth, whether much or little;
if they are poor in mind, they beg for the Dharma, and one gives them the Dharma, whether great or small. "The person before" refers to all people who are impoverished.
According to their needs, there is nothing that does not fulfill their wishes; hence it is said that "everything is bestowed. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"A lay bodhisattva should practice two kinds of giving: first, material wealth; second, the Dharma. A monastic bodhisattva should practice four kinds of giving:
first, paper; second, ink; third, pens; and fourth, the Dharma. A bodhisattva who has attained patience practices three kinds of giving: first..."

The royal throne; second, one's wife and children; third, one's head, eyes, skin, and bones. It should be understood that an ordinary person Bodhisattva practices giving according to what is appropriate.
If one were to completely block [the request] and not give, then one would commit an offense. The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:
"Upon seeing a beggar come, one should give to them according to what is appropriate. To send them away empty-handed is to incur an offense. Based on this, it is known that...
If even householders ought to practice giving, how much more so those who have left the home life—bodhisattvas who train in great compassion? The *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:
"If one sees anyone coming to beg for something, one should give away whatever wealth and goods one possesses according to one's ability.
If one sees those in distress, terror, or peril, one should, to the best of one's capacity, grant them fearlessness. If there are sentient beings who come..."

One who seeks the Dharma should explain it through skillful means according to their own capacity for understanding, so as to personally relinquish stinginess and greed and cause the other to rejoice.
△ Third, the offense incurred for violating the teaching.
Yet, if a bodhisattva, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, does not give so much as a single coin, a single needle, or a single blade of grass;

or if, when there is one who seeks the Dharma, they do not explain even a single word, a single verse, or a fragment of Dharma the size of a mote of dust, but instead further reviles and insults them—[this constitutes a transgression].
This constitutes a transgression against the bodhisattva pāramitās.
A malicious mind is the fear of giving away one's possessions; a hateful mind is a lack of affection for the person—both are causes of stinginess (*mātsarya*).

Not giving is the condition (*pratyaya*) for stinginess. Not explaining [the Dharma] is the stinginess regarding the Dharma (*dharmamātsarya*). Further reviling and insulting is the karmic action (*karma*) of stinginess. And so on...
Regarding material wealth, it ranges from the most abundant down to the absolute minimum—a single needle or a single blade of grass.

This refers to those who possess no wealth and thus cannot give as they wish. Regarding the Dharma, it ranges from extensive expositions down to the absolute minimum—a single phrase or a single verse.
"Even a single mote of dust [of merit]. This is called being of little knowledge and unlearned; one is unable to explain it extensively.

In the past, when the Tathāgata was a Wheel-Turning King, he encountered a world afflicted by famine and famine-slander. He transformed his great body into a mountain of flesh and gave food to sentient beings without any stinginess.
Now, when a beggar comes to him, he does not provide for them; this already violates the Bodhisattva’s original vow, and instead..."
Regarding "insulting": this refers to one who possesses both stinginess and slander; therefore, it is called a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva. Question:
If one’s own principles are not yet clear and one lacks the Dharma to instruct others, what should be done? Answer: This rule prohibits having [the means] but failing to give.

If one truly lacks the Dharma, one should simply state the truth accordingly; one must not deceive by speaking false teachings and thereby misleading the person before, which would instead result in [retribution].

This is a profound fault. If one were to subsume this under the three clusters of precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*): not being stingy with respect to oneself or others constitutes the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint); giving everything constitutes the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas);

and providing for beings according to their needs constitutes the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings). These precepts are collectively established for the seven classes of followers of the Bodhisattvas;

however, there are differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. In the Mahāyāna, one does not distinguish between those who are close or distant; whatever is sought is all given, and if one does not give, it is considered a transgression.

One commits all [offenses]. Because one’s original vow encompasses all beings, whereas in the Hīnayāna the disciples are not taught this method, one commits an offense of the seventh category (*saptama-varga*).

Not giving wealth is not proscribed; adding verbal abuse constitutes an offense according to the specific act, which is not considered grave. This involves both natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) karma.
Being stingy and parsimonious, because it lacks a heart of compassion, violates the Bodhisattva’s original intention; therefore, it is of the same nature [as the preceding offenses].

This is karma. Five conditions constitute its gravity: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of them as a sentient being; third, a mind of stinginess or disparagement; fourth, manifesting the signs of stinginess or disparagement;
and fifth, the other person’s acceptance of it. Regarding "first, a sentient being": this refers to the three types of objects—superior, middling, and inferior.

Regarding those who possess the precepts: all [acts] are grave; the rest are light. Second, regarding the perception of sentient beings: there are four cases—certain, doubtful, and mistaken—making six phrases.

Three are grave; three are light, as explained above. Third, regarding the mind of stinginess and disparagement: this refers to being malicious, angry, and miserly with regard to wealth or the Dharma, wishing to strike, revile, or refuse others.
This constitutes an offense. However, in this case, one's own stinginess and self-disparagement are precisely the primary factors of the karma. To instruct another...

Regarding the fourth [offense], manifesting signs of stinginess and disparagement: whether one conceals and withholds [possessions], or claims they do not exist at all, or drives others away with hands or a staff, or addresses them with abusive insults, or does so oneself, or causes another to beat or revile them—all such acts constitute grave offenses.

Fifth, regarding "the person before one experiences [the offense]": this refers to knowing that the other person perceives signs of one's stinginess and experiences the humiliation of being struck or reviled by one;

depending on the specific action or words, a grave offense is incurred. If that person sends a messenger to request wealth or to ask for the Dharma, and one acts with stinginess toward that messenger, [a grave offense is incurred].
To rebuke or scold from afar does not constitute a face-to-face injury or affliction; as such, it is somewhat lighter and does not result in a grave offense.
Even if an offense were grave, the precept would not be lost. The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "If a petitioner comes three times and one does not give, this is called a grave violation.
The *Śīla-sūtra-mūla* states: "One should observe sentient beings and, through skillful means, benefit them even by using harsh words."
If one refrains from acting out of fear that it will cause the other person distress, this constitutes an offense that arises from non-affliction.

There is no offense if one lacks the means oneself, or if one seeks an object that is not in accordance with the Dharma, or if the object would not benefit the other person, or if one employs skillful means to discipline them.

If that person has violated the king’s law, one may withhold wealth out of regard for the king’s mind; or if one is upholding the monastic regulations (*saṃgha-vinaya*), this clarifies that there is no offense in not giving wealth.
Furthermore, it is said: if a non-Buddhist seeks to find fault; if one is gravely ill; if one is insane; if the Dharma being practiced has not yet been mastered;
if the person is of dull faculties and would give rise to fear upon hearing the profound and sublime Dharma; or if one knows that after hearing it...
If it would increase wrong views, or if one speaks to an evil person—this clarifies that there is no offense in not granting the Dharma.

If the other person would not be fit to hear the Dharma yet would obtain wealth [thereby], it is appropriate to subject them to reproach and humiliation; in all such cases, there is no offense. Question: What constitutes being unfit to hear the Dharma yet obtaining wealth?

They ought to be rebuked. What constitutes cases where none are at fault? The answer is: those for whom it is inappropriate to hear the Dharma—meaning those with inferior faculties who are not suitable vessels, or those who would instead give rise to slander upon hearing it—and those for whom it is inappropriate to obtain wealth—meaning those who would use such wealth to commit evil.

Furthermore, because one may encounter misfortune due to wealth, it is appropriate to subject them to reproach and humiliation. This refers to those who are stubborn and foolish, who will reform and repent through punishment;
and those who are heroic and eminent, who will rise up through being broken and humbled. Such instances of stinginess and disparagement are precisely what bring such individuals to fulfillment;
how could there be any offense in this? Moreover, there are two cases where not giving does not constitute an offense: first, when the petitioner intends to use the wealth for [unwholesome] purposes.

It is evil. To harm others or harm living beings, yet not give and not transgress—these two cases involve returning to the ways of external paths after having requested the Dharma, or assisting in the teachings of external paths;
if one does not speak [of such things], there is no transgression. Even if one is further rebuked, it is still not called a transgression. The *Sutra on the Ten Wholesome Paths of Action* says:
"If one is free from greedy desire, one immediately attains the accomplishment of five kinds of mastery. First, mastery over the three karmas..."
1. Because of the perfection of the faculties; 2. Sovereignty over material wealth, because no enemies or thieves can seize it; 3.
Sovereignty over merit, because all things are provided according to one's heart's desire; 4. Sovereignty over royal status, because rare and wondrous objects are all offered as tribute;
5. The goods obtained exceed what was originally sought, being a hundred times more excellent, because...

In the past, because they were free from stinginess and envy, if they were able to dedicate [their merit] toward Bodhi, then at the time they later attained Buddhahood, they would be uniquely honored within the three realms and be venerated by all.
As for their retribution: the sin of stinginess and disparagement also leads to the three miserable realms.

Furthermore, as a residual retribution for stinginess regarding wealth, one is born into poverty; as a residual retribution for stinginess regarding the Dharma, one is dull-witted life after life. One should know this.

Avarice is subsumed within the wholesome root of non-attachment. According to this precept, it arises from the mind of renunciation, the mind of loving-kindness, the mind of compassion, the mind of giving, and the mind of benefiting, which emerge from the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground Precepts.
△ Ninth: The Three Precepts on Not Accepting Repentance Due to a Mind of Anger. First, the transgression and its cessation.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of anger, incites others to anger, or through the causes of anger, the conditions for anger, the methods of anger, or the karmic actions of anger—
"Anger" refers to a mind of evil wrath. When this mind first arises, it is first seen in the eyes; therefore, anger issues from the eyes.
"Being angry oneself" means harboring resentment within and containing poison in the heart, which then manifests externally through body and speech, giving rise to violence and evil;
thus, all three karmas are unwholesome. "Teaching others to be angry" means instructing another to act as one does oneself. Question:
Anger is not a pleasant thing; why, then, teach its practice? Answer: Ordinary people each have their own inherent nature, and thus they differ in being either fierce and violent or gentle and weak.
If one teaches them patience, they do not rejoice; if one teaches them anger, they gladly follow.

This is like the First Emperor of Qin, who was "wise" enough to expel the guests, or the Han Emperor who delighted in the "sack of wisdom. However, once anger arises, one immediately abandons the mind of compassion.
Among these, hatred and delusion are particularly grave. Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states: "In a single thought-moment, when a mind of anger arises, one million gates of obstruction open.

Furthermore, there are three reasons for teaching others to harbor anger: first, to borrow another's anger toward someone else in order to vent one's own resentment; second, [the second reason]; third, [the third reason].

Third, inciting others to feel hatred toward someone else and taking profit from it; this means causing those whom others resent to harbor mutual hatred and harm one another, thereby making it one's own pleasure.
Regarding the karmic action of dependent origination: the initial arising of a single thought of hatred serves as the cause.
Next, the continuity of the mind acts as the auxiliary condition (*pratyaya*). The various methods of beating and reviling constitute the phenomenon (*dharma*).

The completion of the act of anger and regret constitutes the karma (*karman*). Furthermore, as for the cause (*hetu*): it is the habitual seed of harboring resentment since beginningless time. As for the condition (*pratyaya*):

the object of the person toward whom one is angry appears before one. As for the phenomenon (*dharma*): the arising of a calculation that causes that person to suffer humiliation. As for the karma (*karman*): the three factors combine to produce anger. Therefore, it is so designated.
This is a grave offense. △ Second, regarding the observance of what is to be practiced and the avoidance of what is to be prohibited:
a Bodhisattva should give rise to roots of goodness in all sentient beings through non-contentious matters, and should constantly generate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.
The mind of filial piety and obedience.
"All sentient beings" is a general designation; "root" carries the sense of being able to produce, which is the very foundation for giving rise to goodness.
Not giving rise to a mind of anger is precisely the dharma of non-contention. This dharma of non-contention is itself the source of life.
It is the root of goodness and the essence of the six harmonies. One who can act in this way brings about the non-contentious cultivation of the roots of goodness in all sentient beings.
As for the mind of compassion, one regards all sentient beings equally, cherishing them as one would protect an infant, unable to bear causing them harm.
As for the mind of filial piety and obedience, one views all sentient beings as one’s own parents, unable to bear being contrary to them.

If one indulges in anger without ceasing, creating a barrier between oneself and sentient beings so that they cannot be reached, obstructing the Noble Path so it cannot be traversed, and severing the wisdom-life of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—how could this be the essence of a Mahāsattva? △ Third, the conclusion on the offense for violating the teachings.
On the contrary, if one reviles and insults all sentient beings— and even non-sentient beings— with harsh speech,

further striking them with the hand or attacking them with knives and staves, and if one’s malice still does not cease even when the other person seeks reconciliation and offers sincere apologies and thanks,
this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
Regarding "non-sentient beings," there are two pairs. First, the pair of the Real and the Manifested: this refers to those who transform illusory manifestations.
Although they lack sentience, if one perceives them as sentient beings and acts with anger or contempt, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).
Second, the pair of the Holy and the Mundane: this refers to the Buddhas and holy sages. There are three types of angry, evil karma. First, using internal form: the hand...
First, striking with external objects, such as knives or staves. Second, using both internal and external objects, such as striking with a knife or staff held in one's hand.
Furthermore, there is the verbal karma of committing offenses through harsh speech and insults; the bodily karma of committing offenses by striking with knives, staves, or hands;

and the mental karma of committing offenses because the mind does not cease its malice. These unwholesome actions of the three karmas are more ferocious than wolves or tigers, all arising from hatred.
Therefore, when a person seeks repentance, the physical and mental actions constitute two types of karma; the sincere words of apology and confession constitute verbal karma.

If one sincerely seeks repentance through these three types of karma yet remains unenlightened, they contravene the Buddha’s teachings above, lose their original mind in the middle, and fail to accord with the means of guidance below.
Thus, evil karma increases rather than diminishing, and the Holy Path remains obstructed and cannot be practiced. For this reason, such a person is called a bodhisattva.
Regarding the *pārājika* offense, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "It is better to have attachment than anger. Why? Attachment forms a proximate connection with sentient beings;
there is the Buddha-dharma that can be taught, enabling people to believe and follow it. Anger forms a remote connection with sentient beings;
even if they are fond of the Buddha-dharma, such persons will reject it and not believe. It further says: "I do not see [anyone among] all..."
Among the unwholesome states, there is none more grievous than hatred; therefore, hatred does not manifest in the higher realms, which is why they are called "heavens" (*deva*).

If these are subsumed within the three categories of precepts: not inciting others to anger constitutes the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint precept); giving rise to a mind of compassion constitutes the *kuśala-dharma-śīla* (precept of wholesome dharmas);

and giving rise to a mind of filial obedience constitutes the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings). These precepts are collectively established for the seven classes of bodhisattvas, encompassing both the Mahayana and Hinayana traditions.
They are different. It is the Great Being’s primary concern to gather in sentient beings; therefore, because it runs counter to the way of transformation, it is grave.

The Hīnayāna practitioner, seeking self-benefit and harboring anger toward others, commits an offense of the seventh category. This involves both natural and proscribed karma, arising from the single moment a mind of anger is produced.
Because it can destroy the life-force of wisdom, five conditions constitute a grave offense: first, the sentient being; second, the perception of them as a sentient being;

third, a mind of resentment and obstruction; fourth, manifesting an attitude of not accepting their apology; and fifth, the other person’s understanding of this. Regarding "first, the sentient being":

offenses against superior or middling objects are grave, while those against inferior objects are light. Furthermore, if the object possesses precepts, the offense is also grave, though they do not lose their own precepts. Second...

Regarding the "conception of sentient beings": there are four possibilities—affirmation, doubt, perversion, and the six cases as mentioned above. Third, regarding "the mind being obstructed by anger":
harboring resentment and hostility, one is unwilling to reconcile; this is precisely the primary karmic factor. Fourth, regarding "manifesting the sign of not accepting an apology":

either by closing oneself off and creating a barrier, or by speaking out and refusing to accept it. Fifth, regarding "the other person understanding": knowing that the other will not accept [the apology], one follows their lead.
The gravity of the karmic retribution incurred through verbal actions varies according to their severity. The *Śīla-sūtra* states:

"If a Bodhisattva offends another, or even if he does not offend, should cause another to harbor doubt, he must immediately offer an apology. If he harbors resentment or acts with contempt, and thus fails to apologize in accordance with the Dharma, [he incurs a transgression]."
If one perceives a transgression arising from defilement (*kliṣṭa*), yet does not feel resentment and by nature refuses to accept the confession, this is a transgression that is not defiled.
If one commits a transgression due to indolence or laziness, it is a transgression that is not defiled. Furthermore, it is said:

if one encounters sentient beings who ought to be rebuked, subdued, or punished and expelled, yet fails to rebuke them out of a defiled mind—or conversely, rebukes them [inappropriately]—[this constitutes a fault].
Not to subdue them, nor to punish or expel them, constitutes an offense arising from defilement.
There is no offense if the person before one lacks a sincere heart of repentance or lacks a pressing sense of remorse;

if the Bodhisattva, out of a mind of compassion, intends ultimately to cause them to deeply reform their past errors and never commit them again, and thus displays an appearance of anger or even proceeds to subdue them.
He subdues sentient beings who are stubborn and cruel, those shameless ones of evil nature and false views. Though he manifests outward authority, his heart is truly compassionate;

though his speech rebukes and scolds, his thoughts are filled with pity. This is the great function of a Great Being (Mahāsattva) in taming sentient beings who are fierce and rigid—how could it be compared to those possessed of the three poisons? Furthermore, regarding "not transgressing": if they desire him to act [in a certain way]...

Regarding impure actions: if one subsequently receives [retribution] and does not apologize, there is no offense. If one knows that the other person’s nature is prone to litigation, and that apologizing would only increase their anger, there is no offense in not apologizing.
If one knows that the other person is harmonious and patient, free from resentment, yet fears causing them shame or embarrassment, there is no offense in not apologizing.
Furthermore, regarding those who have committed no offense: if that person again gives rise to defiled attachment toward external paths or slanders the Noble Ones.
He has perfected wrong views. If his painful feelings increase, or if he is incurable, or if he is beyond conversation and difficult to instruct, or if he frequently gives rise to resentment;
or if, upon observation, one fears that because of him there will arise disputes based on what has been heard or contradictions;
or if there is mutual litigation, or strife within the Saṃgha, or a schism in the Saṃgha; or if he is not deceitful and possesses a sense of shame and remorse—gradually...

Regarding "repenting for oneself" and so forth, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra* states: "If one employs skillful means to bring another to submission, yet that person does not repent according to the Dharma and their mind remains unpacified, there is no offense in refusing to accept their confession."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Second Ground," states: "The transgression of anger also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.
If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, they are constantly sought out by others for their faults;
second, they are perpetually tormented and harmed by others. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The habitual tendencies of anger clash together, arising from..."
Because they conflict with one another, there exist the mountain of knives, the forest of swords, the axe, and the halberd. The *Sūtra on the Path of Ten Wholesome Actions* states:
"If one abandons anger and hatred, one immediately attains eight kinds of joyful mental qualities: first, a mind free from harm and affliction; second, a mind free from anger and hatred;
third, a mind free from contention and litigation; fourth, a mind that is supple, upright, and honest; fifth, the attainment of the compassionate mind of a noble one; sixth..."

1. Constantly performing acts of benefit and bringing peace and happiness to the minds of sentient beings. 2. Adorned with the marks of the seven parts of the body, one is universally revered and respected.

3. By means of harmony and patience, one is swiftly reborn in the Brahma-world; if one can further dedicate this merit toward Bodhi, then upon attaining Buddhahood, one will obtain the unobstructed mind of a Buddha, which those who behold it never tire of seeing.
According to these precepts, they proceed from the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground.
It arises from the mind of precept-keeping, the mind of patience, the mind of joy, the mind of loving-kindness, the mind of compassion, and the mind of filial piety.
△ Tenth: The Precept Against Slandering the Triple Gem. Three parts. First: The transgression of failing to practice restraint.

If a disciple of the Buddha slanders the Triple Gem themselves, or teaches others to slander the Triple Gem—whether through the cause of slander, the conditions for slander, the dharma of slander, or the karma of slander—"slander" (bàng) is a term denoting contrariety and opposition.

Generally speaking, when one's understanding does not accord with principle, one's words are not examined for truth, and one offers divergent views and interpretations, all such acts are termed "slander.
To "slander the Triple Gem oneself" means that one has not yet attained right view and has not yet understood.
Regarding profound principles, one may mistake the heterodox for the orthodox and the orthodox for the heterodox.

Whether by seeing heterodox scriptures, hearing the words of non-Buddhist practitioners, or following the criticisms of those in positions of power and influence, one then claims that the sūtras and vinaya of the Bodhisattvas were not spoken by the Buddha.
This constitutes slandering the Buddha; to claim that these are not Mahāyāna sūtras constitutes slandering the Dharma. Furthermore, it is said:
Those who uphold, recite, and study [such works] are not disciples of the Buddha; this constitutes slandering the Sangha.

Either they have conceived false understandings themselves and established false doctrines, claiming them to be correct; or they have received false teachings from evil teachers and composed false books.
It deludes the minds of people and misleads later scholars, causing them to lose the true path forever and fall into heterodox ways.
Because it has been propagated to subsequent generations and spread without ceasing, its sin cannot be pardoned.

To "teach others to slander" means to instruct others to revile [the teaching] as one does oneself, desiring to align with like-minded parties and strike down those who differ. Furthermore, there are those in the world who compose slanderous words and disseminate them.
In later generations, those who are beginners with shallow understanding follow suit and harmonize with this [false teaching]. This is both self-reproach and leading others astray;
it is truly complete in its faults. While seeking gratification for the present moment, they leave behind calamities for successive kalpas.

For those whose karma involves the Dharma, the initial arising of a mind of false views serves as the cause, while the continuous succession of that false mind, which assists in completing the act of slander, serves as the condition. They skillfully expound the methods of false views.

This constitutes a violation of the Dharma. Its function is to cause the person who has accepted it to fail to perceive the marks of the Triple Gem in the future and to undergo the sufferings of the three evil realms.
Furthermore, there are four meanings of "slander": first, establishing one's own sectarian school;
second, displaying one's own skills and arts; third, seeking favor with those in power; and fourth, deceiving and luring the ignorant. This precept is also called "slandering the Bodhisattva-piṭaka."

To preach doctrines that appear similar [to the truth], or what is called "false view," or to preach false precepts—this is termed in the *Śīla-sūtra* as "the precept against slandering and confusing the True Dharma.
This refers to one who, by means of their own false views, slanders and confuses the True Dharma; it does not refer to the slander of verbal abuse.
Even if one were to commit the slander of verbal abuse, the offense would still be light; only this offense is grave. II. The performance of observances and the commission of prohibitions.
When a bodhisattva sees a non-Buddhist or an evil person utter even a single word of slander against the Buddha’s voice, it is as if three hundred spears were piercing their heart;
how much more so when they slander him with their own mouths?

Whether in India or in this land, those among the followers of heterodox teachings—even up to the level of bodhisattvas—who seek the Dharma outside of the mind are all termed "externalists" (tīrthika).

This does not necessarily mean they are utterly perverse; rather, it refers to those who do not believe in the Mahāyāna or the eternally abiding Triple Gem, and thus abandon the great precepts of the mind-ground to study the heterodox teachings of external paths and deny the karmic retribution of good and evil. Such individuals are called "evil persons."

It is not necessarily because of some great crime. As for the "single word," it is so called because it is the very least; yet it is said that even this is like three hundred spears piercing the heart.
How much more so when one speaks at length, allowing slanderous sounds to spread abroad—how could the mind of a Great Being endure such a thing?

That "the sound of slandering the Buddha" is the *dharma* (the literal teaching), while "three hundred spears piercing the heart" is the *upamā* (the metaphor). By means of this metaphor, it illustrates the injury to one's own heart.
This is the ground. Regarding "sound" (*śabda*): it means that the resonance issues forth from that [ground], while the sound itself is what I have heard;

hence, it is called "sound. Question: In the sutras it is only said that one slanders the Buddha; what is the meaning of saying here that one slanders the Triple Gem? Answer: The Buddha is formed by the mind.

The Dharma proceeds from the mouth; the Sangha is manifested through the body. Since the body and mouth have the mind as their master, to slander the Buddha is, in effect, to slander the Dharma and the Sangha.
A Bodhisattva is one who has attained Buddhahood and takes the Three Jewels as his core resolve, universally wishing for all sentient beings to achieve Buddhahood.
Now, if one hears even a single word of slander against the Buddha, one severs the seeds of Buddhahood for the future. Therefore, it is as [stated above].

"Three hundred spears pierce the heart. This means that the harm is most extensive and the pain is all the more acute. When one sees non-Buddhists and evil people slandering the Buddha, the pain is already so piercing;
how much more so for those who have received the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts as his disciples?
To slander him with even a single word from the mouth is to become a non-Buddhist and an evil person. This is truly out of compassion for those of false views. From oneself—
They fall into hell and further lead immeasurable sentient beings to mistakenly enter the sea of suffering; therefore, it is said that this is like three hundred spears piercing the heart.
This does not mean that the precept was established merely to restrain the thought of anger toward those who slander the Triple Gem.
For the essence of the Triple Gem is like the sun and moon; a single finger cannot obscure their brilliance, just as one who hurls an axe to strike at heaven will instead wound themselves.
Furthermore, the Triple Gem will not bring blame upon them. △ Third, the conclusion regarding the offense for violating the teachings:

To fail to give rise to a mind of faith or a mind of filial piety, and instead further assist evil persons and those with false views in slandering [the Dharma], constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a Bodhisattva.
The Buddha is none other than the mind. To slander the Buddha now is to fail to believe that one's own mind is the Buddha; therefore, it is said that "one does not give rise to a mind of faith.
Since this violates the Buddha’s teachings, one lacks a mind of filial obedience; therefore, it is said that "one does not give rise to a mind of filial obedience.
Furthermore, a Great Being originally receives the Buddha’s true precepts through these two minds—faith and filiality—and should always respectfully obey the Three Jewels. Yet, [he] lacks...
To act in opposition is to slander oneself, which is contrary to reason. How could one further assist those of false views and evil persons in their mutual slandering and defamation?

Therefore, it is said that this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva. If these are subsumed within the three clusters of precepts (*trisaṃvara*), then not slandering oneself or others corresponds to the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint).

Viewing [false views] as thorns in the heart corresponds to the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the morality of gathering wholesome dharmas). Giving rise to faith and filial devotion corresponds to the *sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla* (the morality of benefiting sentient beings).

These precepts are collectively established for the seven classes of bodhisattvas, though they differ in their relative gravity. For the Mahāsattva, who takes the welfare of sentient beings as his primary responsibility, these are considered weighty.

In the Hīnayāna, it is taught that killing carries no karmic retribution, that sexual misconduct does not obstruct the path, and that views such as the world being finite or infinite are all termed "evil views.
Each instance of such speech constitutes an offense of the seventh category (*saptama-varga*). If one does not relinquish such views after three admonitions, the third *pārājika* offense is incurred.
Furthermore, if one does not relinquish [the view], the *karma* of "suspension for not relinquishing evil views" (*adṛṣṭi-tyāga-utksepa-karman*) is performed.

Although this is not a formal expulsion (*pravāsanīya*), the disciplinary penalty is the most severe, as it is intended to bring about the permanent abandonment of the evil view. Nevertheless, a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) is ultimately never incurred.

This also possesses both natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed (*prajñapti-sāvadya*) karmic actions; with wrong view as its basis, it further adds the fault of verbal transgression. These ten heavy precepts are all categorized as natural offenses.
Regarding this matter: in the Hīnayāna, alcohol is treated as a prohibitive precept (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*).

However, for a Mahāsattva, whose primary aim is to benefit sentient beings, alcohol is considered an intrinsic transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), because it causes others to become deluded in their mental ground. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "As for intrinsic precepts..."

This *śīla* consists of eight types, namely the three of the body and four of the speech, with the addition of [abstaining from] alcohol to guard the mental ground and thereby ensure a pure livelihood.
Thus, although the number differs, there is no difference in meaning between this and the last three mental actions among the ten wholesome paths of action.
As for "natural offenses" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), these are so called because they are not established by the Buddha's decree; their nature is inherently such.

Because it is evil, it is called an intrinsic offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). The *Zhiguan* states: "Regarding intrinsic precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*), regardless of whether one has received them or not, to violate them is itself an offense;
to observe them, whether received or not, is itself good. If one has received the precepts, observing them generates merit, while violating them incurs guilt."

If one does not receive [the precepts], there is no merit; yet one incurs the offense of violating the precepts, which consists solely of the offenses of misconduct and the paths of karma (*karmapatha*).

To say that "receiving [the precepts] leads to the offense of violation" means that, on top of a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), one further incurs the offense of violating the precepts. This transgression is established as grave when five conditions are met:
first, a sentient being; second, the perception of them as a sentient being; third, the intention to speak; fourth, the actual utterance; and fifth, the completion of the act.
Fifth, the understanding of the person before one. First, regarding "a sentient being": if one slanders with respect to the two higher objects (the Sangha and the Buddha), it is grave;

if toward a lower object (an ordinary person), it is light. Second, regarding the "perception of a sentient being": there are six cases, as can be understood from the previous [explanation]. Third, regarding the "intention to speak."
This refers precisely to the owner [of views]. It means that through the scheming of false views, one holds that "only this is real; all else is false.
Since the mind harbors such erroneous understanding, one delights in speaking of it to others. Although false views are numerous, there are four general categories:

first, the superior; second, the middling; third, the inferior; and fourth, the miscellaneous. The superior consists of the denial of cause and effect, such as among those like the icchantikas. The middling...
This refers to the case where one considers the Three Jewels to be inferior to non-Buddhist paths. If this is established within the mind, one loses the precepts.

However, if the mind recognizes that the Three Jewels are superior while the mouth says they are not, and one has not yet turned back [to the wrong path], the substance of the precepts is not lost; yet for every such utterance, a grave offense (duṣkṛta) is incurred. As for the lesser [offenses]:

To discard the great and take up the small. If one calculates that [the vow] is accomplished, one loses the bodhisattva precepts; if one calculates that it is not yet accomplished, a light offense is incurred. Regarding "mixed" [offenses]:

this refers to either biased attachment, or mixed faith, or being preoccupied with the Hīnayāna, or having erroneous conceptions regarding the meaning. There are two types of biased attachment. First:
To hold fast to the Great [Vehicle] while slandering the Small [Vehicle]. The *Śīla-sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva holds such a view and speaks thus:
'A bodhisattva should not listen to the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas; they should not accept them; they should not study them.

Of what use are the śrāvaka dharmas to a bodhisattva? This constitutes an offense arising from defilement. How could one know that the Buddhas of the three periods appear in the world and establish teachings according to the capacities of beings?"
In all teachings, the Three Vehicles are expounded. To those who are to be delivered by means of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, he manifests in the body of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.
These four fruits of the śrāvaka are, indeed, world-transcending sages and worthies, as well as fields of merit for humans and devas;

how could they be held in contempt? It was because [the Bodhisattvas] lacked the intention to benefit living beings that the Buddha rebuked them. However, he rebuked only their intention, not [their realization].

2. To have once reviled their practice; or, to engage in partial slander of one division of the teachings by claiming within the Vaipulya (fangděng) that a particular division was not spoken by the Buddha—this also constitutes a minor transgression.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva hears the profound meaning and the true meaning of the Bodhisattva Dharma-piṭaka, as well as the immeasurable spiritual powers of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, yet slanders and refuses to accept them, saying they are not beneficial...

The Tathāgata has taught that such [actions] likewise cannot bring peace and happiness to sentient beings; this constitutes a transgression arising from defilement. Regarding those with "mixed faith":

they do not reject cause and effect, nor the Triple Gem, nor the Mahāyāna; however, they merely claim that non-Buddhist spirits and deities also possess awesome power, or they submit petitions to exorcise spirits, or they even encourage others to do so—all these constitute minor offenses. As for those who fix their minds on the Hīnayāna: knowing...

The Mahāyāna is sublime and superior; yet, if one first desires to attain the minor fruits and only later cultivates the Great Vehicle, this is called "regression through thought" (*smṛti-vilopa*) and constitutes a light offense (*laghu-pāpa*).
Regarding those who misconstrue the meaning: if one knows that another is correct, yet forcibly seeks to establish a different view, all such instances constitute a light offense.
Regarding the four types of false speech: whether speaking for oneself, causing others to speak it, or committing it to writing.
Regarding compositions and the like: fifth, as for "the preceding person attaining understanding," this means that if one accepts erroneous speech, one incurs an offense for every word spoken;

*Chù* (黜) is pronounced *chū*. It carries the meaning of "degradation" or "reproach.

*Śīla* is translated here as "cooling," because by being free from the affliction of feverish distress, one attains coolness. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that its nature is wholesome (*kuśala*).
This means that one who delights in practicing the path of goodness and does not engage in negligence is said to possess *śīla*. This is a translation based on its etymological meaning.
It is also translated as "stopping and attaining" (*zhìdé*), because it involves stopping evil and attaining good. The direct translation is "precept" (*jiè*).
A precept is that which restrains; it refers to the ability to restrain all unwholesome phenomena.
Biography of Gao Fayian of Chang’an County, Yongzhou: He was the great-great-grandson of Gao Ying, the Minister of Works (Puyue) during the Sui dynasty.
On the twenty-fifth day of the first month in the third year of the Longshuo era, he went to the Central Secretariat to seek office.

At noon, he returned home. His residence was in Yining Ward, situated in the southern corner with its gate opening toward the street; it was located to the east of Huadu Monastery and belonged to the Gao family.
He intended to exit through Zixi Gate on the western side of the city wall. Once outside the city, two riders on horseback encountered him from within the city and pursued him from behind.
As they drew closer after he had passed through the gate, he found that to the north of the road outside the city wall was Puguang Monastery.
One person said to a mounted man, "Go and guard the gate of Puguang Temple; do not let this man enter. I fear he will be difficult to capture.
Following these instructions, the man galloped there to stand watch at the gate. Fayen was terrified and, unable to enter the temple, fled toward the west.
He eventually reached the south gate of the Jincheng Ward on the west street; to the west of the road was Huichang Temple.
The temple was further reinforced by four mounted riders, who then told the two men on horseback ahead: "Guard the gate of Huichang Temple immediately!
Fearing this, Fayuan hurriedly said to the rider beside him: "Who are you that dares to press upon me?"
The horseman said, "The King has sent me to fetch the Dharma-eye. He asked, "Which king has sent you? The horseman replied, "King Yama has sent me.
Upon hearing that he had been sent by King Yama, Fayen knew with certainty that he was a ghost;
he immediately resisted him. The ghost then became enraged and said, "Quickly cut off my hair! Another ghost seized a knife.

He immediately cut off both topknots of his Dharma-eye, which fell to the ground with the flesh attached. He then proceeded to the western street, where he fainted and fell from his horse, dying suddenly without awareness.
When he reached a major intersection on the main road, he hesitated for a moment; more than a thousand people were watching.
The head of the western street was a noble residence, so he called his family members to carry him toward the house. Only at dawn did he regain consciousness, and he spoke to his family.
The palace lady said: "I entered hell and saw King Yama seated upon a high throne. He rebuked me with anger, saying:
'For what reason did you eat the fruits belonging to the permanent endowment of the monks within the quarters of Master Mingzang at Huadu Temple?
He then compelled me to swallow four hundred pellets of glowing iron. As I swallowed them, my throat constricted and my body was scorched and shriveled."
It turned red; only after swallowing it did he revive. On the twenty-sixth day, when he regained consciousness, various ghosts came again to seize his Dharma-eye and bring him before the king.
The king said, "For what reason do you fail to revere the Triple Gem?"
He spoke of the faults and evils of the Saṃgha, saying: "Once you have swallowed these iron balls until they are exhausted, you shall deserve to have your tongue ploughed by an iron plow.
On the twenty-ninth day of the first month you will awaken; at dawn on the thirtieth day you will die again. Upon reaching hell, you will again undergo the plowing of your tongue by an iron plow.
You will see for yourself that your tongue is several li long, while bystanders see it protruding more than one chi."
The king spoke again to the wardens of hell, saying, "Because this man has spoken ill of the Triple Gem, cut off his tongue with a great iron axe.
The wardens struck it, but they could not sever it. The king spoke again, saying, "Mince his tongue finely with the axe."
He was about to be placed in a cauldron of boiling water to be cooked, yet he did not soften even as he was boiled. The King, again wondering at this, asked for the reason.
Fayen replied to the King, saying, "I once read the *Lotus Sūtra*. The King still did not believe him and ordered that his ledger of meritorious deeds be inspected.
He saw within the records that there was one copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* read by him. When the King verified that this was true, he finally released him from prison, and the man appeared [before him].

Those who observed him were as numerous as a marketplace; those who saw him were inspired to resolve their minds [for enlightenment]. The entire family came to believe and revere him, exerting themselves with diligence and maintaining sincere earnestness without weariness.
This was known by both the clergy and the laity throughout the capital. Excerpted from the *Fayuan zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma).

A bhikṣu who upholds the precepts maintains his discipline like one carrying a life-preserving float across the ocean. He protects living beings so as not to harm them, just as one would handle grass tied together without damaging it.

Regarding the compassionate benevolence of the Cakravartin Kings, it is said that although there are four types of Cakravartins who bring all quarters under their majestic authority, there are also distinctions between them.

The Iron-Wheel King rules the Southern Continent alone; he establishes order only after exerting his martial prowess. The Copper-Wheel King rules the two continents of the East and South; they submit only when his majesty is made to resound.

The Silver-Wheel King rules the three continents of the East, South, and West; they are brought to submission only upon the dispatch of envoys. The Golden-Wheel Universal Monarch’s virtue vibrates throughout the four continents;
they submit to his transformation at the mere sight of his presence. Therefore, he is named a Holy King (*cakravartin*).
The "Three Paths" (*santāpa*) refers to paths or ways, meaning the destinations one approaches. It is also called "coating with fire and charcoal" (*tuotan*), which signifies torment and injury.
The *Sūtra on the Four Deliverances* states: First, the Path of Fire, which is the realm of hell (*nāraka-gati*). This is named after its heat;
it refers to the sentient beings suffering there who are constantly oppressed by boiling cauldrons and furnace coals. Second, the Path of Blades, which is the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*).

This is the realm of ghosts (*preta*). It derives its name from "driving and pressing," meaning that the sentient beings suffering in that place are constantly driven and pressed by blades and staves.
Third is the path of blood, which is the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
It derives its name from "mutually devouring," meaning that the sentient beings suffering in that place—where the strong subdue the weak—devour one another and drink blood.
This is because of eating meat.

Recorded by the Vinaya-transmitting Śramaṇa Shuyu of the Wanshou Precept Platform at Zhaoqing Monastery in Ancient Hangzhou, based on the first volume of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* as expounded by the Buddha. Transcribed by Qinggu.
△ Second, the forty-eight minor precepts. Part one: Continuing from the previous section to introduce what follows. Part two: The formal exposition of the precept characteristics.
Part three: A summary of the observance and recitation.
Now, the first: The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "The ten *pratimokṣa* rules have already been expounded; the forty-eight minor precepts are now [to be taught]."
"It shall be explained.
From "The Buddha told [them]" onwards, this承接 (takes up) what preceded. From "Prātimokṣa" onwards, this initiates what follows.
"Bodhisattvas" refers to all listeners, including those of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sanctity. It does not say "ten pāramitās," but rather says "prātimokṣa."
This means that if one violates it, one incurs an extremely grave offense; if one upholds it, one attains the fruit of liberation. "Minor" is said in contrast to "grave.
As for what shall now be explained, it refers to the Tathāgata’s repeated exhortation to the assembly to listen with a single-minded focus.
△ Second, the correct exposition of the characteristics of the precepts, in five parts: 1. Precepts concerning lack of respect and so forth; 2. Precepts concerning envoys of states and so forth; 3.
Precepts concerning anger and retaliation and so forth; 4. Precepts concerning non-ransom and so forth; 5. Precepts concerning selection and so forth. In the first [section], there are two parts.

First, the enumeration of the ten characteristics. First: The precept against disrespecting teachers and friends. 2. First, the performance of observance and the violation of cessation. 3. First, exhorting others to receive [the precepts].
The Dharma. If,
O Sons of the Buddha, you wish to receive the position of a king, the position of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), or when officials receive their positions,
you should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts.

The meaning of "Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) is as explained above. A "king" (*rājan*) refers to one who governs and oversees the people, such that the whole world looks up to him with reverence.
A "wheel-turning king" (*cakravartin rājan*) refers to one whose virtue shakes the four continents and who employs the wheel [of dharma] to assist in transformation.

"Ministers of state" (*amātya*) refers to those from the Three Ducal Ministers at the top down to the governors and magistrates of the provinces and counties, including all civil and military officials. Regarding those who should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts: this...
This reveals the majestic power of the virtue of precepts. Those who wish to ascend to a position of honor and nobility must first establish their foundation;
once the foundation is established, blessings flourish. It is from this that sagacious sovereigns and virtuous ministers emerge—all of which are benefits derived from receiving the precepts.
Regarding the initial exhortation to the king and his ministers: this means that the Buddha-dharma universally encompasses all, from the highest to the lowest; logically, it ought to be so.

As for not mentioning the monks and nuns: since the method of receiving the precepts is the fundamental duty of the five groups of the ordained, the intention is universal while the phrasing is specific, making further exhortation unnecessary.
Furthermore, the reception of the Dharma comes first, while the reception of rank comes later.
This means that a king possesses the power of transformation and the merit of encouraging virtue; therefore, he is exhorted first. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:
