"If a king receives the bodhisattva precepts and extensively practices the ten wholesome dharmas to transform sentient beings, his body and mind will experience joy, the three calamities will never occur, he will remain far removed from the eight difficulties, and the realm will be peaceful and secure for its people."
This is the joy of fulfillment. Therefore, one first receives the Bodhisattva’s precepts of wisdom, and subsequently receives the position of merit as a king or minister.
Thus, a verse in the *Cittabhūmi-parivarta Sūtra* says: "The various blessings and joys that you, O King, now enjoy, were once maintained through the three clusters of precepts in the past."

This refers to the attainment of the Dharma-body through the retribution induced by the cultivation of the virtue of precepts, thereby obtaining the wondrous fruits of humans and devas. △ Second, the benefits gained from receiving the Dharma:
all ghosts and spirits shall protect the person of the King and the persons of his ministers; and all Buddhas shall rejoice.
"All ghosts and spirits" refers collectively to the various deities who protect the Dharma. "Protecting the king’s person" means not forgetting the Buddha’s command;
thus, they protect the king’s person so that his position may be preserved forever, and they protect the persons of the hundred officials.

Their rank was advanced accordingly. Because the kings and ministers revered the Triple Gem and received the Buddha’s precepts, spirits and deities provided protection and their persons were at peace;
the three calamities gradually subsided, rain and wind were always harmonious, and the myriad people benefited therefrom. Thus it is said:
When the king is at peace, the world is at peace; when the king possesses merit, the world possesses merit. Thus, the *Cittaviśuddhiprabhāsa Sūtra* states:

"If there is a king who achieves right view and transforms the world according to the Dharma, he is called a Lord of Heaven (*devendra*), for he transforms the world with the wholesome dharmas of the heavens.
Consequently, the various heavenly deities and the Four Heavenly Kings constantly come to provide him with protection."

Because he guards the royal palace, although he dwells among humans, he cultivates the deeds of the devas. Because his mind regarding rewards and punishments is free from partiality, such a holy sovereign is called a King of the True Dharma (*saddharmarāja*).
Furthermore, a verse in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says: "Because he is protected by the various devas, he is also named a Son of Heaven (*devaputra*).
The Lord of the Thirty-three Devas divides his power to protect the human king, as do the hosts of stars."

The movements of the planets follow their proper stations; the sun and moon do not deviate from their courses; gentle breezes always accord with the seasons; and sweet rains fall in accordance with the time.
All the hosts of devas fill their respective palaces. Therefore, you, O King of Men, have sacrificed your own person to propagate the True Dharma.
Therefore it is said: "All ghosts and spirits shall protect and defend the person of the king and the persons of his hundred officials.
Now, if even those who uphold the five precepts are still protected by twenty-five deities, how much more so for those who uphold the bodhisattva precepts?

If even commoners who receive the precepts are protected by ghosts and spirits, how much more so for kings and officials? That "all Buddhas rejoice" means that the king and his ministers have faith in and accepted the precepts.

The Dharma is thus joyful; because ghosts and spirits follow its teachings and provide protection, they are glad. Receiving the precepts brings blessings that shelter the netherworld, which is why ghosts and spirits offer their protection.
Furthermore, one can widely propagate and protect the transformative influence of the Dharma, whereby all Buddhas rejoice.
Therefore, anyone who wishes to consolidate their station must first receive these precepts. △ Third, attaining the Dharma and its corresponding practice.
Once the precepts have been received, one should give rise to a mind of filial obedience and a mind of reverence.

Upon seeing elders, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), instructors (*ācārya*), those of great virtue, fellow students, those of the same view, and those of the same practice, one should rise to welcome them, prostrate, and inquire after their well-being.

The mind of filial piety (*kṣiao-jing*) is the very essence of possessing the precepts (*śīla*). To practice according to the Dharma is called "filial" (*xiao*); to not transgress the Buddha’s regulations is called "obedient" (*shun*);
to honor the noble and yield to the virtuous is called "reverent" (*gong*); to maintain solemn decorum and serve with devotion is called "respectful" (*jing*).
These four states of mind all arise from the intention; therefore, it is said that one "generates a mind of filial obedience and reverence. As for "having already attained," it means:
This proclaims that although the precepts were established by the Buddha, their reception must necessarily proceed through a teacher; therefore, one should practice filial piety and reverence.
As for the term "Elder" (*upādhyāya*), it means that there is no one superior to him. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there are three kinds of elders:

first, the elder by seniority of birth, because his years of ordination (*kaṭhināstaraṇa*) precede others; second, the elder by merit, because he is honored and respected by the assembly; and third, the elder by the nature of the Dharma (*dharmatā*).
Because they have entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), this refers to a *śīla-varga-sthavira* (an elder by seniority of ordination).
The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states: "Those who have received the precepts for twenty years up to forty-nine years are called elders.

King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha’s disciples as "superior persons" (*uttama-puruṣa*), because they stand above kings, ministers, officials, and commoners. *Upādhyāya* means "one who gives birth through power" (*balotpādaka*). This is because...
"By the power of the Master, I have given birth to the body of my untainted, wondrous precepts.

*Ācārya*—here translated as "Model" (*guǐfàn*)—is the meaning of "Master," signifying one who can uphold dignified deportment (*vīryāpatha*) to establish a model for others, and who instructs disciples in the rules for maintaining the precepts and the methods of spiritual practice. *Bhadanta* signifies a term of honor, meaning...
It is capable of possessing great merit because it penetrates from above to below. In the case of the Buddha, this means that the Way has been perfected and virtue is complete;

having reached the bottom and exhausted the source, he possesses vast majesty and virtue. In the case of the preceptor and teachers, it refers to their strict observance of the precepts and the protection of dignified deportment, as they possess vast conduct and virtue. Regarding fellow students, it means those who share the same teacher and the same school.
Because they study the Mahāyāna Dharma, those who share the same view possess a single understanding in their minds, for they perceive the principle of the Mahāyāna.
Those who practice the same conduct possess a single karma in their bodies, for they cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna.

As for the aforementioned teachers, they are models for humans and devas and are the vessels that ferry across the world; all manner of goodness is accomplished through them, and the myriad practices are established because of them. Therefore...
The Vinaya states: "One should regard one's *upādhyāya* and *ācārya* as one regards the Buddha; one must not be disrespectful or negligent toward them.

As for a 'friend' (*mitra*), this refers to one who can discern the character of others, assist in cultivating virtue, and aid in spiritual practice. All seeds of awakening do not sprout without a friend; all unwholesome dharmas are not eliminated without a friend.
When a teacher or a friend approaches, one should immediately rise from one's seat to welcome and prostrate to them. (The character "承," *chéng*, means to receive or attend to.)

This refers to serving and welcoming; "welcoming" means receiving with honor. As for "li" (propriety), it signifies principle. To be reverent and humble, advancing and retreating according to measure—this constitutes the great principle.
As for "bai" (bowing), it signifies submission. In secular ritual, there are two bows, taking the two polarities (*liangyi*) as the model; there are also four bows.
The taking of the four bows corresponds to the Four Images (*xiàng*). As for the explanation of the prostrations:

the three prostrations symbolize the dedication of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, through which one takes refuge in the Three Jewels and attains liberation from the three poisons. Regarding "inquiry" (*wèn xùn*): it refers to inquiring with words.

This means that after the prostrations have been performed, one should display a relaxed countenance and a harmonious expression, look straight ahead with right mindfulness, and inquire, saying: "I trust you are free from illness and affliction; how are your daily activities?"
"Are you at ease? Are you well? The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* states: "Is the road clear and peaceful? Are the four great elements in harmony? Are you at peace while sleeping and waking?

One should inquire in this manner according to the occasion, as there is no fixed rule for such matters. All of this constitutes honoring the dharma of the precepts and practicing the way of filial piety and reverence.
Furthermore, one should manifest respect through the mental faculty by welcoming and prostrating; through the physical faculty by inquiring after one's well-being.

Regarding their daily activities, one should show reverence through verbal karma. Thus, with these three types of karma practiced with utmost sincerity, the heart of filial piety and respect is fully realized.
△ Second, violating the teachings and incurring transgression:
yet the Bodhisattva, on the contrary, gives rise to arrogance, pride, delusion, and anger, failing to rise to welcome or prostrate in greeting. First.
First, regarding improper offerings: one must provide for them by selling oneself, or by offering kingdoms, cities, men, women, the seven treasures, and all manner of goods.
Failing to do so constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).
"Those who act contrary to their birth" clarifies that such behavior is improper. "Arrogance" (māna) means exalting oneself; "conceit" (atimāna) means disregarding others;
"delusion" (moha) means failing to recognize those who are worthy sages; and "anger" (dveṣa) means feeling resentment toward those who should be loved.

Thus, arrogance and conceit lead to a lack of reverence, while delusion and anger lead to a lack of filial piety. If one harbors even one of these four mental states within, its characteristics will manifest.
Regarding external [objects], one does not rise to welcome or prostrate. As for "making offerings" (*pūjā*): advancing and practicing with material wealth is called "offering" (*pūjā*);

that which provides sustenance is called "nourishment" (*yā*). Furthermore, presenting what is below to what is above is called "offering"; providing support from a lower position to a superior is called "nourishment."
Any act of making offerings that is not in accordance with the Dharma is not the way of a son of the Buddha.

Selling one's own body is the ultimate expression of teaching others to honor the Dharma and of exhausting one’s sincerity and strength; it is like the example of Sadāprarudita selling his heart and liver to study the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
By extension, this applies to giving away kingdoms, cities, men, and women. This is also a case of citing the most significant instance to illustrate the lesser ones.
This means that one should still perform such offerings; how much more so should one not fail to observe the rites of prostration?

As for the "seven treasures," they refer to gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, crystal, and red pearls. "Hundred things" is a general term for the total number of material requisites for sustaining the body.
However, these include both internal wealth, such as one's own body and life, and external wealth, such as kingdoms and the like, which are more remote.

Furthermore, one’s conditioned environment—cities and towns—and one’s primary retribution—male and female kin—ranging from the noble, such as the seven treasures, to the humble, such as common goods, all may be sold.
Since you have become a child of the Buddha, you should value the Dharma in this way; for even if people today are poor, [they would not sell their own bodies].
It would be better to have no possessions at all than to go so far as to sell one's own children or wife; because one values wealth more highly than the Dharma, one incurs an offense.
Otherwise—that is, if one does not show such reverence and provide offerings as described above—one incurs the minor secondary offense (*āpatti-dukkaṭa*).
Regarding the term "light defilement" (*āpatti-laghu-mala*): although this offense is lighter than the ten grave offenses, it can nevertheless defile the fundamental ground of the mind;
therefore, it is called a "light defilement. One should perform the repentance for a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense. If one does not repent, it will obstruct the Bodhisattva precepts.
At the time of repentance, one must consult those who know the Dharma before the offense is extinguished. This is like the method of repentance for a Bhikṣu’s *duṣkṛta* offense.
This shall be explained below within each individual precept; it need not be further detailed here. According to this principle, this precept should likewise possess four aspects:

cause, condition, dharma, and karma. However, because minor secondary offenses (light stains) are categorized as "misdeeds" (duṣkṛta)—whether they are fully established or not—and because they involve both natural and proscribed karma (*prakṛti-sāvadya* and *prajñapti-sāvadya*), arrogance must not be allowed to grow, as it hinders spiritual progress.

It was established as a precept because it is wholesome. A transgression is constituted by four conditions: first, the presence of a teacher or a spiritual friend, meaning an elder (*sthavira*) or a fellow practitioner;
second, the perception of them as a teacher or spiritual friend (which comprises six permutations: two cases of grave offenses, two cases of light offenses, and two cases of no offense);
third, a lack of respect. As stated in the *Bodhisattva Upāsaka Pañcaśīla Sūtra*: "If one is questioned and does not answer according to reality, one commits a grave defiled offense."
If one commits this offense without the presence of pride, anger, or delusion, it constitutes a minor transgression (*āpatti*). Furthermore, the *Śīla-sūtra* states:

"If, out of arrogance or resentment, one fails to rise to greet or bow in salutation, it is an afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) transgression. If, however, it is due to laziness, indolence, a neutral or distracted state of mind, or forgetfulness, it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There are four cases where one should have greeted but did not, or should have offered hospitality but did not, and so forth."

If the matter is completed, one incurs a minor offense of defilement (*āpatti-dukkaṭa*). If these are subsumed within the three clusters of precepts: filial piety and respect constitute the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint precept);

receiving, welcoming, and prostrating constitute the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas); and providing offerings according to the Dharma constitutes the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings).

These apply equally to the seven assemblies and are common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; however, prohibitions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) are not waived, for teachers, friends, and spiritual mentors (*kalyāṇamitra*) are the great causes and conditions for attaining the Way and are essential for its completion.

Regarding the holy life (*brahmacarya*): if one lacks respect, one will forever lose the benefits of the Dharma and be possessed by Māra. If one possesses respect, one will constantly encounter favorable conditions and accomplish the Buddha-dharma.
As for those who do not commit an offense: if one is ill; if one is listening to or preaching the Dharma; if one has previously been engaged in conversation with another;
or even for the sake of protecting the feelings of many people, as well as in cases of insanity and so forth.
△ Second, the precept against drinking alcohol. This has two parts: first, the offense of commission; second, the observance of restraint. First, the offense of commission:

If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally drinks alcohol—wherein the faults arising from alcohol are immeasurable—and if one passes a vessel of alcohol with one's own hand to another to drink, they shall be without hands for five hundred lifetimes, let alone drinking it oneself.
Therefore, "those who drink" refers to those who intentionally consume it, not those who do so through error or ignorance. Regarding the phrase "the faults arising from alcohol are immeasurable":
this means that alcohol is the gateway to all calamities, and its transgressions are beyond counting; hence, they are said to be "immeasurable.

For example, Sāgata possessed the power to subdue dragons, yet he lay prostrate on the ground in a state of ignorance; likewise, the upāsaka [Vīradatta] led others away from the wrong of stealing chickens.
All their precepts were utterly lost. King Zhou of Shang was powerful and fierce, yet he perished along with his lineage for his "frying-iron" torture and his practice of drinking like oxen.
Kou Qianzhun achieved great merit at the Battle of Shanyuan, yet he failed in his mission because he leaked confidential words. Such are the benefits and harms of the faults of drinking alcohol;
this is precisely why the ancients would rather abandon wine than abandon their own integrity. Furthermore, within the Vinaya, there are thirty-six more [precepts concerning intoxicants].
[These] losses all arise from alcohol. Regarding the act of passing a vessel of wine to others to drink, there are two interpretations:
first, holding the vessel to encourage one another; second, passing an empty vessel to allow for pouring.

As for "being handless for five hundred lifetimes," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: There are five offenses of drinking alcohol, through which one suffers for five hundred lifetimes. First, for five hundred lifetimes...
For five hundred lifetimes they were in the Hell of Salty Dregs; for five hundred lifetimes in the Hell of Boiling Excrement;
for five hundred lifetimes in the Hell of Curved Worms; for five hundred lifetimes in the Hell of Flies and Gnats;
for five hundred lifetimes in the Hell of Ripening Folly like Insects; and for the present five hundred lifetimes, it was because they were in their final existence among humans.
Because alcohol is a medicine for delusion, one receives retribution by being born among the "delusion-maturing" worms.

If giving even a vessel of wine from a broken jar to another person to drink results in such a karmic response, how much more so for one who drinks it themselves—how could they not incur grave transgressions? Question: There are many who drink alcohol.
Question: Why are those without hands so few? Answer: It is not necessarily only among humans; species such as snakes, earthworms, leeches, and eels all receive the retribution of being handless.
Thus, beginning with the brine and ending with the five hundred [years], it is called "the ripening of delusion.

This means that they are dull-witted and intoxicated by their state, remaining stubbornly ignorant; this is precisely the retribution for being handless. △ Second, the observance of prohibitions (śīla).
Furthermore, one must not teach any person to drink, nor should one encourage any sentient being to drink alcohol, let alone drink it oneself.
No kind of alcohol whatsoever may be consumed.
"Any person" refers to those who are householders or renunciants, men or women, young or old, and even those from other regions or foreign lands.
"All sentient beings" refers to non-humans of various species, as well as ghosts, animals, and the like.
"All kinds of alcohol" means that since there are many different types of alcohol, they are mentioned collectively. "One must not drink" is a prohibitive term;
it constitutes the very essence of this precept. While the preceding grave precept prohibited the buying and selling [of alcohol], this precept prohibits drinking it oneself.

Furthermore, not drinking [alcohol] oneself is the virtue of self-benefit; not teaching others to drink is the virtue of benefiting others. When these two benefits are practiced together, all evils cease of their own accord.
The *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: A hungry ghost asked, "Since birth, I have been dull-witted and ignorant. What sin has caused this?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "When you were a human being, you gave alcohol to others and furthermore forced them to drink."

One who encourages others to drink alcohol causes them to become disoriented, their cognitive faculties to become clouded and deluded; they now receive this "flower-retribution," while the actual fruit awaits in hell.

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "If one gives alcohol to those gathered in the Saṃgha, to those who have received the precepts, to those who are tranquil, to those with minds of cessation, or to those who have attained meditative concentration, because it turbidly disturbs such persons, one falls into the Raurava Hell. As it says:
As clarified in the sutras, is this not indeed to be feared? △ Third, the conclusion on the offense for violating the teachings:
If one intentionally drinks [alcohol] oneself or instructs others to drink it, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding the offenses herein: if one violates the Buddha’s prohibitions, whether acting on one’s own initiative or instructing others, both are charged with a light defilement (*āpatti*).
The Vinaya states: "If one consumes *kiṭṭa* (malt) or dregs that can intoxicate a person, one incurs an offense for every swallow; this constitutes a prohibited action (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*).

It is prohibited because it causes the nature to become confused and deluded. An offense is established through four conditions: first, it must be alcohol, meaning a drink that intoxicates a person; second, it must be... [alcohol].
The conceptualization [of this precept] consists of six phrases: two are grave, two are light, and two are non-offenses. Third, there is the intention to drink; fourth, it enters the mouth;

with each swallow, one incurs an offense. If these are subsumed within the three clusters [of training], "not drinking alcohol oneself" constitutes the restraint of the ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), which abandons all faults.

The precept of wholesome dharmas: not instructing others to drink [alcohol] is the precept of sustaining life (*saṃvara-śīla*). It applies equally to the seven assemblies and is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
There is no transgression in cases such as illness where it cannot be cured without alcohol, or in the case of those who are insane or deranged.

The *Compendium of the Essentials of All Sutras* states: Alcohol has many faults and opens the door to negligence. Even if one drinks as little as a mustard seed, the accumulation of transgressions becomes vast.
If it is for the sake of curing illness, this was not among the prohibitions established previously; rather, it is the Tathāgata’s great compassion that permits it for the sake of disease.
However, one must not drink before being ill, nor greedily consume it while forgetting the Vinaya, as was the case with the consort of King Prasenajit in the past.

Māluṅkyāputra, after receiving the precepts from the Buddha, she encountered a situation where the king intended to execute a kitchen official. The lady served wine to the king at a banquet and encouraged him with shared merriment.
Delighted by the lady’s drinking, the king became so absorbed in his pleasure that he forgot about the execution, and the punishment was consequently suspended.
The lady went to the Buddha to confess her transgression. The Buddha said, "One who drinks in such a manner attains great and wholesome benefit.
Seeing the capacity [of the recipient], he employed skillful means; thus, it was not a violation of the precepts. This was a temporary expedient; how can it be constrained by ordinary rules?
If one lacks the mind of Mallikā yet imitates the deeds of Mallikā, the offense is difficult to escape. Only if one can truly be like Qi..."

As for the monk Tanyuan, who, while intoxicated, contended in debate with the Daoist priests (huángguān) and caused countless Daoists to submit to the Buddha-dharma—causing the Dharma to flourish greatly thereby—he incurs no transgression. Should it not have been so, the retribution would have been according to the law.
△ Third: The Precept Against Eating Meat. Part Two. First: The Transgression of Committing the Act and the Maintenance of Abstinence. First: The Transgression of Committing the Act.
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally eats meat—no meat whatsoever may be eaten—one who eats meat cuts off great compassion.
The seed of Buddha-nature is seen and abandoned by all sentient beings;
therefore, it is clear that those who eat meat are not mistaken.
"All meats" refers to any being, whether of water, land, or air—provided it is the body of a sentient being—it is entirely impermissible to eat. Thus, all meat...

This arises from the taking of life. To inflict injury and slaughter, to harm living beings, and to cause others to undergo death in order to provide for oneself—merely fearing one's own hunger while disregarding the suffering of death; to kill another to sustain oneself—is this endurable in the heart?
It severs the seeds of Buddha-nature, which possess three meanings: first, it injures loving-kindness (*maitrī*); second, it injures compassion (*karuṇā*); and third...
It violates the Buddha-nature. This means that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature and are of the same essence as oneself;
how, then, could one eat their flesh? Furthermore, the Bodhisattva takes compassion as his foundation and the benefit of others as his concern.

Compassion entails uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness, while the intent to benefit entails extensively practicing acts of utility. To eat meat violates both of these practices. How [could this be permissible]?
They are called "sons of the Buddha. Furthermore, that which possesses great compassion is the unsurpassed bodhicitta.
To sever this mind is to sever the seed of buddha-nature. Once the seed is severed, what will then serve as the root for attaining Buddhahood?
Therefore, it is said that severing great compassion is to sever the seed of buddha-nature. As for all sentient beings who see [this] and abandon it:

This means that because the habituation to killing has not been eliminated, one still gives rise to fear and terror. It is like the seagull fleeing from the fisherman’s trap, or the pigeon startled by the shadow of the Arhat;

trembling and alarm do not cease. How much more so when one eats its flesh, or sees and hears its form, color, and breath—how could one not be struck with awe and dread, and thus distance oneself from it?
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Hunters, butchers, those who catch fish, and those who net birds..."

When evil persons and the like see him, dogs bark in alarm; when beasts see him, they flee in haste. All sentient beings—whether flying in the air, moving on water, or dwelling on land—upon seeing him, all think to themselves:
"The breath of this person is like that of a rākṣasa; now that he has come here, he will surely kill me.
For the sake of protecting their lives, they all run away to avoid him; hence it is said that "seeing him, they abandon [the place] and depart. Question:
The Sūtra states that when a person who eats meat enters a mountain forest, tigers, wolves, and lions all gather around him.
Why, then, is it said here that all sentient beings see him and depart? Answer: Those who depart do so because they are startled by his murderous intent and distance themselves;
those who gather come because they smell their own kind and seek one another out. Whether they depart or gather, both actions stem from evil.
This is the causal condition. △ Second, the observance of restraint:
For this reason, no Bodhisattva may eat the flesh of any sentient being; to eat meat incurs immeasurable transgressions.
"Therefore" summarizes the meaning of the preceding text: if there is compassion, one approaches; otherwise, one departs.
"All Bodhisattvas" refers to those from the very first who have received the precepts, up to those who have not yet attained the stages (*bhūmi*).

As for those Bodhisattvas who have already ascended to the stages, they themselves know the fault of eating meat while maintaining the precepts. Regarding the Small Vehicle, it initially permitted three kinds of "pure" [meat].
Regarding meat: it is said that in those lands, the ground abounds with sand and gravel, and grasses and vegetables do not grow.

Out of compassion, the Tathāgata, through his supernatural power, manifested these as a temporary expedient; they were truly not the physical parts of sentient beings, and immediately after [the manifestation], they vanished.
How could there be anyone who eats meat and yet be called a child of the Buddha? Therefore, it is said: "No Bodhisattva whatsoever may eat even a single [bit of meat]."
This refers to the flesh of all sentient beings. To say that eating meat incurs immeasurable sins means that such karmic offenses are manifold and not of a single kind.
With one's mind shrouded by false views and craving for the pleasures of the palate, one accumulates evil with every thought and inflicts injury upon compassion with every morsel.
As days and years pass, the karmic offenses become beyond counting; thus it is said that one incurs immeasurable sin.
Nevertheless, although all sentient beings may change their heads and faces and differ in physical appearance, their Buddha-nature—the instinct to cling to life and fear death—remains no different.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* clearly explains that there are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat, stating that [sentient beings...]
Because one is constantly associated with the six types of kin; because one is produced from the growth of impure elements;
because all sentient beings who smell one’s breath give rise to terror, like a dog that barks in alarm upon seeing a *caṇḍāla*; because compassion does not arise; because incantations do not succeed;
because one is abandoned by the various devas; because there are many evil dreams at night; and because tigers and wolves scent one’s odor.
Because of many various diseases. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Those who eat meat, even if they attain an opening of the mind that resembles *samādhi*, are all great *rākṣasas*;
when their retribution ends, they will inevitably fall into the bitter sea of birth and death.
How could such people escape the three realms? A ghost asked Maudgalyāyana: "Since my birth, I have had many sons, all of whom were handsome..."
It is truly a matter for joy. Yet they all died young; when I think of it, my heart breaks and the pain is beyond words. What sin has caused this? Maudgalyāyana replied:

"When you were a human being, you saw your children kill living beings, and you rejoiced in it while eating their meat. Because of the killing, their lives were short; because of your rejoicing, you suffer this bitter agony.
You are now receiving the 'flower-retribution' (the preliminary fruit), and as a result, you shall enter hell. By witnessing an act and rejoicing in it, one receives its retribution."
It is so. How much more so for doing it oneself! Question: The harm caused by silkworms is cruel; why is it not prohibited? Answer: Because the texts mention them interchangeably.

Boiling cocoons and severing life is subsumed under the ten grave precepts against killing. Using cauldrons and boiling water or the silk-reeling wheel as instruments of slaughter is subsumed under the precepts regarding the means of killing.

By analogy with raising domestic livestock, it is subsumed under the precept against harming sentient beings. When done for the sake of profit to support one's body, it is subsumed under the precept against wrong livelihood.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* also prohibits [the use of] silk, cotton, and fine silks. Thus we know that monks are called "patch-robed ones" (*nàzǐ*) and laypeople are called "plain-clothed ones" (*bùyī*);

there is no need for further discussion. As for kings and ministers, they detest coarse clothing and prize the embroidered robes and ceremonial caps; this is because there are established teachings from the ancients on this matter.
2. Violating the Teachings and Incurring Offenses.
If one intentionally eats [forbidden meat], one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

Regarding the transgression herein: it refers to being personally greedy for the flavor while failing to consider the bodies of others; thus, the offense is categorized as a light defilement. Question:
Since the taking of life has already been prohibited within the previous ten heavy precepts, why is eating further prohibited here? Answer: It is because there may be those who say...

To kill constitutes a violation of the precepts; however, to purchase food for consumption does not pose such an obstacle. Yet one fails to realize that if there were no purchasing of food, there would likewise be little killing.

It is simply that killing constitutes a grave offense, whereas eating it constitutes a minor one. Nevertheless, although the characteristics of these offenses are unequal, [the causal relationship remains].
None of these are the path to liberation. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "To kill sentient beings for profit, or to purchase various meats with wealth—both are evil karmas;
upon death, one falls into the Raurava Hell. It is clear that neither the light nor the heavy offenses should be committed.
A sin is established through four conditions: first, the meat itself, which refers to the physical parts of a sentient being; second, the six permutations regarding the perception of meat.

Two cases are grave; two are light; two are non-offenses. Third, having the intention to eat constitutes the primary offense. Fourth, once it enters the mouth, for every swallow, an offense is incurred.

If these are subsumed within the Threefold Pure Precepts: abstaining from meat is the *vinaya-śīla* (precept of restraint); possessing Buddha-nature is the *kuśala-dharma-śīla* (precept of wholesome dharmas);

and the compassionate mind that gathers in all beings is the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering and benefiting sentient beings). These apply equally to the seven classes of followers, though the Mahayana and Hinayana do not fully coincide in their application—referring to the former.

In the Hīnayāna, at first, three kinds of pure meat were permitted: that which one has not seen being killed, has not heard was killed for oneself, and does not suspect was killed for oneself—all such meat was permitted.

Furthermore, if one knows that water contains insects, or suspects it may contain insects, yet uses or drinks it without examining or filtering it, this is prohibited for both monastics and laypeople alike. There is no offense in cases of insanity and so forth.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Because humans eat sheep, when the sheep dies it becomes a human; when the human dies it becomes a sheep.
Continuing thus for ten lifetimes, death after death and birth after birth, they prey upon one another in turn. Their evil karma arises together, persisting until the end of the future.
Thus one knows that eating meat results in the retributive punishments of the three miserable realms."
△ Fourth: The Precept Against Eating the Five Pungent Herbs (2). First: Abstinence and Maintenance; Transgression through Action.
If a Buddha’s disciple, one must not eat the five pungent herbs: garlic, leek, scallion, chives, and asafoetida.
These are the five pungent herbs; among all foods, one must not eat them.
The "large garlic" (*la su*) is the *húcōng* (onion); it is so called because it was brought from the land of *Hú*. The "wild onion" (*gé cōng*) is the *xiècài* (leek).
The "compassionate onion" (*cí cōng*) is so named because its stems and leaves are soft and supple. The "orchid onion" (*lán cōng*) is the small garlic (*xiǎosuàn*).
The *xìngqú*—also called *xìngyí*—has leaves resembling those of the turnip and roots like those of the radish; it is edible both raw and cooked.
"Stench. This originates from the kingdom of Khotan; as it does not exist in this land, it is not translated [into Chinese].

Regarding "these five pungent vegetables and so forth," this clarifies that among all foods, one must not eat them. There are four categories: first, those that are savory but not pungent, such as asafoetida (*hinguppu*);
second, those that are pungent but not savory, such as ginger and mustard; third, those that are both savory and pungent, which are the five pungent vegetables (*pañca-gandhaka*).

Furthermore, the four non-fleshy and non-pungent items refer to grains and vegetables. These five pungent roots (pañca-gandha) are such that eating them cooked arouses lust, while eating them raw increases anger.
Since they must not be consumed if present in any food, it is said that "one must not eat them among any kinds of food.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* clarifies five disadvantages: first, the increase of transgressions; second, being distanced from the heavens; third, being drawn near to ghosts; and fourth, the loss of merit.
[It] eliminates [them]. The Five Assemblies of Māras. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "If there is food in a household, they are driven out beyond the city gates.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* enumerates six [reasons]: namely, that the body and mind are foul and filthy; one lacks a good reputation; incantations do not succeed;
one is abandoned by the various devas; the breath is constantly foul; and it obstructs the various holy paths. Mahāmati asked: "Regarding wine, meat, and [vegetables such as] *śiṅgī*..."
"How is this? I pray that you will explain for me the merits and faults of eating and not eating. The World-Honored One replied:

'All meats and onions, as well as various leeks, garlic, and the like, and all kinds of intoxicating liquors—those who practice the path should always keep far from these. Food and drink give rise to heedlessness;
heedlessness gives rise to false thoughts; from such thoughts arises craving; and craving causes the mind to become deluded and intoxicated. Delusion..."

Intoxicated by long-standing craving for sensual desires, one is not liberated from birth and death. Alcohol, meat, scallions, leeks, and garlic all constitute obstacles to the Noble Path and contradict the outward signs of a sage;
therefore, they should not be consumed. Question: Drinking alcohol clouds the spirit, and eating meat harms living beings.
The transgression is indeed appropriate. As for the five pungent vegetables (*pañca-garaka*), they do not cloud the spirit and cause no harm to living beings.
Since the sutras permit these five [types of] faults, is this not already extreme? Answer: Although they do not harm living beings, they can still cloud the spirit.

Because their foul and turbid vapors assist in arousing the mind of desire, and their acrid and sharp flavors increase the nature of anger, when desire and anger shroud the mind, one suddenly forgets clear awakening. This is not...
How can one be deluded? Therefore, one must be cautious. △ Second, the conclusion regarding the offense for violating the teachings:
If one intentionally consumes [forbidden food], one commits a minor offense (light impurity).
One who upholds the precepts and distances themselves from defilement should head toward the path of purity; as such, all pungent, acrid, or foul-smelling substances must not be eaten. If...

Therefore, one who violates this incurs a minor offense of defilement (*āpatti-kaṣāya*). This is a prohibitive act (*pratikṣepa-karman*), established because foul and impure substances obstruct pure dharmas.

The offense is completed through four conditions: first, the substance is pungent; second, there are six permutations regarding the perception of it as pungent—two cases of heavy offenses, two cases of light offenses, and two cases of non-offense;
third, there is the intention to eat; and fourth, the offense is incurred with every swallow once the substance enters the mouth. If [the food] consists of the three clusters...

Inclusion: Refraining from eating the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*) constitutes the *vinaya-śīla* (precepts of discipline). Not eating these pungent roots constitutes the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precepts of gathering wholesome dharmas), which involves restraining oneself and exhorting others;

this is the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precepts of benefiting sentient beings). These apply equally to the seven classes of followers and are established by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. While the Mahāyāna’s meaning regarding the prevention of transgressions is profound, it is somewhat more restrictive than the Hīnayāna.
Exceptions for non-transgression include cases of illness where garlic or similar items cannot be cured otherwise, necessitating that one eat them in a secluded place or a separate room.
He must not enter a Buddha shrine or a monastic hall; he must not enter a monastic bathhouse; he must not enter the upper latrine.

He shall wait until seven days after the cessation of his fasting, when the foul odor has completely vanished, and then bathe, wash his clothes, and enter the community after perfuming himself with incense, as explained in detail in the Vinaya.
Furthermore, there is no offense in cases such as those who are insane or deluded.

The *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra* states: "If a person who consumes pungent roots and scallions can expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the celestial seers and immortals of the ten directions will loathe their foul odor and all depart from them.
Various hungry ghosts will lick their lips and mouths; though they practice *samādhi*, it cannot be pure.
Virtuous deities will not protect them, and at the end of life, they will naturally become members of the retinue of Māra."
When his demonic merit is exhausted, he falls into the Avīci Hell.
△ Fifth, the precept against failing to instruct others to repent of their offenses, in two parts: first, the practice of observance and the offense of non-observance.

If a Buddha’s disciple sees any sentient being who has violated the eight precepts, the five precepts, the ten precepts, or who has broken prohibitions or committed one of the seven heinous crimes or the eight [grave offenses]...
It is difficult. One should instruct all those who have committed offenses against the precepts to perform repentance.
"All sentient beings" refers to the eight classes of gods and dragons, humans and non-humans, and others who have received the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna precepts of the Buddha;
even those who have not received the Buddha’s precepts, such as practitioners who commit evil deeds and act unlawfully, are included.
Regarding "matters": it refers to being able to skillfully admonish and instruct others so that they do not commit [certain acts], thereby revealing the mind of a bodhisattva.

Regarding the "eight precepts": there are two vehicles, the Great and the Small. As for the Great Vehicle, these are the eight grave prohibitions found in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* (Dizhi jing), namely: killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

Lying, slandering, causing distress, anger, and calumny. In the Hinayana, this refers to the Eightfold Precepts of the Fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), which consist of abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, [slandering, causing distress, anger, and calumny].
Drinking alcohol; wearing flowers, perfumes, and necklaces; anointing the body with fragrant oils; using high or grand beds; performing or attending musical performances and spectacles;
and eating at improper times. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "I, [name], receive and practice the eight precepts, following and training in the teachings of all Buddhas;
this is called *poṣadha*. By means of the merit and reward of this *poṣadha*, may I [be sustained] in birth after birth."

One shall not fall into the three evil realms or the eight difficult conditions. I also do not seek the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, nor that of the Brahma or Śakra Devas, nor the pleasures of the world.
My wish is for all afflictions to be exhausted, to attain *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), and to accomplish the Buddha-way. Question:
For what reason does one receive the eight precepts and cultivate merit on the six fasting days (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*)? Answer: On these days, evil spirits pursue [beings].
When people wish to take another’s life, it brings about illness, misfortune, and decay, making one inauspicious.

For this reason, in the beginning of the aeon (*kalpa*), the sages taught people to observe the fast (*upavāsa*), cultivate goodness, and perform meritorious deeds in order to avoid such misfortune and decay. At that time, the method of fasting did not involve receiving the eight precepts;
rather, simply abstaining from food for one day was considered the fast. Later, when the Buddha appeared in the world, he taught them, saying: "You should..."
For one day and one night, as the Buddhas observe the eight precepts, they abstain from food after midday; this merit leads people to Nirvana.

In cities, towns, villages, and all such places, wherever there are virtuous people who observe the fast and receive the eight auxiliary precepts, malevolent spirits will keep their distance and their dwellings will be peaceful and secure. For this reason, one should observe the fast and receive the precepts on these six days.
The merit obtained will increase and be beyond measure. This is also called the "Intermediate Precepts," meaning they are situated above the five precepts and below the ten precepts.

The five precepts are the first five items among the eight precepts; for laypeople, these merely prohibit deviant and improper conduct, whereas for those who have left the household life, they are completely severed. The ten precepts are the ten precepts of the śrāmaṇera, as well as those in this very sūtra.

These are the ten grave precepts (*daśa-guru-śīla*). Of these, the eight precepts apply exclusively to lay practitioners; the ten precepts apply exclusively to those who have left the household life (*pravrajita*);
and the five precepts encompass both the laity and the ordained alike. Regarding "violation of prohibitions": "violation" (*hui*) means to transgress; "prohibition" (*jin*) means to forbid.

This refers to the disciplinary laws (*śīla-dharma*) established by the Tathāgata, which prohibit one from deviating. Regarding the "seven reversals" (*sapta-ānantarya*): they are explained in the subsequent text. The "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭāv-akṣaṇāḥ*).
These are the retributions for violating the precepts: first, hell; second, hungry ghosts; third, animals; fourth, long-lived devas;
fifth, the continent of Uttarakuru; sixth, being blind, deaf, or mute; seventh, possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence; and eighth, being born before or after a Buddha.
These eight types are all hindrances to the Path, preventing one from seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma; therefore, they are so named.

It is difficult [to overcome]. However, these eight matters may arise because of sins committed in previous lives, resulting in such hardships; or they may be the result of actions performed in this life that will be requited in the future.

Therefore, one should instruct them to repent for their transgressions. For example, committing acts such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, or lying invites retribution as a denizen of hell, a hungry ghost, or an animal;
practicing the "attainment of non-conception" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) of the non-Buddhists invites rebirth in the Heaven of Long Life (Ābhāsvara).
The retribution for five hundred kalpas: failing to recognize the Triple Gem and performing only worldly merits invites rebirth in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru).

Giving rise to wrong views and feeling no joy upon hearing the Dharma invites the retribution of blindness and deafness. Lacking faith in the Triple Gem and slandering the Sangha invites the retribution of being mute and dumb.
Disbelieving in the supramundane Dharma and indulging in worldly teachings invites the retribution of perverse intelligence and eloquence. Such is karma.

Heavy conditions outweigh light ones; therefore, one receives retribution either before or after the Buddha’s appearance. Regarding the phrase "all offenses for violating the precepts that should be confessed":

"all" is used here as a comprehensive summary. To ruin and break [the precepts] is called "violation. The laws and teachings of all Buddhas are called "precepts. Faults and transgressions are called "offenses.
That which is logically appropriate is called "should. To admonish and exhort is called "instruction. To reform the past and cultivate the future is called "confession" (*chān-huǐ*).
This refers to a summary of the aforementioned offenses, whether light or heavy, whether natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) or prohibited (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).

It is logically appropriate to admonish and encourage [the offender] to confess their actions before the Triple Gem, so that they may reform and turn toward the good, vowing not to commit them again. Therefore, it is said:
"All transgressions of the precepts should be taught as requiring repentance. △ Second, the conclusion on the offense for violating the teachings.
If a Bodhisattva does not instruct [a fellow practitioner] to repent, yet lives with them, shares the same monastic provisions, and performs the *poṣadha* together—

dwelling in the same community and reciting the precepts alongside them— yet fails to bring their offense to light and fails to instruct them to rectify their transgression, they commit a minor offense (*laghu-pāpaka*).
"One who does not teach repentance" means that their mind for the dual benefit [of self and others] is entirely deficient.
"Dwelling together and sharing the same monastic gains" means residing within the same *sīmā* (monastic boundary) and collectively receiving the offerings of donors.

"Participating in the *poṣadha* and dwelling in the same assembly to recite the precepts" means that within the same boundary, the community of monks collectively performs the *poṣadha* every half-month.

"Sā" refers to the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*). However, both "reciting the precepts" (*poṣadha-vācanā*) and "recitation of the precepts" (*śīla-vācanā*) share the meaning of *poṣadha* (the Uposatha).

Within a single great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) in the Western Regions, there may be two separate residences that perform the recitation of the precepts together while receiving offerings separately; now, it is said they are "identical" because they share both the Dharma and the food.
For instance, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, if there is one who has committed an offense, and the three roots [of perception] are certain and firm...
One should immediately bring up the offense committed and cause that person to repent, so as to manifest harmony in precepts and practice together.

If one neither brings it up nor instructs them, yet partakes in the community's offerings and accepts the faithful laity’s gifts in vain, one incurs the minor secondary offense (*āpatti*) due to concealing another's transgression.
Because it defiles one's own mind. The *Bodhisattva Upāsaka Pañcaśīla-Ācāra Sūtra* states:

"When a bodhisattva serves as a leader for many people, if he sees that his kinsmen and dependents are engaged in unrighteous activities, he should reprimand them or expel them. The *Upāsakaśīla Sūtra* states:
"It would be better to accept evil precepts for a single day and thereby sever the life-faculties of immeasurable beings than to ever harbor [a harmful intent]."
To nurture corrupt and evil disciples whom one cannot subdue—why is this? Because such a corrupt discipline brings calamity solely upon oneself;
it fails to instruct evil disciples and instead causes immeasurable sentient beings to commit evil, for they are able to slander immeasurable sublime dharmas.
This constitutes an obstructive karma (*vāraṇa-karma*), established by the prohibition against relying on the wicked to increase transgressions. A sin is completed through four conditions.
First, there is the offense itself; second, the perception that it is an offense; third, the lack of intent to instruct—these constitute the primary factors of the offense.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "To fail to admonish out of anger is a defiled offense; to fail to do so out of indolence or laziness is a non-defiled offense.

Fourth, to remain silent and cohabit with the offender without instructing them to repent constitutes one offense. Furthermore, to eat together and participate in the same Dharma activities with them constitutes one offense each, according to the specific circumstances.

Regarding the fetters (*saṃyojana*): if they are subsumed within the three categories of precepts, one should instruct them to perform repentance. The *śīla* of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) involves participating together in the *poṣadha*.

The *śīla* of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-śīla*) involves purification through the confession of transgressions. This also encompasses both natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) karmas, and applies to all seven classes of followers who may equally commit offenses.
Yet, there are also differences; a *bhikṣu* should point out the offenses of all seven classes, whereas a *bhikṣuṇī* [is subject to different rules].

One may expose the offenses of the group of six, but one may not expose the offenses of a bhikṣu. If they are relatives or acquaintances, there is no offense in privately exhorting or admonishing one another.
A śikṣamāṇā may expose the offenses of the five groups [of monastics], but she may not expose the offenses of a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī.
A śrāmaṇera may expose the offenses of the four groups [of monastics], but he may not expose the offenses of the three higher groups. A śrāmaṇerī may...
One may bring forth the offenses of the three assemblies, but one must not bring forth the offenses of the four higher assemblies.

The two lay assemblies may bring forth offenses within their own respective classes, but they must not bring forth the offenses of the five monastic assemblies. When close friends and intimate acquaintances privately exhort and admonish one another, there is no offense in any case.
Regarding those who do not commit an offense, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If that person is violent, or if they rely on the power of the king... [The text continues: ...great...

If one encounters the force of a subject or the force of a violent person, or if there arises a cause for the taking of life that would harm a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārin*), one should form this thought:
"The karmic retribution for those sinful deeds must surely come to him; he himself shall know it. This is like a house fire: one should only save oneself;
how can one concern oneself with other matters? At such a time, guarding the sense faculties accordingly is faultless, and furthermore, one does not commit an offense.

Regarding those who are insane and so forth, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If a virtuous bhikṣu, upon seeing one who destroys the Dharma, remains indifferent and fails to reprimand them, expel them, or report their case, such a person is an enemy within the Buddha-Dharma.
If one can indeed reprimand and expel them, know that they shall obtain inexhaustible merit. It does not say otherwise.
It can be measured. The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "Even those such as caṇḍālas and butchers, though they perform evil deeds, cannot destroy the True Dharma of the Tathāgata;

they will not necessarily fall into the three evil realms. However, if one acts as a teacher yet fails to instruct and admonish their disciples, they thereby destroy the Buddha-Dharma and will certainly fall into hell."
△ Sixth Precept: Not Providing for Those Who Request the Dharma. Part Two. First, the practice of observance and the violation of restraint; this further has three sections. First, the introduction:
"If a disciple of the Buddha sees a Mahāyāna Dharma Master, a fellow student of the Mahāyāna, one of like view and like practice, entering the monastic quarters..."

Whether from a residence, a city, or from as far as a hundred or a thousand *li*, those who come first designate the Mahāyāna Dharma Master, followed by the Mahāyāna fellow students—the three types of friends in view and practice—in order to distinguish them from teachers and friends of the Hīnayāna.
While the initial precept merely required revering and honoring teachers and friends, this section additionally requests that they preach the Dharma. Therefore...

Furthermore, it is prescribed: A "Dharma Master" refers to one who has thoroughly mastered the nature and characteristics of the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, and is even capable of transforming and guiding sentient beings so that they may enter the stage of Buddhahood.
A "monastery" (saṃghārāma) is a place where those who have left the household life reside.
A "household" is a place where those who remain in the household reside. A "city or town" is a place where kings and officials reside. [These may extend for] a hundred li or a thousand li.
Regarding the path traveled by teachers and friends, regardless of whether it is far or near, the etiquette for meeting them ought to accord with the Dharma;
one must not be negligent. △ Second, the ritual of prostration and offering.
He immediately rose to welcome him when he arrived and saw him off when he departed; he prostrated and made offerings to him, serving the Dharma Master three times each day.
He provided the Dharma Master with food costing three *liang* of gold per day, along with meals of a hundred flavors, bedding, and seats. Whatever was required was given to him in its entirety.
"To rise immediately" means that there must be no moment of negligence. "Welcoming" means that the etiquette between guest and host is not lacking.

"Seeing off" means that the thought of teacher and friend is never forgotten. "Prostrating" means that the mind directed toward the Dharma is earnest. "Making offerings" means that the rite of reverence is performed with utmost sincerity.
Regarding the three periods of *chen*, *si*, and *wu*, the time for offering food is clearly observed without fail; this is the daily meal.

"Three or two taels of gold" signifies that he has prepared the offerings with all his might and without stinginess. "Food and drink of a hundred flavors" refers to all the sweet and delicious things in the world.
"The beds have the distinction of cords and wood; the seats have the difference of high and low"—this means that he provides everything necessary as described above in the offerings.
Yet, fearing that this may still not suffice for his teachers and friends, he now gives whatever they desire.
Give everything freely; do not go against their wishes. Therefore it is said that all necessities shall be provided.
If even one's own body can be relinquished, how much more so external things? △ Third, requesting the Dharma.
One should constantly invite Dharma masters to preach the Dharma during the three periods of the day; pay homage three times every day; harbor no thoughts of anger or resentment;
sacrifice one's body for the sake of the Dharma; and request the Dharma without weariness.
"Always requests" clarifies that this is not for a single day or a single moment.
"The three periods" refers to the first part of the day, the middle part of the day, and the latter part of the day; these are the times for requesting further instruction.

"Not giving rise to a mind of anger" means that while receiving the Dharma, one does not resent the teacher’s detailed and meticulous admonitions. "Not giving rise to a mind of distress or vexation" means...
This means that within the act of making offerings, one receives [the teacher’s] countenance with a joyful mind and is entirely without stinginess.
"To sacrifice one's body for the sake of the Dharma and to seek the Dharma without weariness" refers to external renunciation; this [passage] clarifies internal renunciation.

It means that by forgetting the self for the sake of the Way, one attains the Dharma; by seeking it with courageous diligence, the Dharma increases. This is the wondrous function of a Bodhisattva of Right View.
It is as when the Buddha, during his causal stage, sacrificed his entire body to seek half a verse; he gouged out his flesh to light a thousand lamps to request the preaching of the Dharma;
he gave his wife and children as food to a yakṣa because he wished to hear the essentials of the Dharma; and even used his own body as a bed and seat.
Spreading his hair to cover the mud—this is the model for the Tathāgata’s seeking of the Dharma.
One who cultivates the bodhisattva practices should likewise act thus. Therefore, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva told Sudhana:
"Within this ocean of Dharma, there is not a single word or a single phrase that was not obtained through renunciation and giving. His constant entreaty is merely verbal.
Sincerity means that one’s affection for the Dharma is profound. Reverence means that this body is sincere and never ceases its service to the Dharma.

Freedom from anger and vexation means that the mind is sincere and does not treat the Dharma with arrogance. When the three karmas are thus devout and sincere, they are perfected in goodness and beauty.
Indeed, when a person possesses the Dharma, they flourish; without the Dharma, they wither. To obtain the Dharma is to attain wealth and honor; to lose the Dharma is to...

"Poor and lowly. It is further said: "One who realizes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) becomes a sage in a single instant; one who is deluded regarding the nature of phenomena sinks into saṃsāra for eternal kalpas.
How could this be comparable to the worldly, trivial arts and crafts, or the diligent pursuit of meager profit and status?
The *Dṛṣṭānta-sūtra* states: "In a past life, the Venerable Ānanda was once a young incense seller. He saw a śramaṇa..."
The śrāmaṇera was begging for alms while reciting a verse from a sutra. [The boy] asked him the reason for this, and the śrāmaṇera replied, "My master studies the Way in the mountains;
he requires me to deliver one *sheng* of rice daily and, in addition, to recite one verse.
He asked again, "If you were not to deliver the rice, how many verses could you recite each day? He replied, "I could recite ten verses. The boy said, "From now on, do not..."
He went out to beg for alms once more, and I offered to pay for his rice in exchange. The śrāmaṇera was filled with joy and was able to sit in quietude to study.
When nine *shu* of rice had been paid for, he was tested on the scriptures; he mastered them all with complete fluency.

By virtue of this meritorious retribution, he was later reborn as a disciple of the Buddha, becoming foremost in extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), fully endowed with the three types of clear knowledge (*trividyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and entrusted with the seal of the Buddha’s mind (*cittamudrā*). Thus one knows:

If even a *śrāmaṇera* who merely provides sustenance for one who upholds the sūtras receives such a superior reward, how much more so for those who provide offerings to a teacher or friend of the Mahāyāna who is able to preach the Dharma—how could anyone fathom the superior reward they obtain? Now, if these two [distracted] thoughts do not arise, one will be diligent in seeking the Dharma.
2. Contravening the Teaching and the Incurrence of Offenses.
If one does not act thus, one commits a minor offense (āpatti).
Just as with being stingy with material wealth, to be arrogant toward the Dharma and disrespectful toward the teacher constitutes a minor offense;

this is a prohibitive action (vārita-karman) established because it results in the loss of the benefit that sustains the spirit. The offense is completed through four conditions: first, there is a Dharma master; second, the perception of them as a Dharma master; or...

If one does not know [the offense], there is no transgression. Regarding the three types of non-requesting intentions: if it is due to anger or vexation, it is a defiled transgression; if it is due to forgetfulness, error, or negligence, it is a non-defiled transgression.

Fourth, to pass time indifferently and in vain constitutes an offense according to the specific circumstances. If these are subsumed within the three clusters of precepts: providing for one's teachers and friends pertains to the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint precepts);

not giving rise to anger or vexation pertains to the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precepts for gathering wholesome qualities); and requesting [instruction] at the three times pertains to the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precepts for acting for the benefit of sentient beings).
The Dharma encompasses the precepts for sustaining life. These apply equally to all seven assemblies, yet they are not entirely shared between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions.

In the Hīnayāna, those who have not completed five years of seniority and are not yet conversant with the Vinaya-piṭaka should invite a person who maintains the Vinaya when such a person arrives; others are not subject to this requirement.
In the Mahāyāna, one seeks the Dharma without weariness and should therefore invite everyone. There is no offense if one is ill, lacks physical strength, or knows that the person [invited]...
This constitutes a perverted explanation. [It applies] if one is personally learned and powerful, or if one has already received the Dharma previously, or in cases such as insanity and so forth.

The *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states: "Sentient beings of the final age who wish to practice cultivation should, throughout their lives, make offerings to virtuous friends and serve spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*).
When those spiritual teachers come to approach you, you should sever arrogance. Furthermore..."
One should remain detached and sever all resentment. When confronted with circumstances that are either adverse or favorable, one should regard them as being like empty space.

One must thoroughly understand that one's own mind is ultimately equal, sharing the same essence as all sentient beings without distinction. Only by practicing in this manner does one enter Perfect Enlightenment.

Furthermore, the Commentary states: "When a virtuous friend guides others through various skillful means, the minds of teacher and disciple must reach a point of resonance before the intent of the Dharma can truly be realized."

The Tradition states: "Therefore, by looking down upon things and responding to the opportune moment, one draws others close through mutual affinity. Yet the ignorant lack discernment, and arrogance immediately arises.
Once arrogance obscures the mind, one no longer enters the Way."

△ Seventh: The Precept Against Laziness and Not Listening to the Dharma. This section has two parts. First, the establishment of what is to be maintained and what constitutes an offense, which further has two parts. First, the citation of the locus:
"If a disciple of the Buddha, wherever there is the preaching of the Dharma—the Vinaya, Sūtras, and Śāstras—whether in a great residence or at a place where the Dharma is being preached..."
"All places" refers generally to both monastic quarters and secular grounds. "Expounding the Dharma" (*jiangfa*) is a general term for preaching the teachings and debating their meaning.
To analyze the meaning according to the text is called "expounding" (*jiang*); that which maintains all things is called "Dharma" (*fa*). *Vinaya* is translated as "extinction" (*mie*).

This extinction has three meanings: first, the extinction of unwholesome karma; second, the extinction of afflictions (*kleśa*); and third, the attainment of the fruit of extinction. This is the intended meaning.
The term "refers to" indicates that which is expressed (*vācya*). The two characters "Sūtra" and "Vinaya" indicate that which expresses (*vācaka*).
That is to say, the Sūtras express the Dharma, and the Vinaya expresses the *vinaya*. *Vinaya* is translated as "discipline" (*lü*). "Sūtra" is taught as "constant dharma.
While both types—Sūtra and Vinaya—are common to the world, worldly sūtras do not necessarily express the True Dharma, and worldly vinayas do not necessarily express the *vinaya*. Only the Buddha...
The Sūtras and Vinaya can expound the *dharma* and *vinaya*; therefore, they are called "Dharma-Vinaya. The Sūtras and Vinaya are also termed the "Buddha’s Exhortations.
These are practiced by all seven classes of followers and are honored equally by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna adherents; they are not restricted solely to the Śrāvakas.

Furthermore, the Sūtras constitute the "Transformative Teaching" (*pariṇāmanā-śāsana*), meaning they open the way and guide through transformation. The Vinaya constitutes the "Regulatory Teaching" (*niyama-śāsana*), meaning it restrains and governs one's conduct.
Therefore, the *śāstras* explain the intent of the Sūtras and Vinaya; thus, they are not cited here.

Furthermore, *vinaya* is translated as "skillful governance" (*śan-zhi*), meaning that it is well able to govern one's own lust, anger, and delusion, and is also able to govern the faults and evils of sentient beings.

This name is derived from its functional capacity. Its direct translation is "discipline" (*lü*). "Discipline" means "dharma. This name is derived from the teaching itself, meaning that it... cuts off [evil].
Because the distinctions between light and heavy, permitted and prohibited, and the upholding or violating of precepts are not fixed according to what is non-Dharma;

furthermore, "Vī" means to depart and "Nī" means truth—meaning to depart from various forms of non-truth and proceed toward the truth. Now, this truth is precisely the original source, the mind-ground.

Furthermore, when both Sūtra and Vinaya are referred to as "Vinaya," the Sūtra refers to the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* (Fanwang jiejing), and the Vinaya refers to the Dharma and Vinaya of the Mind-Ground, as well as all other [related texts].
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka refers to all Mahāyāna sūtras, as they all contain the meaning of extinguishing evil and generating goodness;
therefore, they are likewise called *vinaya*. Furthermore, those who lecture on the *dharma-vinaya* are in fact lecturing on the sūtras and the vinaya.
As the subsequent text states: "A novice bodhisattva should take a scroll of the Sūtras or Vinaya to the place of a Dharma Master to listen, receive instruction, and inquire about its meaning.
Regarding "within a large residence," this specifically refers to the houses of kings or officials where a master is invited to preach the Dharma.
△ Second, going to listen.
A newly initiated bodhisattva should carry the volumes of the sutras and vinaya to the place where the Dharma Master resides to listen, receive, and inquire about them;
or they should go to all places where the Dharma is preached, whether in mountain forests, beneath trees, or within the precincts of the Sangha.
"In the former case," it means that the Bodhisattva came to me, and I requested him to preach the Dharma. "In this case," it means that the Bodhisattva was there, and I went to listen to the Dharma.
In the former instance, I was the head of the assembly; in this instance, I am among the listeners. Regarding "new learners," this refers to those who have newly received the Bodhisattva precepts.
Carrying the scrolls of the sutras and the vinaya is the proper etiquette for listening to the Dharma. Once one's conduct is thus complete—
"One should go there. Regarding "listening and receiving through inquiry": "listening" refers to hearing with focused auditory consciousness;

"receiving" refers to internalizing with mental consciousness—namely, the two wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī* prajñā). "Inquiry" refers to posing questions; that is, reflecting deeply upon what has been heard.

He contemplated this but could not yet fully comprehend it, so he again raised his doubts for inquiry. Once his doubts were resolved, he relied upon them to advance in practice and enter the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground of the Mahāyāna.
If one does not listen, there will be no cause for receiving nourishment; if one listens but does not inquire, there will be no cause for growth.
Entering understanding through hearing fulfills the requirements of learning the Dharma. This [is taught] lest new learners of the Bodhisattva path...
If one's karma has not yet been perfected, one will be unable to revere the Dharma and will naturally give rise to indolence, thereby losing the great benefit of the Dharma.

Without daily progress, one will ultimately regress from the stages of the mind. Therefore, you must exert yourself with diligence; for this reason, you should listen, receive, and inquire about it. As for "mountains, forests," and so forth:
This clearly defines the monasteries and temples as all places for the preaching of the Dharma. If one is indolent and does not listen, it constitutes negligence.
Negligence leads to the loss of right mindfulness; the loss of right mindfulness leads to much distraction; much distraction leads to a lack of correct awareness;
a lack of correct awareness gives rise to ignorance, whereby one commits various evil deeds. Since you are a child of the Buddha, you must...
One must seek the higher and transform those below; this is the fundamental causal mind. Extensive study and vast learning constitute the supreme skillful means.

If one does not extensively study and possess vast learning, how could one be fit to uphold the Triple Gem? Therefore, wherever there is any place for preaching the Dharma, [one should apply these principles].
One should go to that place in all cases to listen and receive [the teachings]. △ Second, the conclusion regarding the offense for violating the teaching:
If one does not go there to listen and receive [the teachings], one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).
The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma becomes deeper as one enters it; to sit idly without advancing is to violate the Buddha’s teaching, and thus the offense is concluded as minor.

This is a defilement. It is a prohibited action (*pratiṣiddha-karman*), established as such because one neglects and loses the benefits of the Dharma through indolence. A transgression is established through four conditions: first, there is the actual teaching of the Dharma;

second, the perception that it is the teaching of the Dharma; third, the state of mind of not going—whether out of anger, pride, or other such defiled states, which constitutes a defiled offense, or out of laziness, which constitutes a non-defiled offense;
fourth, the failure to go and listen, for which a daily offense is incurred. —From *Śraddhākaravarman’s Śīlasamuccaya*.

The sūtras prescribe that one must go within forty *li*; this case should be treated likewise. If categorized according to the three groups of precepts: going to listen [to the teachings] constitutes the *vinaya-śīla* (precept of discipline);

holding the scrolls of the sūtras and vinaya constitutes the *kuśala-dharma-śīla* (precept of wholesome qualities); and listening, receiving, and inquiring [about the teachings] constitutes the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings).

These apply equally to the seven assemblies (*sapta-saṃgha*), though there are slight differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as explained in the preceding discussion on the precepts. There is no offense if... [if not...]
Explanation: If one is ill; if one lacks strength; if the other person speaks erroneously; if one protects the mind of the speaker;

if one has heard it repeatedly, already mastered it, and understood its meaning; if one is highly learned; if one practices according to the teaching; if one is practicing meditative concentration and does not wish to interrupt it even for a moment;
or if one is of dull faculties and finds it difficult to master, or is insane or deranged—in these cases, not going [to hear the Dharma] does not constitute an offense.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In this land, the true essence of the teaching lies in the purity of hearing and sound.
By means of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, the aggregate of precepts becomes pure, and only then can one enter samādhi.

This is why the youth [Bodhidharma] traveled south through a hundred prefectures, Zhaozhou wandered for eighty years, and others ascended the mountain three times and visited it nine times, traversing a thousand peaks before finally attaining clear realization.
This is a matter of great importance. How could there be a Maitreya born by heaven, or a Śākyamuni who appeared spontaneously?

△ Eighth: The Precept of Turning Away from the Great and Toward the Small. Part One: Committing Transgressions and Ceasing to Maintain [the Precepts]. This also has two parts. First: Turning Away from the Great.

If a disciple of the Buddha, in their heart, turns their back on the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya that are eternally abiding, saying they were not spoken by the Buddha—though the intention is to say this before the words have even been uttered—it is called "turning one's back in the heart. Regarding the term "eternally abiding" and so forth:
it means that these Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya flow forth from the ground of the mind of Vairocana; their nature is fundamentally eternally abiding, neither arising nor ceasing, and unchanging.
It is unchanging. It is that which all Buddhas take as their teacher and the mother of Bodhisattvas.
Abiding in the world, it teaches and transforms sentient beings, enabling the lineage of the Buddhas to remain uninterrupted; therefore, it is called the eternally abiding Sūtra and Vinaya.

This is the Tathāgata’s sudden teaching of the single reality, not the provisional, expedient, or minor teachings of gradual regulation according to circumstances. As for those who say it was not spoken by the Buddha:

It is not that they do not believe the Buddha’s words; rather, because these newly initiated bodhisattvas do not understand the profound and subtle mysteries of the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, they claim that the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya were not spoken by the Buddha.
