Therefore, in the *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā* (The Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra), the Tathāgata instructs all Bodhisattvas to exert themselves in practice for three months without being bound by a retinue of disciples.
Consequently, even when Arhats instruct their disciples, they still possess residual afflictions; such was the case with [the masters of] Mount Nanyue and Tiantai.

There is the lamentation regarding the five grades of the iron wheel. "Every day one commits three types of karma; verbal offenses are immeasurable" means that beating and striking are bodily karma (*kāyakarma*);
reviling and insulting are verbal karma (*vākkarma*); and when the body and speech have not yet been set in motion, but a mind of anger has already arisen first, this is mental karma (*manaskarma*).
Once these are performed, they constitute completed offenses. Question: Since you speak of the three types of karma, why do you single out verbal offenses here? Answer:
Because of the arising of a mind of anger, one proceeds to strike and beat others. Striking and beating must first be preceded by verbal abuse;
at the time of such abuse, every word is harsh speech, for which one incurs immeasurable sin. Therefore, it is said that the offenses of the mouth are limitless.
As for those who commit the seven heinous crimes, you should know that these are metaphorical expressions. For example, as I today seek revenge against my father, so too does he...
He has formed an enmity with my father and sown the causes for his future harm; therefore, taking revenge is what may be called the seventh transgression.
The remaining cases may be understood by analogy. △ Second, the conclusion of the offense for violating the teachings.
If an ordained bodhisattva, lacking a heart of compassion, deliberately seeks revenge even against those among their six kin, they commit a minor offense (light impurity).
This rule specifically distinguishes the ordained from other groups; that is to say, a lay bodhisattva may still employ secular laws concurrently.
Requiting an injury with rectitude. For a renunciant bodhisattva, a mind of loving-kindness is the foundation; they regard enemies and kin with equal vision.

Whether an adversary is great or small, near or distant, one must never retaliate against them. By not retaliating, one resolves enmity and unties the knots of resentment, so that there is forever no further opposition.
If one retaliates, then mutual hostility and harm will continue without end. To deliberately retaliate would be to violate the fundamental mind of loving-kindness.

This constitutes a light offense of defilement (*āpatti-kaṣāya*). It involves both natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibitive transgression (*prajñapti-sāvadya*), as it violates loving-kindness and patience, and further binds one to future enmity;

therefore, it was proscribed. Five conditions constitute the offense: first, the person is an enemy; second, the perception that they are an enemy. There are six permutations [of these two factors]; the first two permutations are light offenses.

That is to say: regarding an enemy, one perceives them as an enemy; or regarding an enemy, one is uncertain [of it], yet proceeds to strike out in anger in retaliation—these two phrases are somewhat grave. Regarding one who is not an enemy, one perceives them as an enemy;

or regarding one who is not an enemy, one is uncertain [of it]—these two phrases are even more grave. Regarding one who is not an enemy, one does not perceive them as an enemy, yet regarding one who is an enemy or one who is not an enemy, one strikes out in anger—this is subsumed under the ninth grave precept.
Third, there is the mind of seeking retribution; fourth, one carries out the act of striking out in anger.

The matter: fifth, the person receiving it, meaning that if one receives their beating or abuse, a light offense (*dukkaṭa*) is incurred; if life is harmed, it falls under the first precept of killing.

If categorized according to the three clusters (*tri-skandha*), not seeking revenge is the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint); following the path of filial piety is the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas);

and not killing is the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings). This applies equally to the seven classes of followers and is established by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. If one is a lay bodhisattva...
The Bodhisattva relies on a judicial official to adjudicate according to the law without any personal bias; in such cases, whether one strikes or kills, no offense is committed.
The *Śīla-sūtra* states: "If a Bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of resentment toward another and maintains it without relinquishing it, this is an afflicted offense.
This precept may also be understood as concurrently governing such conduct. Furthermore, a Bodhisattva should not retaliate against an enemy, but rather should repay kindness when it is shown.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If there is a filial son who can exhort his parents toward the Three Jewels and the teachings on cause and effect, causing them to develop faith and take refuge;
and furthermore, causes them to cultivate precepts, generosity, meditation, and wisdom to discipline themselves—this alone is called truly repaying the kindness of one's parents.
Moreover, the *Śīla-sūtra* states: "Having received the kindness of others, [one should not harbor] a heart of resentment..."
To respond to them with an equivalent or greater [offense] constitutes a defiled transgression. To do so out of laziness or indolence constitutes a non-defiled transgression.
There is no transgression if one lacks the power despite having made an effort; or if one employs a skillful means to subdue them;
or if they refuse to accept it despite one’s desire to repay their kindness; or in cases such as insanity and the like.
The *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: The Buddha said to Sāgaramati, "Furthermore, there may be someone who comes with an evil mind, reviling and insulting you with anger.
You should then think: 'This person is indolent and has abandoned the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*). I shall now arouse diligence.'"
Diligently seek and practice cultivation, planting all roots of goodness, and do not give rise to complacency.
May this person first sit at the site of enlightenment, and may I be the very last to attain perfect awakening. Even until I rely upon this Dharma, what is this that is called anger?
How is it that there is no anger? One investigates these two [states] and finds neither to be obtainable.

Furthermore, whether it be anger itself or the one who is angry—whether toward oneself or another—both anger and the angry person are unobtainable. Being thus unobtainable, one is even free from this [conceptual] view;
this is what is called patience (*kṣānti*). If one can investigate in this manner, it constitutes the equal contemplation of enemies and kin; yet, an enemy cannot be found.
It is so. △ The twenty-second precept against arrogance and failing to request the Dharma has two parts. First, ceasing transgressions and practicing observance, which further has two parts.
First, relying on arrogance.
If, O sons of the Buddha, at the very beginning of your renunciation you have not yet attained any understanding, yet you rely on your own cleverness and intelligence;

or you rely on your noble status and advanced age; or you rely on your prestigious lineage and high social standing, your great learning, or your great wealth and abundance of the seven treasures—and because of such arrogance, you do not consult or receive instruction from the Dharma masters who have studied the sutras and vinaya before you.
Regarding those who have newly gone forth from the household life: it is understood that their defilements are not yet deep.
Because their defilements are not yet deep, they frequently engage in self-exaltation. As for "having no realization," this means they lack the correct understanding within the Buddha-dharma;

therefore, they give rise to arrogance. Regarding "relying on oneself" and so forth, there are seven types: first, relying on worldly cleverness and wisdom; second, relying on high status; third, relying on... [text continues]

Eighth, relying on seniority. Ninth, relying on one’s lineage and clan. Tenth, relying on one’s views and understanding. Eleventh, relying on one’s merit and virtue. Twelfth, relying on wealth and abundance.

By means of these, one gives rise to arrogance and refuses to receive instruction. Furthermore, conceit (*māna*) consists of both the root afflictions and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). As for *mada* (intoxication/arrogance):
It is characterized by deep attachment to one’s own prosperity and has the nature of arrogance and intoxication; its function is to obstruct non-conceit and to serve as a basis for defilement.
It is the cause for the arising of pride (*māna*) and is one among the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). As for pride:
it consists of relying on oneself and disparaging others, having the nature of haughtiness; its function is to obstruct non-pride and to produce suffering. Indeed, it is because of pride that...
It is the lack of humility toward those who possess virtue. Because of this, one revolves endlessly in the cycle of birth and death and undergoes various sufferings;
it is thus one of the six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). These two afflictions are able to obstruct the Noble Path, such that no spiritual merits whatsoever are accomplished.
By relying on them, the mountain of pride becomes loftily towering, blocking one's own progress forward. Therefore...
There are those who possess prior learning and knowledge, yet do not move even a single step forward, thereby forfeiting the great benefit of receiving instruction.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Good son, it is by being sustained by spiritual friends that bodhisattvas do not fall into the evil realms;
it is through the guidance of spiritual friends that they achieve liberation from the world; and it is by relying upon spiritual friends that they awaken to the Path."
Having eliminated the obstacles of karma and afflictions, one leaves the city of birth and death and reaches the place of purity.

Furthermore, one should conceive of one's own body as being afflicted by illness, regard the spiritual friend as a king of physicians, and, following their instructions, regard them as a skilled healer.
Regarding the correct practice being cultivated, one should maintain the perception that it serves to eliminate illness. The *Sūtra on the Four Dharmas of the Mahāyāna* states:

"O Bhikṣus, for as long as life lasts, even if you encounter circumstances that threaten your very survival, you must never abandon a virtuous spiritual friend. △ Second, regarding pride toward those of superior virtue:
As for that Dharma Master, he may be of humble lineage, young, from a lowly family, poor, and of low station;
his faculties may be incomplete, yet he truly possesses virtue and understands all the sutras and vinayas.
"Of low birth" means they are not from a distinguished lineage. "Young in years" means they are not venerable elders. "From humble origins" means they are not from a great clan.
"Poor" means they are not wealthy. "Lowly" means they are not of noble status. "With impaired faculties" refers to those whose character and qualities are deficient;
yet those who actually possess virtue are truly people of authentic cultivation and practice. All...
One must fully understand the Sūtras and Vinaya; this excludes those with shallow or limited knowledge and insight. A bodhisattva at the initial stage should regard the Dharma as paramount.
One may only seek understanding for what has not yet been understood; one must not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, thereby losing the Dharma for the sake of the person.
△ Second, the violation of the teaching and the resulting offense.

If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not inquire of or receive instruction from a Dharma Master regarding the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) because they have failed to observe the Dharma Master’s lineage, they commit a minor offense.

The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is the supreme dharma of unsurpassed bodhi. A Dharma teacher such as this, possessing both excellence in understanding and practice, is fit to serve as a model for future generations.
If a newly initiated Bodhisattva, considering their own spiritual lineage, does not come to consult and receive instruction from such a teacher, they incur the fault of a light defilement.
This constitutes both a natural and a proscribed offense, arising from the obstruction of pride.

It was established as a rule because of the Dharma. That is to say, pride is like a high mountain; the water of the Dharma does not abide upon it, and thus one loses the benefit of transformation through the teaching.

A transgression is established through four conditions: first, the Dharma teacher; second, the six permutations regarding the perception of the Dharma teacher—two heavy, two light, and two non-offenses;

third, the mind of arrogance, which is precisely the primary factor (the *karmic lord*); this differs from the sixth [condition], the affliction of anger, mentioned previously; fourth, the failure to...
Consultation and reception [of teachings]. One incurs an offense according to whether one should have consulted but did not. Previously, the seventh rule prohibited laziness;
this [present rule] concerns arrogance and failing to request [teachings]. If one does not go to listen out of a mind of pride, one should incur an offense identical to this precept.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "To treat the teacher of the Dharma with contempt, failing to give rise to reverence, ridiculing and disparaging them, and merely clinging to the literal words..."

According to the ultimate meaning, this is a defiled offense, and it is also governed by this precept. If categorized according to the three clusters of pure conduct (*tri-śikṣā-pada*), [not relying on pride] constitutes the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint);

"consulting and receiving the Dharma" constitutes the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas); and "first studying the Sūtras and Vinaya" constitutes the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings).

These apply equally to the seven classes of followers; however, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not entirely coincide. In the Hīnayāna, one may act with pride toward those who are worthy of being consulted.

If one does not invite [the preceptor], one commits an offense. Otherwise, one must simply avoid arrogance; there is no prohibition against inviting everyone. In the Mahāyāna, the primary task is the seeking of the Dharma;
therefore, one should invite all and never be arrogant. Only that which is prohibited should be avoided, while nothing else is forbidden.
△ Twenty-third: Arrogant Deviation in Reciting the Precepts. Part Two: First, the performance of observance and transgression; second, obtaining the precepts upon seeing the signs.
If, O Sons of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one wishes to receive the Bodhisattva precepts with a sincere heart, [one should do so] before a Buddha or a Bodhisattva...
Before an image, one should take the precepts through a self-vow. One must perform repentance before the Buddha for seven days;

if one obtains a favorable sign, one then attains the precepts. If one does not obtain a favorable sign, one should practice for two weeks, three weeks, or even up to one year, until a favorable sign is obtained.

Once one has obtained a favorable sign, one may then receive the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva. If one does not obtain a favorable sign, even if one receives the precepts before an image of a Buddha, one does not obtain the precepts.
"Regarding 'after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa': this is said in contrast to the time when the Buddha was in the world.

The Tathāgata has eternally extinguished the great affliction of birth and death, transcended the four currents, and, having completed his work of transforming those with whom he has a karmic connection, has returned to the limit of reality; therefore, it is called 'parinirvāṇa.

While the Tathāgata is in the world, one takes the Buddha as one's teacher; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one takes the precepts as one's teacher, regarding the teacher of the precepts as the Buddha."
"Those with good intentions" refers to those who, desiring to seek upward the unsurpassed, wondrous Way of all Buddhas and to transform sentient beings downward, give rise to the great bodhicitta.

"Those who vow to receive the precepts themselves" refers to those who, before images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, discipline their own minds and make great vows, seeking to behold the Tathāgata place his hand upon their heads and confer the precepts. "Repentance" refers to...
Having made this vow, one should further practice diligent repentance before the Buddha for seven more days regarding all karmic obstructions.
If one wishes to store lion’s milk, one must first cleanse the crystal flask thoroughly. As for auspicious signs:
whether during the time of repentance, within meditative concentration, or in dreams, one may see flowers, light, or the Buddha and Bodhisattvas.
At the summit of Mount Sāma, one beholds the various auspicious marks of the Tathāgata and thereby attains the precepts.
If one does not perceive these auspicious marks—perhaps because one’s afflictions are too deep-seated and one is unable to see them—one must further arouse a superior resolve (*adhimukti-citta*).
Before the Buddha, for two weeks, three weeks, seven weeks, or even up to a year, one must take the perception of these marks as the definitive goal; only then will one attain the Buddha-bodhi.

Receiving the precepts before an image of the Buddha may not necessarily result in their attainment; thus it is said that although one receives the precepts before a Buddha image, one does not obtain them.
Formerly, the śramaṇa Daojin of Northern Liang sought to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from Dharmakṣema, but Dharmakṣema did not grant them.
Instead, he ordered him to repent for seven days and nights. When this period had ended, Daojin went to Dharmakṣema to request the precepts once more. Dharmakṣema...
He refused, saying he would not permit it. Zhi Jin reflected that his karmic obstacles had not yet been eliminated, so he redoubled his sincere repentance for three years from beginning to end.
In a dream, he saw Śākyamuni Buddha bestowing the precepts upon him. The next morning, when he went to see Huichan, before he had even reached his presence, Huichan exclaimed, "Excellent!
You have already received the precepts; I shall serve as your witness. Subsequently, before a Buddhist image, he expounded [the precepts] for him.
The characteristics of the precepts are such that when the water is clear, the moon appears; this is the mutual resonance between the faculty of the practitioner and the Way.

Furthermore, the Vinaya Master Zhenbiao sought the precepts through arduous repentance, vowing that Maitreya would personally bestow them upon him. He doubled his efforts at night compared to the day.

After seven days and nights had passed, he beheld the Great Being Kṣitigarbha, who shook his golden staff to serve as an exhortation for the precepts. Thereupon, Zhenbiao redoubled his courageous diligence. Until—

After twenty-one days, he saw the mountains and rivers become level and full, forming a world of silver color. He was moved by the appearance of the King of Tuṣita Heaven, who came to circumambulate the stone altar.
Maitreya arrived slowly, lowered his hand to stroke [the practitioner's] head, and praised him, saying: "Excellent, O man!
To seek the precepts in such a manner—Mount Sumeru may be pushed aside with one's hand, but your mind shall never retreat. Thereupon, he bestowed upon him the dharma of the precepts.

He personally entrusted [the master] with his robe and bowl, and further conferred upon him the name Vinaya Master Zhenbiao. When the water of the sentient beings' minds is pure, the reflection of Bodhi appears therein.
If one's heart of repentance is not earnest, the nature of transgression will not be empty; the Buddha will not appear before one, and the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) cannot be attained.
△ Second, receiving the precepts in the presence of a master.
If one receives the Bodhisattva precepts before a Dharma Master who has previously received them, it is not necessary to see auspicious signs.

Why? Because this Dharma Master has transmitted the lineage from master to master; therefore, auspicious signs are not required. Thus, by receiving the precepts before a Dharma Master, one immediately attains the precepts.
This is because, through the arising of a mind of profound respect, one thereby attains the precepts. If within a thousand li there is no one capable [of conferring them]...
Regarding the precept-bestowing master: one may receive the precepts through self-vow before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, provided that one seeks a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*).

In cases where the transmission proceeds from master to master such that a favorable sign is not required—because it has been handed down through successive generations—one is indeed the legitimate son of the Tathāgata, and this is also the eternally abiding Dharma-body. Therefore, by receiving the precepts before a Dharma Master, one immediately attains the precepts.
Therefore, the Vinaya-piṭaka states: "One who upholds the Vinaya is one who occupies the place of the Buddha. Regarding the matter of profound respect:
those who receive the precepts should regard their teacher as the Buddha and give rise to a heart of earnest devotion; it is through this that they obtain the precepts.

If there is no preceptor capable of conferring the precepts within a thousand *li*, although receiving them before an image is permitted, it must emphasize the presence of the visible signs (*dṛṣṭalakṣaṇa*);

only then is it called "attaining the precepts. To say one "attains the precepts" means that one attains the essence of the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*). Regarding the method of receiving the precepts:

taking the arousal of the resolve (*cittotpāda*) as the internal cause and the body and speech as the external conditions, when causes and conditions are fully assembled, they evoke [the realization].
Regarding the essence of the precepts (*śīla-sarīra*), there are two kinds: first, non-manifest precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*); second, manifest precepts (*vijñapti-śīla*).

Non-manifest precepts are the essence of the precepts; manifest precepts are the characteristics of the precepts. Essence belongs to nature (*prakṛti*); characteristics belong to cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Essence is made manifest through characteristics—this is cessation (*śamatha*). Characteristics are cultivated by means of essence—this is practice (*pratipatti*). Although the precepts are immeasurable, they are fully subsumed within cessation and practice. Thus, Fan...
Master Shi explains: "This precept-essence (śīla-bhāva) may not arise; if it does arise, it is entirely the nature (dharmatā). Thus, nature and cultivation mutually accomplish one another.
There must necessarily be unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa). As for 'unmanifest form,' it means that the nature must rely upon manifest form-dharmas to be manifested.
It is also called untainted form-dharma (anāsrava-rūpa-dharma). However, once the unmanifest has been produced, it functions spontaneously from its essence."

It stops evil; because it does not require repeated action, it is called "non-action" (*avijñapti*). It allows for the spontaneous operation of goodness without ever lapsing into indolence, and thus it is also called "action.
Furthermore, it is said that this precept-essence is operated solely by the mind and is accomplished without relying on deliberate fabrication;
therefore, it is named "non-action. However, its reception consists of three grades: superior, middling, and inferior. The *Yingluo jing* states: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas..."
Receiving [the precepts] in the presence [of a teacher] is called the superior grade of precept. Receiving them in the presence of a Bodhisattva Dharma Master is called the middle grade of precept.

Where there is no teacher for a thousand *li*, one vows and receives them before a scripture or an image; this is called the inferior grade of precept. Regarding the superior grade of reception, its essence is obtained from the arising of the mind (*cittotpāda*).
Regarding the middle grade of reception, its essence is obtained from the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). Regarding the inferior grade of reception, it values only the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Focus the mind. Upon seeing a favorable sign, one then attains the substance (*tattva*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the section on mindfulness of the precepts, states:
"Although this substance has no form or color, it can be guarded and maintained; although it has no tactile contact, through skillful cultivation of means, it can be made complete.

Thus we know that there is a distinct substance of non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) which is obtained through the ritual of formal motion (*karmavācanā*). This also applies to those who undertake the vow by personal resolve.

It is obtained from the three white [foods] at the time of receiving the precepts, or it is obtained at the time of seeing auspicious signs. Furthermore, regarding untainted (*anāsrava*) form-dharmas:
immediately upon completing the initial reception of the precepts, one obtains the form of non-killing toward sentient beings within the dharma-realm;

one obtains the form of non-stealing toward both sentient and non-sentient beings within the dharma-realm; and one obtains the form of non-sexuality toward sentient beings within the dharma-realm. One obtains...
One does not take on the appearance of one who speaks falsely, even regarding the Dharma-realm or the Three Jewels; thus one attains the appearance of one who does not slander them.

Furthermore, among the various forms of disrespect, one does not take on the appearance of one who is arrogant toward teachers and friends within the Dharma-realm; thus one attains the appearance of one who is humble. Regarding alcohol within the Dharma-realm, one does not take on the appearance of one who drinks it; thus one attains the appearance of one who abstains from drinking.
Regarding the flesh of the dharma-realm, one attains the form of non-consumption; even regarding the dharma-gates of the dharma-realm, one attains the form of non-destruction.
Although these dharmas such as non-killing and non-stealing have no visible forms or characteristics, they are manifested by means of form.
That which is called "form not belonging to the sense-base of the eye" is form belonging to the sense-base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

Furthermore, acts such as killing and stealing are outflowing phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), whereas non-killing, non-stealing, and so forth are non-outflowing phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*); therefore, it is said that the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*) is a non-outflowing phenomenon of form.
Consequently, although one may not necessarily commit acts such as killing or stealing in every moment prior to receiving the precepts, throughout the ten directions...
The world is nothing other than the field where I practice killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and falsehood;

all sentient beings of the ten directions are nothing other than the objects upon which I exercise killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and falsehood. Yet, as soon as one has received the precepts, the worlds of the ten directions become nothing other than the ground of my benevolence, goodness, purity, and uprightness;
all sentient beings of the ten directions become nothing other than those whom my benevolence, goodness, fulfillment, and uprightness pervade.
This is the pivotal mechanism. Thus, within a single thought-moment, one accomplishes untainted, subtle, and wondrous wholesome form (*rūpa*), each instance pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.
All subsequent thoughts are likewise so. Furthermore, the eighty-four thousand *dharma*-gates are the very essence of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
The multitude of virtues possessed therein—compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—are the marvelous functional power of the precepts of non-action. Therefore...
It is said that one attains the precepts upon seeing a "good sign" (*lakṣaṇa*). "Must" means it is absolutely necessary. As for "good signs," there are both false and true ones;
since demonic activities (*māra-karman*) are numerous, they are not easily distinguished. One must examine them with great care and must not hastily take anything to be a good sign.
Even for Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*), Māras may still manifest in the form of a Buddha and bestow [precepts] upon them.
Commentary: Should not ordinary people in the final age be cautious? △ Second, the conclusion regarding the offense for violating the teachings, which has two parts.
First, relying on arrogance:
If a Dharma Master, relying on his own understanding of the sutras and vinaya, and having studied the Mahāyāna precepts, [associates with] kings, crown princes, and the hundred officials...
Regarding "acting as a virtuous friend" for those who rely on themselves, there are two meanings: first, relying on one's own internal ability to understand the sutras and vinaya;

second, relying on external associates such as kings, crown princes, and the various officials as virtuous friends, thereby giving rise to arrogance. Indeed, [such a person] serves as a teacher and model for others.
One should regard those who seek the Dharma with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, as if they were one's own newborn infant.
Whenever they have questions, one should provide instruction on each point, speaking with total sincerity to inspire in them a heart of joy and lead them toward the Buddha-dharma.
One must not, on the inside, rely on one's ability to learn and understand while disparaging those who are newly trained;
nor, on the outside, rely on the influence and status of one's associates to treat others with arrogance and fail to answer their inquiries. The *Yingluo jing* states:

"If a Dharma Master can, within any land, teach and transform a single person so that they leave the household life and receive the Bodhisattva precepts, the merit of that Dharma Master is superior [to all else]."
If one constructs eighty-four thousand jeweled stupas, how much more so for two people, three people, or even hundreds of thousands of people;
the fruit of their merit is beyond measure. △ Second, the discourse on pride.
If a newly initiated bodhisattva comes to inquire about the meaning of the sutras or the meaning of the vinaya, and one, with a light mind, a malicious mind, or a conceited mind,
does not answer each question well, one commits a minor offense.

The meaning of the *sūtras* refers to dharmas such as the cultivation of good and the abandonment of evil. The meaning of the *vinaya* refers to dharmas such as the gravity of offenses and the permissions or prohibitions regarding them.
A "light-minded" person is one who disregards the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas out of ignorance, and treats kings, officials, and even those who are not virtuous friends with contempt.
An "evil-minded" person is one who is stingy with the Dharma and deceives others because they lack a compassionate heart. A "proud-minded" person is one who relies on their own merit and wisdom.
Because one treats others with contempt, one does not provide thorough and excellent answers to their questions. These three mental states obscure the mind’s vision;
relying on one's own understanding and power, one fails to answer well, causing the principles of meaning to vanish and the characteristics of phenomena to be inverted.
Therefore, this is categorized as a light offense. This also involves both natural and prohibitive karma, and is established because it deviates from the path of guidance and instruction.

Four conditions constitute the offense: first, the person seeking the Dharma; second, the perception that they are seeking the Dharma; third, a mind of arrogance, which is the primary factor for the karmic retribution;

and fourth, the actual speaking of the erroneous explanation, with each word constituting an offense. If these are subsumed within the three clusters [of ethical discipline], it is as follows: receiving [the teaching] in accordance with the Dharma.
The precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) is not to rely on oneself; the precept of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-śīla*) is to delight in answering questions;

and the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgraha-śīla*) is such that all seven assemblies equally commit [the offense] when they all obtain the right to preach the Dharma. This applies to both the Great and Small Vehicles, for even in the Lesser Vehicle, biased preaching is not permitted.
Regarding those who do not commit the offense, the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi-saṃvara-śīla-sūtra* states: "If one knows that the person before them holds evil and heterodox views and seeks out faults..."
There is no offense. If one knows that by not speaking, the person will be disciplined; or if one knows that the person before one is incapable of respectful compliance;

or if one knows they are of dull faculties and would give rise to wrong views upon hearing the profound meaning; or if one knows that after hearing it, they would proclaim it to evil people and thereby destroy the True Dharma and so forth—in all such cases, there is no offense.
△ Twenty-fourth: Not Training in the Buddha’s Precepts (3). First, ceasing transgressions to practice upholding.
If a disciple of the Buddha possesses the Buddhist sūtras and vinaya, the Mahāyāna Dharma, right view, right nature, and the true Dharma-body, yet is unable to diligently study and cultivate them.
The "Buddha’s sūtras and vinaya" refers collectively to the Mahāyāna teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
it is stated as such to distinguish them from the sūtras and vinaya of the Hīnayāna. This Mahāyāna Dharma is the precious raft that transcends birth and death and crosses the ocean of suffering.
Without this raft, one could never emerge from the ocean of birth-and-death suffering. This is right view.
This refers to the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, which fundamentally possess the correct understanding of the original source, the mind-ground;

therefore, they are called "right view" (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). As for "right nature" (*samyak-svabhāva*): because they possess the correct understanding of the mind-ground, they accord with the correct cause of the mind-ground.
This correct cause is precisely the Buddha-nature of Śākyamuni; therefore, it is called "right nature. As for the "right Dharma-body": because one awakens to Śākyamuni’s...

Buddha-nature is my own intrinsic nature. By practicing the six perfections and the myriad deeds, such that conduct and understanding correspond and principle and phenomena are thoroughly integrated, one realizes the wondrous essence of the true, eternal fruit-virtue; therefore, it is called the "True Dharma-body.
If one does not diligently cultivate and study such Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas—the true cause and true fruit of the mind-ground—one cannot be considered a Great Being.
One has become deluded regarding correct practice and has instead entered onto a deviant path. Since one is a child of the Buddha, there is a Buddha to whom one may return;
he is my original teacher. There is a Dharma to be studied; it is my parent. As this is my original teacher and parent, I ought at all times to draw near to them and train therein.
△ Second, the commission of transgressions and the cessation of non-observance.

Yet they abandon the seven treasures to instead study false views, the two vehicles, non-Buddhist scriptures, secular classics, the Abhidharma and miscellaneous treatises, and all manner of written records;
these are causes and conditions that sever the Buddha-nature and obstruct the Path, and are not the practice of one who follows the Bodhisattva path.
The seven treasures have two meanings. First is the meaning of excellence, which refers to their surpassing all other teachings that are partial, biased, or inferior.
Second is the meaning of benefit and relief, which refers to their ability to bestow upon all sentient beings the wealth of merit and Dharma.
These are the aforementioned seven types, such as the Buddha, the Sūtras, and the Vinaya. However, regarding the seven treasures of gold, silver, and so forth, the world—

It is the most precious, for it can rescue one from poverty and suffering and bring peace and happiness to the body. Now, this Great Vehicle teaching of the Mind-Ground is the most rare and supreme among all dharmas;
it can eliminate the destitution of sentient beings and cause them to obtain the wealth of the Dharma’s merit, thereby adorning the body of Śākyamuni’s myriad virtues.
For these reasons, it is metaphorically called a "jewel. Yet, you are unwilling to study it with diligence.

This is the meaning of relinquishment. Regarding "false views": this refers to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*), and even all secular scriptures that lack the correct teaching of the groundless mind;
therefore, they are called false views. Since the view itself is false, then both the causal nature and the resultant phenomena are entirely false.
This means that the followers of the two vehicles fall into a biased emptiness, while non-Buddhists cling to erroneous calculations, and secular classics merely discuss [worldly matters].

Worldly affairs (*lokadharmas*), the *Abhidharma*—here translated as "Incomparable Dharma," which refers to the treatises of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka-yāna* and *pratyekabuddha-yāna*)—the *Saṃyukta-śāstra* (Miscellaneous Treatises), and all the treatises of the various schools of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) as well as the monastic systems of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). As the *Śata-śāstra* states:

"The ninety-six paths (consisting of ninety-five types of paths plus the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle) are all unable to attain the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. Therefore, those who follow the path of the *śrāvakas* all...
All of these are false. "All written records" refers to treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) and all worldly languages and scripts.

"Severing the Buddha-nature" means that those of the two vehicles (the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) wither the sprout of bodhi, while non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) gouge out the seed of perfect enlightenment;
thus, all their speech lacks true meaning, which is why it is said they "sever the Buddha-nature. These are the causes and conditions for obstructing the Path.

This means that taking false understanding as the cause and erroneously practicing deviant conduct as the condition, one thereby obstructs the right path of the Mahāyāna and forever loses the fundamental source-ground of the mind; hence it is called "the causes and conditions for obstructing the Path.
"Not practicing the Bodhisattva path" refers to those with false views, whose every action is entirely improper; hence it is called "not practicing."
This is the path of the Bodhisattva. △ Third, the conclusion regarding the offense for violating the teaching:
If one acts intentionally, one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).
Regarding those who commit this offense: it is not even permitted to turn one's back on the Buddha-ground and pursue the path of the Śrāvaka, let alone to study and practice it.

Regarding the secular texts of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika), they are thus categorized as light offenses of defilement because they deviate from the path leading to liberation; therefore, they are proscribed.

For example, if one practices exclusively the "lesser" [vehicle], it is merely an obstructive act (*pratikṣepa-karman*) and not a defiled offense. If one practices exclusively the "external" [paths], it constitutes both natural (*prakṛti*) and obstructive acts, and is a defiled offense.
Furthermore, if a Bodhisattva denies the existence of the two vehicles, this is also termed an offense. Moreover, regarding a Bodhisattva Bhikṣu...
A bhikṣuṇī who does not study the śrāvaka vinaya also commits a minor offense. The *Bodhisattva Upāsaka Pañcaśīla-veiyi jing* states:

"If a bodhisattva possesses the Buddha’s sūtra-piṭaka yet fails to diligently study and practice it, instead diligently studying the secular texts of non-Buddhists, they commit a grave offense. The *Śīla-mūla sūtra* states: "Regarding secular texts, the bodhisattva..."
To delight in and fail to abandon the heterodox and erroneous treatises of non-Buddhists, and not to regard them as poison, is called an offense.

If one is subsumed within the three clusters [of precepts] to study and practice the Mahāyāna: the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint precepts) means not giving rise to false views; the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precepts for gathering virtuous dharmas) means practicing the bodhisattva path;

and the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precepts for benefiting sentient beings) is the same for all seven classes of followers. All should first study this sūtra, and only when they have the remaining capacity [to do so] may they [study other texts].

They are practiced separately; the Great and Small Vehicles do not fully coincide. That is to say, for the Great Vehicle, failing to study the Vinaya is an offense; for the Small Vehicle, failing to study this sūtra is not an offense.

As for what constitutes no offense: if one studies the Small Vehicle to assist the Great, or if one studies the dharmas of the Two Vehicles with the desire to guide and transform those of the Two Vehicles so that they may enter the Mahāyāna, there is no offense.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "For the sake of debating the meaning, for the sake of refuting..."
Because of wrong views; because one wishes to know that the non-Buddhist scriptures are false while the Buddha-dharma is true;

and because one wishes to understand worldly affairs—for these reasons, there is no offense. Question: Previously it was said that "one turns away from the Great [Vehicle] and heads toward the Small";

next, "deviating from the teaching"; here, "not practicing"; and later, "momentarily thinking [of it]. These four precepts seem to overlap. Answer: First, because their orientations are contrary; second, because of the teaching...

First, they lead [beings] toward partiality and heterodoxy. Second, they habitually practice the Small Vehicle with complacency, not intending to study the Great Vehicle. Third, they habitually practice the Small Vehicle for the time being, planning to study the Great Vehicle gradually.

For these reasons, they do not overlap [in their approach]. Question: The *Fuxing* (Explanations of the Practice) states that the Small Vehicle permits practicing the external paths for one period among the twelve periods of the day in order to subdue non-Buddhists;
however, for those at the initial stage of the Great Vehicle, this is strictly not permitted. This continues until the sixth...

Regarding the stage of purity of the faculties (*indriya-viśuddhi-avasthā*), it should not be difficult for those in training (*śaikṣa*). This is accepted by the Hīnayāna. What is the refutation offered by the Mahāyāna?
Answer: There are two points. First, the wisdom of the Hīnayāna is inferior; they do not practice the external [sciences] and thus cannot subdue them. The wisdom of the Bodhisattva is superior;

even before practicing the external sciences, he is already able to subdue them. Therefore, there is no necessity to study them with such urgency. Second, the Bodhisattva studies one aspect of the Buddha’s...

All-encompassing wisdom is the root; once this wisdom is realized, one attains the root, and with the attainment of the root, the branches follow as a matter of course. Thus, there is no need to study them in haste.
For now, let your progress toward the Great Vehicle be your primary concern; how could you prioritize other matters? Those śrāvakas have no intention of attaining Buddhahood.
If one does not cause them to study, they will ultimately remain isolated, narrow-minded, and ignorant.
△ Twenty-fifth: Not Skillfully Knowing the Multitude of Precepts. Part Two: First, the performance of observance and the cessation of transgression.
If you are a disciple of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, whether you serve as a master of the Dharma, a master of the monastery, a master of instruction,

a master of seated meditation, or a master of communal affairs, you should give rise to a heart of compassion. You must skillfully reconcile disputes and skillfully guard the property of the Triple Gem,
never using it recklessly as if it were your own.
During the Buddha’s lifetime, although the great disciples were sent to various regions to propagate the teachings, they all regarded the Buddha as their master.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, each established his own school and propagated the Way of the Dharma; it was not without those who took charge of administrative affairs.
Fearing that over time things might gradually diverge, the Tathāgata therefore anticipated this by mentioning them in advance.
The "Master of Dharma" refers generally to those who preside over the dharma assembly. The "Master of the Monastery" is the *karmadāna* in Sanskrit, which here means "abbot";
he is the one who presides over the administrative affairs of the monastery, namely the *karmadāna*. The "Master of Instruction" refers to one who teaches people to cultivate merit.

To transform people toward goodness and cause them to know that the Three Jewels are a fertile field of merit (puṇyakṣetra), so that they may place their faith, take refuge, and promote offerings to them;
the "president of seated meditation" refers to one who presides over matters such as seated meditation;

the "president of arrivals and departures" refers to one who presides over matters such as the coming and going of guests—what is known as the *kalyāṇamitra* (host/guest master); and "one should give rise to a mind of compassion" refers to this context.
There are two matters, both of which take a mind of loving-kindness as their primary basis. First, by means of a mind of loving-kindness, one skillfully reconciles disputes.

This means that when those who uphold the Dharma see those engaged in conflict, they should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and skillfully subdue them with gentle words, causing them to dwell in peace and happiness so that the Buddha-dharma may endure for a long time.
Second, by means of a mind of loving-kindness, one skillfully guards the property of the Triple Gem. That is to say:
Those who manage the property and wealth of the Triple Gem, upon seeing an administrator waste or squander these resources, should give rise to a heart of compassion.

They should instruct them with kind words to make them understand the distinction between transgression and merit, so that they may cherish the permanent endowment (*sādhāraṇa-vastu*) and clearly perceive the law of cause and effect.

Thus, their own body and mind will attain benefit. Let there be no one who uses such things without restraint. "Restraint" (*du*) means the Dharma; it refers to the Buddha’s property being used for the Buddha, and the Dharma’s property [being used for the Dharma].
Regarding the application of property: monastic goods are for monastic use. Even when monastic goods are used for monastic purposes, one must still act with clarity and precision.
For example, if one uses goods intended for feeding the Sangha to construct a monastic hall, one will fall into the Hell of the Fire-Brand Shackles after death.

Furthermore, one must not transfer property belonging to the Triple Gem from this location to be used at another, nor may one transfer property belonging to the Triple Gem from that location to be used here.
Regarding the application [of resources]: there must be no application without measure. This clearly elucidates the meaning of properly maintaining [the property]. The Vinaya states:

"One should cherish and protect the communal property (sangha-sādhāraṇa-dravya) as one would guard the jewel in one's eye. The lamp-stand of Yangqi and the ginger of Baoshou serve as paradigms for all time.
Generally speaking, those who hold administrative authority, upon seeing the wealth and goods of the Triple Gem, whether it be a single coin, a *sheng* or a *he* of grain, or even a single...

A grain of salt, a single blade of grass, or a single needle must not be used interchangeably. In this present age, such matters are easily overlooked; in future generations, they will be difficult to repay.
If one possesses these items oneself, one should cherish them as if they were one’s own property and must not use them improperly.

This does not mean that it is permitted to encroach upon or misappropriate the wealth and property of the Triple Gem. Some say that one must not use them interchangeably, nor should one treat them as one's own.
It is one's own property. △ Second, regarding the violation of the teachings and the resulting offense:
to instead cause disorder among the assembly through strife and contention, and to recklessly use the property of the Triple Gem, constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).
"Those who cause disorder and engage in strife" refers to those who are unacquainted with the Vinaya and adjudicate matters contrary to principle, thereby causing the community to be unsettled.

"Those who act according to their own whims regarding the two types of precious objects" refers to those who do not understand the distinction between sin and merit, and thus [misappropriate] the property of the Triple Gem.
To act according to one's own whims and self-will is to be an unvirtuous leader who fails to settle the community.

To guard property without knowing how to manage its expenditure harms both oneself and others, thereby losing the compassionate and harmonious mind of a Mahāsattva; for this reason, it is classified as a light offense. Since one has already become the head of a monastery, [one must act with care].
One should be compassionate and harmonious toward all. Cause and effect are distinct; one must not act with license or indulge one's own whims.

This constitutes an obstructive karma (*vāraṇa-karma*), established because it harms oneself and others. It is unwholesome for extinguishing disputes, as it results in the accumulation of faults regarding the matter at hand.

It is unwholesome for guarding property, as it results in the accumulation of faults according to its use. If the Three Jewels are used interchangeably, it falls under the precept against stealing. If it gives rise to disputes...

Regarding the matter: one separately incurs a nature-offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). If categorized according to the Threefold Aggregate (*tri-koṭi*), guarding the property of the Triple Gem constitutes the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint precept);

generating a mind of compassion constitutes the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas); and skillfully reconciling disputes constitutes the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings).

Monks (*bhikṣu*) and nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*) incur the offense in its entirety; as for the other five assemblies, they do not incur the offense if they are unaware of the monastic affairs. Even if they hold office, they still incur the offense, whether the matter is major or minor.
Both are prohibited; it is strictly forbidden with no exceptions.
△ The twenty-sixth precept: Receiving Offerings Alone. Part Two: First, the practice of observance and the nature of transgression. Three sections. First, receiving guests and offering greetings.
If a son of the Buddha is already residing in a monastic dwelling, and sees a visiting bodhisattva bhikṣu entering a monastery,
a private residence, a city, the palace of a king, or even a place for summer retreat or a great assembly,
the resident monks should welcome him upon his arrival and see him off upon his departure.
"Seng-fang" (Monastery) refers to the temple where monks reside. In Sanskrit it is called *saṃghārāma*, which means "Garden of the Community.
This signifies a place where the sprouts of the Buddha's sons and the fruits of the Path are cultivated.

Alternatively, it is called *vihāra*, meaning "place of wandering," referring to the temple grounds where the monastic community traverses. The term "Bodhisattva Bhikṣu" distinguishes them from the Śrāvaka Saṃgha.
"Assembly" refers to the king’s residence, specifically the halls and chambers built by the king to provide a place for the Saṃgha to dwell.
"The place for the summer retreat" refers to where the Saṃgha is invited by the king, his ministers, or lay donors (*dānapati*) to observe the three-month summer rains retreat.
"Within the great assembly" refers to either the first day of the month, the eighth day, or the fifteenth day; these three days are [the times for the assembly].
In India, there is a monthly assembly where food is provided as an offering for the monks.
Furthermore, there is a five-year assembly held in honor of the Buddha’s *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance); a six-year assembly held in honor of the Tathāgata’s ascetic practices;
or assemblies for the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his birth, and his attainment of enlightenment; or the Ānanda assembly, held in honor of the Buddha’s younger brother.
The Rāhula Assembly is held for the sake of the Buddha’s sons. These seven assemblies were established by the Elder Sudatta out of his reverence for the Buddha;
they may be either Unrestricted Assemblies (pāṭihāriya-saṅgha) or the Sangha’s Invitation Assembly (pravāraṇā).

Regarding the offerings at these aforementioned locations, whether one is a newcomer or a long-time resident, all present have a share. Those who reside first are the hosts; those who arrive later are the guests.
As for guests: since one acts as their host, one should fulfill the Way. Welcoming them with arrival shows the presence of propriety;
seeing them off upon departure sufficiently demonstrates the mind of the Way. △ Second, providing what is required.
One should provide food and drink, dwellings and bedding, as well as rope beds and wooden couches, giving them all such things.

If one lacks material goods, one should sell one's own body, or even the bodies of one's sons and daughters; one should even cut off the flesh of one's own body and sell it to provide whatever is required, giving it all to them.

He provided food and drink as offerings to satisfy their hearts; he gave them lodgings and bedding to comfort their bodies; and he provided rope beds and wooden benches for sitting and reclining at their pleasure.
He bestowed these things upon them one by one without any stinginess or regret. He even sold his own body and cut off his flesh for the sake of his guests—this was the height of his devotion.
If it is said that even his flesh could be cut and sold, how much more so his wealth, which is but an external possession?
If this is so even for those who possess nothing, how much more so for those who do? The rules regarding men and women apply equally;
that is to say, a lay bodhisattva should likewise not begrudge body, life, or family members in order to provide for visiting monks.
Although the text mentions only "bodhisattvas and bhikṣus," śrāvaka monks should also be included in the distribution of guests and hosts; one must not fail in propriety. Regarding the provisions:

The phrase "must be equal" (*xū děng jù*) serves as a summary of the preceding text; it means that whatever items are used, one should give them with all one's heart and must not be stingy. △ Third, the sequential invitation.
If a donor (dānapati) comes to invite the community of monks, the visiting monks shall receive a share of the offerings.

The master of the monastery (vihārasvāmin) should assign the visiting monks to the invitations in due order, first clearly explaining the etiquette for reception and providing for their needs; this refers to assigning them to the invitations in sequence. Regarding the term "dānapati": *dāna* is a Sanskrit word.
"Yu" (語) means "to speak. "Ci" (此) means "this," which here refers to "giving" (*dāna*). "Yue" (越) means "to transcend.
This signifies that if a person can practice giving, they will immediately transcend the ocean of suffering of poverty.

"Guest monks" (*ātithi*) refers to all itinerant monastics from the ten directions, whether of the Mahayana or Hinayana, who have no patron (*dānapati*). "Those entitled to a share of offerings" refers to...

Regarding the offerings bestowed by a donor—whether food, clothing, undergarments, general invitations, or specific invitations—their substance extends equally to all beings of the ten directions, both ordinary and holy, regardless of whether they are guests or hosts; thus it is said that visiting monks have a share in these provisions.
As for "successive appointment and invitation," this refers to cases where a donor is unable to invite the entire assembly and instead limits the invitation to five persons.

From ten people up to thirty or fifty, they should be dispatched from among the monastic quarters in their proper order; one must not select individuals based on whether they are newcomers or long-term residents.

If there is no donor, one should even sell one's own body to provide for the community, let alone when there are patrons—how could one fail to dispatch visiting monks according to the established order?
△ Second, the conclusion of the offense for violating the teaching.
If the resident monks alone accept the invitation while failing to appoint visiting monks, the abbot of the monastery incurs immeasurable sin;
he is no different from a beast, not a śramaṇa, and not of the Śākya lineage, having committed a minor offense (laghu-āpatti).

When a donor invites the Sangha, there is originally no distinction between guests and long-standing residents. If the abbot, acting out of personal bias, does not admit the visiting assembly, this is called "receiving alone.
Every mouthful of food and drink consumed by the resident community incurs transgression; every item of wealth received constitutes an offense when its value is calculated.
Since the faults of the entire group fall upon the leader, it is said that he incurs immeasurable sin. Know only this: I...

Being full, they disregard the hunger of others; therefore, it is said they are no different from animals. As for the term "śramaṇa," this refers to a śramaṇa of the inner path—one who diligently cultivates precepts, concentration, and wisdom;
who extinguishes greed, hatred, and delusion; and who realizes the mind and attains its source. Thus, he is called a śramaṇa.
Now, by violating that source and receiving [offerings] solely out of a greedy heart, he is said not to be a śramaṇa. As for the "Śākya clan," this is...
A disciple of the Buddha ought to forget their own person for the sake of the assembly and practice the Bodhi of the Buddha.

Now, by focusing exclusively on your own self-interest, you contravene the Buddha's teachings above and diminish the merit of those who give below; internally, you violate the essence of the six harmonies, and externally, you block the path of the Sangha throughout the ten directions.
Therefore, it is said that one is not of the Śākya lineage. This constitutes a deficiency in the donor’s mind of equanimity and a failure in the Great Being’s practice of benefiting others;
it is a transgression resulting in a light impurity. This involves both natural and proscribed offenses when, during the sequential invitation of the Saṃgha, [one acts improperly].

All those within the boundary (sīmā) should have a share. The present rule against appointing visiting monks (*āgantuka-bhikṣu*) was established because of a failure to distribute the offerings and gains accordingly.
However, to receive [the gains] alone constitutes a derivative of the precept against stealing (*adattādāna*). The offense is established through four conditions:

first, there is a visitor, meaning one who is entitled to a share of the offerings and gains and has arrived within the boundary; second, there is the perception of such a visitor, which consists of six permutations (two grave and two light).
Second, there is no offense. Third, the individual who receives [the portion] in their own mind is precisely the owner of the property. Fourth, regarding the conclusion of the appointment:
if one knows that it is specifically the turn of a certain person according to the monastic order (*saṃgha-krama*), yet does not appoint them, one incurs only a minor defilement (*laghu-pāpaka*).

This is because at the time of the appointment, someone might still arrive from outside the boundary (*sīmā*), and thus the share has not yet been exclusively theirs. If, after the appointment is concluded, one gives it to another person instead, that other person [incurs an offense]. If the person themselves...

Knowing that one should not accept an invitation, yet accepting and receiving food from a donor’s house worth five *kārsāpaṇas* such that it enters one's hand, constitutes a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) identical to that of one who has been appointed [to perform the invitation].
If these are subsumed within the three clusters of precepts: welcoming and seeing off [guests] pertains to the *pratimokṣa-śīla* (the morality of restraint);

providing for every necessity pertains to the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the morality of gathering wholesome qualities); and sequentially appointing and inviting [monks] pertains to the *sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla* (the morality of benefiting sentient beings). This applies to both *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs*.
This constitutes a full offense. For the other five assemblies, it is not an offense if they are unaware of the monastic affairs. However, there may be times when food is distributed;

if it is distributed with partiality—whether being excessively generous or stingy, or being present for some while absent for others—all such instances constitute a minor offense (*laghu-āpatti*). The *Susheng jing* (Sūtra on Good Birth) states:
"If, among the Sangha, food is being served and one shows partiality toward one's teacher by selecting the finest portions and giving them in excess, this Upāsaka incurs a fault."
The offense of the mind. Whether great or small, both are prohibited; they are only forbidden and never permitted.
△ Twenty-seventh: Receiving Individual Invitations. Part Two: First, the transgression of failing to maintain restraint.

If a disciple of the Buddha, one must under no circumstances accept individual invitations so that gain and offerings enter one's own person. For such gain and offerings belong to the ten [directions].
Regarding the phrase "the Sangha of the ten directions": to separately accept an invitation and thereby take property belonging to the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself constitutes an offense.

The expression "all such [equal] items" is a general designation; it refers to whatever offerings are made to the Sangha by kings, ministers, commoners, or the populace—whether lay or ordained—and regardless of whether they are within or outside the monastic boundary (*sīmā*), one must never seek to appropriate them for oneself.
It is for oneself. Regarding "benefits and offerings" (*līyǎng*): these are things that are beneficial to one's body and mind.

This means that when a donor (*dānapati*) resolves to provide for the assembly, the substance [of the offering] pervades the ten directions and all beings have a share in it; therefore, it is said that these benefits and offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions.
To receive them separately by oneself, thereby preventing those [beings] of the ten directions from obtaining the benefits and offerings, carries the sense of a remote act of deprivation.

Therefore it is said: "This is equivalent to taking the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself. To seize and use the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for one's own benefit—how could this be tolerated?
The retribution for sin and merit, and the principles of cause and effect, are perfectly manifest. 2. Violating the Teachings and Incurring Guilt.
Among the eight fields of merit, if one uses for oneself the goods belonging to the Buddhas and sages, individual teachers and monks,
parents, or the sick, one commits a minor offense.

Regarding the eight fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), they all share the principle of being entitled to receive the benefits and offerings due to the monastic community (*saṃgha*), such as when the Buddha appears in the form of a monk or similar manifestations;
the rest may be understood accordingly. Furthermore, when the Saṃgha receives offerings and alms, it constitutes a field of respect (*gurutā-kṣetra*) for superior offerings.
The middle [field of merit] is the field of gratitude (*en-tien*), and the lower is the cultivation of the field of compassion (*pei-tien*).

If one accepts a private invitation, one not only takes the property of the Sangha from the ten directions for oneself, but also seizes the goods belonging to the eight fields of merit (*pu-tien*) for personal use.

Since a Bodhisattva benefits sentient beings universally for the sake of all, to accept a private invitation is to divert the property of the Sangha into one's own possession; therefore, this is defined as a minor transgression (*qing-gou*).

This is a prohibitive action (*pratiṣedha-karman*). It is established as a precept because it causes the donor to lose their impartiality and deprives the Saṃgha of the ten directions of its regular offerings.

A transgression is incurred through three conditions: first, there is a specific invitation; second, there are six permutations regarding the perception of that specific invitation—two heavy, two light, and two non-offenses.
Alternatively, if one is invited to receive ordination or to preach the Dharma, or if one knows that the person is not one's own [monastic kin], then one does not attend to them.

In all such cases of merit, there is no offense. Third, regarding the conclusion of accepting invitations: if one summarizes these according to the three groups [of precepts], one does not separately accept individual invitations.

This is the *vinaya-śīla* (precept of restraint). Not taking monastic property is the *kuśala-dharma-śīla* (precept of wholesome qualities). That benefits belong to the ten directions is the *sattva-anugraha-śīla* (precept of gathering and benefiting sentient beings).

These offenses are common to the five groups of the ordained; for laypeople, there is no matter of receiving offerings. The *Susheng jing* (Sūtra on the Origin of Goodness) states: "If a *upāsaka*..."

If one accepts bedding, seats, or furniture for the *sāṃghika* (monastic community) on behalf of the *caitya* (the universal community), one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. This precept should also be understood as concurrently regulating this matter;

although the regulations differ between the Great and Small Vehicles, the Small Vehicle prohibits eating separately from the community (*pṛthag-bhakta*). If among four people there is one who belongs to the sequence of the monastic community, there is no offense.
It does not prohibit receiving invitations separately. The *Prātimokṣasūtra* states: "When a donor comes to invite [the Sangha], if..."

When [a donor] comes to one's own residence, or to a monastery, or to another's house, and offers clothing, food, or various requisites, if a bodhisattva refuses to accept them or does not go because of anger or pride, it is an afflicted offense, as it involves abandoning sentient beings.
If it is due to laziness or indolence, it is a non-afflicted offense. There is no offense if one is ill, lacks physical strength, is insane, or is far away.
If the location is dangerous or the road is perilous; if one knows that [the donor] will not accept [the meal]; if one wishes to subdue them; if one has previously accepted an invitation;

or if one is practicing wholesome dharmas and does not wish to abandon them even for a moment, desiring instead to hear unprecedented teachings and their beneficial meaning—in all such cases, there is no offense.
△ Twenty-eighth: The Precept on Inviting Monks Individually. Part Two. First, the practice of maintaining and ceasing violations, which has two sections. First, inviting the Sangha and making a vow:
"If, O Sons of the Buddha, there are renunciant bodhisattvas, lay bodhisattvas, or any donors who invite the Sangha for the sake of merit..."

When seeking to fulfill a vow through a field of merit, one should enter the monastic quarters and inquire of the administrative official: "I now wish to invite monks to seek the fulfillment of a vow.
Are they ordained or lay? Are they those who have already received the Bodhisattva precepts, or are they all donors (*dānapati*) who have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts?

Regarding the invitation of monks as a field of merit to seek a vow, this refers to both monastics and laypeople inviting monks; wherever there is an invitation of monks, there must necessarily be a specific aspiration or request.
Some may seek to be reborn in heaven to enjoy blessings; some may seek liberation from saṃsāra; some may seek longevity and peace; and some may seek the extinction of nirvāṇa.
The recipient should declare their aspiration before the Triple Gem so that it may be fulfilled. Regarding the *karmadāna* (the administrator):
this refers to one appointed by the Saṅgha to oversee the affairs of the community. As with the aforementioned aspirations, [one should likewise proceed].
He entered the monastic quarters and questioned the administrative officers (karmadāna). He requested that the host not act unilaterally. △ Second, the superiority of merit through impartiality.
The officer replied: "One who invites according to the prescribed order obtains the assembly of worthy and holy monks from the ten directions; whereas worldly people invite [only] individually."
A community of five hundred arhats and bodhisattvas is not equal to a single ordinary monk (pṛthagjana) according to the order of the assembly.
Regarding the statement "the administrator reports," this refers to the person in charge of monastic affairs who should explain matters according to the Vinaya.

Having set aside the mind of discrimination, once one has entered the midst of the assembly, one must abide by the regulations of the Saṃgha; therefore it is said that by requesting [food] in order, one obtains it.

These are the worthy and holy Sangha of the ten directions. These worthies and sages possess both the provisional and the real. The real refers to those who have already realized the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path], as well as the three ranks of worthies and the ten ranks of sages.
The provisional refers to those who, though still ordinary beings, have already received the great precepts of the original source mind-ground.

Because they cultivate and study the true path of the noble ones (ārya), they are also called the Noble Sangha (āryasaṃgha). However, the term "Sangha" generally encompasses both ordinary beings and sages;

when alms are given universally throughout the ten directions with a mind of equanimity, the resulting merit is as vast as the realm of space. Yet, if the mind gives rise to discrimination, the retribution will be limited.
Moreover, since it is difficult to distinguish between the noble and the ordinary, how could one possibly fathom their relative superiority? For this reason, Piṇḍola was struck, and the śrāmaṇera—
One must not refuse clothing offered as alms; thus, it is known that by not being selective, one immediately gains the status of the noble Sangha (āryasaṃgha).

How much more so for the Tathāgata, who has already commanded the sixteen great Arhats—each leading hundreds of thousands of disciples, all of whom have realized the four fruits [of the path]—to manifest their traces as ordinary beings while secretly receiving offerings, thereby enabling donors to obtain supreme karmic rewards and benefiting sentient beings, such that no human being can [fathom this].
The Vidyādharas: 1. Piṇḍola, 2. Kāṇakavatsa, 3. Kāṇakavarṇiśreṣṭhin, 4.
Subhūti, 5. Nāgārjuna, 6. Bhadra, 7. Kālika, 8. Vajraputra, 9. Śubhaka, 10. Paṃtaka, 11. Rāhula, 12. [Name missing].
13. Nagasena; 14. Indaka; 15. Vanavāsi; 16. Aśvajit; 17. Cuḍapanthaka.
When worldly people separately invite Arhats and Bodhisattvas as the Saṃgha: the Arhat belongs to the Hīnayāna, while the Bodhisattva belongs to the Mahāyāna.
If they are invited separately, these worthies and sages are then merely the assembly of ordinary persons (pṛthagjana).
If one invites according to the sequential order [of the Sangha], then ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are themselves the noble Sangha (*āryasaṃgha*).

Therefore, it is said that a single ordinary monk invited according to the Sangha’s sequence is superior [to inviting many individually]. The *Śīlapratyaya-sūtra* states: "The mother Viśākhā separately invited five hundred arhats.
The Buddha said: 'Mother Viśākhā, you are without wisdom and lack skill; you shall not obtain great merit. Had you invited them sequentially from within the Sangha...'"
A single person attains great merit, the most excellent of karmic fruits, and infinite benefit. Question:

Is it then that five hundred noble monks do not equal a single ordinary monk? Answer: One must understand that when discussing the field of merit, even hundreds of thousands of millions do not equal the noble ones.
For example, in the past, Aniruddha offered a bowl of rice to a Pratyekabuddha; from that time onward—
Henceforth, for ninety-one kalpas, they shall receive inexhaustible blessings among devas and humans; this depends on the mind and not on the field [of merit].
Furthermore, to invite separately violates the Dharma-gate of equality and formlessness, and results in the loss of vast and perfect merit.
To not invite separately is like a single drop cast into the ocean, instantly becoming one with the body of the sea. △ Third, the conclusion regarding the violation of the teachings.

This is a transgression. To invite the Sangha individually is the practice of non-Buddhists; none of the Seven Buddhas had such a method of individual invitation, nor does it accord with the way of filial piety.
If one intentionally invites the Sangha individually, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
"A separate invitation" implies a mind characterized by high and low. As for the methods of the non-Buddhists, it is because their minds are not impartial.
That the seven Buddhas had no separate invitations clearly demonstrates the impartiality of the Buddha-mind.

Furthermore, the reason many sutras cite the seven Buddhas as proof is to make it easy for those with faith to understand. Moreover, they all manifested their traces through transformation within this Sahā world.
Within the span of a hundred kalpas, these have all been seen by those in the Heaven of Longevity (*dīrghāyus-deva*).
First is Vipaśyin Buddha, also called Vīra; this is translated as "Victorious Vision. Second is Śikhin Buddha, also called Śikhi; this is translated as "Fire.
Third is Viśvabhū Buddha, also called Suvarṣa; this is translated as "Omnipresent Sovereignty. These are the three World-Honored Ones.
All appeared during the past *Vibhūṣaṇa-kalpa* (Adornment Aeon). Fourth was Krakucchanda Buddha; some call him Krakutsunda.
This translates as "That Which Should Be Severed. Fifth was Kanakamuni Buddha; this translates as "Golden Silence," or alternatively, "Golden Sage" (*Kanakarṣi*).
The sixth was Kāśyapa Buddha, here translated as "Drinking Light. The seventh was Śākyamuni Buddha, which translates as "Able Sage" or "Able Scholar.
If even these seven Buddhas still followed the order of the monastic assembly, how much more so should a Great Being?

To invite [monks] out of order is to offend the Buddhas and oppose the Sangha; therefore, it is said that this does not accord with the way of filial piety. If one intentionally invites monks separately...
That is to say, whenever one prepares an offering, one should practice impartial giving. To make any distinction is to violate the Buddha’s precepts; such merit will likewise be limited.

This is like honoring one's father while being disrespectful toward one's mother; it incurs the offense of a light impurity (*mṛdula-āpatti*). This constitutes an obstructive karma (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
This was established because [the donor] discriminates between fields and non-fields, and because their mind is narrow and inferior, failing to accord with the Dharma-gate of equality.

If one gathers [the Sangha] through the three groups (triskandha) and does not invite them individually, this constitutes the *vinaya-śīla* (precepts of discipline), which accords with the way of filial piety; the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precepts for gathering wholesome dharmas), which involves inviting according to the order of the assembly;

and the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precepts for benefiting sentient beings). These apply equally to the seven classes of followers and are common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The aforementioned precept regarding the exclusive acceptance of offerings is...

To fail to send a guest monk to attend an invitation constitutes an offense. Next is the precept against accepting individual invitations: this refers to incurring an offense by personally accepting an individual invitation from another.

The present precept concerns incurring an offense by personally selecting and inviting monks. There is no offense in cases where one is not seeking merit by feeding the Sangha, or when there is a specific discussion to be held with acquaintances, relatives, or friends; in such instances, making individual invitations does not constitute an offense.
△ Twenty-ninth: The Precept Against Living by Wrong Means of Livelihood. Part Two. First: Abstinence from Committing Offenses. Part One: The Evil Mind.
If, O sons of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, for the sake of profit and sustenance...
To act with a malicious mind for the sake of gain and offerings reveals that one lacks the intention to benefit sentient beings according to their needs.
Because this involves a malicious mind directed toward evil matters, the Sūtra says: "Those who have many desires seek many gains, and therefore their suffering and affliction are also many."
If one performs wholesome deeds with a wholesome mind, then much merit will be generated. △ Second, listing the specific activities: trafficking in the sexual favors of men and women;
preparing food with one's own hands; grinding and pounding grain oneself; practicing physiognomy on men and women; interpreting the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of dreams;
