determining whether a child will be male or female; incantations and arts; methods for training hawks; and compounding a hundred kinds of poisonous medicines—these [are the ten unwholesome paths of action].
Poisoning with various poisons, snake venom, the poison of raw gold and silver, and *gū* (sorcery) poisons;
and those who traffic in the sexual services of men and women—meaning they purchase young men and women to sell them for carnal pleasure.
This is to sever ties with one's own kin, to defile the family reputation, and to disregard all sense of shame; it is something that both monastics and laypeople alike must prohibit.
To "prepare food with one's own hands" means to personally tend the hearth and cook the meals. To "grind and pound with one's own hands" means to grind and husk the five grains oneself.
Even regarding the Buddha’s prescribed rules for a bhikṣu’s meal, he would only eat after the food had been received from a *śrāmaṇera* (lay attendant); how could a śramaṇa [do otherwise]?

[This] gate [leads to] making plans for a livelihood. Having already lost one’s dignified demeanor (*vīryā*), it also fosters the greed of others. This matter applies solely to the regulation of those who have left the household life.

Regarding "divining the marks of men and women": *zhan* (占) refers to divination, determining the fortune or misfortune of individuals; *xiang* (相) refers to examining physical forms and observing the vital breath (*qi*).

Both are false judgments concerning whether a person is male or female, and their longevity, early death, poverty, or success. Regarding "interpreting the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of dreams": *jie* (解) means...
They describe events seen in a person's dreams, whether auspicious or inauspicious, as well as whether the fetus in the womb is male or female.

Regarding "incantations" (*mantra*), these refer to the heterodox and erroneous incantations, talismans, and registers of non-Buddhists that can summon spirits and dispatch generals, or seize the eight souls and seven spirits.
Regarding "arts" (*kalā*), this refers to illusionary arts capable of manifesting various illusory phenomena to delude people.

"Mind. "Skillful" means a master craftsman; "expert" means a skilled artisan. This refers to a master craftsman or skilled artisan who creates exquisite objects to manifest their extraordinary talent.
Regarding the method of training hawks: it refers to being adept at training hawks and dogs to seize the lives of living beings.
Regarding the hundred and thousand kinds of poisons: it refers to taking all manner of worldly poisons and compounding them into a decoction.
Ointments, pills, and powders are used to harm living beings. Regarding "snake venom": the venom of a snake resides in its head or its tail;
one may extract its brain or its seminal fluid to injure people. Alternatively, it may be compounded with other malevolent substances such that contact with it inevitably causes death.
It is like a venomous snake biting a person, for which there is no remedy. "Gold and silver poison" refers to raw gold.
Raw silver is of an extremely poisonous nature; if ingested, it will immediately end one’s life. As for "poisonous *gū*," it refers to concocting toxic medicines;
if consumed, they cause the abdomen to swell and form a *gū*-worm. To engage in such practices as these to obtain offerings and support oneself is called "wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*);
it is not the path of a Great Being’s compassion. 2. Conclusion on the Offense of Violating the Teachings.
To have no heart of compassion and no heart of filial obedience—if one intentionally acts [in this way], one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding "having no heart of compassion": a Mahāsattva should take loving-kindness as their primary thought, pitying sentient beings as if they were their own infants.
They should sacrifice themselves to benefit others; yet instead, they live for themselves and harm others, which is like eating the flesh of one's own child. Therefore—
It is said that they lack a heart of compassion and lack a heart of filial piety. A Bodhisattva regards sentient beings as his own parents;
yet to instead harm those "parents" for the sake of one's own self-interest is the height of rebellion. Therefore, it is said that they lack a heart of filial piety.

If one acts intentionally, it demonstrates that the act was not committed by mistake. As a disciple of the Buddha, maintaining the Way and abiding in integrity, sustaining one’s life through purity—only then does one not violate the outward appearance of a śramaṇa.
How could one, for the sake of profit, engage in trade or pursue various means of livelihood?

Internally, one loses the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); externally, one harms social customs. This constitutes a minor defilement offense (*āpatti-avadya*). However, if the object dies, one commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).

This involves both natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibitive offenses (*prajñapti-sāvadya*); it is established because of the absence of compassion and filial piety. Nevertheless, among these, only the two matters of selling medicine and [administering] poison possess both types of natural offenses;

the remainder are merely prohibitive offenses. These are subsumed under the precept against harming sentient beings. Regarding poisonous drugs, the offense is incurred at the time of compounding them.
Light [offense]. If one harms living beings at that time, a grave offense is incurred accordingly. The same applies to training hawks.
If a layperson supports themselves through incantations, crafts, or medicine in accordance with the Dharma, and does not harm living beings, there is no offense.

For those who have left the household life, it is also permitted to use authentic incantations to rescue those in peril and alleviate distress, provided they have no intention of seeking profit. Question: Regarding the pounding and grinding used to prepare food, for a layperson... [is this permissible?]
Exemption. Answer: There are two meanings to this. First, for the sake of one's own livelihood, it is not the practice of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa). Second, regarding the five grains:
because there are many insects within firewood and rice, if one does not harm living beings, it is not an improper means of seeking a livelihood.

This is also permitted for the two lower groups of the ordained. If these are subsumed within the Threefold Aggregate, it constitutes the morality of restraint (saṃvara-śīla) by not sustaining one's life through wrong livelihood.

To give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and filial piety, and to observe the precepts of wholesome dharmas so as not to harbor evil thoughts, constitutes the precept of protecting living beings. This applies equally to the five groups of renunciants.

For laypeople, with the exception of three types—selling women, training hawks, and dealing in poisons—all other means of livelihood conducted in accordance with the Dharma do not constitute a violation.
The *Sūtra on the Good Life* states: "If an upāsaka requires agricultural work, he should not seek [to use] water that is not pure, nor [land that is] dry."
In places where seeds grow, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrong thought); this may also be subsumed under this precept. "Pure water" refers to water free of insects.
Regarding "places where plants grow on land," this refers to areas where land-grown grains, wheat, and so forth are cultivated; it is unnecessary to use water that would cause injury to insects.
This is prohibited for both monastics and laypeople alike. There is no offense if, for example, a renunciant uses such means incidentally for divination, incantations, or technical arts.
One may employ expedient means to guide sentient beings and cause them to enter the Buddha-way; this is not a transgression provided it is not done with a mind seeking profit.
As for incantations (*mantra*), they are used for treating illnesses and rescuing those in distress; therefore, they are found throughout both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.

According to the sūtras and śāstras, there are five or four types of wrong livelihood, which correspond to the precepts mentioned here. The first is feigning extraordinary abilities for the sake of gain and offerings.
Specifically: first, for the sake of gain and offerings, one speaks of one's own merits; second, for the sake of gain and offerings, one divines omens of good and ill fortune;
third, for the sake of gain and offerings, one raises one's voice and displays an air of authority to inspire awe and respect in others;

fourth, for the sake of gain and offerings, one speaks of the offerings one has received to move the hearts of people—these are the five kinds. As for the four kinds: first, eating with the mouth lowered.
First, eating from the ground: this refers to practicing medicine, geomancy, and cultivating fields and gardens. Second, eating by looking upward:

this refers to observing celestial phenomena, such as the sun, moon, and the five planets. Third, eating by looking around: this refers to fawning upon those with power and influence, acting as a messenger to the four quarters, using clever speech to seek much gain.
Fourth, eating by looking downward: this refers to studying various incantations and arts, divining good and bad fortune through astrology and calculation, or engaging in [such practices].
The opposite of the above is called "pure livelihood sustenance" (*pariśuddhājīva*). Regarding pure livelihood sustenance, there are four kinds:
first, fruits and vegetables from deep mountains; second, constant practice of begging for alms; third, food sent by donors; and fourth, pure food within the Sangha.
One sustains life by means of these without defiling the mind-ground; therefore, it is called pure livelihood sustenance.

△ Thirty: The Precept Against Disrespecting the Auspicious Time. This has two parts. First, the cessation of what should be maintained and the commission of what should not be done; this also has two parts. First, disrespect:
"If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, personally slanders the Triple Gem, feigns intimacy and attachment, and speaks of emptiness with their mouth..."

To engage in worldly existence, acting as a go-between for laypeople to facilitate the sexual union of men and women, creating various bonds and attachments—this is the cause of covetousness for those with evil minds.
"One's own person" means to exclude others; "slanderer" means one who defames.
This is a general designation for such matters as acting as a go-between for men and women, which destroys the essence of the Sangha; thus it is said with the mouth.

To speak of emptiness and so forth [in such a manner] is to destroy the meaning of the Dharma; to fail to practice the precepts of the fast (upavāsa) and to engage in killing, robbery, and the like is to violate the Buddha’s prohibitions.

Therefore, it is said that these constitute slandering the Triple Gem. "Fraudulently appearing to be close" means feigning dignified deportment and falsely assuming the appearance of a practitioner to draw near to the Triple Gem, thereby inducing others to have faith and respect so as to seek gain and offerings. "Speaking of emptiness" refers to...
This refers to those who verbally profess words of liberation while in practice engaging in schemes for profit. Regarding "acting as intermediaries for laypeople":
*tong* (通) means to communicate; *zhì* (致) means to convey an intention. This refers to carrying a man's intent to a woman, or a woman's intent to a man, thereby causing them to meet.
"Engaging in various forms of bondage" refers to committing the aforementioned impurities.
These matters are all the entanglements of self and others; by means of them, one wanders through birth and death within the three evil realms and fails to attain liberation.
Therefore, they are called "bondage and attachment. △ Second, the favorable time.
Regarding the six fast days (*upoṣadha*) and the three months of the long fast (*trai-māsa*).
As for the six fast days, the *Caturmahārāja-sūtra* states: "On these days of fasting for the various devas, they observe the good and evil of human beings.
Each of the Four Heavenly Kings governs one quarter of the world and regularly dispatches messengers on the eighth and twenty-third days of the month to conduct inspections."
14. They travel among humanity to examine good and evil. On the twenty-ninth day, they dispatch the Crown Prince to descend.

On the fifteenth day of the following month, the Four Kings descend in person, commanding the sun, moon, five planets, and twenty-eight lunar mansions to diligently observe the good and evil of sentient beings.
If they see that those who cultivate goodness are numerous, they ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to inform Śakra Devendra and the various devas.

They congratulate one another and protect the boundaries of their realm. When they say that the asuras have diminished and the hosts of devas have increased, they bestow auspicious blessings, bestow emoluments, and increase the lifespan.

If they see that those who practice virtue are few, the devas become anxious and distressed, saying that the race of asuras has multiplied while the hosts of devas have decreased; they then send down misfortune, diminish emoluments, and shorten the lifespan.
The realm is beset by many calamities; therefore, the Buddha said that if one practices the fast on these six days, the merit shall be double that of other days.
As for the three months of the "Great Fast" (*trīṇi dīrgha-vrata-māsāḥ*), they refer to the first, fifth, and ninth months of each year.

These are auspicious months, the months during which Śakra-devendra conducts his inspection tours. Within this celestial palace, there is a great precious mirror. From the first month of the year, it [reflects]—
In the second month, it illuminates the western continent; in the third month, the northern continent; in the fourth month, the eastern continent;
and in the fifth month, it again illuminates the southern continent. Thus, through these three cycles, it observes the good and evil of human beings.
Whenever an ordinary person raises a thought or stirs a mind, it appears clearly and naturally within the mirror. Such is the sun and such is the moon; they exhaust [all things].
This is a day and month when spirits and deities gain power, a favorable time for the Heavenly Kings to successively conduct their tours of inspection.

It is precisely at such a time that one ought to avoid evil and cultivate goodness. Not recognizing this as a favorable occasion, yet instead becoming negligent and violating the precepts without giving rise to shame or fear—this is what is truly called an "evil mind. △ Third, the conclusion on the offense for transgressing the teachings.
To commit acts of killing or robbery, or to break the fast and violate the precepts, constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding "killing and robbing": this refers to failing to cultivate pure conduct, managing worldly affairs and attachments, losing the bodhicitta, and severing the lineage of the Buddhas;
this is called "killing. To preach that emptiness functions as existence, thereby deviating from the holy path while receiving the faithful offerings of others—this is called "robbery."

To commit such offenses with one's own mouth is called robbery. If one actually instructs others to kill or rob, they incur both the karma of nature (*svabhāva-karma*), which falls under the two precepts against killing and stealing. Regarding those who break their fasts and violate the precepts:

a lay bodhisattva, on the six fasting days (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*) and during the months of long fasting, should observe the eightfold *upavāsa* precepts, taking the abstention from food after midday as the fast. If...

To consume food at an improper time constitutes a violation of the fast; hence it is called "breaking the fast. For those who have left the household life, one must never eat at an improper time for the rest of their lives.
To violate this rule incurs the aforementioned offenses. The *Adornment Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) states:

"If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the pure dharmas of the six perfections and concurrently cultivates the eight precepts—the prohibitory laws of all Buddhas—then these good sons and good daughters..."
The six perfections constitute the complete and pure practice of the Dharma. To fail to cultivate them is called violating the precepts.

Associating with laypeople, engaging in unrighteous acts, diminishing the merit of others, destroying their Dharma-wealth, and thereby harming both oneself and others constitutes a minor transgression.

This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited action), established because of managing the affairs of laypeople. If one summarizes these by means of the three clusters (*tri-skandha*), they are as follows: [the cluster of restraint, the cluster of merit, and the cluster of wisdom].

Returning [to lay life], one must not personally associate with laypeople (*avadātavasana*). The *vinaya* precepts consist of not slandering the Triple Gem. The precepts of wholesome dharmas consist of not committing killing or theft;
these constitute the precepts for sustaining life. These are uniformly regulated for the five groups of monastics. That is to say, at all times, one must not manage the affairs of laypeople.
For the two groups of householders who have already received the Bodhisattva precepts, failing to show respect during auspicious times also constitutes a minor offense.

[This constitutes] a defilement. The *Śubhasūtra* states: "If an upāsaka is unable to observe the eight precepts and make offerings to the Triple Gem within one month, he incurs the offense of 'loss of resolve.
This is regulated for both major and minor [offenses], being strictly prohibited without exception. △ Second, the exhortation to uphold [the precepts].
These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart. They are explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Formulation of Precepts" (Chūjin, Volume 6).
[Note on terminology:
Regarding the phrase "internally harboring the virtue of a lion," *saṃgha* in Sanskrit means "lion" in this context; it refers to the Great Lion’s Roar.
When the young lions hear it, they all become brave and robust; the hundred beasts hide away.

When the Buddha-lion roars, the Bodhisattvas who hear it increase their spiritual powers, the hosts of Māras are terrified and disperse, and those who are disciples of the Buddha learn the Buddha’s dignified deportment, increase their power of faith, and should ever mind his virtue.

The majestic gaze of the King of External Phenomena is called *gaja* in the Sanskrit language, which here means "elephant. An elephant’s backward glance involves the entire body turning along with it;
this is a mark of the Great Being, the Tathāgata. With body and mind focused as one, whenever he observes something, his head and body turn together.

For this reason, humans and devas revere him, and the hosts of māras are struck with terror. As a model for the sons of the Buddha and a guide for future generations, one should likewise [emulate this].
Thus it is. One must not act with frivolity or recklessness.
When Śāriputra beheld the dignified and composed deportment of Aśvajit, faith and reverence arose within him, and he immediately asked:
"Who is your teacher? What Dharma do you profess? Aśvajit replied: "All phenomena arise from conditions; when conditions cease..."
"The Dharma leads to cessation. My teacher, Śākyamuni, always speaks thus. Upon hearing this, Śāriputra immediately realized the first fruit [of the path].
Yulü was Cūḍapanthaka; this means "born by the side of a small road. His elder brother taught him a single verse. Four...
Candra could not remember it; he forgot the preceding and lost the subsequent. His elder brother sent him back home, where he wept and wailed outside the gate.
The Buddha observed the causal conditions and saw that this was not one whom a śrāvaka could deliver. Therefore, he led him out. The Tathāgata took pity on him and comforted his mind.

He then used his supernormal power to transform the verse Candra had been reciting, saying: "The one who has entered into tranquility rejoices; Seeing the Dharma, they attain peace and happiness. The world..."
Freedom from anger is the supreme joy; not harming living beings is the highest happiness. There is no worldly pleasure equal to freedom from desire; renunciation of sensual craving is bliss.
To subdue one’s own pride—this is the foremost joy. He was further instructed, and immediately upon reciting it, he realized the fruit of arhatship.
The *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) states: "In principle, dharmas are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished;

now, we speak only of their non-arising, hence they are called 'unborn' (*anutpāda*). When a bodhisattva, regarding these unborn dharmas, endures suffering and endures pleasure, remaining unmoved and non-retrogressive, this is termed 'endurance of the unborn nature of dharmas' (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."

Regarding the five grades of the Iron Wheel: formerly, when the Chan Master Huisi of Mount Nanyue attained the purity of the six sense faculties, his disciples were doubtful at his death as to whether he had realized the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
The Master said, "In my lifetime, I hoped to enter the Copper Wheel [grade] because I led disciples too early."
"To harm oneself while benefiting others is possible only under the Iron Wheel-turning King.

Furthermore, when the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai—successor to Nanyue—was nearing his end, his disciples asked him, 'We do not know in what stage of realization you have entered. The Master replied, 'You are too lazy to plant roots of goodness and instead ask about my merit.
It is like a blind man asking about milk; what benefit would there be in telling you the truth? I shall now act to shatter your delusions.'"
I doubt it. I do not lead a multitude; I must purify my six sense faculties. To harm oneself for the sake of others is merely the stage of the five ranks.

This refers to the five ranks of the external ordinary person (*bālapṛthagjana*) within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). First, the mind of sympathetic joy; second, reading and reciting; third, preaching the Dharma;

fourth, concurrently practicing the six perfections; fifth, correctly practicing the six perfections. The iron wheel is the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) within the Perfect Teaching. This is heard through the Perfect [Teaching].

One cultivates perfect practice through perfect faith. By progressing from the preceding stage of external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), one becomes doubly and repeatedly more profound and clear, thereby attaining entry into the ten stages of perfect faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Regarding the two categories of afflictions—the root and the derivative—the root affliction is the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā-kleśa*). That is to say, this root...
The delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*) is able to give rise to all afflictions (*kleśa*). There are six roots (*mūla*): namely, greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and views.

Second, the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), which follow [the primary ones], number twenty and are divided into three categories. The first category consists of eight major [afflictions]: namely, greed and so forth. (Note: *śraddhā* appears to be a textual error for *lobha* or is listed as a distinct factor here).

Laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), lethargy (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), and distraction (*vikṣepa*).

The two intermediate [defilements] refer to shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). The ten minor [defilements] refer to anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāsa*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), arrogance (*mada*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*).
*Sāṃkhya* (僧佉): This is translated as "owl" (*ulūka*), which is the name of a non-Buddhist school.

This person appeared eight hundred years before the Buddha and attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). The treatise he composed is named *Vaiśeṣika*, which is translated as "Unconquerable" (*asādhya*).
It consists of one hundred and sixty thousand verses; that is, the treatise on arts and mathematics (*śāstra*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speaks of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*): first, grammar (*śabdavidyā*), which explains glosses and defines characters, clarifying their categories and distinctions;

second, the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*), including technical skills, mechanical devices, and the calculation of yin-yang and calendrical cycles; third, the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*), involving prohibitions and incantations to ward off malevolent influences.
1. Medicine (Cikitsāvidyā); 2. Logic (Hetuvidyā), which examines and determines the heterodox and the orthodox, and investigates and scrutinizes the true and the false; 3.
Inner Science (Adhyātmavidyā), which thoroughly elucidates the subtle principles of cause and effect within the five vehicles.
Yangqi’s Lamp Vessel at Mount Yangqi. When Chan Master Fange was attending upon Ciming, he served as the head of the administrative office (jianyuan).

He installed two lamp vessels; when his fellow practitioners looked on in curiosity and asked for the reason, the Master said: "The lamp vessel beneath the pillar is the communal property of the monastery;
it is used for public affairs. The lamp vessel atop the pillar is my own; it is used for private matters. They said: [This is indeed so.]
"Why do you slight the permanent property of the Sangha while valuing your own? The Master said:
'What you do not know is that one may take a drop of oil from oneself and place it in the Sangha's bowl, but one must never take a drop of oil from the Sangha's bowl and place it in one's own.
Because of this, his reputation spread in all directions and his fame was transmitted for a thousand ages."
Baoshou Shengjiang Baoshou. When Master Mubao was attending upon Wuzu Keqin, he served as the head of the administrative office (kusi).
When Keqin fell ill, he ordered an attendant to go to the storehouse to fetch ginger for decoction. Baoshou scolded him. The attendant reported this to Keqin, who told him to take money and buy some.
Baoshou gave him the ginger. Later, the Prefectural Governor of Yunchou sent a letter requesting that Keqin recommend someone to succeed to the abbacy of Dongshan.
The abbot Jie said, "A man who sells raw ginger can dwell [in this way]," whereupon his fame resounded throughout the world.
Master Pan—Song Zhipan, the Vinaya Master—widely propagated the study of the Vinaya; he was a contemporary of the Repentance Master Ciyun and the Venerable Siming.

Pindola was beaten. Pindola means "The Immovable. Long ago in the Western Regions, there was an elder who heard that the Arhat Pindola had received the Buddha’s command to serve as a field of merit for people of the future age. He immediately prepared a great assembly and invited the Sangha;
however, Pindola did not appear at three successive gatherings. The elder then went before an elderly senior monk (*sthavira*) and offered a formal confession.
The Elder said, "I accepted your invitation for all three assemblies. Yet you yourself employed a slave who barred me at the gate.
Seeing that I was old and my robes were tattered, he took me for a *caṇḍāla* ascetic and struck me on the right side of my forehead with a staff, breaking it.
When I came for the second assembly, he struck me again on the middle of my forehead, breaking it so that I could not enter. When I came for the third assembly, he struck—"
"The left side of my forehead has split. Having said this, he vanished. [The monk] then realized it was indeed [the disciple].
A śrāmaṇera did not receive the gift of robes from the Song dynasty śramaṇa Huìquán. He had a disciple who had attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
While waiting for Huìquán’s illness, the disciple said, "When you pass away, Ācārya, you will be reborn into a Brahmin family. Huìquán said, "I—"

"By accumulating the karma of sitting in meditation, how could one possibly be reborn there? The disciple said, "The Ācārya’s faith in the Way is not yet firm, and furthermore, your engagement in external studies has not ceased.
Although you possess meritorious karma, it is insufficient for transcendence. If you were to organize a superior assembly and provide food for a single Sage, you could achieve the fruit of the Path.
You should then offer your saṃghāṭī robe as a gift; if anyone requires it, do not discriminate."
When the assembly was being held for the elders and juniors, it reached the time for the distribution of robes. A śrāmaṇera approached Quan and requested a robe.
Quan, thinking he was his own disciple, said, "I wish to offer this to the Holy Monk; how can I give it to you?
However, reflecting on his previous words that he could not choose between people, he joyfully gave it to him. On another day, seeing this śrāmaṇera, he asked him:
"I previously gave you a robe; does it not feel too large? The śrāmaṇera replied, "I simply could not obtain the robe, as I had other business;
I am ashamed that I was unable to attend the assembly. Only then did Quan realize that the former śrāmaṇera was one transformed by a sage.
Viśākhā (Visheshaka), here translated as the *Dī* (氐) lunar mansion, refers to the month in which the moon is in conjunction with the *Dī* constellation.

Regarding the construction of a monastic hall for the Sangha’s property at Mount Yungai in Hunan: Shouyong took the Sangha’s property to build a monastic hall, but after his death, he fell into the Hell of the Fire-Brand Shackles (*agnimālā-naraka*).
Carrying the shackles, he sought out Zen Master Zhizhe, who appraised the value of the hall and used it to provide offerings for the monks.
The Master acted according to his words. [Feng] Mengyong thanked him, saying, "I have been reborn among gods and humans.

*Dili* refers to one who can know the dragon veins, sand, and water of the earth, as well as the principles of movement, stillness, and consolidation, in accordance with the transformative operations of Yin and Yang;
it is also called *kan-yu*. This is because the earth can carry all things like a carriage (*yu*), and thus it is so named.
The "person who selects the site" is the geomancer (*kānyu*).
The five stars refer to Mars (*Hing-fuk-sing*), Saturn (*Chen-sing*), Jupiter (*Sui-sing*), Venus (*Tai-pai-sing*), and Mercury (*Chen-sing*).
The eight winds are: first, gain; second, loss; third, defamation; fourth, praise; fifth, renown; sixth, insignificance; seventh, suffering; and eighth, pleasure.
These eight types are said to be called "winds" because they can fan the human mind, giving rise to love and hatred.
The First Tide of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Seven.
Recorded by the Vinaya-transmitting Śramaṇa Shuyù of the Qing-gǔ Hángzhōu Zhāoqìng Wànshòu Ordination Platform.
△ Four: Precepts on Not Redeeming [Slaves], Part Two. First: Listing the Characteristics, Nine Sections. Thirty-first: Failing to Practice Redemption.

The second section on Precepts. First, the two aspects of maintaining what is practiced and ceasing what is transgressed. First, regarding the act of seeing someone selling [the Dharma], which has two parts.
First, the seller. The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, after my parinirvāṇa, in this degenerate age, if you see non-Buddhists or any evil persons..."

"Robbers" refers to those who appear after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; this specifically reveals the degenerate age of the Final Dharma. During the time when the Buddha was in the world, all people knew what was wholesome, and such things did not exist.
Because they do not comprehend their own minds, they give rise to various heterodox views, desiring to surpass the Buddha-way. Therefore...
They are called non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Having given rise to unwholesome thoughts, they desire to bring harm to all and sever the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom;

therefore, they are called evil persons. They forcibly seize the images of the Triple Gem and of their parents, and they harm those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta; therefore, they are called bandits.
Such people as these do not revere the Triple Gem, are unfilial toward their parents, and act with transgression and malice;
therefore, it is called an evil age. △ Second, that which is sold.
To sell images of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, or one's parents; to sell the sutras and the Vinaya; to trade in monks and nuns;

or even to sell those who have resolved their minds for enlightenment—bodhisattvas and practitioners of the Way—so that they may be conscripted into government service or made into slaves for all manner of people.
Regarding the phrase "selling images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or one's parents":

this refers to cases where a person, possessing a heart of faith and reverence, mindful of repaying the Buddha’s kindness, fashions images using precious incense materials and the seven treasures for the purpose of making offerings.
Or, it may refer to a child who, longing for their parents whose labors were boundless, likewise paints or constructs such images for the sake of offering them. Because of these [circumstances]...
These are objects that may be sold; therefore, they are prepared in advance. Furthermore, parents and children possess great kindness and virtue equal to that of the Triple Gem;
thus, they are grouped together. Moreover, the Buddha is the Great Compassionate Father and the Bodhisattvas are the Great Compassionate Mothers;
they are able to bestow happiness upon sentient beings and able to extract them from suffering. If these [objects] were to be forcibly seized by evil persons, or stolen by bandits and thieves...

To sell [the Sangha] is to destroy the Jewel of the Buddha. As for the Sūtras and Vinaya: the Sūtras open the mind to reveal one’s true nature, while the Vinaya restrains the three karmas and the six sense faculties;
to sell them is to destroy the Jewel of the Dharma. Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs are the field of merit for humans and devas, and the monastic Jewel dwelling in the world;
to sell them is to destroy the Jewel of the Sangha. Although only two categories are mentioned here, they encompass all.
This applies to all seven assemblies. A "bodhisattva who has resolved their mind" refers to one who has first generated the great resolve and received the bodhisattva precepts.

A "practitioner of the Way" (dàorén) refers to one who has long cultivated the bodhisattva path. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One who has attained the Way is called a practitioner of the Way.
Other members of the monastic community, although they have not yet attained the Way, are also called practitioners of the Way because they cultivate the supramundane path. All of these are included.

They belong to the Three Jewels. Like those mentioned above, they may be kidnapped, stolen, or sold by others, or conscripted into government service, or forced into labor for the classes of scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants, thereby losing their autonomy;
hence it is said that "they may be employed by officials" and become slaves to all people. This is called bringing disgrace upon the Three Jewels and causing the virtuous to sink into ruin.
This is why it is called an "evil deed. △ Second, regarding redemption:
When a Bodhisattva sees such a matter, he should give rise to a heart of compassion and, through skillful means, rescue and protect them, teaching and transforming them everywhere.

To take property to ransom a Buddha image, a bodhisattva image, or the images of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as all the sūtras and vinayas—when a bodhisattva sees such matters, it is an external encounter with objective conditions.
To give rise to a mind of compassion is the internal arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
This means that by giving rise to compassion, one causes others to attain the joy of nobility; by exercising pity, one causes them to leave behind the suffering of lowliness.
Furthermore, regarding "providing protection through skillful means": this refers to seeing such matters as those before one's eyes.

In this very final age of degeneration, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) should properly uphold the Buddha-dharma amidst these evil times, extensively perform virtuous deeds, and transform and guide sentient beings.

Through skillful means, he should exhaust his strength to provide protection; if he himself is incapable, he should exhort and convert donors to redeem and liberate [beings], and must not conceal [the suffering].
"Endurance" means to sit by idly watching. Yet, if one does not rescue [the Dharma], one fails in the two benefits; if one rescues it, one fulfills the two adornments.
If one sees the Three Jewels being destroyed and remains indolent, failing to redeem them, the Three Jewels will from this point on be cut off and extinguished;
the human life-force of wisdom and the field of merit will likewise have no recourse. 2. Violating the Teachings and Committing Offenses.
If one does not redeem [the victim], one commits a minor offense (laghu-pāpaka).

Regarding the transgression herein: it is not the conduct of a Great Being (mahāsattva) for a Bodhisattva to see a situation requiring intervention and yet fail to rescue; therefore, this is defined as a minor offense.

This constitutes a prohibitive act (pratikṣepa-karman), established by the rule that failing to do so brings disgrace and humiliation upon the Triple Gem and one's parents. The offense is completed through four conditions: first, one ought to redeem [the victim].
The object refers to sacred images, sūtras, vinaya texts, monks, and so forth. Second, there are six permutations regarding the intention to ransom them:

two cases of grave offense, two cases of light offense, and two cases of no offense. Third, there is the absence of any intent to ransom them. Fourth, if one causes them to be defiled or insulted, an offense is incurred according to the specific act.

Even if one lacks the power to intervene, to remain indifferent and unconcerned also constitutes a light offense. If these are subsumed within the Threefold Refuge, it is an offense upon seeing [the objects] being sold.

Giving rise to loving-kindness; the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*); protecting through skillful means; the precept of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-śīla*); and the precept of gathering and saving sentient beings through teaching and ransoming them—these constitute the "precept of gathering and saving beings.
These apply equally to all seven assemblies of disciples, yet the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not fully coincide. In the Hīnayāna, one incurs an offense if one does not ransom one's parents;
for other cases, no such prohibition is seen. For a Bodhisattva, the great task is to protect and save others; thus, all should be ransomed. There is no transgression if one lacks the power to do so.
Or, as in the case of circulating the scriptures according to the Dharma.
△ Thirty-second: The Precept Against Harming Sentient Beings. Part Two: First, regarding the commission of offenses and the observance of restraint.
If a disciple of the Buddha, one must not keep swords, staves, bows, or arrows for sale; nor use light scales or small measures; nor rely on official authority or influence.
One must not seize the property of others, bind them with malicious intent, or sabotage their successful undertakings.

One must not raise cats, wildcats, pigs, or dogs, nor keep weapons such as knives, staves, bows, or arrows—these being instruments of harm. Furthermore, one must not hoard or sell false weights and small measures.
These are instruments of deception and should not be used. All things should be treated with equality; the same principle applies to short measures.

To act out of official influence or power, such that matters are handled like a forced seizure, is not the conduct of a Son of the Buddha. If one should obtain anything [in such a manner], it is improper.
This also pertains to the precept against stealing. "Binding with a harmful intent" refers to injuring their physical bodies.
"Destroying completed works" refers to ruining their already accomplished undertakings; both result from failing to obtain what one seeks. "To nurture" means to raise or keep as livestock.
For instance, a cat that can catch mice is called a "rākṣasa that walks on the ground," and a *lī* (weasel) that can seize prey likewise possesses [such qualities].
There are many different kinds. The small ones are like mice; the large ones are like cats. They are adept at catching rats and seizing prey; none of them may be kept as pets.
As for the two species of pigs and dogs, they will ultimately cause harm. While sustaining life, they inflict injury; within their kindness lies enmity.
Although one does not kill others directly, the causes for killing are fully present. These six aforementioned types all possess the evil discipline (*akuśala-saṃvara*) of harming living beings.
This harms compassion and is not what is appropriate. In the Vinaya of the Hīnayāna, keeping dogs is permitted for the purpose of guarding one's dwelling place.
△ Second, the violation of the teaching and the incurrence of guilt.
If one intentionally maintains [such practices], one commits a minor offense (laghu-āpatti).
Regarding the transgression herein: to trade in instruments of killing, to seek wealth through unrighteous means, and to unjustly harm all beings—therefore, these are defined as minor offenses.

These implements involve both natural (prakṛti-sāvadya) and proscribed (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya) actions; they are prohibited because they create distant obstacles to harm and contradict compassion. This concludes the tenth [precept].

Keeping implements for killing constitutes the offense of selling and binding for the purpose of harming. Number twelve: selling persons of noble birth and coffins; this refers to selling implements such as blades and staves.

Number seventeen: specifically clarifying reliance on power; this enumerates six types [of offenses] while simultaneously establishing prohibitions. Thus, the preceding and succeeding sections differ.

If these are subsumed within the three categories of training, "not selling implements for killing" pertains to the *vinaya-śīla* (precepts of restraint), while [the regulation of] weights and measures pertains to the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precepts of gathering wholesome qualities).

The precept of using things fairly: this is the precept of maintaining life without relying on official power. It applies equally to all seven assemblies of the Sangha. The *Sūtra on the Good Life* states:

"If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) engages in trade for the sake of his own livelihood, when selling goods with measures or scales, once the price has been stated, he must not retract it or shift from the cheap to the expensive.
When measuring goods with measures or scales, he must use them fairly according to what was previously established. As it says:

If it is uneven, one should speak so as to make it level. If one does not do so, one incurs an offense of mental derangement (duṣkṛta). This applies even to laypeople, let alone those who have left the household life;
the precepts are established for both the great and the small, being strictly prohibited and never permitted.
△ Thirty-third: The Precepts on Wrong Actions and Discursive Thought (2). First: Refraining from and Maintaining [the Precepts], and Violating through Action (2).
First: With an Evil Mind. If a Buddha’s disciple, with an evil mind...

"Those with evil minds" refers to those who do not discern the opportunity to benefit sentient beings, but instead harbor perverse thoughts and perverse perceptions, flowing along with their passions.
This is because they violate the fundamental mind. A Bodhisattva should contemplate the supramundane path and its practices; they must not involve themselves in worldly, miscellaneous affairs.

If one involves oneself in such miscellaneous affairs, right mindfulness becomes obscured and confused, leading to the commission of all manner of unwholesome acts. Once such karma has been produced...
It is not correct; that perception is also erroneous, and is therefore called an "evil mind. △ Second, listing five matters: first, observing combat.
One observes the combat of all men and women, as well as the combat of military arrays, generals, soldiers, bandits, and so forth.
"Contemplation" refers to the mind that contemplates; "all" refers to the objects being contemplated. Regarding the fighting of men and women, there are two types:
first, the playful dancing and competitive play of men and women; second, quarreling and physical combat. Regarding the fighting of military arrays and the like, there are also two types:
first, the battle between two nations; second, the combat between enemy troops. As the Great Sutra says: "Elephants, horses, oxen, dogs, and..."
One must not watch fights between chickens, pheasants, parrots, and the like; nor should one watch even the brawls of those who are violent, addicted to wine, or unruly.
To watch such things will inevitably lead to injury and damage, cause one to give rise to unwholesome thoughts, cause one to lose one's own dignified deportment, and invite the ridicule of the laity.
This is not the way of one practicing the Bodhisattva path. △ Second, listening to music.
Furthermore, one must not listen to the sounds of conchs, drums, horns, lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, *konghou* lutes, singing, shouting, or the music of courtesans.
The "conch" (*bèi*) refers to a sea shell; it is blown to initiate musical performance. The "drum" (*gǔ*) is made by carving wood for the frame and stretching leather over both sides;
it is struck to accompany the music. The "horn" (*jiǎo*) refers to a cow horn; it is blown within the army as a signal and can also startle horses.
The *qín* is the stringed lute. In this land, Fuxi first fashioned it with five strings; later, King Wen added the "lesser *gong*" and "lesser *shang*" strings, making it seven-stringed.
The *sè* was first made by Paoxi with fifty strings, which Yu Shun later changed to twenty-five strings.
The *zhēng* has thirteen strings and was created by Meng Tian. The *dí* (flute) is one foot four inches long, with seven holes, held horizontally.
The *chuǐ* (flute): made of bamboo; created by Qiu Zhong. The *kōnglóu* (harp): twenty-four strings; created by Shi Yan. Both are also made of bamboo.
These eight items above all produce sound by means of external objects. As for singing and chanting: men and women produce sounds through their own voices to sing and recite.
Although these human pleasures differ from one another, once they enter the faculty of the ear, they cause the mind to flow and wander.

There is no difference; for this reason, they are not permitted to be heard. As for "music and dance" (*gīta-vādya*), this refers to items ranging from conch-shells and drums up to the *sheng* (reed organ), *huang* (mouth organ), *xiao* (flute), *guan* (transverse flute), *pipa* (lute), *sanxian* (three-stringed lute), *erxian* (two-stringed lute), and so forth. Furthermore, singing performers and the like all belong to the category of music and dance.

In ancient times, women were often employed to perform these arts; thus, the character is written with the "woman" radical. All of these are gateways to negligence and obstruct the practice of the Way.

This merely increases sensual pleasure and is of no benefit to body or mind. Even if one perceives the opportunity and acts with appropriateness, manifesting what appears to be an unwholesome deed, such an act is not inherently unwholesome;
it is unwholesome because of the mind. Therefore, the mind is mentioned first. If the intention is to lead those who are errant back to the correct path, then it is not an unwholesome mind;
it entirely belongs to the Bodhisattva’s playful exercise of supernatural powers within samādhi.

This is the case. Although the *Yìshū* (Commentary on the Meaning) opens up the possibility that one may perform offerings to the Triple Gem, it does not permit doing so for one’s own amusement, nor does it permit the Sangha to perform it themselves;
rather, it directs laypeople to do so. △ Third, miscellaneous performances.

One must not play *chūpú* (backgammon), *weiqi* (go), *bōluosè xī* (the game of the Bodhisattva), *tánqí* (dama), *liùbó* (six-sided dice), *pàigu* (ball games), *zhìshí* (stone-throwing), *tóuhú* (pitch-pot),
*qiāndào* (pulling the path), *bādào* (eight-path games), or *xíngchéng* (city-storming).
*Chupó* (樗蒱) refers to the game of *bóchóu* (博籌). *Wéiqí* (圍棋), that is, the large board game of nineteen lines (*shíjiǔ lù*).

Regarding *páluosè xì* (波羅塞戲): *páluo* is a Sanskrit term, while *sèxì* is a Chinese word; *sè* is pronounced like *sài*. It refers to *bósè* (博塞), meaning "to block" (*sè*) by means of dice (*cǎi*), where victory is determined by the throws.
The *Shuōyuàn* (說苑) states: "When the pieces move and block one another, it is called 'blocking' (*sè*). As for *tánqí* (彈棊), according to... [text continues].
In this region, Han palace women used their cosmetic trunks as playthings; they would strike one another with chess pieces, which is also called *tánqí* (board-game).
*Liùbó* (six-sided game) was a *shuānglù* (double-six) game invented by the Wei Prince of Chen-si. *Pàigu* refers to the present-day game of kicking a ball.
As for "throwing stones and tossing into the pitch-pot," in antiquity stones were used for throwing, whereas today arrows are used for tossing; [the game] is won by those who hit the mark.
"To win" refers to the eight paths that lead to the city. The "city" refers to the board with four gates and eight paths, as described above.
Although these various matters differ from one another, they all belong to the category of gambling.

Since a Great Being cultivates the emptiness of persons, the emptiness of phenomena, and the Great Way, how could he harbor a mind of victory or defeat to deceive sentient beings? △ Fourth, divination by lot and stalks.
They perform divination using fingernail mirrors, *shichō* stalks, willow branches, alms bowls, and skulls.
As for the "fingernail mirror," it refers to the method of the circular light (*maṇḍala*): that is, applying medicinal ointment to the fingernails or employing incantations (*dhāraṇī*).
By reciting mantras over the fingers, they become as clear as a mirror; hence it is called the "claw-mirror" (*zhaojing*). It reflects human affairs to manifest good and ill fortune.
As for the *shichao* stalks, they emerged from the tomb of Fuxi and Wenwang in this land. Above, they are shrouded in vapors; below, they guard the numinous tortoise.

Their clusters must number one hundred, and their stalks must be a fathom long. They are used to divine calamities and blessings. Although these stalks originated in this land from Fuxi and Wenwang, [they were brought here].
...their tombs. This practice already existed among the Indians of old; they all used this grass as divining stalks (*śi*).
As for the willow branch (*yángzhī*), if the *shí* grass was unavailable, they would simply use a willow branch as the stalk.

This is similar to how in this region (China), one employs a sorcerer’s incantations to consecrate a *zhāngliǔ* tree as a deity, naming it the "Zhāngliǔ Spirit," to inquire about auspicious or ominous signs, and so forth. Regarding the alms bowl (*póbēn*): it is made from a basin...
Fill a vessel with water. Reciting incantations aloud, use a knife to stir the water until it becomes still; this determines good or bad fortune. This is the method for stirring the bowl of water.
As for the *dúlóu* (skull), one takes the skull of a person who has recently died and performs a sacrificial rite over it using heterodox arts;
it can then predict calamities and blessings from the side of a person's ear. This is called the "Spirit of Ear-Notification. Regarding divination (*bǔshì*): using a tortoise shell is called *bǔ*.
"Divining with *shī* stalks is called *shi*. This summarizes the five preceding matters; using them to determine good or ill fortune is collectively termed "divination" (*bushi*).

Although the way of divination allows even sages and worthies to seek auspiciousness and avoid misfortune as a skillful means, those who have received the Buddhist precepts should not perform it for the sake of profit. △ Five: The Use of Thieves.
One must not serve as a messenger for thieves; one must not do so in any instance whatsoever.
"Must not" means that since one should not even approach thieves, how much less should one act as their messenger? Therefore, it is prohibited.
"Must not do so in any instance whatsoever" means that, as in the aforementioned case of watching a fight, it can give rise to a mind of cruelty and merriment.
Music can give rise to a mind of lustful dissipation; theatrical performances can give rise to a mind of distraction; divination can give rise to a mind of delusive attachment;
and acting as a messenger can give rise to a mind of treachery and guile. These five types are all wrong livelihoods (*mithyājīva*).
Since each matter disturbs the Path, it is said that one must not engage in any of them. △ Second, the conclusion regarding the offense for violating the teachings.
If one intentionally commits such acts, one incurs a minor transgression (light defilement).

Regarding the offenses herein: to be greedily attached to sights and sounds, for both mind and form to be deluded, to seek wealth through gambling and arts, or to act as a messenger for profit—these are not the practices of one who walks the Bodhisattva path;
therefore, they are defined as minor transgressions. These constitute obstructive karma (*pratikṣepa-karman*). If one acts as a thief...

The purpose [of this precept] is that both types of karma—those involving volition (*cetanā*) and those involving restraint (*virati*)—are governed by what is set in motion; since neither constitutes primary karma (*maula-karman*), they are regulated [by this rule].
If one engages in improper mental application (*vitarka-vicāra*) regarding wrong action, it obstructs and abandons the Right Path, causing one to lose the benefits of both worlds.

If one does not engage in such improper mental application regarding wrong action, one remains free from agitation and regret, and concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) easily arise. If these are subsumed within the three clusters (*tri-skandha*), the *vinaya* prescribes not going to witness or listen [to improper performances].
The precept of decorum: not serving as a courtesan. The precept of wholesome dharmas: not acting as a messenger for bandits. This is the precept of gathering in sentient beings.

Now, one who is a son of the Buddha should be non-active and desireless, maintaining purity within himself. If one serves as a messenger for bandits, one debases one’s will and disgraces one’s person, thereby ruining the Buddha-dharma.
As it was said of old: "One does not serve kings or lords, holding one’s own principles in high esteem. How much more so when it concerns one’s outward appearance and robes?
To transcend the world, how could one willingly serve as a messenger for thieves? The *Śīla-sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva is indolent, lazy, or addicted to the pleasure of sleep;
or if they do not know moderation regarding improper times—this is a defiled offense. If such afflictions, being sharp by nature, arise repeatedly, this precept may also encompass them.
This rule is established equally for the five groups of the ordained, while those in the household life offer support.
Regarding the Three Jewels: it is permitted to perform music and dance for them. However, those who have left the household life (the ordained) may not do so themselves.

Even when making offerings to the Three Jewels, it is permitted to have laypeople (white-robed ones) perform such acts. This regulation applies equally to both the great and the small [monastic orders].

There is no offense in cases where one perceives an opportunity to benefit sentient beings, as was the case with the former Chan Master Huiquan, who, despite his long accumulation of merit through seated meditation, did not cease his study of external teachings and consequently could not avoid being reborn as a Brahmin.
Family. Therefore, the harm it causes is no small matter. The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xianyu jing*) states:

The Buddha said, "In a past age, there was a king named Dharmavardhana. He possessed a heart of compassion and governed the kingdom with righteous laws. Having no affairs and being at leisure, he engaged in board games with others.
At that time, a man committed a crime, and the ministers reported to the king: 'Outside, there is a man who has committed an offense...'"

"According to the royal law, how is a crime to be punished? At that time, the king was distracted by his gambling and failed to answer. The minister immediately executed him according to the penal code.
After the king finished playing, he asked his ministers, "Where is that criminal now? The ministers replied to the king, "He was dealt with according to the laws of the land;
he has already been executed. Upon hearing this, the king fainted and fell to the ground; after a long while, he finally [regained consciousness].
Sū replied, "I shall immediately abandon the kingdom and enter the mountains to dwell in self-restraint.
At that time, the king passed away and was reborn in the great ocean as a makara fish, six hundred yojanas in length. Many insects devoured his body because it was afflicted with itching.
They scrape against the Crystal Mountain, crushing and killing all the insects; their blood flows, polluting the sea until it is crimson for a hundred li.
Due to these karmic conditions, at the end of their lives they fall into the Great Hell. Since there are such transgressions, how could one not exercise restraint?
△ Thirty-fourth: Briefly Contemplating the Precepts of the Hīnayāna. Part One: The Initial Practice of Maintaining, Ceasing, and Transgressing. Sub-part One: Guarding the Precepts.

If a Buddha’s disciple guards and maintains the prohibitive precepts, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, during the six periods of day and night, they shall read and recite these precepts. Just as...
Like a vajra; like one wearing and carrying a life-preserving float when wishing to cross the great ocean;

like a bhikṣu bound by grass—this refers to those who guard and maintain the prohibitive precepts. "Guarding" (hu) means to prohibit and defend, for Māra is unable to invade them; "maintaining" (chi) means to hold fast.
Because the mind does not regress, it is "prohibition" (*gami*); this has the meaning of restraint, as it causes the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) to remain unmoved.

Because it is "precept" (*śīla*); this has the meaning of cessation, as it prevents the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) from arising. Furthermore, these fifty-eight precepts were all personally proclaimed by the golden mouth of Śākyamuni.
Like a royal prohibition or edict, no one dares to willfully transgress them; therefore, they are called "prohibitory precepts" (*gami-śīla*). This is the general heading.
This refers to practicing the conduct of the Bodhisattva precepts. "Walking, standing, sitting, and lying down" refers to the four modes of deportment.
"Six periods of day and night" means three periods each during the day and the night. During these times, one upholds the Buddha's precepts and guards the city of the mind.
Thus, one will not be tossed about by the winds of external objects. To "read and recite" these precepts clearly elucidates the meaning of upholding and protecting them.

"Reading" means consulting the original text to examine the words and thereby understand what constitutes observance and violation. "Reciting" means detaching from the text to investigate the mind and clarify its ultimate purpose.
As for "Vajra," it is named after a metaphor and possesses two meanings. First, it is a metaphor for how the precepts can shatter all...
The afflictions are like bandits. Second, the analogy for the Great Being’s mind being firm in its protective maintenance is like a vajra.
As for the life-preserving float, it is a device for crossing the sea; people crossing the sea in India sometimes make one from bird feathers or a hair bag.
Alternatively, one may use the hide of an ox or a sheep, or carry an ox bladder, always wearing it upon the body.

Should a sea vessel be wrecked, one can blow air into it to float the body across the great ocean. This is illustrated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. Formerly, there was a merchant who carried a leather bag while crossing the sea.
A rākṣasa came to beg for it, but he resolutely refused. The rākṣasa then begged for half of it, and so on, down to a mere thread or a speck of dust.
In all cases, he gave nothing away; this serves as a metaphor for one who maintains the precepts.

While adrift in the ocean of birth and death, even if such a person encounters the rākṣasas of affliction that seek to destroy their grave precepts—down to even the slightest minor transgression, not even so much as a single speck of dust—nothing can be taken from them.
Regarding the "monk bound by grass," the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* states: During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a monk who was robbed by bandits while on a journey.

They seized his robes and belongings. Fearing that the assembly would sound the gong to pursue them and further desiring to take his life, one thief among them who knew the rules of the bhikṣus said to the others, "There is no need to kill him; simply bind his hands and feet with living grass."
Regarding that precept, it means that since grasses and trees possess life, one dares not harm or injure them, remaining personally unmoving. The bandits followed his words and bound him.
The bhikṣu maintained his precepts; he would rather die than waver. Once the bandits had gone far away, a traveler came along and finally untied his bonds.
Now, it should be understood that when a Great Being protects and upholds this Bodhicitta precept, they should likewise act in this manner.
Regarding the śrāvaka’s observance of the disciplinary code (vinaya-saṃvara), it would rather be better to die than to transgress it. △ Second, generating faith:

one should constantly generate wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna, knowing for oneself that "I am a Buddha who is not yet perfected," while "the Buddhas are Buddhas who have already attained perfection."
"One who constantly gives rise to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna" means to keep this in mind at all times, without interruption. This follows from the preceding text:
although one may be able to protect the precepts, if one lacks the pure cause of right faith, then wealth and precepts will merely result in mundane, scattered goodness.
"To know for oneself that one is an unperfected Buddha" means realizing that the sentient being and the Buddha are fundamentally without two minds;

that all sentient beings will certainly become Buddhas, with the distinction being merely between those already perfected and those not yet perfected. In reality, what difference is there between a prior Buddha and a subsequent Buddha?

This is what is meant by "constantly maintaining such faith," which constitutes the full perfection of the category of precepts (*śīla-skandha*). Because the followers of the Two Vehicles lack this faith, they do not [possess it].
One does not hope for oneself to become a Buddha, nor does one hope for all sentient beings to become Buddhas.
Because the Mahāsattva possesses true faith and is free from doubt regarding this, he is able to deliver himself and others, attaining equal perfect enlightenment together with them.

That "the Buddhas are those who have already become Buddhas" means that the Buddhas have already attained the perfection of the three bodies (*trikāya*), are fully endowed with the ten thousand virtues, have exhausted the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*), and [transcended] the two...
Upon death, one perishes forever. Therefore, I am able to cultivate the causes in this manner, and will necessarily realize the fruit in this manner.
If there were even the slightest negligence, I would lose the fruit of the Buddha’s future adornments. △ Third, the generation of the resolve.
Generate the bodhicitta, never letting it depart from the mind for even a single thought-moment.
"To generate" means to bring forth and develop. "Bodhicitta" is precisely the Buddha-mind; as it is said: "This very mind is the Buddha."
This Buddha is this very mind. Because one has previously been mired in delusion, it must now be awakened.
This means that although one may have possessed the wholesome faith of the Mahāyāna, if one does not give rise to the bodhicitta, that faith will have nothing upon which to rely;

therefore, one should give rise to this great mind in order to strengthen its nature. Furthermore, guarding and maintaining the prohibitive precepts is "conduct" (śīla), and constantly giving rise to wholesome faith is "faith" (śraddhā).

"I am a Buddha who has not yet attained completion. This is the interpretation. It refers to the bodhicitta, which is the essence of the wisdom of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*) within the stages of faith, understanding, and practice.

Although these three—faith, understanding, and practice—possess this essence, when realizing the fruit of Buddhahood, one must take the Mahayana bodhicitta that has been generated as the primary factor. Question: From what does the great bodhicitta arise?
Yes. The answer is: it arises from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). As the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"For the sake of wishing to rescue and deliver all sentient beings, one gives rise to the power of compassionate vows and so forth to seek unsurpassed bodhi. If it were not for the purpose of delivering sentient beings..."
I would not have generated this bodhicitta. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:
"From the first bhūmi up to the tenth bhūmi, within each and every bhūmi, great compassion is the primary factor. The *Bodhicittavivaraṇa* states:
"The great bodhicitta arises from compassion; all the most excellent qualities of the Buddha-dharma have compassion as their root."
The *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta* states: "That which exists at the time of the cause is the bodhicitta;
when the fruit is perfected and its qualities are complete, it is called Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). The dharma of bodhicitta is inconceivable, and all Tathāgatas praise it.
The *Vimalaprabhā-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "The merit produced by generating the bodhicitta is as vast and supreme as the realm of empty space."

It is inexhaustible. Even if someone were to fill Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with precious jewels to offer to the World-Honored One, and if another person were to join their palms with utmost sincerity and once give rise to the unsurpassed mind of right and equal enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*), the merit of this latter person would surpass the former merit beyond all calculation. As stated in the *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood*:
All phenomena are signless; they have the characteristic of empty space. Having cultivated this contemplation, it is called the ultimate bodhicitta.
One should know that all phenomena are empty, for by awakening to the fact that phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, the essence of mind remains as it is, and neither body nor mind is perceived.
Abiding in quiescence, the wisdom of ultimate equality and reality ensures that there is no retrogression.

If deluded thoughts arise, recognize them and do not follow them; when delusions subside, the source of the mind is empty and still, endowed with all virtues and possessing inexhaustible wondrous functions.
Therefore, the Buddhas of the ten directions all take the practices and vows of the ultimate truth as their precepts; it is simply by possessing these that [one attains liberation].
The mind is that which can turn the wheel of Dharma, bringing benefit to both oneself and others.
To have this mind not depart from one’s thoughts at every moment is the meaning of upholding the precepts through right view; it means that within each *kṣaṇa*, one does not abandon this bodhicitta.
Only when the practice of the precepts is thus matured into bodhi can the fruit of Buddhahood be expected. Furthermore, one should know that my own mind is...
Because it is the mind of all Buddhas, one seeks the Buddha-way above; because they further know that my mind is the very mind of sentient beings, one transforms sentient beings below.
Yet, regarding this mind and this thought, one must not be separated from them for even a moment. If there were separation for even a single thought-instant, [the practice would fail].

This refers precisely to giving rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles that seeks only self-deliverance. The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* states: "To regress from the Great [Vehicle] and adopt the Small is what all the Sages condemn.
A Bodhisattva does not do so; seeing the suffering of sentient beings as identical to their own, they give rise to great compassion and love them as if they were their only child.
Just as a mother who has obtained food constantly thinks of her child, if one dwells in emptiness alone, one is then abandoning others."
Furthermore, they would be unable to purify buddha-fields, transform sentient beings, or fully perfect the Buddha-dharma;
none of these could be accomplished. Therefore, although a bodhisattva enters the world, birth-and-death and afflictions cannot impair their wisdom.
Although the path to Buddhahood is long and distant, they do not regard it as remote. Although the number of sentient beings is vast, their resolve remains courageous.
With a firm mind free from retreat, one advances with diligence and never succumbs to weariness or indolence. Thus it is said:
"The Bodhisattva possesses courage regarding birth-and-death (saṃsāra) and does not relish nirvāṇa.

To be courageous in birth-and-death means to manifest birth without being born, remaining unstained by birth-and-death—just as a lotus flower in the mud is not defiled by the mud. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states that the sutra...
It is said that lotus flowers do not grow on high plateaus or dry land, but rather in low-lying, damp mud;

thus we know that the "high plateau" of nirvāṇa does not produce the flower of a bodhisattva’s great compassion. It is within the mud of saṃsāra that a bodhisattva possesses the supreme function of benefiting sentient beings.
Although they remain within saṃsāra, they are unstained by it—this is because the vows of the Great Being are firm.
His resolve is courageous; therefore, it is said that [this thought] does not depart from his mind for a single moment. △ Second, the conclusion regarding the offense for violating the teachings:
If one gives rise to even a single thought of the two vehicles or of non-Buddhists, one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).

If one should give rise to even a single thought of the mind of the Two Vehicles or of non-Buddhists—meaning that within what is believed, understood, practiced, or resolved—one should not give rise to even a single thought of seeking self-deliverance.
If one gives rise to even a single thought of self-deliverance, one immediately departs from the bodhicitta and abandons the bodhisattva vow;
such a person is called a non-Buddhist. Therefore, they are equated with the Two Vehicles. Thus it is said:
They are also non-Buddhists (tīrthika). It should be seen that one who upholds the Bodhisattva precepts ought not to give rise to even a single thought of the Two Vehicles.
To give rise to such a single thought is to be the same as a non-Buddhist. As it is said: "The slightest admixture is the cause of suffering in the three miserable realms."
Therefore, one incurs the defilement of transgression. Question: How can this single thought constitute a transgression? Answer:
Although it is but a fleeting thought, it injures the seed of the Buddha and causes one to lose the bodhicitta.
For example, in a past kalpa, Śāriputra gave rise to the bodhicitta and practiced great generosity. A brāhmaṇa came to him and begged for his eyes. Śāriputra said, "The eyes are..."
"My own body is of great utility; to give it to you would be utterly useless. The brahmin firmly sought his eyes.
Śāriputra gouged out his eyes and gave them to him. The brahmin looked at them and threw them away;
having thrown them, he spat upon them, uttering words of foul abuse, and departed treading upon them with his feet. Śāriputra said, "I previously spoke to you about these eyes."

"It is useless. You stubbornly desired it, yet now you cast it aside as worthless. Sentient beings are so dull and inferior that they are almost impossible to transform. It would have been better to seek early on your own liberation;
instead, you have withdrawn your great resolve and returned to practicing the Lesser Dharma. Only upon reaching the time of Śākyamuni Buddha did you finally realize the stage of an Arhat.
By seeking self-liberation through a single thought-moment, you have lost the great benefit of the Great Vehicle. Should you not be cautious? This is an obstructive karma."

Because one deviates from what was originally practiced, a restriction is established: if one intends to turn away from the Mahāyāna toward the Hīnayāna, the offense constitutes the eighth [grave offense] before the plan is completed;

once the intention to turn away from the Mahāyāna is finalized, it constitutes a loss of the precepts and is ranked as the tenth grave offense. This precept is established because one does not wish to turn away from the Mahāyāna.

It is specifically stated that the Hīnayāna is easy to practice, and thus one might wish to sever the fetters first and subsequently bring about the transformation of beings; for this reason, it is prohibited. If, by means of the three clusters (*tri-skandha*)...

To gather and return [to the path]: to guard and uphold the prohibitive precepts is the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint); to constantly give rise to wholesome faith is the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas);

and to resolve upon the bodhicitta is the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings). These seven groups of followers share these precepts in common, though the Mahayana and Hinayana do not fully coincide in their entirety. "Common" means that they equally must not give rise to the mind of an externalist (*tīrthika*).
While the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*) were their original practice, one does not violate [the precepts] if one temporarily enters the state of the two vehicles or externalists.
One does not commit an offense for the sake of transforming others.
△ Thirty-fifth: The Precept Against Not Making Vows. Part Two. First: The Practice of Observance and the Offense of Non-observance. Three sections. First: Making Vows.
If a Buddha’s disciple, one should always make all vows.
"Constantly" means that it should not be merely a single arousal [of the mind], but should arise repeatedly so that the bodhicitta continues in an uninterrupted succession.
"All" refers to the ten matters mentioned below. "Vow" (praṇidhāna) carries the meaning of aspiration and longing;
for if there were no aspiration and longing for all the sublime causes, wondrous fruits, and immeasurable wholesome dharmas, [they would not be realized].
Such desires as these can never be fulfilled. Therefore, a Bodhisattva should always aspire to and seek superior matters, directing the mind toward wholesome objects;
in the future, one will thereby achieve fulfillment. Thus, one should constantly bring forth such aspirations. △ Second, explaining the matters.

I shall be filial and obedient toward my parents, teachers, and monastics. May I encounter a good teacher and virtuous companions in study who constantly instruct me in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya,

the ten stages of setting forth (*daśa-prasthāna*), the ten stages of nurturing (*daśa-poṣaṇa*), the ten adamantine stages (*daśa-vajra*), and the ten bhūmis, so that I may attain understanding and practice according to the Dharma,
firmly upholding the Buddha’s precepts.
"To be filial toward one's parents and respectful toward one's teachers and monks" refers to the benefit of knowing how to repay kindness; it is the vow of upholding the precepts.
Since filial piety is itself called the precepts, it constitutes the foundation of the ten vows. If this foundation is deficient, the remaining nine vows will likewise be lost.
Therefore, the first vow specifically mentions filial piety. "May I obtain a good teacher" refers to the benefit of becoming a vessel for the Dharma. [The text notes: "The father above..."

To serve one's mother and preceptor is called filial devotion; to seek out a "good teacher" is to choose an enlightened master. One is said to be "good" when both practice and realization are fully perfected.
If one possesses realization but lacks practice, how can they lead me forward? If one possesses practice but lacks realization, [how can they do so?]
"How can I open my mind-ground? It is for this reason that I repay my parents and ensure the flourishing of the Triple Gem;

all of this is accomplished through the power of the teachers' instruction. Thus, among the ten vows, the teacher is the most essential. Although roots of goodness may have been planted in previous lives, awakening depends upon a virtuous teacher.
Yet, though a disciple may possess faith, without the guidance and training of a virtuous teacher, they cannot undergo the process of refinement."
One polishes and refines oneself; yet, without becoming a vessel for the Dharma, one must therefore seek a good teacher as the second aspiration.

A fellow student who is a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend) serves as a supportive assistant. Such a person is one who shares the Mahayana precepts and teachings with you, and is a friend who skillfully understands the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground.
This means that even if one encounters an enlightened teacher who provides explanation and liberation, one still requires the guidance of a virtuous friend.

"Carrying [the Dharma] forth: Just as Linji inspired the head seat and Changli gained entry through the attendant, one must therefore regard seeking a teacher as paramount and visiting friends as a priority;
thus, the third aspiration is to obtain fellow students and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
May those who constantly instruct me in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya provide this definitive meaning and benefit—namely, that I may always have such teachers and friends."
