While he was secretly listening to the recitation of the precepts, the Vajrapāṇi yakṣa crushed him with his mace until his body was reduced to fine dust.
Thus we know that one who acts as a teacher must not fail to be cautious. △ Second, clarifying the rejection of heterodoxy and the lack of faith.

These evil people do not receive the Buddha’s precepts and are thus called "beasts"; life after life they do not see the Triple Gem, being as heartless as wood or stone, and are thus called "heretics.
These people of false views are no different from wooden stumps.
"These groups of evil people" is a general summary of the aforementioned categories of externalists (*tīrthika*) and those with evil and heterodox views.

It means that because they do not distinguish between good and evil or the wise and the foolish, they are like animals; they do not receive the Great Precepts of the thousand Buddhas and lose the seed of Bodhi.
Therefore, wherever they are born, they do not perceive the Triple Gem. Though they dwell among human relations, they do not know how to turn toward the Great Way that transcends the world.
Thus, like wood or stone, they lack a mind; from delusion to further delusion, their six sense-faculties are darkened and obstructed, no different from a block of wood.
When one speaks to such people as these, they not only fail to understand, but they even give rise to derision.
Because it would constitute slander, one should not speak [of these matters]. Second, the violation of the teaching and the resulting offense:
if a Bodhisattva preaches the seven Buddhas' teachings and precepts before such evil persons, they commit a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).
Regarding the "Precepts Taught by the Seven Buddhas": this refers to the Great Precept of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi*).

Although it has been taught by all Buddhas of the three periods of time, it has been transmitted through successive reception from the Seven Buddhas of the past; this is precisely what makes it so intimate and personal.

One must therefore exercise discernment and hold oneself in high regard, refraining from lightly explaining it to those of external paths who have not received the precepts, lest one cause harm to oneself and lead others into ruin.

The transgression is no small matter. The Dharma-water of the Tathāgata moistens only the sprouts that possess roots; I fear that those who lack faith will, on the contrary, increase their doubts and deliberations.
Although the Dharma is equal for all, its exposition must be appropriate to the capacity of the recipient.

If the giver does not show honor and the receiver does not show respect, a light defilement of sin is incurred; this constitutes an obstructive karma (*pratikṣepa-karman*). Because it was preached prematurely, the recipient will be unable to give rise to realization later.

This is established by way of earnest and profound intent. A transgression is completed through four conditions: first, the person has not received the Bodhisattva precepts; second, one perceives them as such (with six permutations of perception);
third, there is a mind that intends to speak for the sake of profit—two cases are grave, two are light, and two are non-offenses;

fourth, the offense is incurred at the moment the other person hears it. If these are subsumed within the three clusters of pure conduct (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), one should not speak to wicked people; this is the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Regarding the precepts: those spoken before kings are the precepts of wholesome dharmas; they are not spoken for the sake of profit, but are the precepts for sustaining living beings.
These are common to the seven assemblies, yet the Great and Small Vehicles do not fully share them.

At all times, one must not explain the five categories of offenses to śrāmaṇeras and others of the Lesser Vehicle, for if they were to understand them, it would constitute the grave offense of stealing the Dharma. In the Mahāyāna, however, these are recited only during the fortnightly assembly.
When performing the *karmavācanā* for ordination, those who have not yet received the precepts must be sent away; at other times, this is not required.
It was stated previously that Bodhisattvas—whether bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs—should expound this sutra and its vinaya at all times.

Furthermore, the subsequent text states that one should encourage all sentient beings to receive the three refuges and the ten precepts, and so forth. Thus, it is clear that this differs from the vinaya of the Hīnayāna.

This is also a transgression. Furthermore, Bodhisattvas—whether bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs—at no time whatsoever shall speak of the offenses categorized under the five groups to those who have not received full ordination.

Likewise, Bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras and others must not preemptively learn the names and meanings of these five groups of offenses, lest they incur grave difficulties that would forever obstruct their attainment of full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) in this life. Only...
Prohibition against not opening [the door].
△ Forty-third: The Precept Against Receiving Alms Without Shame. Part Two: First, the observance of restraint; second, the commission of an offense.
First: One should not accept offerings.
If a disciple of the Buddha has left the household life with faith and received the Buddha’s true precepts, yet deliberately conceives the thought of violating these sacred precepts,
they shall not receive the offerings of any donors; nor shall they walk upon the ground of the king, nor drink the water of the king.

"One who leaves the household life out of faith" refers to one who, having resolved to seek the supreme [enlightenment] for themselves and to transform others below, departs from the home of birth-and-death and enters the family of the Tathāgata.
"One who receives the Buddha’s true precepts" refers to these bodhisattva great precepts, which are the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Therefore, it is called "right precepts. These constitute a most excellent field of merit, capable of receiving offerings.

Thus, one who conceives the thought of violating the holy precepts is said to fail to maintain their original resolve; such a person is like a field with defects, so how could they be worthy of receiving offerings?
Regarding the phrase "one who does not walk upon the ground of the king": the king is the lord of the great earth, and even a single sip of drink or a morsel of food [is his domain].
This matter belongs to the relevant authorities. Since you possess no virtue of the precepts, how can you be worthy of receiving such offerings? The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"For a person who has broken the precepts, regarding communal meals and monastic dwellings, the Buddha did not permit such a person to consume even a single morsel of food or to set foot upon even a single square of ground.
Observing this, one knows that for a breaker of the precepts, though heaven and earth are vast, there is nowhere to rest. This is the case for the donor (*dānapati*).

Even a small amount of water is difficult for such a multitude to digest; how much more so, then, the four types of offerings provided by donors, or the property belonging to the Sangha of the ten directions?
Therefore, it is said that they must not accept any offerings from patrons, nor even drink the water of a king.
II. Both the hidden and the manifest world resent them.
Five thousand great ghosts constantly block his path ahead. These ghosts cry out, "Great thief! Whenever he enters a room, a city, or a house, the ghosts further sweep away his footprints.
All people of the world revile him, saying, "A thief within the Buddha-dharma.
No sentient being wishes to see him with their eyes; such a person who violates the precepts is no different from a beast, no different from a piece of wood.
Regarding the "five thousand great ghosts," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "A bodhisattva is fully endowed with five hundred precepts.
For each precept, the Heavenly Emperor dispatches ten spirits to provide protection for the practitioner who upholds the precepts; thus, there are five thousand benevolent deities.

If one maintains the precepts with faith, then five thousand benevolent deities will provide protection. If, however, one violates them with an evil mind, then [five thousand malevolent spirits will follow]."
A thousand great spirits follow him at all times, just as carriages, horses, and servants constantly attend and protect those of high worldly rank.

When one violates the king’s law, cangues, shackles, and black-clad guards always follow to restrain and guard them. These are all distinctions between the paths of good and evil; their principle is fundamentally natural.
To "block his way" clearly indicates that he is not permitted to travel upon the king's domain. The term "great thief" refers to one who has failed [in his duty].
This harms the great precepts of the thousand Buddhas. Those who sweep away their traces will fail to ascend because they have destroyed the precepts, like a turtle dragging its tail.
They detest the filth in monastic quarters and on the roads. Such are the thieves within the Buddha-dharma; they steal by donning the robes of the Buddha.
To steal the food intended for the Buddha is, within the Buddha-dharma, to instead harm the Buddha-dharma; therefore, such a person is called a thief.

Yet, those who maintain the precepts and proper deportment are gazed upon with reverence by both humans and devas, whereas the signs of one who has violated the precepts are such that sentient beings do not wish to see them with their eyes.
All of this is a calamity brought upon oneself. As the Sūtra says: "The places where sages and worthies recite the sūtras and practice the Way—those lands are all..."

It becomes diamond. When devas and humans scatter flowers as an offering, the ground where a person who has broken the precepts walks becomes covered in rubble and debris, while sand and stones fly through the air.
For this reason, ghosts and spirits constantly sweep away their tracks. Furthermore, the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states:
"When a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts steals the Dharma of others, all the robes he wears and the food he receives [are likewise defiled]."

This is what they have stolen. For this reason, people of the world all revile them, calling them "thieves within the Buddha-dharma. Not knowing what constitutes upholding or violating the precepts, how are they different from animals?
Having no essence of the precepts in their bodies, they are no different from blocks of wood. △ Second, the conclusion of the offense for violating the teachings.
If one willfully violates the right precepts, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).

The monastic observance of the precepts is a field of merit; if the precepts are not maintained, how can there be a field? To harbor offenses without shame is to be reviled by both humans and spirits;
therefore, this is defined as a minor offense. This constitutes both natural and proscribed transgressions, arising from a disregard for the precepts.

According to the Vinaya, an offense is established through three conditions: first, the actual transgression; second, the perception of having committed the transgression; and third, the arising of the intention to commit it.

Each moment of such thought constitutes a minor defilement (*pāyattika*). The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "To give rise to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) and fail to cultivate awakening constitutes a defiled offense (*kliṣṭa-āpatti*)."

This is also subsumed within these precepts. If categorized according to the three clusters (*tri-skandha*), they are as follows: receiving the Buddha’s true precepts constitutes the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint);

leaving the household life with faith constitutes the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas), which means not violating the true precepts; and the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings) is common to all seven assemblies.

However, for a renunciant bodhisattva who serves as a field of merit for the world, the responsibility is doubly heavy; thus, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna establish prohibitions. In the Hīnayāna, it is as follows: [text continues].
This refers to the offense of a light transgression against the precepts. Depending on the specific offense committed, one further incurs the offense of a light transgression against the precepts.

The Bodhisattva’s commitment to the mind is more rigorous than that of the Śrāvaka. If one originally lacks such intent yet deliberately violates the mind, one is only charged with the primary offense according to the specific act;

this additional offense is not added. If one simply gives rise to this thought without having committed the act, for a minor case one merely reproaches the mind, while for a major case it should likewise be so.
Confession. Only *vichā* (obstruction) is not permitted.
△ Forty-fourth: The Precept Against Not Making Offerings to the Scriptures. Part Two: First, the practice of observance and the transgression of cessation.
If a disciple of the Buddha, they should always with a single mind receive, uphold, read, and recite the Mahayana sutras and vinaya. Even if one must flay one's own skin to make paper and pierce...

Using blood as ink, marrow as water, and splitting bones to make brushes, one should write down the Buddha’s precepts. One should likewise transcribe them upon tree bark, rice-husk paper, silk, or bamboo slips, and always maintain these copies.
Furthermore, one should use caskets and bags made of the seven precious gems, priceless incense and flowers, and all manner of miscellaneous jewels to store the volumes of the Sūtras and Vinaya.
"One should always maintain a single mind" means that "always" (*nitya*) refers to the uninterrupted continuity of mindfulness, while "single" (*eka*) refers to the mind being free from distraction;

this reveals the ultimate degree of diligent application and resolute commitment. If one recites the sutras and vinaya with the mouth while the mind dwells on external objects—whether those objects be wholesome or unwholesome—it constitutes discursive thought (*vikalpa*), and thus wisdom and understanding cannot arise. Now, this single-mindedness is capable of...
The mind of faith. The sutras and vinaya are the dharmas that are to be believed. These consist of both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*). As for phenomena:
it means guarding the precepts with the mind, upholding them without wavering, reciting them without forgetting, having no rebellious heart, and having no distracted intent.

When the mind does not oppose the precepts and the precepts do not oppose the mind, this is called "single-mindedness in phenomena. As for principle: it means the mind merges with the precepts to the point of non-duality, such that there is no longer anything to uphold.

Yet one maintains it; this maintenance is without the characteristic of maintaining. One recites without reciting; this recitation is without the characteristic of recitation. Thus, the mind is itself the precept, and the precept is itself the mind.

One does not perceive a subject that maintains nor an object that is maintained. There is neither transgression nor non-transgression; maintenance and transgression are fused as a pair. This is called "single-mindedness in principle.
Regarding those who receive, maintain, read, and recite, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The power of faith is called 'receiving' (*upādāna*); the power of mindfulness is called..."

To uphold [the teachings] means to read them by looking at the text; to recite them means to do so without forgetting; to explain them means to proclaim them; and to understand them means to resolve what is difficult to comprehend.

This constitutes one method of making offerings. Now, because all Buddhas attain equal and perfect enlightenment through studying the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, one should know that the sūtras and vinaya are the mothers of all Buddhas. If one does not make offerings with such sincerity and according to the Dharma, this is...
To slight the Mothers of the Buddhas of the three periods is called unfiliality; thus one incurs sin.

The passage regarding "flaying the skin to make paper" and so forth is an instance of citing the heavy to illustrate the light, thereby manifesting that the aspiration for the Dharma is most urgent. This has two meanings:

first, the flesh and blood of one's own body are connected to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); among the world’s most precious and weighty things, these are the very body and life itself which one is willing to sacrifice.
Thus, the life-force of wisdom is sustained. Second, the four great elements are false and provisional, ultimately resulting in decay and ruin; among worldly things, these are the most useless.
By relinquishing what is useless, one accomplishes the Great Function. As for "tree bark, grain, and paper": [this refers to the materials used for writing].
*Gǔ*: This refers to the *chǔ* tree. Paper is made from its bark; hence it is called "wood-bark *gǔ*-paper.
Regarding "silk, plain cloth, bamboo, and silk-fabric": *jiàn* (silk) refers to sleeve-silk; both *jiàn* and *bó* (plain cloth) are woven from *sù* (plain silk). *Sù* is also white gauze.

In the high antiquity of this region, paper-making was not yet known, so bamboo slips and wooden tablets were used extensively. However, the materials employed by various nations have varied across time and place.
The same applies here; one should act according to the time and according to the region. For example, in the five regions of India, birch bark, *tāla* leaves, and white woolen cloth are used.
In this land (China), the creation of thin paper began from the Former Han through the reign of Emperor Huan of the Later Han.
At that time, Cai Jingzhong manufactured paper using tree bark, worn-out cloth, and fish nets. Nowadays, bamboo slivers and—
It is made from *zhū* (mulberry) bark. By using this to transcribe and circulate [the teachings], one performs both the giving of material wealth and the giving of the Dharma;

thus they are widely disseminated without end. The *Sūtra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground* states: "The Dharma-Jewel has four kinds: first, the Dharma of teaching; second, the Dharma of principle; third, the Dharma of practice; and fourth, the Dharma of fruition.
All are untainted (*anāsrava*), capable of destroying ignorance, afflictions, and karmic obstructions. They consist of sounds, names, and phrases..."
The teachings are called the Dharma of Instruction. All phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, are called the Dharma of Principle.
The practices of precept, concentration, and wisdom are called the Dharma of Practice. The unconditioned, wondrous fruition is called the Dharma of Fruition.
These four kinds of Dharma guide sentient beings across the sea of birth and death to reach the other shore. For these reasons, one should wholeheartedly make offerings to them at all times.
Regarding the phrase "with the seven treasures and so forth," this serves to manifest that the mind of reverence for the Dharma is exceedingly profound.
Furthermore, there are two meanings: first, internal reverence, such as using peeled skin as paper; second, external reverence, such as using wealth, jewels, silk, and cloth.

The skin and bones represent internal renunciation, while the wealth and jewels represent external renunciation. By renouncing both the internal and the external, one’s devotion reaches its ultimate limit. As for the boxes and bags, all...
It is the vessel for storing the Dharma-treasure. △ Second, the conclusion regarding the offense for violating the teachings:
If one does not make offerings according to the Dharma, one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).
Regarding "making offerings," as mentioned above, there are five types: first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, transcribing; and fifth, [offering] incense.
Flowers. Each and every one must be offered according to the Dharma. Why is this? The Jewel of the Dharma is that which all Buddhas take as their teacher;
the Buddhas of the three periods of time rely upon it to practice, severing all obstacles and attaining Bodhi.
Until the end of the future, they benefit sentient beings. Therefore, the Tathāgata’s life of wisdom is entrusted to the Tripiṭaka. If it were not for its illumination...
If one fails to protect it, damage will inevitably occur. Such damage severs the seed of the Buddha, which is a grave act of filial impiety; therefore, this constitutes a light offense.

This is a prohibitive action (*vāraṇa-karman*), established because of a lack of reverence for the Dharma. If these are categorized according to the three groups of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*): reciting and chanting the Mahāyāna constitutes the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint);

copying the Buddha’s precepts constitutes the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas); and making offerings in accordance with the Dharma constitutes the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings).
This applies to all seven assemblies. While the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not entirely coincide, the Hīnayāna does not incur an offense for failing to recite or uphold the Vinaya;
however, the Mahāyāna practitioner should cultivate five matters. Furthermore, failing to make offerings to the Triple Gem also constitutes an offense. The *Śīla-sūtra* states:
"Within a single day and night, whether the Buddha is present in the world, or at a stupa or temple, or with a scripture, or regarding a Bodhisattva’s practice..."

Regarding the Sūtra Piṭaka and the Vinaya Piṭaka, if one does not offer even a small amount of worship to the community of bhikṣus, the assembly of great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, or fail to praise their virtues with even a single verse;

or if one is unable to purify the mind for even a single thought-moment; or if one is disrespectful, indolent, or lazy—this constitutes a defiled offense. If it is due to forgetfulness or error, it is not so.
This is not a defiled offense. The *Susheng jing* (Sūtra on the Birth of Goodness) states:
"If one obtains new grain, fruits, melons, or vegetables and does not first offer them to the Triple Gem before consuming them oneself, the upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence (*āpatti*).
If one gives leftover food to the fourfold assembly [of disciples], one incurs an offense of negligence. This is strictly prohibited and never permitted."

△ Forty-fifth: The Precept Against Not Transforming Sentient Beings. Part Two. First: The Active Maintenance and the Negligent Transgression. Part One: Exhorting Others to Receive the Refuges and Precepts.
If a Buddha’s disciple constantly gives rise to a heart of great compassion, and upon entering any city, town, or residence, sees any sentient being...
When giving birth [to disciples], one should proclaim: "All you sentient beings, you must all receive the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts.

Regarding the phrase "constantly giving rise to the mind of great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā-citta*): because a bodhisattva takes the transformation and deliverance of others as their primary concern and feels an urgent sense of pity for those suffering, they constantly give rise to the mind of great compassion.
This mind must not be forgotten for even a moment; therefore, it is called "constant. It does not say "great kindness" (*mahāmaitrī*).
This clearly demonstrates that the urgency of uprooting suffering outweighs that of bestowing happiness. Regarding "all sentient beings," this originally encompasses the six realms;
however, as long as a Bodhisattva has not yet attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), it is not easy to perceive them in cities, houses, or crowded places.
Among gods, *asuras*, hell-beings, and hungry ghosts who can be seen, there are only humans and animals. Now...
In this passage, the purpose is to cause human beings to resolve their minds [on enlightenment]. Since humans have distinctions of high and low, noble and base, the text says "all.
Next, it causes animals to resolve their minds; subsequently, it enters into forests, mountains, rivers, and wilds—solitary places—and includes spirits, ghosts, and so forth.
One should first employ various skillful means to teach them and cause them to give rise to great faith, and only then bestow [the precepts].

Regarding the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts: if one does not first instruct [the recipient] to generate the resolve for enlightenment before administering the precepts, it is equivalent to bestowing the precepts upon an evil person.
As for the phrase "one should chant," etc., this is a term used for calling out and providing a reminder;

it means that within the field of the eight consciousnesses of all sentient beings, the seeds of both the out-flowing (sāsrava) and non-out-flowing (anāsrava) dharmas are inherently and fully present. Yet, alas, because there is no such reminder, for many kalpas...
Burying it in the dust, if one encounters a timely reminder, one will naturally be able to awaken to it.

It is like an eighty-year-old man who, when called by his childhood nickname, never fails to have his heart alert and respond with his voice. Or again, like a beautiful mountain or fine river visited decades ago;
long after the fact, upon encountering someone who mentions it, the sublime scenery appears as vividly as before, such that one cannot help but dance with hands and feet.

"Trample. This present proclamation and reception is likewise so. There are three reasons why one should receive [the teaching]: first, it has existed inherently from the beginning and does not come from without;
thus, one should receive it as a matter of principle. Second, this alone is the reality while the other two are not true; thus, one should receive it according to its meaning.

Third, having been lost in delusion for a long time, one suddenly encounters a pointing-out instruction; thus, one should receive it at this opportune moment. The *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* says: "The Dharma..."

The Master first provides an explanation to inspire the student’s devotion, and only then confers the precepts. The Three Refuges consist of taking refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
This is because the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha is the true and pure field of merit. Furthermore, "taking refuge" is a term of turning back;
whereas in the past one turned away from the correct path to follow the deviant, wandering through the realms of rebirth, now one turns [toward the truth].
That deviant mind is turned toward the right path; hence it is called "turning back. One can thus perceive the inconceivable power of the Triple Gem.

By taking refuge and entrusting oneself to them, they are able to provide protection and rescue. Karmic obstructions are eliminated, merit and wisdom increase, and various demons and enemies cannot cause further harm.
Therefore, one should take refuge. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "By means of the Three..."

The Triple Gem is that to which one returns, for the purpose of seeking protection so as not to be subjected to oppression or violation. As stated in the *Chai-fu luohan jing* (Sūtra on the Subduing of Arhats):
When the life of a son of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven was about to end, he was destined to receive the body of a pig; he went to the Buddha to seek salvation.

The Buddha taught him to take refuge in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Thereupon, for seven days and seven nights, he applied himself with diligence to the Three Refuges and attained [liberation].
Previously, he was the son of an elder. Furthermore, the *Mukhaṇḍika-sūtra* states that the Buddha told King Virūḍhaka:
"If you pierce mukhaṇḍika seeds while reciting the names of the Triple Gem, you shall sever the karma of fetters and attain the unsurpassed fruit. Thus, one knows the Triple Gem.
This is the place of refuge for all sentient beings. As for the "ten precepts," they are the ten grave *pratimokṣa* rules of a bodhisattva.

One does not speak of the five precepts but rather the ten precepts because the five precepts are the cause for rebirth as a human or deva, whereas the ten precepts are the very foundation of a bodhisattva; therefore, it is proclaimed: "All you sentient beings, each of you possesses..."

Regarding the precepts of Buddha-nature: because you have been lost and deluded from beginningless time until this present life, I now point out for you the path of awakening to which you should return;
this is the primary cause for attaining Buddhahood. The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "If a person hears the names of the Triple Gem, they shall not fall into the three evil realms;
how much more so if they take refuge in the Triple Gem with a sincere heart? Furthermore, regarding the Bodhisattva...
The Bodhisattva sees that all sentient beings are none other than Buddhas; those who are not currently Buddhas are precisely those who must undergo [the process of realization].
If one does not receive the Three Refuges, one does not know the self-nature of the Triple Gem; if one does not receive the Ten Precepts, one does not know the self-nature of liberation.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "When a Bodhisattva goes to the home of a layperson, if they cannot preach the Dharma to open [their minds]..."
He instructs them to make offerings to the Triple Gem; [if they do not], they incur offense. △ Second, he causes them to resolve upon the Great Mind (bodhicitta).
If they see oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, or any other animals, they should mentally reflect and verbally declare: "You are the master of these animals; resolve upon bodhicitta.
Thus, wherever the Bodhisattva enters—whether mountain forests, rivers, or fields—he causes all sentient beings [to likewise resolve].

Regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta through mental reflection and verbal expression: when a Bodhisattva beholds all sentient beings, they should give rise to great compassion, reflecting that since beginningless kalpas these beings have lost their true nature, falsely created deluded karma, and have needlessly endured the retributive suffering of saṃsāra. Thus one acts...
Having formed this thought, he spoke these words aloud: "You are an animal; you should seek liberation. Do not endure this suffering in vain, without end.
In this way, he caused them to recognize their suffering and know it, so that their minds would seek deliverance and turn toward the Great Being (Mahāsattva).
Only then did he instruct them to resolve upon Bodhicitta; thus it is said, "the mind thinks and the mouth speaks. Furthermore, "you are an animal... [and so forth].
Regarding those who have been born: first, their karmic retributions are shown; subsequently, they are taught the essentials for transcendence.
The bodhicitta is the perfectly luminous enlightened essence of all Buddhas and the fundamental nature of sentient beings;
it is precisely the Three Refuges of Self-Nature and the Ten Precepts of the Mind-Ground. Because one is deluded regarding this mind, it remains hidden and fails to manifest.

This is why one revolves through the three miserable realms without end. Now, having encountered a true guide who has awakened this mind, spiritual awareness becomes profoundly clear, and the obscurations of darkness, ignorance, and folly are instantaneously extinguished.
Thus, one perceives that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different in their threefold nature.
Regarding the phrase "entering all places equally," it means that after first causing humans and animals to give rise to the bodhicitta, [the text] now summarizes—
In every direction and at every place where he encounters beings—whether human or animal—he causes them all to resolve their minds [upon enlightenment].
This clearly demonstrates the Great Being’s mind of universal transformation; there is nowhere he goes that is not beneficial, and his thought of salvation is never not urgent.
△ Second, the violation of the precepts and the resulting offense.
If this Bodhisattva does not give rise to the mind to teach and transform sentient beings, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).

It is the fundamental aspiration of a Great Being that benefiting sentient beings be their primary concern; if they do not give rise to this mind, the offense is bound as a light defilement. Question:

When preaching the Dharma to humans, if the people still do not believe, and one then directs the mind toward animals—since animals have no awareness, how can they know? Answer: The awakened nature (bodhi-mind) is inherent within all sentient beings.
Many do not lose their way. For example, the parrot that heard the Four Noble Truths was reborn in heaven and eventually attained the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha.
The monkey that offered honey was subsequently born as a renunciant and realized the Way. The bird that listened to the sutras was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The geese that heard the Dharma were reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three. The fish in the pond that heard the verses of the sutra became a son of heaven. The sea whale that heard the Buddha...
In each case, the boat was spared from disaster. Such instances as Peng’s reverence for the precepts and the clam’s rebirth in heaven are too numerous to mention.
Do not say that because these moving creatures are ignorant, they cannot be transformed. Even if they are deluded and unaware, through the empowerment of the Dharma, they may still obtain benefit.
For example, when Śāriputra spoke the Three Refuges to a sick dog and a venomous snake...
The Dharma-seals: born into the family of a wealthy householder, he later attained the fruit of sainthood;
by hearing the title of a sutra while in hell, he was entirely delivered from the fiery pit. Furthermore, as for mantra incantations, how could humans understand them?

Yet if one upholds them, they fulfill whatever wishes the mind desires—even to the point of causing a withered tree to bloom again. If even insentient things respond thus, how much more so sentient beings?
Is there benefit to be gained? Not a single word or syllable proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata can be fathomed by ordinary minds;
therefore, the Vinaya prescribes that whenever a bhikṣu arrives at a shrine, or at places such as beneath trees or beside water, he must recite gāthās.
Now, this Great Being knows that all sentient beings are fully endowed with the nature of awakening; thus, he teaches and transforms them, universally delivering them through his mind.

There is no interruption [in the offense]. This is a prohibitive karma (*pratiṣedha-karman*), established because it contravenes the great vow (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). A transgression is constituted by four conditions: first, a sentient being;

second, the perception of that being as a sentient being; third, the absence of a mind to transform them; and fourth, the failure to perform the transformation—failing to transform one who is capable of being transformed.
The fault is determined according to the specific act. However, the Great Being’s transformative deliverance does not exceed the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*): first, giving (*dāna*)...
Generosity consists of three types: material gifts, the gift of Dharma, and the gift of fearlessness. There are also four [means of attraction]: second, kind speech; third, beneficial action;
and fourth, cooperation. The *Śīla-sūtra* states: "To fail to follow those who seek transformation out of a mind of resentment constitutes a defiled offense.
This refers to the inclusion of beneficial action (*anugraha*). It further states: "Seeing sentient beings engaged in activities—whether it be farming, herding cattle, or..."

Regarding the settling of disputes: if one does not join others in meritorious deeds out of a mind of resentment and hatred, it is an afflicted offense; if it is due to laziness or indolence, it is a non-afflicted offense. This is what is meant by "gathering through common purpose.
If categorized according to the three clusters [of pure precepts], it consists of: encouraging others to receive the precepts of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*);

giving rise to a heart of great compassion, which is the precept of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-śīla*); and teaching and transforming sentient beings, which is the precept of gathering in sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgraha-śīla*).
...is also [the case]. It applies equally to the seven assemblies. It is not prescribed [as a transgression] in the Hīnayāna because it lacks the principle of transforming others.
Regarding those who do not commit an offense, the *Śīla-sūtra* states: "If that person intends to perform an improper act; or if one is ill; or if one lacks the strength;

or if one is upholding the regulations of the Saṃgha; or if, although the act is proper, it would cause many people to engage in an unrighteous act; or for the sake of subduing non-Buddhists; or by means of..."
Thus, they are appropriately subdued and none of them commit an offense. △ The forty-sixth precept:
Preaching the Dharma in an Unlawful Manner. Part Two. First, the transgression of failing to maintain what should be maintained and ceasing what should be ceased; this further has two parts.
First, regarding the universal illumination of all:
O Sons of the Buddha, you should always teach and transform others, giving rise to a heart of great compassion.

When entering the homes of wealthy patrons or noble families, you must not stand among the assembly to preach the Dharma to laypeople. You should instead occupy a high seat in front of the assembly of laypeople.

That which one should constantly practice as a teacher is the conduct for one's own benefit (*svārtha-caryā*). Entering the homes of wealthy patrons (*dānapati*) is the conduct for the benefit of others (*parārtha-caryā*).
This means that, being endowed with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one constantly expounds the Dharma for both the laity and the ordained.

However, at the time of teaching, it must be done in accordance with the Dharma; if one teaches in a manner that is not in accordance with the Dharma, both the speaker and the listener incur the fault of treating the Dharma with contempt.
"Among all the assembly" refers to being amidst kings, ministers, scholars, and commoners.
"One must not stand to preach the Dharma to laypeople" means that one should maintain reverence for the Dharma oneself. "Laypeople" (baiyi) refers to those who prefer to wear plain white clothing;
hence this designation. "One should [stand] before the assembly of laypeople" means that one must not [stand]... [in the midst of them].
"Behind him" means that one who ought to sit upon a high seat must not be taught while sitting on a low seat;
these are all protocols for honoring the Dharma and must not be treated with levity or disrespect.
This is not for the sake of seeking personal exaltation. If it is merely a brief instruction, there is no fault in both standing. △ Second, specific cases.
The fourfold assembly:
A Dharma-preaching bhikṣu must not stand upon the ground to preach the Dharma to the fourfold assembly of laypeople.

When preaching the Dharma, the Dharma-preacher shall occupy a high seat, honored with incense and flowers, while the fourfold assembly of listeners sits on lower seats, listening with filial piety toward their parents and with respectful obedience.
Regarding the "Teacher’s Instruction": it is like the case of the fire-worshipping Brahmins.
While previously [the teachings] were expounded universally for laypeople and those who had not yet received the precepts, now they are explained specifically for the laity and the ordained.
As for the high seat, incense, flowers, and offerings, these represent the utmost sincerity of the invitation to the Dharma.
This is sincerity. Regarding the members of the fourfold assembly who listen from the lower seats: this exhorts those who listen to the Dharma to practice filial piety and reverence.

The preceding section clarified that the teaching should accord with the Dharma; this section clarifies that listening should likewise accord with the Dharma. "As one is filially obedient toward one's parents" means that the Dharma is the parent of the Dharmakāya;
therefore, one must be filially obedient toward it. "Reverently obeying the teacher’s instruction" means that the Dharma is the [parent] of all Buddhas.
Regarding the gates of the teachings that reveal, cause one to awaken to, and lead one into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, these must necessarily be received from a teacher;
therefore, one should respect and comply with them without opposition. This is like the story of the fire-worshipping Brahmin:

at the beginning of the kalpa of this world, a son of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven descended from heaven to observe the gardens, groves, and flowing springs of Jambudvīpa; having observed them, he returned once more.

In the heavens, the radiance of the body is like fire. Seeing this from afar, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) outside the grove falsely claim that because worldly people make offerings to fire, they are reborn in the celestial realms.

Therefore, whenever the sun was about to set, they would light a great bonfire at night, prostrate toward it, and pay their respects with utmost sincerity and devotion. This is used as a metaphor for reverence.
One should follow the teacher’s instructions with the same utmost sincerity as one shows in reverently serving the sacrificial fire. △ Second, the offense for violating the instructions:
If the one who expounds the Dharma does not explain it according to the Dharma, they commit a minor secondary offense.
"To speak contrary to the Dharma" means to deviate from the proper etiquette of teaching the Dharma; it does not mean that the teaching itself is poorly delivered.
However, when a Great Being bestows the Dharma, it must not be treated as an ordinary matter. The speaker must maintain self-respect, and the listener must show reverence.

If this is not done, a minor defilement offense (*āpatti*) is incurred. This constitutes a prohibitive act (*vāraṇa-karma*), for by insistently providing an explanation, both parties harbor arrogance toward the Dharma.

Because of these faults, the rule was established. A transgression is constituted by three conditions: first, the ritual procedure is not in accordance with the Dharma; second, there is the perception that it is not in accordance with the Dharma; third, the teaching of the Dharma itself.
If it is done for the sake of fame or profit, it is a defiled offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*). If it is due to forgetfulness or error, it is a non-defiled offense.

If categorized according to the Threefold Aggregate (*tri-skandha*), the speaker occupies the high seat [of the teacher]; this is the fragrance and flower offering of the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint precepts). The *kuśala-dharma-śīla* (virtuous conduct precepts) [is fulfilled by]...

The listener sits on a lower seat; this is the precept for maintaining life. This applies equally to the seven classes of followers, because it is permitted for śrāmaṇeras and others to preach from a high seat, and because even a layperson (avadātavasana) who explains the meaning of a single phrase or verse must likewise act in accordance with the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Sūtra of Good Birth* states:
"If the Saṃgha does not permit the preaching of the Dharma or the offering of praise, yet one proceeds to do so oneself, such a person is merely an upāsaka."
This offense of violating the intention [to remain seated] is also governed by this precept; it is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.

Regarding those who do not commit the offense, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu, for the sake of stūpa affairs or Sangha affairs, goes before a king or a local lord, and that person says, 'May the Bhikṣu preach the Dharma to me,' he must not speak to him to ask him to rise, for fear of giving rise to suspicion. If there is someone standing nearby, [he may speak to them]."
Regarding the term "person": this is established as referring to a person who has formed the intention [to listen]. Even if a king listens to the Dharma, the bhikṣu incurs no offense.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu is on a dangerous path in a state of fear, if a guard says, "Venerable sir, preach the Dharma for me," even if that person carries a sword or a staff, there is no offense in preaching for him.
△ Forty-seventh: The Precept Against Unlawful Restrictions. Part Two. First: The Prohibition on Making and Maintaining [Such Restrictions]. Part One: The Person Receiving the Precepts.
"If, O Sons of the Buddha, there are those who have received the precepts with sincere faith..."
"All who receive the precepts with a mind of faith" is a general indication of both that which restrains and that which is restrained;

it means that all receive the Buddha’s true precepts with a mind of faith. "That which restrains" clarifies the method of establishing the regulations, while "that which is restrained" refers to those who act as messengers for officials.
Once one has given rise to faith, one should not violate that resolve. △ Second, the matters of restrictions, in two parts. First, regarding the destruction of the Triple Gem:

If kings, crown princes, officials of the hundred ranks, or disciples of the four assemblies, relying on their own high status and nobility, destroy the Buddha’s Dharma and its precepts, openly enacting restrictive laws to constrain my disciples of the four assemblies, forbidding them from leaving the household life to practice the Way, nor furthermore...
They permitted the creation of images, Buddha-stūpas, and the copying of the Sūtras and Vinaya; they established systems to govern the masses and required monks to register their names.
Bodhisattvas and bhikṣus stood upon the ground while laypeople occupied high seats, widely practicing what is contrary to the Dharma, like soldiers or slaves serving their masters.
Regarding the "fourfold assembly of disciples": according to various sūtras and vinayas, these are the four classes of disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Kings and officials are also included among those of pure faith. Those who rely on their own high status refer to those who possess power and sovereign authority.
To destroy the Buddha-dharma means to give rise to unwholesome thoughts and to act with deliberate intent.
To establish restrictive laws is to create unwholesome karma. To prohibit those from leaving the household life to practice the Way is to destroy the Sangha Jewel.
To prohibit the construction of images and Buddha-stūpas is to destroy the Buddha Jewel. To prohibit the copying of the Sūtras and Vinaya is to destroy the Dharma Jewel.
To establish a central authority to control the masses and maintain registers of the monks is to clarify [the regulations].

This concerns matters of restriction. It refers to establishing separate registers of affiliation, prohibiting [unauthorized entry] among the multitude, and maintaining ledgers to record the names of monks, so that they may be accounted for like householders in the world and required to perform public service no differently than the common people.

"Bodhisattva-bhikṣus standing on the ground" refers to those who are subject to the jurisdiction of these registers. For laypeople to occupy high seats and extensively practice what is improper [is likewise restricted].
As for the Dharma, it means that the responsibility rests upon one’s person; all coming and going is conducted through it.

It is like a soldier or a slave serving a master who, being constrained by the master’s power and authority, causes those above to go below and those below to go above. Yet, such is the case for the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu.

These are those who cultivate the Noble Path; they are able to cause the Buddha-dharma to abide in the world, to teach and transform all sentient beings, to protect and sustain the realm, and to bring benefit to the people.
They ought to be revered and honored; how could they possibly be subjected to such humiliation?
The *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed King Prasenajit: "After my parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma..."
I wish to extinguish this Sūtra and its Three Jewels, entrusting them to various kings to establish and protect.
Great King, you should know that in the future age of the five corruptions, kings, princes, and ministers, relying on their own high status, will destroy my teaching.

They will arbitrarily enact restrictive laws, failing to rely upon the Buddha’s teachings, and will constrain my disciples, forbidding them from leaving the household life and the construction of Buddhist stūpas and temples. Sūtra...

The establishment of the system of official administrators, the recording of monastic affairs in registers, the positioning of bhikṣus on the ground and laypeople on high seats, and so forth—what is taught in that sutra is essentially identical in intent to the present disciplinary regulations. Since monks and nuns have already left the household life, [these measures are necessary].

Furthermore, they were compelled to return to lay life; the two assemblies of householders were not permitted to leave the home life. Thus, it is said that they arbitrarily established restrictive regulations. Question:

While kings and officials may establish such regulations, how could the fourfold assembly possibly regulate the fourfold assembly? Answer: Sometimes parents, siblings, children, or grandchildren impose restrictions and create obstacles for one another;
therefore, [the assembly] does not permit it. This is as described in the *Dharmatrāta-parivarta* (The Entrustment of the Dharma-treasury).
The Sūtra says: When the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin went to the city to beg for food, he saw a crow and smiled.
His disciple asked him about it, and the Venerable said: "In a past kalpa, I wished to leave the household life, but my parents would not permit it.
They forcibly betrothed me to a wife, and when I had a son who was six years old, I again desired to depart. My parents then instructed their son to embrace my feet."
Weeping, he said: "Father, if you abandon me, upon whom shall I rely for sustenance? You should first kill your son, and only then depart;

because of this child, you will not be able to leave the household life. From that time on, for ninety-one *kalpas*, they transmigrated through the six realms of existence and never again saw one another.
Now, observing with the eye of the Way, [the Buddha] saw that the crow was none other than his former son. Out of compassion for his ignorance, [he spoke].

They have long remained within birth and death; for this reason, [the Buddha] smiles. If one obstructs another from leaving the household life, they will suffer the retribution of rebirth in the evil realms;

even if later born among humans, they will be afflicted by blindness and lack eyes. Therefore, when a wise person sees someone wishing to leave the household life, they should use skillful means to bring it to fulfillment and must not create obstacles.
Furthermore, the *Old Woman Sūtra* says: At that time, there was a poor old woman who heard the Buddha speak...
The Dharma. Her mind was opened and her understanding attained. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, "Why is this woman’s wisdom so great?
The Buddha said, "She was my mother when I first resolved to study the Way in a previous life. He asked again, "Why was this mother so poor?
The Buddha said, "In the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, I wished to become a śramaṇa, but this mother, out of loving-kindness, would not permit it."
"I went there. I grieved for not having eaten for a single day, and because of this, I was poor for five hundred lifetimes. Now my life span has ended;

as the sutras state, I shall be reborn in the Land of Amitābha Buddha. If the karmic retribution for obstructing one's parents or being obstructed by them is such as this, how much more so for husbands and wives, brothers, or friends who mutually create obstacles? What will their transgressions be like? Good!
Those who have received the Buddha’s precepts from the heart must at all times exercise self-restraint. II. Exhorting through examples to uphold them:
A Bodhisattva ought to receive offerings from all people; yet, if they instead serve as a messenger for government officials, it is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor the Vinaya.
If kings and their officials receive the Buddha’s precepts with a sincere heart, they must not commit such sins as destroying the Triple Gem.
The Bodhisattva is a field of merit for the world and should receive offerings from humans and devas to bring benefit and joy to all;

yet, instead, he acts as a servant to government officials. Therefore, it is said that this is neither Dharma nor Vinaya. Thus, on the occasion of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, [the Buddha] earnestly and repeatedly entrusted [this matter to his disciples].
[Regarding] the statement: "How could it be so? Even if kings and ministers were to coerce [us] by force, a monk may be killed but must not be humiliated.
It is better to die once and preserve the True Teaching than to live a life of expediency that ruins the Dharma-gate.

As for the passage beginning with "If the king, the various officials," etc., this is the Tathāgata’s great compassion, a word of exhortation to kings and ministers, meaning that since they have already given rise to a good heart and accepted [the teaching]...

The Buddha’s true precepts should be followed as they were at the beginning. Before entering the Buddha-dharma and while not yet associated with a monastic community that has violated the Dharma, one should give rise to faith and cause the Triple Gem to flourish.
One should adhere to the Buddha’s discipline without establishing separate regulations; this is because the secular laws of foreign kings do not apply here.
Therefore, it is said: "Do not commit the sin of destroying the Triple Gem. If one destroys the Triple Gem, it is equivalent to being in rebellion.

"Rebellion. Question: Since it is called "rebellious offense," why is it that one only incurs a minor defilement? Answer: Because kings and ministers live as householders, they cannot yet be subjected to heavy restrictions;
thus, although their offense is light, the retribution they receive is indeed heavy. △ Second, the conclusion of the offense for violating the teachings.
To willfully act as one who destroys the Dharma constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).

Regarding those who commit this offense: the four assemblies who receive the precepts are all children of the Buddha; they should embody the Buddha’s great compassion and propagate the transformative teachings of the Dharma.
If, through illegal restrictions, they cause the destruction of the Triple Gem, they incur the bond of a minor offense. This includes both natural and proscribed offenses.

There are two types of karma. They are established as prohibitions because they obstruct wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*). Four conditions constitute an offense: first, it concerns an object belonging to the Triple Gem;

second, there is the perception that it belongs to the Triple Gem; third, there is a restrictive intention; and fourth, the restriction is fulfilled. An offense is incurred according to the specific object. If these are subsumed within the three categories of discipline:
not relying on one’s own high status is the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint morality); not destroying the Triple Gem is the *kuśala-dharma-śīla* (wholesome dharma morality). Not...
The "Method of Establishing Regulations" refers to the precepts for governing sentient beings. For the two groups of lay followers, this constitutes a full offense if violated.

For the five groups of monastics, although they lack independent authority or power, if they were to establish unlawful restrictions even according to their capacity, it would likewise constitute an offense; thus, these regulations apply equally to both the great and the small.
However, as in the case of Maitreya, who was formerly a king, if he were to provisionally establish unlawful restrictions in order to promote the True Dharma, there would be no offense.
△ Forty-eighth: Breaking the Precepts of the Dharma, Part Three. First, the transgression of failing to maintain what should be maintained.
If, O Sons of the Buddha, you have left the household life with a sincere heart, yet for the sake of fame and profit, you [act] before kings and high officials...

Those who preach the Buddha’s precepts arbitrarily impose restrictive measures upon bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, bodhisattva precept-holders, and disciples—treating them like prisoners in a jail or like soldiers and slaves.
This is like worms within a lion’s body devouring the lion’s own flesh, rather than other external insects;
thus, it is the disciples of the Buddha themselves who destroy the Buddha-dharma, not external paths or celestial māras.
Originally, one left the household life with a sincere heart and received the Buddha’s true precepts; for this reason, one was held in high esteem by kings and officials.
Later, however, being deluded by fame and profit, one could not maintain oneself in accordance with True Suchness (Tathatā) and thus lost one's initial resolve. This is no longer a sincere heart.
To preach the Buddha’s precepts and so forth before kings and high officials while lacking actual practice within means manifesting external deportment while having no internal realization.

Deceiving others by falsely claiming to uphold the Buddha’s precepts, they exaggerate their own conduct and virtue to mislead those who listen and place their trust in them, thereby causing worldly punishments to be inflicted.
Consequently, the internal disciples suffer penalties for which they are innocent; hence, this is called "arbitrary" (heng).

As for "inflicting acts of confinement," it refers to shackling the hands and feet or imprisoning the body, thus being described as "according to the laws for prison inmates. Alternatively, it may refer to irreverent and frivolous behavior.
They are base; they are reviled, censured, and humiliated. Thus it is said that this is like the law for military slaves.

Yet, how can the various forms of punishment and humiliation endured by those within the assembly be tolerated in one’s heart? Though you disregard yourself, you leave behind calamities for your descendants; moreover, regarding the present moment, how can you remain without shame?
Why do you covet fame and profit to ruin your own virtue, relying on kings and officials while losing your fundamental nature?

Conscience. To profit from the Dharma while failing to acknowledge its grace, instead acting with malice and harming it, thereby destroying the Dharma-gate—this is precisely what is meant by an "evil Māra bhikṣu.
The previous prohibitions were for the two groups of lay followers; this precept, which destroys the Dharma, is for the two groups of renunciants.
Yet, for the sake of fame and gain, they violate the very essence of this precept.
As for kings and their officials who have already received the Bodhisattva precepts: although they are fellow practitioners of the Dharma, one may recite the Bodhisattva precepts before them;
however, one must not arbitrarily inflict unlawful punishment upon them.
There are three reasons for this. First, such persons are of noble status and are objects of long-standing veneration; therefore, one remains before them [with respect].

They shall preach the Buddha’s precepts to cause others to believe and accept them, thereby increasing their roots of goodness and enabling them to protect the Dharma, because they keep their minds focused on the Triple Gem.
Second, regarding those of noble status who possess sovereign power:
relying upon that power, they may oppress their own companions and arbitrarily subject bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or disciples of the bodhisattva precepts to confinement, as if in a prison.

The practice of imprisoning [disciples] prevents them from attaining liberation. It is like the practice of treating soldiers as slaves, forcing them to obey orders; this serves only to humiliate their peers.

Furthermore, when a disciple commits a transgression, one should punish them according to the Dharma, but one must not subject them to imprisonment or bondage as if they were prisoners or military slaves, for such acts violate the monastic code. Thirdly, because one is unable to maintain the precepts oneself, seeing those who do...

Regarding the precepts: one who instead slanders them will, before those of noble status, claim that the Buddha’s precepts—by which the upholder of the precepts is made manifest—are actually inferior.
The phrase "the worm within the lion's body" is a metaphor used to clarify the characteristics of one who destroys the Dharma.
The lion is the king of beasts, capable of subduing all other animals; who could possibly harm it? Only...

The worms within one’s own body are able to eat its flesh. This is a metaphor for the radiant Vajra-precepts, which can destroy all afflictions (*kleśa*) and cannot be broken by external paths or celestial Māras;
yet they can only be destroyed by one who has left the household life within the Buddha-dharma but does not rely upon the Buddha's teachings.
There are two ways in which these precepts may be destroyed by oneself: first, having already received the Buddha’s precepts...
Not protecting the Dharma is called destroying the Buddha-Dharma. Second, when the Sangha receives the Buddha’s precepts, if I insult them, this is also called destroying the Buddha-Dharma.
If there are transgressions among the five groups of monastics, they should be disciplined and punished according to the Buddha’s laws and regulations.
Whether one causes them to perform repentance or carries out formal acts such as expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*), how could it be appropriate to insult them with secular laws?
This would cause royal officials to lose merit and benevolent deities to depart from the realm; thus, it not only destroys the Dharma but also brings calamity upon the state.
Since the sutras contain clear evidence of this, how can one remain without fear? △ Second, the practice of what is to be done and the cessation of what is to be avoided.
If one has received the Buddha’s precepts, they should protect the Buddha-Dharma as if cherishing an only son or serving their parents; they must not violate or destroy them.

When a Bodhisattva hears the sound of heretics or wicked people slandering the Buddha’s precepts with evil words, it is no different from three hundred spears piercing the heart or being struck by a thousand swords and ten thousand staves upon the body. Rather than endure such things, they would sooner enter hell themselves.
For a hundred kalpas, one shall not hear even a single harsh word or sound of slander against the Buddha’s precepts, let alone personally breaking them.
Those who ought to protect the Buddha-dharma—meaning those who have received the Buddha’s precepts—should cherish and maintain them with gravity; they must not be transgressed.
However, the Dharma-body is accomplished through precepts, and sentient beings are saved through precepts; therefore, one must guard them with care.

"As if mindful of an only child" is a metaphor for the height of love. Just as parents compassionately cherish an only child, keeping them in their thoughts at every moment, if that child were lost, they would have no support for the rest of their lives. If the precepts are broken, then the Dharma-body...
It is without dependence. "As in serving one's parents" is a metaphor for the ultimate degree of reverence.

Just as a child reverently serves their parents, performing every task without opposition, so too is this precept the parent of all Buddhas. To uphold this precept is like reverently serving one's parents;
one must not allow even a hair’s breadth of negligence that would lead to its violation. Furthermore, "mindful of one's children" refers to...
The mind of compassion is the very same as the filial heart used to serve one’s parents; when compassion and filiality are both perfected, the Dharma remains unbroken.

As for the "three hundred spears," if even a single spear piercing the heart is unbearable, how much more so are three hundred? This illustrates the ultimate degree of dread felt toward the sound of being accused of slandering the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "a thousand blades and ten thousand staves," it means that a Bodhisattva would rather undergo such suffering than [slander the Dharma].
One must endure even the sound of slander that breaks the Buddha’s precepts. Why is this? Although one may undergo ten thousand forms of physical torment, these affect only one's own single body.

However, to slander the precepts is to destroy the True Teaching and ruin the Buddha’s Dharma-body, causing immeasurable sentient beings to lose their faith, sink into the sea of suffering, and fail to attain liberation. Therefore, it is said: "Rather than [suffering for oneself]..."
They enter hell and remain there for a hundred kalpas, yet they do not hear even a single harsh word of slander against the Buddha or his precepts.
If such words cannot even be heard, how much less can one personally destroy them? △ Third, the conclusion on the offense of violating the teachings.
To teach others the causes and conditions for breaking the Dharma, and to lack a heart of filial piety—if one intentionally acts in this way, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding "teaching others the causes and conditions for breaking the Dharma," it means that a disciple of the Buddha must not direct monastic affairs toward laypeople.

If one speaks in such a way as to cause others to lose faith, thereby creating the causes and conditions for the destruction of the Dharma, acting in opposition to the Triple Gem, and lacking a heart of filial piety and obedience;

or if, having received the Buddha’s precepts, one fails to guard them with sincerity, treats the Buddha’s wisdom-life as if it were a mere craving for fame and profit, or brings disgrace upon the Saṃgha—these constitute offenses of light impurity (*āpatti*).

Such acts possess both the nature of being inherently unwholesome (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and the nature of being prohibited by rule (*prajñapti-sāvadya*), because they involve the disparagement of the gateway to the Dharma.

The Regulation: Five conditions constitute an offense. First, one is a disciple of the Buddha—meaning a member of the seven assemblies of the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna—who has not committed a pārājika offense (a border-line transgression) and has not renounced the precepts.
Second, the perception of the person as a disciple of the Buddha, which consists of six permutations: two heavy cases and four light cases.

Although this does not apply to those who are not disciples of the Buddha, they likewise should not perform acts of binding; however, because such instances are relatively rare, no specific regulation was established for them.

Alternatively, it may be subsumed under the precept against harming through anger. Third, the mind of punishment and retribution, which intends to cause the other person to suffer humiliation, constitutes the actual basis of the offense.
Fourth, the person addressed, such as a king, official, or others who likewise possess the precepts;
because they share the same precepts, only a light offense is incurred. If one punishes someone who has not received the precepts, it falls under the sixth grave precept. Fifth, the actual...

[This concerns] the practice of administering disciplinary punishment according to the specific offense. If these are subsumed within the three categories of precepts (*tri-skandha*), one should protect the Buddha-dharma as follows:

the *śīla* of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) is like serving one's parents; the *śīla* of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-śīla*) is like cherishing an only son; and the *śīla* of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*) is [the intent to] gather and sustain all beings.

These offenses are common to the five groups of monastics. As for the two groups of lay followers, if a disciple of the Buddha is to be punished, it falls under the aforementioned precepts and is governed by them concurrently.

Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna prohibit [the use of weapons]. There is no offense if, in an age of corruption and turbidity, a bhikṣu who upholds the True Dharma may rely on the power of kings and great ministers to arm himself for self-defense, as clarified in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
However, he must not punish others through illegal means. Question: Suppose there are wicked monks who do not observe the Buddha’s precepts and violate the laws of the state...

Regarding the Dharma: if one admonishes them and they do not comply, or if one expels them and they do not leave; and if internal discipline is applied but fails to rectify the situation—then what should be done?
