Thus it is said: the Mahāyāna cause is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, and the Mahāyāna fruit is likewise the true reality of all phenomena.
This true reality is simply another name for buddha-nature. Now, as for the cause...
The Buddha-nature is the fruit, and the fruit is also the Buddha-nature. Since the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding, both cause and fruit are likewise eternally abiding.
Universally, all dharmas are termed the treasury of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature of cause and fruit. Specifically, this refers to such sections as the "Source of Buddha-nature" chapter.
Furthermore, regarding the first being the mind, the second the stages, and the third the precepts: this precisely clarifies that these precepts belong to the Bodhisattva.
It is the ground of the mind. Great practices and great vows arise from this precept; the true cause and true fruit are attained through this precept;
the eternally abiding Buddha-nature is realized through this precept. How magnificent is the precept! This is its ultimate perfection.
When all Buddhas speak [of it], they are universally referring to the fundamental Buddhas and the manifested Buddhas upon the thousand-petaled lotus throne. It is immeasurable and one.
"Every treasury of all dharmas" refers to the treasuries of all dharmas such as the ground of mind (*cittabhūmi*) and so forth. Because the mind is immeasurable, the dharmas are also immeasurable.
Since the treasury of the mind is thus, the other treasuries are likewise. Therefore, it is called the "immeasurable treasury of all dharmas. "Concluded" means to cease;
it signifies that the exposition of the Dharma stops at this point. The preceding five [sections] are distinct, while this one is—
In summary: △ Fourth, the conclusion revealing that the great assembly receives and practices it.
Within the worlds of the hundreds of thousands of millions, all sentient beings receive, uphold, and joyfully practice it.
If one were to extensively open up the characteristics of the mind-ground, it would be as described in the "Chapter on the Seven Practices" regarding the Buddha Flower-Light King.

The preceding section clarified the Buddhas and the teachings that are capable of benefiting others; this section concerns the sentient beings who are the objects of such benefit, which is precisely the Dharma-treasury of the ten inexhaustible precepts.

Furthermore, throughout the hundreds of thousands of millions of worlds, all sentient beings—each and every one—respectfully receive and uphold, and joyfully practice, the immeasurable treasury of all dharmas taught by the Original Buddha and the Trace Buddha.

This clearly explains the mutual resonance between the capacity [of the practitioner] and the teaching. Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of the mind-ground," the precepts are the characteristics of the mind-ground.

Fundamentally, the mind-ground is without characteristics, yet the precepts possess the aspects of observance and violation; this is precisely the characteristic of the mind-ground. These characteristics have both general and specific types:
the ten grave prohibitions are the general, while the forty-eight minor rules are the specific. However, since the general is immeasurable, the specific is likewise [immeasurable].
It is inexhaustible, layer upon layer without end; all phenomena are perfectly interfused like the net of Indra. This is the very mark of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
hence it is called "mark upon mark. As it is said: "These phenomena abide in their own positions; the marks of the world are eternally abiding.
This is a brief explanation of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground. If one wishes to open it extensively and clarify the matters and principles of the Mind-Ground:
Its characteristics should be understood as explained in the "Seven Practices Chapter" of the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka-rāja-sūtra*. Alas, this chapter has not yet reached us.
△ Third, the general praise for its circulation, in three parts. First, praising the benefits of upholding the precepts, in two parts. First, the general praise:
although these verses were not spoken by the Buddha himself, they are complete in both phrasing and meaning; they may have been composed by sages or noble ones of the Western Land (India), or—

This was arranged by the translators of this region as a text for praising the observance of precepts, exhorting the study [of them], and encouraging the salvation of sentient beings through the making of vows and the dedication of merit.
It is like the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which begins with verses of praise, enumerates the characteristics of the precepts in the middle, and concludes again with verses of dedication;
only thus does it accord with the meaning of the "Threefold Invocation. Now, the initial verses of praise are missing, because the present scripture is not a complete edition.
This is because the categories encompass both the superior and the inferior.

A person of clear understanding possesses strong patience and wisdom; they are able to uphold such a Dharma. Until they attain the path of Buddhahood, they will securely obtain five kinds of benefits.
"An enlightened person" refers to this Great Precept of the Mind-Ground. It is not something that can be received by those who are ignorant, small-minded, or of shallow wisdom;

rather, only one who is clear-sighted and wise is able to uphold it. Because they possess the power of patience and wisdom, they are called "enlightened persons. "Patience" (kṣānti) refers to *anurakṣaṇā-kṣānti* (endurance), which specifically indicates the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Wisdom" (prajñā) refers to transcendent wisdom, which specifically indicates the power of outflow-free insight (*anāsrava-bala*). By virtue of possessing the power of concentration, and...
The mind is unmoving; by the power of the outflow-free (anāsrava), one severs delusions and realizes the Truth.
To have wisdom without patience is called "mad wisdom"; to have patience without wisdom is called "foolish concentration. Furthermore, patience is the mind’s steadfastness;
because this patience is most firm, it is called "strong patience. Wisdom is the mind’s spiritual penetration; because this wisdom is most sharp, it is called "wisdom."
Patience is powerful; when patience is strong, one is not turned by external things. Wisdom is powerful; when wisdom is strong, one can transform external things.

Furthermore, when patience is strong, one can maintain [the state] eternally, remaining unshakable from beginning to end. When wisdom is strong, one can maintain it skillfully, being perfectly integrated and free from stagnation.
However, those of the Two Vehicles have much concentration and little wisdom, and thus do not see the Buddha-nature. The Bodhisattvas of Expedient Wisdom have much wisdom and little concentration.
Although they have seen the Buddha-nature, it is not yet clear; because both their patience and wisdom are strong, they are able to uphold such a Dharma-gate of the mind-ground.
The phrase "until the Buddha-way is attained" is an extreme praise for the excellence of upholding the precepts, intended to inspire people to delight in learning them.
It means that by being able to uphold these precepts, one will certainly attain Buddhahood; though one has not yet attained it now, [one is certain to do so]. Regarding this...
In the intervals between lives, throughout successive births, one first attains these five kinds of meritorious benefits.
As for "attaining with ease," it is because of the power of the virtue of the precepts that they are naturally and spontaneously acquired; it is not a matter of vain hope or forced seeking.
△ Second, the specific manifestation.
First, the Buddhas of the ten directions will compassionately regard and constantly protect them. Second, at the time of death, they will possess right view and their minds will be filled with joy.
Third, in every place of rebirth, they will become friends to all bodhisattvas. Fourth, they will fully accomplish the accumulation of merit through the perfection of ethical discipline.

Fifth, regarding the present and future lives: one’s nature-precepts, merit, and wisdom will be fulfilled. These are the benefits for the sons of the Buddha (these five kinds of benefits are set forth in the *Bhūmivastu-sūtra*).
As for those who are protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, it means that this Dharma is the Mother of the Buddhas;
all Buddhas emerge from it. Therefore, those who uphold it connect with the vital essence (*dhātu*) of all Buddhas. If one does not uphold this Dharma, then...
To sever the Buddha-nature is to cut off the lineage; to be able to uphold this Dharma is to continue the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom.

Therefore, all Buddhas constantly hold those who uphold the Dharma in their compassionate regard and protection, ensuring that they advance on the Path without demonic interference and are able to perpetuate and flourish the Buddha-seed.
Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata skillfully protects and regards all Bodhisattvas. [At the] end of life...

Regarding those whose minds rejoice in right view: these are the upholders of the Dharma who have already attained the Buddha-eye. At the time of their passing, by the power of their virtuous precepts, they attain clear and distinct right view;
they remain far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, ultimately reaching *nirvāṇa* and attaining great peace and bliss.
This is what is meant: even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one's head, their concentration and wisdom would remain perfectly luminous.
Because one never loses [this], one gives rise to joy. Regarding "being born life after life as a friend to Bodhisattvas": this refers to those who uphold the Dharma;

their status is equal to that of Great Awakening, and they are truly the children of the Buddha. In every place where they are born, the three grades of worthies (*sāraṇyaka*) and the ten stages of sages (*ārya*), all Bodhisattvas, are their fellow students and companions.
Regarding "the perfection of merit and the *pāramitā* of ethical discipline" (*śīla-pāramitā*): ethical discipline...
It is the foundation of all merits, just as the great earth is able to bring forth all things.
Now that the perfection of precepts (*śīlapāramitā*) is complete, then all other perfections, the myriad practices, and the wealth of meritorious dharmas will be fully accomplished and perfected.

Regarding the "fulfillment of the merit and wisdom of the nature-precepts" (*prakṛti-śīla*): this means that these precepts are the precepts of the fundamental source of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
By nature, one is inherently virtuous and good; the actions of body and speech are pure. One spontaneously ceases evil and spontaneously gives rise to goodness.

Ceasing evil is wisdom (*prajñā*); giving rise to goodness is merit (*puṇya*). Because of ceasing evil, the field of merit and wisdom are fulfilled; because of giving rise to goodness, wisdom is fulfilled by means of merit.
Now, by firmly maintaining the pure precepts, one’s merit and wisdom will increase spontaneously day and night.
In future lives, one will perfect the two provisions and attain the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood, becoming known as the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings;
thus it is said that in future lives, the precepts of nature, merit, and wisdom will be fulfilled. Furthermore, all sons of the Buddha are born from the precepts; now, one is able to uphold them.
When merit and wisdom gradually become full, one is truly a son of the Buddhas; such a person shall succeed to the Buddha-position in the future.
Therefore, it is said, "These are the sons of the Buddhas. This refers to the meaning of having previously received the Buddha-precepts and entered the rank of the Buddhas.
△ Second, the account of the practice of the precepts, in two parts: first, observing the essence of the Dharma.

The wise person reflects skillfully: those who calculate based on a self and cling to signs cannot believe in this Dharma; nor is one who seeks to extinguish their lifespan a field where seeds may be sown.
If you wish to grow the sprouts of Bodhi, which illuminate the world with light, you should observe with tranquil discernment.
The true nature of all phenomena is neither arising nor ceasing; it is neither eternal nor discontinuous, neither identical nor different, neither coming nor going.
Within this single mind, the Bodhisattva should perform their duties through skillful means, diligent effort, and adornment.
One should train in the proper sequence; regarding those in training and those beyond training, do not give rise to conceptual discrimination.
This is called the primary path, and it is also called the Mahāyāna. All evil conceptual proliferation is extinguished from this source; [it leads to] the *sarvajñatā* of all Buddhas.

Because all [phenomena] emerge from this source and are definitively understood, it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). "Skillful deliberation" means that one should skillfully employ the mind to examine and deliberate with the discerning wisdom of *prajñā*.
As for "the nature of precepts," regarding those who calculate and cling to a self and its characteristics: it means...

As for the non-Buddhist practitioners who calculate a self, and the ordinary people who cling to appearances: their minds are scorched by the three poisons and their bodies are fettered by the five desires.
They falsely take the four great elements as the characteristic of their own body and the shadows conditioned by the six sense objects as the characteristic of their own mind.
Bound by both the faculties and the sense objects, they are deluded regarding their original true mind; therefore, they are unable to believe in this precept-dharma of the source-ground of the mind.
Furthermore, regarding those who extinguish their lifespan to attain realization: the former refers to ordinary beings who conceive of a self within their bodies and cling to illusory appearances;
this is called "clinging to existence. The latter refers to those of the Two Vehicles who extinguish their life-span to realize quiescent extinction; this is called "clinging to non-existence."
Thus, those who reduce the body to ashes and extinguish wisdom, taking such a state as their realization of peace—a withered and silent nirvana—do not provide a locus for planting the seeds of bodhi.
Yet, since the Buddha’s precepts are impartial, how could he exclude them? It is only because these men of lowly service do not exercise proper reflection that they all lack a share [in the Dharma].
If one wishes to cause the sprouts of the bodhi-path to grow and achieve equality in the future, [one must act accordingly].
The Perfectly Awakened One, with the sun of wisdom, illuminates the world and destroys the dark abode of the afflictions of all sentient beings.
There is no need to seek outward; simply now, within this ground of mind and these precepts, give rise to unimpeded, pure wisdom.
When purity reaches its limit and light penetrates everywhere, the sprouts of the Path will flourish. "Observing in stillness" means:

One should properly employ the mind as described above. "Quiescence" (śamatha) is a synonym for "stopping" (sthiti); "examination" (vipaśyanā) refers to the meticulous observation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
When stopping and contemplation are non-dual, that alone constitutes true cultivation. As for the "true reality of all phenomena" (*dharmatā*), it refers to all phenomena.
All things arise from conditions. That which arises from conditions has no inherent nature; its very substance is emptiness. Emptiness is true emptiness. True emptiness is signless;

therefore, it is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This is precisely the essence of the original source-mind. However, this true emptiness and true mark do not belong to the conditioned body and mind;
therefore, it is said to be neither born nor extinguished. It does not fall into the two extremes; therefore, it is said to be neither eternal nor... [discontinuous].
It is uninterrupted; it does not fall into numerical categories. Therefore, it is said to be neither one nor different. It is fundamentally free from movement and stillness;
therefore, it is said to neither come nor go. Such phenomena are, in essence, but the single mind.

When a Bodhisattva wishes to adorn the original source, the ground of the mind, they again give rise to function from their own mind, using the wisdom of skillful means to illumine the realm of the mind. As for that realm—

The realm (*dhātu*) is itself the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); therefore, it is called "serene contemplation. Furthermore, both contemplation and the observance of precepts are termed "adornments of skillful means" (*upāya-vyūha*).
Contemplation is the skillful means of principle (*li*), which is termed the "adornment of wisdom" (*prajñā-vyūha*).

The observance of precepts is the skillful means of phenomena (*shi*), which is termed the "adornment of merit" (*guṇa-vyūha*). Moreover, if one applies diligent skillful means without serene contemplation, then...

If one observes conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as being with outflows (*sāsrava*) and devoid of adornment, and remains in quiet contemplation without applying diligent skillful means (*upāya*), then one will become withered and empty, incapable of adornment.
Therefore, within a single mind, one must adorn it with skillful wisdom and skillful means.
This adornment is the task that a bodhisattva ought to perform; one should study this in its proper sequence and thereby consolidate it.
This is indeed appropriate. Regarding those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): the stage of training consists of investigating reality and severing delusions;

the stage beyond training consists of exhausting reality and eliminating delusions. Furthermore, those at the initial stage of the Three Worthies (*trividha-ārya*) who practice sequential contemplation are all termed beginners (*ādikarmika*).

This is the cause for those in training (*śaikṣa*). The mind at the conclusion of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)—that which does not observe sequentially—is called the final fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
However, regarding these states of training and no-more-learning, do not give rise to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

If one gives rise to the thought of discrimination, that is a conditioned mind-consciousness (*saṃskṛta-citta-vijñāna*) and not the true wisdom of *prajñā*; thus, one will be unable to enter the [first] stage.
First is the Middle Way. Because it does not give rise to discrimination, it abides in the center; the Middle Way is thus perfectly manifest. This is called the primary path.
Because it does not fall into the two vehicles, it is named the Mahāyāna, the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, it is the wondrous cultivation of non-action.
It is entirely identical to the principle of reason and is called the First Path. This wondrous nature of the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) arises from true cultivation and is named Mahāyāna;
it signifies the conveying of both self and others together into the city of Great Nirvāṇa. All those who harbor evil through conceptual proliferation—

This refers to the fact that because this is the foremost path, it is able to extinguish the dualistic attachments to existence and non-existence held by ordinary beings and followers of external paths, as well as their calculations of "that" and "self.

All such conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and evils are completely purified without remainder; therefore, it is said that all conceptual proliferations and evils are extinguished from this very source.
Because this is the Mahāyāna, it is able to bring forth the fruit of the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) of all Buddhas. *Sarva...* [text fragment]
*Sarvajñā* (婆若). This is translated as "the wisdom of all-knowledge. When in the state of cause, it is called *prajñā*; when in the state of fruition, it is called *sarvajñā*.
It is the general name for the ultimate, perfected fruit of the threefold contemplation within a single mind. By means of the primary path, one is capable of transporting the Mahāyāna vehicle;
by means of the Mahāyāna vehicle, one is capable of reaching the stage of *sarvajñā*; by means of *sarvajñā*...

If one perfectly accords with the principle that is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), then the wisdom, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and samādhis of all Buddhas will all be manifested through this very point.
Therefore, it is said that the *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) of all Buddhas emerges entirely from this place.

Thus, the "Mind-Ground" (*citta-bhūmi*) of the Brahma Net Sutra penetrates the fruit and encompasses the cause; its fundamental principle reaches its ultimate limit here. △ Second, the Protection and Maintenance of the Precepts.
Therefore, O sons of the Buddha, you should rouse great courage and protect the pure precepts of all Buddhas as if they were a bright jewel.
All Bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in this; those of the future shall train in it; and those of the present are training in it now.
This is the sphere of action of the Buddhas, praised by the Holy Lord.

As for the phrase "therefore," it refers back to the aforementioned ground of the true mark of reality (*bhūtatathatā*). That is to say, if one wishes to return to the true mark of the single mind, one must cultivate the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground;
and if one wishes to cultivate the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground, one must first give rise to a courageous and resolute mind.

The cultivation and observance of the pure precepts of all Buddhas serve as the foundation for entering the Path. Regarding the protection and maintenance [of these precepts] like a bright pearl, there are three meanings:
first, the meaning of purity; one should protect and maintain them so as not to allow defilement. Second, the meaning of perfection;
one should protect and maintain them so as not to allow them to become incomplete or deficient. Third, the meaning of radiance; one should protect and maintain them so as not to allow...

Its darkness is dispelled; its purity is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*); its perfection is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya-guṇa*); and its radiance is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*).
This clarity, purity, and perfection are all the characteristics and virtues of the jewel. Within these characteristics and virtues, there are further three meanings:
first, its substance is that of a supreme, peerless treasure; second, its characteristics are perfect, luminous, and pure; and third, its function is able to...
The rain of material goods relieves the poor; its essence is the *dharmakāya*, its marks are *prajñā*, and its function is *vimukti*.
These are correlated with the three clusters of sublime precepts (*tri-śīla-skandha*); the correspondence between the dharma and the metaphor is perfectly clear.

The phrase "all bodhisattvas of the past," etc., is a statement for citing evidence, concluding the exhortation, and dedicating the merit for its widespread circulation. It means that this radiant Vajra Jewel Precept is [the standard] of the three periods of time.
This is what Bodhisattvas practice together to realize Bodhi, and what the Buddhas of the ten directions collectively traverse to proceed toward Nirvana.
The Buddha is the saint among saints; therefore, he is called the Holy Lord.
When a son of the Buddha thus courageously upholds the pure precepts, cause and effect correspond perfectly. How could the Tathāgata not praise such excellence?
Therefore it is said: "This is the sphere of action of the Buddha, praised by the Holy Lord. △ Third, the vow to deliver sentient beings:
"I have expounded this in accordance with the truth; may the immeasurable mass of merit resulting therefrom be dedicated to all sentient beings, that we may together proceed toward omniscience."
"May those who hear this Dharma all attain the path of Buddhahood.
"I" refers to the person composing the verse, and may also be used by one reciting the precepts. "In accordance with" (sui) means...
"Not to turn one's back on the scriptural texts" means to follow them without contradicting the intent of the precepts;

that is, from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas above, all have revered this Great Precept of the Mind-Ground, reciting it according to the Dharma every half-month. I now follow in accordance with this noble mind.
Recite it in this manner, and there will be an immeasurable and vast accumulation of merit. Therefore, it is said:

"I have spoken in accordance with the truth; this is an immeasurable mass of merit. Yet, one does not keep this merit for oneself, but dedicates it entirely to all sentient beings, so that they may all together proceed toward the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna), and not toward anything else.

Because [this precept] causes humans, devas, and those of the two vehicles to attain small fruits, it is said that one "dedicates it by bestowing upon sentient beings" so that they may together proceed toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
This is truly because every single word and syllable of this precept flows forth from the mind-ground of Vairocana;
it is the source of all Buddhas and the root of Bodhi. Since it is received through the arousal of the bodhicitta, one now recites it.

The merit of these precepts is further dedicated toward Bodhi. Furthermore, it is vowed that those who hear such Dharma of the precepts shall, upon its passing through their faculty of hearing even once, forever become seeds of the Buddha;
by practicing according to the Dharma, they shall all complete the path to Buddhahood. Therefore, it is said:
"May those who hear this Dharma all attain the path to Buddhahood. Moreover, this is dedicated and bestowed upon sentient beings, which is the downward transformation.
The mind that [regards all beings] as one's own kin is called compassion (*karuṇā*). The mind that seeks upward toward omniscience is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
The simultaneous operation of both compassion and wisdom is called the bodhicitta. Because one has generated this mind, one receives these great bodhisattva precepts;
because one upholds these great bodhisattva precepts, one is able to fulfill the two wheels of compassion and wisdom. As the ancients said:

That is to say: to initiate the *saṃnāha* (armor) at the first thought of enlightenment and, concluding with great compassion, to rush to the rescue of those in distress—this may be called proceeding directly from the bodhi of names toward the ultimate goal.
As for the aforementioned wondrous precepts of the mind-ground, this dharma-gate is profoundly deep and inconceivable.
I universally pray that all sentient beings, in every life and every birth, shall receive, uphold, read, and recite it, always following along with these [precepts].

The Buddha’s cultivation and study were completed as he, together with others, realized the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment and preached the Brahmajāla Sūtra; thus his great task was finished.
*The First Tide of the Buddha’s Brahmajāla Sūtra*, Scroll Eight (End). Postscript.
The Sūtra states: "One should, throughout the six periods of each day and night, uphold the Bodhisattva precepts and understand their underlying principles and the nature of Buddha-nature.
It further states: "If one receives the Bodhisattva precepts but does not recite them, one is not a Bodhisattva and lacks the seed of Buddhahood.
Yet today, while there are many who receive the Buddha’s precepts, those who understand the Buddha’s words are few. If one receives them but does not recite them, where do the precepts abide?
There are those who recite it without understanding its rational nature; thus, the sprouts of the Way do not emerge even though their minds have received its grace.
Therefore, the Tathāgata himself recited it every half-month as a permanent model for all Bodhisattvas to study well, never daring to alter it.
I pray that all Mahāsattvas will give rise to a courageous and vigorous mind: once you have received it, you must uphold it; once you have upheld it, you must understand it. The ground of the mind—

Open it! The Buddha-seed manifests of itself. Teach and transform sentient beings so that we may together repay the Buddha’s kindness, lest we fail the earnest instructions bestowed upon the thousand-petaled lotus throne.
Written on the fifth day of the *Poṣadha* (Long Jing) during the winter of the Jia-Mao year of the Kangxi era, by Fo-an, recorded with the brush of Yu-ge.

The phonetic gloss explains that the six kinds of "nature" (*gotra*) are identical to "seeds," in the sense of having the meaning of production. "Nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the "essential constituent," which carries the meaning of being one's own portion that does not undergo change.
The *Āḍakavatī-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng) correlates these with the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten stages of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*).

Regarding the discussion of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) and Wondrous Enlightenment (pratyak-saṃbodhi), there are thus six kinds of natures (gotra). However, while "nature" (gotra) applies throughout all six stages, "kind" (bīja) is restricted to the causal stage;

therefore, the preceding four stages are termed "kinds. Although Equal Enlightenment is still within the causal stage, it excels those preceding it and may be designated as "enlightenment" (bodhi); hence, it is not called a "kind."
Regarding the six wheels and their corresponding stages, there are two meanings: first, turning; second, crushing.

This means that when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas turn the Wheel of Dharma, they are able to crush the afflictions and karmic actions of sentient beings; therefore, the six wheels are correlated with the various stages.

"Omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*) refers to the ability to know and understand all internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*) and internal designations, as well as all external phenomena (*bāhya-dharma*) and external designations;

this is called omniscience, which is the wisdom of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*. Regarding "internal phenomena": because the Buddha’s teachings are expounded in accordance with the principle (*yukti*), they are termed "internal.
As for "external [teachings]," such as those of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they are termed "external" because they involve arbitrary conceptualizations that contradict the principle.

The *Wu-bai-wen jing-lun* (Treatise on the Sūtra of Five Hundred Questions) concerning the Mountain of Flesh-Camels states: In the past, there was a bhikṣu who begged extensively and accumulated wealth.
He neither performed meritorious deeds nor practiced the Path. At the end of his life, he was reborn as the Mountain of Flesh-Camels, spanning several tens of li in breadth.

It happened that a year of famine occurred, and the people of the country took its flesh daily for food; yet as it was cut away, it grew back again. Shortly thereafter, a neighboring country began to take it as well. Immediately—
He then cried out loudly. When asked the reason for this, he replied: "I was originally a man of the Way.
Because I coveted wealth and failed to practice charity, I have incurred a great debt to the people and things of this kingdom. Therefore, I am repaying it with my flesh; I owe nothing to you."
The *Chapter on the Vows and Practices of the Avataṃsaka* states:

"If there should be a person who constantly abides in pure precepts and receives, maintains, reads, and recites these great vows, then all demonic armies, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and all evil spirits and ghosts shall [be unable to obstruct them]."

They have all distanced themselves from it. Even when they occasionally give rise to the aspiration [for awakening], they should approach and protect it; for if one has violated the pure precepts, would one not rather harbor a mind of anger to block them from proceeding?
Regarding "by the power of faith one receives, and by the power of mindfulness one maintains":

as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states, when one has deep faith in the principles of the truths, it further increases, enabling one to ward off doubt and remain unshakable; to resist heterodox outsiders and remain undeluded;

and to destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*) so that they cannot cause harm. Regarding "the power of mindfulness," it refers to the growth of the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), which is able to destroy [the obstacles].

Regarding wrong thoughts: because one must accomplish all supramundane right mindfulness, if one lacks the power of faith now, regarding [the teaching] as trivial, how could one receive it with the mind?
If one lacks the power of mindfulness, immediately forgetting it, how could one maintain it in memory?
Thus, it is by the power of faith that one receives it, and by the power of mindfulness that one maintains it.
The *pātra* leaf—here translated as "bank-shaped"—resembles a *tāla* palm; it is straight and tall, with long and broad leaves that are lustrous in color.
These are gathered for the purpose of writing.
*He ti, ti*. This is an ancient form of the character *ti*, a name for paper.
It refers to paper made from peeled animal hides. Long ago, in the past, incalculable eons ago, there was one named Most Victorious (*Jiēshèng*).

He dwelt among the mountain forests, practicing the way of the immortals and attaining the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). He constantly practiced a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in order to hear [the Dharma].
For the sake of the Dharma, he traveled to cities and villages, seeking everywhere for a teacher who could preach the Dharma.
At that time, a celestial Māra came and said to the Rishi: "I have a verse; if you can flay your skin to serve as paper and draw blood to serve as ink,"
"I shall break my bones to make a pen and write down this verse; I will then explain it for you.

Having heard this, the seer thought to himself, "Throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have undergone all manner of suffering and affliction without any benefit. Now I shall cast off this unsubstantial body to obtain the sublime Dharma.
With great joy and exultation, he immediately used a sharp knife to flay his skin, prick himself with blood, and break [his bones].
He knelt with palms joined toward the heavens and requested that the Buddha’s verses be spoken. Seeing this, Māra became distressed and immediately vanished.
The rishi then said, "For the sake of seeking the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, I do not begrudge my own body or life; my sincerity is not in vain.
If there be one in another world who possesses great compassion and is able to preach the Dharma, may he appear before me. At that time, [a being] came from the east.
In the twenty-second land, there was a buddha-world named Universal Stainless.

A buddha named Pure Name King suddenly appeared before him and emitted a great radiance that illuminated the body of the immortal; his suffering was immediately dispelled, and he was restored to his former state.

He then extensively expounded for him the *Sarvapuṇyasamuccayasamādhi-sūtra*. Upon hearing the Dharma, the rishi attained unimpeded eloquence (*asaṅgapratibhāna*) and extensively preached the sublime Dharma for all sentient beings, causing immeasurable beings to abide in the path of the Three Vehicles.
After passing through a thousand years, at the end of his life, he was reborn in the land of Samantavimala under the Buddha Viśuddhanāman.
Because of his reverence for the Dharma, he has now attained Buddhahood.
When the parrot heard the Four Noble Truths, there were two parrots belonging to the elder Sudatta; one was named Lati and the other was named...
Śāradvatīputra, the Venerable Ānanda, went to the house of the elder and expounded for him the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Having heard the Dharma, the bird rejoiced and recited it; however, while staying overnight in a tree, it was eaten by a wild mongoose.
By means of these roots of goodness, he was born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; passing through successive births, he was born in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations.
Having thus been born seven times among the six heavens of the desire realm, he was subsequently born among humans, where he left the household life and became a pratyekabuddha.
In the past, when the Buddha was sitting in a forest with the bhikṣus, there was a monkey who took the Buddha’s bowl, climbed a tree, filled it with honey, and offered it to the Buddha.
After the Tathāgata had accepted it, he distributed it among the assembly of monks until it was completely exhausted.
The monkey, filled with joy, leaped and danced about; he fell into a pit and died, immediately being reborn [in heaven].

He was born into the household of the elder Sādhuka. Possessing a handsome and upright appearance, he left the household life and became an arhat, known as the Elder Madhuvāsiṣṭha (Hsien-mi Shang-tso).
In the past, there was a bhikṣu who was reciting a sutra in a forest; his voice—
The discourse was harmonious and elegant. At that time, there was a bird that, having heard the Dharma, received it with reverence; it sat upon a tree to listen.

It was struck by a hunter and died, but by virtue of these roots of goodness, it was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Immediately taking celestial incense and flowers, it went to where the bhikṣu was and made offerings with deep respect.
The bhikṣu then preached the Dharma for it, and it attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

The Geese Heard the Dharma and Were Reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Long ago, when the Buddha was in a forest grove in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī preaching the Dharma to humans and devas, there were five hundred geese traveling in a flock through the air. Hearing the Buddha’s voice, their bodies and minds were filled with joy;
they circled and descended. At that moment, a hunter spread a net and killed them, yet they were all reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The devas descended from heaven, holding flowers to offer to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained the first fruit of enlightenment.
As for the fish in the pond that heard the verses: in the past, incalculable kalpas ago, Śākyamuni Tathāgata was the son of a wealthy householder named Flowing Water.
In a pond within a desolate marsh, he recited the name of the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin for ten thousand fish.
He preached the verses on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. At the end of the night, ten thousand fish all passed away simultaneously and were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
When the Tathāgata attained enlightenment and first turned the Wheel of Dharma, they descended from heaven;
hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, they all attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
The sea whale is renowned by its Sanskrit name *makara*, which here is translated as "whale-fish.
It is a massive fish of the ocean, with a body length ranging from three hundred to seven hundred *yojanas*. When it encounters a ship, it is capable of swallowing it whole.
At one time, five hundred merchants were traveling by ship into the sea to gather treasures when they encountered a whale opening its mouth above the water. The water—
They rushed and flowed along as if entering a great pit. The boatman said, "We are all going to die. The merchants each offered prayers to their respective deities, but to no avail.
Among them was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who addressed the crowd, saying, "The Buddha is the compassionate father of all sentient beings.
Let us together cry out 'Namo Buddha' and we shall be saved. The multitude immediately chanted it with one voice. When the fish heard the name of the Buddha, they immediately closed [their mouths].
They recited it together with one voice, and the multitude was thus spared from calamity.

The *péng* bird, who reveres the Vinaya, is a Golden-Winged Bird King (*garuḍa-rāja*) who constantly intends to seize dragons for food; however, when a dragon wears the *kāṣāya*, he does not give rise to harm.
When the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, a frog emerged from a pond and entered the grass to listen to the teaching.
A farmer digging the grass accidentally injured it, and the frog died and was reborn in heaven.
The Case of the Dog and the Poisonous Snake: Long ago, there was a dog that stole food from a traveling merchant.

The merchant immediately cut off its four paws and cast it into a pit. There, the dog could neither find life nor find death. Śāriputra, observing this with his divine eye, filled his alms bowl with rice and flew to where the dog was.

He used the rice to extinguish the fires of hunger and then preached the Three Seals of the Dharma for it, saying: [The three seals are: All conditioned phenomena are impermanent (*sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ*); all phenomena are selfless (*sarvadharmanairātmyam*); and nirvāṇa is peace (*śāntaṃ nirvāṇam*).]
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all dharmas are without self; nirvāṇa is peace and extinction. You should now, toward me, give rise to a pure mind.
Cast off this body of an animal and you shall be reborn in a happy realm. Furthermore, there was a great venomous snake.
In a mountain forest, they were scorched by a great fire until their skin was charred and their flesh consumed.
Śāriputra went there as well and taught them the Three Dharma Seals. Later, both were reborn into the families of wealthy householders;
they left the household life to become disciples of Śāriputra, and both attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Hearing the Title of the Sutra and Escaping the Fire Pit of Hell: Once, a man died a violent death and entered hell.
The hell-wardens impaled him with iron forks and cast him into a cauldron of boiling oil. He immediately cried out, "Namo to the Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra.
At that moment, the cauldron of oil transformed into a lotus pond, and all who heard it were delivered from hell.
*Gāthā* is translated here as "verse. These are stanzas spoken by the Buddha that possess great spiritual power, capable of benefiting both oneself and others. The verse says:
"The worldly pleasures of the five desires, or even the joys of the various heavens, when compared to the bliss of the exhaustion of craving, do not equal even one-thousandth part of it.
From accumulation (*saṃskāra*) arises suffering; from suffering, accumulation arises again. The Noble Eightfold Path can transcend them and reach [Nirvana]."

The wondrous state of nirvana: namely, those who practice giving will certainly obtain its benefit and profit. If one gives for the sake of happiness, they will certainly attain peace and joy in the future.
Regarding the Sangha as a field of merit: if a person makes offerings to this Sangha, they will obtain immeasurable blessings and shall not suffer poverty from lifetime to lifetime.
From the suffering of poverty, one attains great wealth and happiness, just as a fertile field yields abundant harvests.

Nowadays, there is a vulgar distortion that calls those who do not diligently observe the precepts and fasts, yet sit and eat upon the "fields," "Field-Merit Monks" (Futián Sēng). This greatly violates the meaning of the scriptures.
